## Chapter 1
## (a) Concerning the Bodhisatta Setaketu Deva
In this manner, our Great Bodhisatta Gotama, during the period of four asankheyya and one hundred thousand aeons, received the definite prophecy (niyata-byākata) from twenty-four Buddhas, beginning with Buddha Dīpaṅkara and ending with Buddha Kassapa, among the twenty-seven Buddhas who appeared during that time. They proclaimed, "This person will surely become a Buddha among the three types of beings." Having received this garland of prophecy, he fulfilled the perfections (pāramī), sacrifices (cāga), and conducts (cariya) for the aforementioned four asankheyya and one hundred thousand aeons.
2:
2
Having cultivated and practiced the four meditations (bhāvanā) and reached the pinnacle of all qualities required for Buddhahood, he reached the end of all lives in the period of fulfilling perfections in his existence as the Great King Vessantara. In that life, he performed noble practices to such an extraordinary and incomparable degree that the inanimate great earth shook and trembled seven times. After living out his lifespan and passing away, he was reborn in Tusita heaven, as is the nature of Bodhisattas. He became a deva named Setaketu, who surpassed other devas in ten attributes: (1) longevity, (2) beauty, (3) happiness, (4) great wealth and retinue, (5) sovereignty, (6) superior visual objects, (7) superior sounds, (8) superior smells, (9) superior tastes, and (10) superior tangible objects.
(In this regard, it is said that the mass of water in the great ocean gradually deepens from the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and upon reaching the base of Mount Meru, the depth of that water is eighty-four thousand yojanas. Upon deep reflection, one realizes that the drops of water in that great ocean are so numerous they cannot be counted. Similarly, when it is briefly stated or read that "the Bodhisatta practiced the perfections, sacrifices, and conducts without rest through the four meditations for four asankheyya and one hundred thousand aeons," the virtuous should deeply reflect that during those four asankheyya and one hundred thousand aeons, in countless existences even more numerous than the drops of water in the great ocean,
3:
3
the Bodhisatta cultivated the perfections in every single life, and they should revere the qualities of the Bodhisatta's conduct.)
## The Appearance of the Buddha-uproar
The Bodhisatta Setaketu Deva enjoyed great celestial bliss for the full lifespan of the Tusita devas, which is four thousand (4,000) celestial years, or five hundred and seventy-six million (576,000,000) human years. When his celestial lifespan was nearing its end, with only one thousand human years remaining, the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas proclaimed:
"O friends, one thousand years from today, a Fully Enlightened Buddha will appear in this world of men!"
Because they shouted and proclaimed this from the sky, the "Buddha-uproar" (Buddha-kolāhala)*—the excited and widespread rumor among people saying, "A Buddha is about to appear! A Buddha is about to appear!"—occurred one thousand years in advance.
(Regarding the name of the Bodhisatta Deva, in the Ratanacaṅkama section of the Buddhavaṃsa Pali, it is taught: "Yadāhaṃ Tusite kāye, Santusito nāmahaṃ tadā," indicating his name was Santusita. The Buddhavaṃsa Commentary and the Jinālaṅkāra Ṭīkā also explain him as Santusita Deva according to this Pali. However, in the commentaries on the Pārājika (Verañjakaṇḍa Pubbenivāsakatha) and
* The five types of uproar (kolāhala) are explained in detail in the Anudīpanī.
4:
4
the Mūlapaṇṇāsa (Bhayabherava Sutta), the Bodhisatta Deva's name is given as Setaketu. The lineage of ancient Burmese Buddhavaṃsa authors, such as those of the Tathāgata-udāna-dīpanī, Mālālaṅkāra-vatthu, and Jinatthapakāsanī, also wrote and referred to the Bodhisatta Deva's name as Setaketu. Therefore, teachers state that the name "Santusita" is a general title acquired in relation to the Tusita celestial realm, while the name "Setaketu" should be understood as the specific name of the Bodhisatta Deva.)
## The Request to the Bodhisatta Deva
Having heard the Buddha-uproar—the excited talk that a Buddha was about to appear—the Four Great Kings, Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Sunimmita, and Vasavatti devas from each of the ten thousand world systems, as well as the Mahābrahmas, gathered together in this single world system. When only seven human days remained before the end of his celestial lifespan, and the five signs of a deva's passing (pubbanimitta)* were clearly appearing to the Bodhisatta Setaketu Deva, they approached him in unison and, with hands raised in prayer, made this request:
"O Noble Bodhisatta, you have fully practiced the ten perfections. You did not practice these perfections desiring the bliss of Sakka, Mara, Brahma, or a Universal Monarch.
* The five signs of a deva's passing are described in detail in the Anudīpanī.
5:
5
O Noble Bodhisatta, you practiced those perfections solely aspiring for Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) for the sake of liberating yourself from the three worlds and liberating many humans, devas, and brahmas as well. O Noble Bodhisatta, the time has come for you to become a Buddha. Now is the right time for you to become a Buddha. May you be conceived in the womb of a mother in the human world, become a true Buddha among the three types of beings, save the multitude of humans and devas from Saṃsāra, and teach them the Dhamma of Nibbāna, the state free from death."
Thus they made their request.
## Making the Five Great Observations
To the devas and brahmas who had gathered from the ten thousand world systems to make this request, the Bodhisatta Setaketu Deva did not give his promise immediately. Instead, he made the Five Great Observations (Pañca-mahāvilokana), which is the custom of all previous Bodhisattas:
(1) Observing the time (kāla) for becoming a Buddha,
(2) Observing the continent (dīpa) for becoming a Buddha,
(3) Observing the region (desa) for becoming a Buddha,
(4) Observing the family (kula) in which the Bodhisatta (in his final birth) would be born,
(5) Observing the lifespan of the Bodhisatta's mother—
6:
6
He made these five observations.
(1) Among these five great observations, he first considered the time: "Is it the right time to become a Buddha in the human world, or is it not yet time?" In this consideration, a period when the human lifespan is increasing and exceeds one hundred thousand years is not the time when Buddhas appear. The reason is that during a period when the lifespan is longer than one hundred thousand years, the suffering of conception, the suffering of aging, the suffering of sickness, and the suffering of death are not apparent to beings. Because of the concealment provided by such a long lifespan, people live in negligence of this mass of suffering. Furthermore, the Dhamma to be taught by the Buddhas is never devoid of the characteristics of impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta). If Buddhas were to appear when the lifespan is over one hundred thousand years and teach the nature of anicca, dukkha, and anatta, the people of that era would be unable to distinguish or understand, wondering, "What are they teaching?" They would not listen or believe. If they do not listen or believe, they will not realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation. Teaching the Dhamma of the three characteristics, which can liberate one from the round of rebirths, to those who do not accept or believe it would be fruitless and would not achieve the goal of liberation from Saṃsāra. Therefore, a period when the lifespan is longer than one hundred thousand years
7:
7
is not the time when Buddhas appear.
A period when the human lifespan has decreased to less than one hundred years is also not the time when Buddhas appear. The reason is that beings born in a period when the lifespan is less than one hundred years have abundant and thick defilements (kilesa). The instruction of the Buddha given to those with thick defilements would not last long, disappearing quickly like a line drawn on the surface of water with a stick. Therefore, a period when the human lifespan is less than one hundred years is also not the time when Buddhas appear.
Only the period between a lifespan of one hundred thousand years and one hundred years is the time when Buddhas appear, as birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa) are easily apparent; the teaching of the three characteristics and the way to liberation from Saṃsāra is easily understood; and defilements are not too thick in the continuum of beings. (At the time the devas and brahmas requested the Bodhisatta Deva, the human lifespan was one hundred years.) At that time, the Bodhisatta Setaketu Deva clearly perceived the time for becoming a Buddha, thinking, "This is indeed the suitable and proper time to become a Buddha."

(2) Then, as he investigated the island where the Buddhas are born, among the four great islands each surrounded by five hundred small islands, he clearly perceived the island of birth to be this great island of Jambudīpa, where the Jambu (rose-apple) tree grows and after which it is named, for it is the constant rule that former Buddhas are born only in this Jambudīpa.

(3) Then, reflecting, "This Jambudīpa is very vast; in extent, it measures ten thousand yojanas. In such a vast Jambudīpa, in which region did the former Buddhas appear?" he investigated the region of birth and clearly perceived the Majjhimadesa (Middle Country), the central region of this Jambudīpa, as the place where former Buddhas were born.

(Majjhimadesa refers to the region bounded by these five landmarks: to the east, the great Sāla tree to the east of the market town named Kajaṅgala; to the south-east, the Salalavatī River; to the south, the market town named Setakaṇṇika; to the west, the brahmin village named Thūna; and to the north, the Usīraddhaja Mountain. It measures three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in breadth, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference. Regions outside this Majjhimadesa are called Paccantarit (border regions). It is only within this Majjhimadesa that the Omniscient Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Disciples, and Universal Monarchs are born, as well as other powerful and wealthy Khattiya-mahāsāla, Brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla, and Gahapati-mahāsāla families.)

Within this central part of Majjhimadesa lies the royal city of Kapilavatthu, belonging to the Sakyan kingdom. The Bodhisatta Setaketu Deva decided that it was there he should be born.

(4) Then, as he investigated the family in which the Bodhisattas in their final existence are conceived and born, he reflected: "Former Buddhas are not born into the merchant class or the poor class in their final existence; they are born only into the Khattiya (warrior-noble) or Brāhmaṇa (priestly) castes, whichever is esteemed as supreme by the people. In an era when the Khattiya caste is esteemed as supreme, Bodhisattas in their final existence are born into that supreme Khattiya caste. In an era when the Brāhmaṇa caste is esteemed as supreme, they are born into that supreme Brāhmaṇa caste. At present, the Khattiya caste is esteemed as supreme; I shall be born into that Khattiya caste. Within that caste, King Suddhodana, the lord of the royal city of Kapilavatthu, is a supreme king of pure Sakyan lineage, an Asambhinna-khattiya-rāja, descended without break from the Great Elect, King Mahāsammata, at the beginning of the world. This King Suddhodana, of such pure and noble lineage, shall be my father." Thus, he clearly perceived the family of birth.

(5) Then, as he investigated the mother of the Buddha, he reflected: "The mother of a Buddha must be one who is not at all frivolous or flirtatious, and who never consumes intoxicants. She must be one who has fulfilled the meritorious perfections to become a Buddha's mother for a period of one hundred thousand aeons.
10:
"From the time she was born into the life destined to be the mother of a Buddha, she must be one who has always strictly observed and protected the five precepts without ever breaking or marring them. Queen Siri Mahāmāyā, the chief consort of King Suddhodana, is fully endowed with all these aforementioned virtues and qualities. This Queen Siri Mahāmāyā shall be my mother." (Then, as he further investigated how much of the life-span of the one worthy to be his mother remained, he clearly perceived that the remainder of his mother's life was only ten months and seven days.)

## Giving Consent to the Devas and Brahmas

Having thus thoroughly investigated and perceived the Five Great Investigations, the Bodhisatta Setaketu Deva resolved and decided, "I shall indeed descend to the human world and become a Buddha." Then, to the assembly of Devas and Brahmas who had come from the ten thousand world systems to make their request, he gave his word of consent:

"O friends, Devas and Brahmas! Now is the proper time for me to become a Buddha, as you have requested. You may return to your respective abodes. I shall descend to the human world and become a Buddha."

Having given this promise and permitted the assembly of Devas and Brahmas to depart, he entered the Nandavana Grove in that Tusita heaven, surrounded by the host of Tusita devas.

## (b) About the Nandavana Grove

I shall now describe the Nandavana Grove as explained in the commentaries such as the Sagāthāvagga Saṃyutta Aṭṭhakathā and the Nandana-vagga. This grove is called "Nandavana" because it causes delight and joy to all the devas who enter it.

Such a Nandavana Grove exists in each of the six deva realms. The Nandavana groves in the lower deva realms and those in the higher deva realms are similar in their nature of providing delight; therefore, the scriptures describe the Nandavana Grove in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in detail as a representative.

This Nandavana Grove is a place so magnificent, diverse, and beautiful with celestial jeweled trees, flowering plants, mansions, vehicles, and various wish-fulfilling objects (padesā) that worldlings (puthujjana) could never finish seeing, enjoying, or describing its wonders. It is a grand garden complex, a special place of frolic and joy, where various celestial dancers and musicians compete to entertain with diverse forms, colors, sounds, and radiant glows, presenting an array of sensual pleasures from all four directions, as if displaying the height of divine luxury.

As a crowning glory and ornament of their respective deva realms, it is a noble grove that can delight and enchant all devas who arrive to experience the five cords of sensual pleasure: sights to see, sounds to hear, scents to smell,
12:
tastes to eat, and objects to touch. 

Even when devas and devīs are about to fall from their divine state and die, and are weeping in intense agony and anxiety as they reflect on having to abandon their divine luxury due to the appearance of the five great omens of death (cuti-nimitta), upon entering this Nandavana Grove, the fires of grief and lamentation that previously tormented them vanish in an instant. Through the entertainment of the Nandavana Grove, they immediately find joy, clarity, and relief, making it a place of great delight.

No matter the cause of their arrival—be it in exhaustion, weeping, or burning with sorrow—once they step into that Nandavana Grove, their anxieties and grief are extinguished in a moment, just as a mass of dew or frost melts and disappears under the heat of the sun, or as a lamp flame is extinguished by a gust of wind, while they indulge in the enchanting sensory objects. It is so beautiful and filled with delightful objects for the worldlings of the sensual realm that it is said, "One who has never reached the Nandavana Grove, the gathering place of all various sensual pleasures esteemed as good in the world, cannot understand the nature of what is called 'happiness' in the world."
13:
In the commentary to the Verañja-kaṇḍa in the Vinaya Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Volume I, page 268, it is explained: "The Nandavana Grove in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is sixty yojanas in extent. (According to some teachers, it is five hundred yojanas wide.) It is beautifully adorned with a thousand species of celestial trees."

In the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā, in the explanation of the Threefold Buddha-field (Tividha-buddhakkhetta) on page 90, it is stated: "That Nandavana Grove is situated on the eastern side of the royal city of Sudassana in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, surrounded by walls, battlements, and gate-towers made entirely of jewels. It is one thousand yojanas in circumference and is a place of delight and joy for the devas. Between the Nandavana Grove and the city of Sudassana, there are two lakes: the Mahānandā Lake and the Cūḷanandā Lake. These lakes are pure and clean in every direction, and their water surfaces bear a dark blue-green hue, resembling the cloudless sky." Thus it is described.

## The Time for the Bodhisatta's Departure

When the Bodhisatta Setaketu Deva entered that Nandavana Grove, the devas and devīs of the Tusita realm who accompanied him said to him:

"Noble Deva, when you pass away from this deva realm, may you go only to a happy destination (sugati) where those of merit reside."

Thus, they repeatedly encouraged him to reflect upon and remember his previously performed meritorious deeds.
14:
While he was wandering within the Nandavana Grove, surrounded by the host of devas who were thus urging him to reflect repeatedly on his past merits, the time for the Bodhisatta Setaketu Deva to pass away (to decease from the deva realm) arrived.

## (c) The Manner of Conception

At the time when the Bodhisatta Setaketu Deva's time to pass away arrived, Queen Siri Mahāmāyā was enjoying great royal luxury as the Chief Queen of King Suddhodana in the city of Kapilavatthu. She was then in the third part of the second stage of life, known as Majjhimavaya (middle age).* (At that time, the human lifespan was one hundred years, and Queen Siri Mahāmāyā was approximately fifty-five years and four months old. This is explained in detail in the Samantacakkhu-dīpanī.)

## Celebrating the Festival of the Stars

In the year 67 of the Great Era (Mahā Sakkarāj), on the 9th waxing day of the month of Āsāḷha, when Queen Siri Mahāmāyā was about fifty-five years and four months old, the festival of the Uttarāsāḷha constellation (Nakkhatta), which was traditionally celebrated in the royal city of Kapilavatthu, took place. The citizens, marking it as a grand festival, celebrated joyfully, shouting and cheering to one another.

* The reason for conception taking place in the third part of the second stage of life is mentioned in the Anu-dīpanī.
15:
15
Queen Mahāmāyā Devī also enjoyed the festival, which was complete with flowers, perfumes, incense, and adornments, and free from the consumption of intoxicants, for six days from the 9th to the 14th day of the waxing moon of Āsāḷha. When the full moon day of Āsāḷha arrived, which was the seventh day from the 9th of the waxing moon, Queen Mahāmāyā Devī bathed early in the morning with scented water and performed a great act of charity by spending four hundred thousand coins. Then, adorned with all kinds of ornaments and having partaken of a delicious and excellent morning meal, she took upon herself the Eight Uposatha Precepts (from the hermit Devala). She then entered the beautifully decorated auspicious royal chamber and remained there, practicing the Eight Uposatha Precepts upon her auspicious bed.

## The Vision of the Dream
While she was thus practicing the Uposatha and dwelling there, during the last watch of the night of that full moon day, she lay down upon her auspicious bed and fell into a light slumber. Then, Queen Sirimahāmāyā Devī saw the following dream, which was a precursor and omen of the Bodhisatta’s conception.

In the dream, the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika) lifted Queen Sirimahāmāyā Devī together with her bed and carried her to Lake Anavatatta in the Himālaya. They placed her under a great Sal tree, seven leagues in height, upon the Manosilā (red arsenic) rock plateau, which was sixty leagues in extent.
16:
16
[They placed her] under a great Sal tree, seven leagues in height, upon the Manosilā rock plateau.

Then, the goddesses who were the queens of those Four Great Kings came and took Queen Sirimahāmāyā Devī to Lake Anavatatta, where they bathed her to remove all impurities. They dressed her in divine garments, anointed her with divine perfumes, and adorned her with divine flowers. Thereafter, they made Queen Sirimahāmāyā Devī lie down with her head toward the east in a golden mansion within a great silver mountain situated not far from Lake Anavatatta.

While Queen Mother Māyā Devī was thus sleeping and in a state of light slumber, a noble white elephant wandered about on a golden mountain situated not far from the silver mountain where the golden mansion of the Queen Mother was. Descending from that golden mountain, it climbed the silver mountain where the golden mansion stood, entered the golden mansion, circumambulated Queen Mahāmāyā Devī three times to the right, and then, appearing to pierce her right side, entered her womb. This was the dream she saw.

## The Conception of the Bodhisatta
At that very moment when she saw the dream, the Bodhisatta, the celestial being Setaketu,
17:
17
while wandering and enjoying various sights, sounds, and pleasures in the Nandavana Garden of the Tusita heaven, passed away (cuti) from the celestial realm without losing mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña). He took conception in the womb of the Queen Mother during the last watch of the night at dawn on Thursday, the full moon day of Āsāḷha, in the year 67 of the Mahā Sakkarāj (the era remaining after King Añjana’s reduction), while the moon was in the Uttarāsāḷha nakshatra. Among the 19 types of rebirth-linking consciousness, he took conception with the first great resultant consciousness (paṭhama mahāvipāka citta), which is the fruit of the first great wholesome consciousness (paṭhama mahākusala citta) accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and unprompted (asankhārika), which he had cultivated in previous lives as the preliminary practice (parikamma-bhāvanā) leading to the mettā-jhāna.

(The mention of the specific year and the names of the days like Thursday for the Bodhisatta’s conception and birth is based only on the records of worldly astrology and chronicles; there is no mention of these in the Pali texts, Commentaries, or Sub-commentaries. The Gotama Purāṇa states that "the Buddha Gotama appeared in the year 2570 of the Kali Yuga.")

## The Great Earthquake
Simultaneously with the Bodhisatta’s conception, the entire ten thousand world systems shook violently in six ways. The surface of the earth in the ten thousand world systems, which is the field of birth (jāti-khetta), [shook as follows]:

(1) It rose up in the east and sank down in the west.
18:

(2) Then it rose up in the west and sank down in the east.
(3) In the same manner, from north to south.
(4) From south to north.
(5) From the center to the periphery.
(6) It rose up from the periphery and sank down in the center.

## The 32 Great Omens
Furthermore, at the time of the final conception of Bodhisattas, 32 types of great omens, which are natural laws (dhammaniyāma) and are extraordinarily great, wonderful, and amazing, appeared clearly so that the wise could know beforehand that "the Bodhisatta has taken conception." I shall describe these 32 great omens as they appear in the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā-nidāna. When the Bodhisatta took conception:

(1) An immeasurable great light spread throughout the ten thousand world systems.
(2) As if wishing to behold the glory of the Bodhisatta, those who were blind from birth gained their sight at that moment.
(3) Those who were deaf regained their hearing and heard sounds.
(4) Those who were mute and could not speak regained their speech and began to talk at that moment.

(5) Those with crooked, hunched, or deformed bodies became straight-bodied at that moment.
(6) Those who were lame (unable to walk) regained their ability to walk and could move about well on their feet.
(7) Those who were held in prisons and bonds (shackles, stocks, chains, etc.) were released from all such various bonds at that moment.
(8) The fires in all the hell realms were extinguished and became cool.
(9) In the realm of hungry ghosts (peta-loka), hunger and thirst were appeased and ceased.
(10) Animals faced no danger whatsoever. (They were freed from all fears.)
(11) All living beings who were diseased were cured and freed from all their ailments.
(12) All beings spoke only pleasant and affectionate words to one another.
(13) Horses neighed joyfully with sweet and pleasant tones.
(14) Elephants trumpeted with sweet and pleasant tones.
(15) All musical instruments, such as drums and lutes, played their own natural sounds without being struck or blown.

(16) Human ornaments, such as bracelets and anklets, produced sounds spontaneously without striking against one another.
(17) All directions and open spaces became pure and clear.
(18) Gentle and soft breezes blew mildly, bringing coolness and happiness to all beings.
(19) An unseasonal great rain fell. (Even though it was not the rainy season, a great and heavy rain fell with much clamor.)
(20) Water gushed forth spontaneously from this great earth and flowed here and there.
(21) Many birds did not fly in the sky. (At that moment, there were no birds flying in the sky.)

(23) The water in the great ocean, which is naturally salty in taste, became sweet at that moment.

(25) All land flowers and water flowers bloomed simultaneously at that moment.
(26) On the trunks of trees, trunk-lotuses (khandha-paduma) bloomed wonderfully.
(27) On the branches of trees, branch-lotuses (sākhā-paduma) bloomed wonderfully.
(28) On the vines of trees, vine-lotuses (latā-paduma) bloomed wonderfully.
