These 32 great omens are also called the 32 great wonders. These 32 wonders are the same 32 great omens that were promised to be described here in the section on the birth of the Bodhisatta in the Catuvisati-buddhavaṃsa section below.

Because the ten thousand world systems of the birth-field (jāti-khetta) were adorned with these 32 great omens and wonders, they reached a state of supreme glory, fragrant with the scent of flowers everywhere, like a great ball of flowers thrown together, or like a great bouquet tightly bound without gaps, or like a great flower bed prepared and laid out, as if being fanned by a yak-tail fan.
23:
After having pleased and satisfied them, the King related the dream of Queen Mahāmāyā Devī and inquired, “What are the benefits or ill effects of this dream? Please read and interpret this omen.”

The Brahmins replied, “O Great King, do not be anxious or worried. A conception has taken place in the Queen’s womb. The one who has been conceived is not female but truly male. A son will be born to you, O King. If he leads a domestic life and remains in the human world, he will become a Cakkavatti, a Universal Monarch ruling over the four islands. If he leaves the domestic life, renounces the world, and becomes a monk, he will surely become an Omniscient Buddha, who breaks open and removes the roof of defilements in the three worlds.” Thus they interpreted the omen and submitted their report.

## The Guarding by the Four Great Kings
From the moment the Great Bodhisatta was thus conceived, for the purpose of warding off ogres, distorted figures, and ill-favored forms of animals and birds from the places where the Bodhisatta and his mother might see or encounter them, the Four Great Kings of this universe, such as Vessavaṇa and others, each holding a sword, entered the royal chamber of Queen Mahāmāyā Devī and guarded her closely day and night. In the ten thousand universes of this birth-field (jātikkhetta), forty thousand Great Kings (four from each universe) drove away ogres and other such beings to other places, and from the door of Queen Mahāmāyā Devī’s
24:
royal chamber to the edge of the universe, they maintained their guard.

This guarding was not done out of concern that any being could actually harm the lives of the Bodhisatta and his mother. Indeed, even if a hundred thousand Māras were to come, each carrying a hundred thousand Mount Sinerus to harm the lives of a Bodhisatta in his final birth and his mother, those Māras and those Mount Sinerus would only vanish and be destroyed; they would be unable to harm the lives of the Bodhisatta and his mother.

Although they could not be harmed, because it was possible that the Bodhisatta and his mother might experience fear or terror if they saw or heard foul and distorted forms or sounds, the Four Great Kings held their swords and stood guard solely to prevent such ill sights and sounds. (Alternatively), they guarded them because they were prompted and urged by the profound sense of reverence and respect (garu-gārava) that arose in their hearts due to the Bodhisatta’s glory and power.

A question may arise: Did those Four Great Kings who came to guard and stay within the Queen’s royal chamber make themselves visible to the Bodhisatta’s mother, or did they not? The answer is: Those Great Kings did not make themselves visible when Queen Mahāmāyā Devī was bathing, dressing,
25:
taking her meals, or attending to her personal hygiene. However, when she entered the noble royal chamber and reclined on her noble couch, they made themselves visible to her.

Although ordinary humans who see deities are usually terrified, Queen Mahāmāyā Devī felt no fear or terror at all when she saw those Great Kings, owing to the Bodhisatta’s glory and her own glory. It was just as if she were seeing the regular palace guards.

## Constant Natural Virtue
The mothers of Bodhisattas in their final birth are naturally constant in their virtue (sīla) during that lifetime. Before the appearance of a Buddha, people usually pay homage to hermits and wanderers, sitting in a crouching position to receive the precepts. Queen Mahāmāyā Devī had also received the precepts from the hermit Kāla Devala before the Bodhisatta’s conception. However, once the Bodhisatta was conceived, it was not the custom for her to prostrate herself on the ground before another; nor did she receive the precepts in a manner that required her to be placed in a lower position (not as a pupil). She merely reflected upon them. Therefore, from the time the Bodhisatta was conceived, Mahāmāyā Devī herself undertook and reflected upon the precepts. It should be understood that she did not observe them as a pupil of the hermit Kāla Devala.

## Freedom from Lustful Thoughts
The mothers of Bodhisattas in their final birth, from the time the Bodhisattas are conceived,
26:
never have any lustful attachment or desire toward any man, starting from the Bodhisatta’s father. It is their natural way to be pure and free from lustful desires. It cannot be said, however, that worldlings (puthujjana) who saw the Bodhisatta’s mother did not experience lustful thoughts or desires. This is because the physical form of the mother of a Bodhisatta in his final birth possesses such beautiful, graceful, and marvelous splendor—due to the accumulation of meritorious perfections (pāramī) practiced over many lifetimes—that even master sculptors or painters who have reached the pinnacle of their craft would be unable to replicate it.

If those who saw the Bodhisatta’s mother, endowed with such beauty and marvelous splendor, were not satisfied with merely looking and attempted to approach her with lustful intent, their feet would be unable to move from the spot where they made that attempt. It would be as if both their feet were firmly fastened in celestial stocks or shackles. Therefore, it should be well understood that the mothers of Bodhisattas in their final birth are exceptional and noble women whom no deity or human can violate or offend.

## The Mother’s Womb Like a Shrine
The auspicious womb, the dwelling place of the Great Bodhisatta’s conception-element, is as noble as a shrine (cetiya) that is an object of worship.
27:
As it is so noble, it is truly not fitting for any other person to enter, dwell in, or use it. During the lifetime of the Bodhisatta’s mother, it is also impossible for any other woman to be installed as the Chief Queen (Aggamahesī). For this reason, it is the natural law that seven days after giving birth to the Bodhisatta, the mother of the Bodhisatta passes away and is reborn in the Tuṣita heaven. The precious golden womb of Mahāmāyā Devī, where the Bodhisatta resides, is like a chamber filled with vajra jewels and diamonds.

## The Arrival of Gifts
Upon hearing the good news that a son of such glory and splendor had been conceived by Queen Mahāmāyā Devī, the consort of King Suddhodana of Kapilavatthu, many kings from the surrounding regions sent gifts and offerings suitable for the Great Bodhisatta, such as very costly and fine garments, ornaments, and musical instruments, to King Suddhodana. Due to the past merits of the Bodhisatta and his mother, the gifts and tributes sent from various places were so numerous that they could not be counted or recorded.

## The Mother Seeing the Son in Her Womb
Although Mahāmāyā Devī was carrying the Bodhisatta in her womb, she did not experience the swelling of hands and feet or any other
28:
ailments, nor any physical pain, heaviness, or exhaustion like other pregnant women. Being free from such suffering, Mahāmāyā easily and happily passed through the early stages of pregnancy, such as the time of the kalala (embryo). When the five branches (limbs and head) were well-formed and distinct, and the Bodhisatta’s conception-element reached maturity, she would occasionally look to see whether her son within her womb was in a good position and whether he was comfortable, as is the custom of mothers, so that she might adjust if necessary. When she looked, she could clearly see the Bodhisatta sitting comfortably, cross-legged (pallaṅka), facing the front of his mother’s abdomen, leaning his back against his mother’s spine as if it were a backrest—much like a brilliant silk thread passed through a clear and beautiful veluriya (beryl) gem with eight facets, or like a noble Dhamma preacher (Dhammakathika) sitting gracefully on a pulpit (dhammāsana) leaning against the backrest.

(In this world, other ordinary humans who must dwell in a mother’s womb sit in misery and discomfort, like an old monkey
29:
hiding in a hollow tree during a rainstorm, sitting on the foul and malodorous stomach (the place of old food) while carrying the stomach (the place of new food) on their heads, leaning their backs against the mother’s front abdomen, with their knees drawn up and their chins resting on their hands.)

## The Reason for Seeing the Son in the Womb
The reason why Queen Mahāmāyā Devī could see her son within her womb from the outside is that, due to the exceptional merits she had fulfilled and accumulated in her previous lives, there were no thick, coarse, or dark layers of physical matter in Mahāmāyā’s body that would obstruct the view. Because of this absence, Mahāmāyā’s body was exceedingly pure, clean, and subtle. The skin of the auspicious womb that arose in such an exceptionally pure and subtle body was as clear as a sheet of crystal or a slab of ruby. Such extremely clear and subtle skin did not prevent or hide the son within from being seen from the outside. Therefore, Queen Mahāmāyā Devī could clearly see the Bodhisatta residing in her womb with her natural eyes, penetrating the skin of the abdomen (like an object placed inside a glass box).

It should be specially noted that although Queen Mahāmāyā Devī could see her son in the womb clearly, the Bodhisatta residing in the womb could not see his mother, because “eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa) does not normally arise within the mother’s womb.”
30:
## (d) The Birth of the Bodhisatta
Except for the mothers of Bodhisattas in their final existence, other women give birth with varying durations, either exceeding ten months or less than ten months, without a fixed number of days or months. They may give birth in any of the four postures—lying, sitting, standing, or walking—often unexpectedly. Some give birth while lying down, some while sitting, some while standing, and some while walking.

However, the mothers of Bodhisattas in their final existence are not like that. From the day of conception, they carry the womb for exactly ten months, reaching the full duration of two hundred and ninety-five (295) days, and they invariably give birth while in a standing posture. At the time of birth, they are not smeared or stained with any repulsive impurities but are born pure and clean, appearing as magnificent and radiant as a precious gem placed upon a fresh cloth from the Kāsī kingdom.

Unlike Bodhisattas, other beings, when the birth-winds (kammaja-vāya) of the mother move, are turned upside down by the force of those winds (with feet up and head down). They experience extreme pain and suffering, as if being squeezed through a thick mass of flesh at the mother's birth canal, feeling as though they are falling into a hundred-fathom deep abyss, or as if a great elephant is being
31:
pulled and extracted through a very narrow keyhole, thus being born with great pain, exhaustion, and distress.

Bodhisattas, however, are not like that; they are born with ease and comfort, like water flowing from a water-strainer (dhammakaraka). (For example) they are born peacefully and mindfully, with eyes open, limbs extended, and palms spread, like a noble Dhamma-preacher (dhammakathika) gracefully descending from the preaching throne after a sermon, or like a man calmly descending a staircase, or like the thousand-rayed sun emerging and shining through a golden mountain. They are born without any fear or trembling, fully endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension.

## Queen Mahāmāyā's Journey to Devadaha
Queen Mahāmāyā, having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb for ten months as carefully as one would carry oil in an alms-bowl, felt the desire to go to her native home of Devadaha when the time of birth drew near. She requested King Suddhodana, saying, "O Great King, I wish to go to the city of Devadaha, the residence of my relatives."

King Suddhodana consented, saying, "Very well," and ordered the road from the royal city of Kapilavatthu to the city of Devadaha to be leveled and prepared. Along both sides of the road, he had plantain trees planted, full water-pots placed, areca-nut trees planted, and banners and flags raised, thus preparing the entire route.
32:
The road was beautifully decorated like a celestial path. He then had Queen Mahāmāyā seated upon a new golden palanquin and ordered a thousand ministers to carry it. With a large retinue of guards and ceremonial honors suitable for the occasion, he sent her forth to the city of Devadaha.

(The differing opinions of various scholars regarding Queen Mahāmāyā's journey from Kapilavatthu to Devadaha are mentioned in the Anu-dīpanī.)

## The Lumbinī Sal Grove
Between the two royal cities of Kapilavatthu and Devadaha, there is a Sal grove named Lumbinī, which was used by the people of both cities. When Queen Mahāmāyā arrived at that Sal grove, every tree was in full bloom from the base to the tips of the branches.

Among the flowers and branches of the Sal trees, swarms of five-colored bees and various species of birds flew about, singing sweet and melodious songs. The entire Sal grove was endowed with extraordinary and marvelous qualities, no different from the Cittalatā garden of Sakka, the King of Devas. It was filled with the continuous and thunderous sounds of joy, much like a pleasure garden well-prepared by a king of great power and glory. (This is the explanation from the Jātaka Commentary.)
33:
In the Lumbinī Sal grove, from between the branches and blossoms of the Sal trees, female bees—intoxicated by the scent and nectar of the Sal flowers, rejoicing and flying about (carrying nectar for others)—sang melodiously and delightfully, making the Lumbinī Sal grove resemble the Nandavana garden cherished by the devas.

[Refer to the Anu-dīpanī for the explanation of the text in parentheses.]

Vibūsitā bālajanāticālinī,
Vibūsitāṅgī vaniteva mālinī,
Sadā janānaṃ nayanālimālinī,
Vilumbinīvātiviroci lumbinī.

Bālajanāticālinī = capable of agitating and stirring the minds of young people. Vibūsitāṅgī = having limbs and parts adorned with various ornaments like beads and earrings. Mālinī = wearing various kinds of flowers. Vanitā = like a young woman. Ativiroci iva = just as she is exceedingly beautiful. Vibūsitā = being adorned with various and diverse decorations. Sadā = at all times. Janānaṃ = of all people. Nayanālimālinī = being like a cluster of flowers where the bees of people's unblinking eyes gather and rest. Lumbinī = the garden called Lumbinī. Vilumbinīva = as if competing in beauty with that young woman. Ativiroci = was exceedingly and marvelously beautiful. (This is the poetic description of the Lumbinī garden by the author of the Buddhavamsa Commentary, Venerable Buddhadatta Thera.)
34:
Upon seeing the exceedingly beautiful Lumbinī Sal grove, Queen Mahāmāyā felt a strong desire to enter and enjoy herself in the grove.

The ministers, having informed King Suddhodana, took Queen Mahāmāyā in the golden palanquin and entered the auspicious Sal grove.

## The Gathering of Devas and Brahmās
At the very moment Queen Mahāmāyā entered the Lumbinī Sal grove, all the devas cried out and proclaimed, "Today, the Great Bodhisatta will emerge from his mother's womb and be born!" causing a thunderous echo to resound throughout the ten thousand world-systems. The devas and brahmās from the ten thousand world-systems, intending to perform an auspicious worship for the birth of the Bodhisatta, brought various auspicious gifts and gathered together, filling this entire world-system. They covered the whole sky with divine white umbrellas, sang auspicious songs, and stood there making the sounds of divine musical instruments and conch shells resonate simultaneously.

As soon as Queen Mahāmāyā reached the interior of the auspicious Sal grove, she desired to reach out and hold a branch of a Sal tree, which had a straight, round trunk and was fully adorned with flowers. That auspicious
35:
Sal branch, as if it were a sentient being, moved and amazed the hearts of the people by bending down automatically like a rattan shoot softened in hot water, coming within reach of Queen Mahāmāyā's palm.

Queen Mahāmāyā stood holding the Sal branch that had come to her hand with her right hand, which was beautiful and pleasant, with fingers as round and smooth as lotus stems and fingernails as bright red as a bird's beak, adorned with newly worn golden bangles. Standing there holding the Sal branch with her right hand, Queen Mahāmāyā was exceedingly beautiful, like the crescent moon just emerging from between dark, rain-threatening clouds, or like a flash of brilliant lightning, or like a goddess appearing in the Nandavana garden.

## The Birth of the Bodhisatta
While Queen Mahāmāyā stood with great beauty, wearing a golden-threaded sarong and a fine white upper robe patterned like the eyes of a carp reaching down to her feet, holding the auspicious Sal branch with her right hand, the birth-winds (kammaja-vāya) moved, signaling the birth of the Bodhisatta. At that time, the attendants, ministers, and others surrounded Queen Mahāmāyā with curtains and then withdrew from her presence.
36:
While Queen Mahāmāyā stood gracefully holding the auspicious Sal branch with her right hand, the entire ten thousand world-systems, including the great oceans, roared and shook like a potter's wheel. Simultaneously, the thirty-two great and marvelous omens (pubbanimitta) appeared, such as the devas and brahmās shouting praises, the raining down of divine flowers, the spontaneous playing of divine and human musical instruments, and the opening of the entire world-system from top to bottom. It was the year 68 of the Great Era (Mahā-sakarāj), on the full moon day of the month of Kason (Vesākha), a Friday, under the Visākhā nakshatra. Just as a flying radiant gem from the peak of Mount Vipulla gracefully descends into a waiting golden casket, the Great Bodhisatta, adorned with the major and minor marks, was born from the womb of his mother, Queen Mahāmāyā, which was like a shrine-house.

At the moment of this pure birth, two streams of water—one warm and one cool—spontaneously emerged from the sky to honor the mother and son, who were already pure by nature, and to balance the temperature of the bodies of the Bodhisatta and his mother.

(The explanatory remarks on this matter are provided in the Anu-dīpanī.)
37:
## Successive Reception by Brahmas, Devas, and Humans

At the very moment of birth, the four Great Brahmas, whose minds were purified from defilements, first received the noble Bodhisatta, the royal son, with a golden net. Placing him before his mother, they said:

“O Queen, be joyful in heart; a son of great power and majesty has been born to you.”

Then, from the hands of the four Great Brahmas, the four Great Kings (Cātumahārājā) received the royal son with a skin of the black antelope, which is traditionally designated as auspicious.

Again, from the hands of those four Great Kings, humans received the royal son with a wrap of fine white cloth.

Then, releasing himself from the hands of the humans, the Bodhisatta stood firmly on the ground with his two feet placed evenly like golden sandals, and he looked towards the eastern direction. As he looked, thousands of world systems (Cakkavāḷa) in the eastern direction became a single expanse; there was no distinction between one world system and another, appearing as an open, continuous, and vast space. The devas and humans residing in that eastern direction worshipped the noble Bodhisatta with scents, flowers, and other offerings, and said:
38:
“O Great Man, in this direction, there is no one equal to you. Where could there be anyone superior to you?”

In this manner, he looked successively at the ten directions: the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, the downward direction, and the upward direction. Seeing no one equal to himself in all those ten directions, he took seven strides towards the north from the place where he stood.

As he thus strode, the Great Brahma held a white parasol over the Bodhisatta; the deva Suyama held a yak-tail whisk; and other devas followed behind the Bodhisatta, each holding the royal regalia: the sandals, the sword, and the crown with its diadem. Although the devas and Brahmas followed while holding these five royal regalia, the people could not see the devas and Brahmas themselves, but saw only the royal regalia.

Great Miracles: When he thus strode, the noble Bodhisatta walked only on the actual ground; however, in the minds of the multitude, it appeared as if he were traveling through the sky. He strode with his natural body just as he was born, without any clothing or ornaments; however, in the minds of the multitude,
39:
it appeared as if he were walking fully dressed and adorned with ornaments. He strode in the form of a newborn infant; however, in the minds of the multitude, it appeared as if he were sixteen years of age.

(What has been described now regarding the noble Bodhisatta taking seven strides to the north is written according to the explanations in the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, the Mahāpadāna Sutta Commentary, and the Jātaka Commentary. In the Vijātamangala section of the Jinālaṅkāra Ṭīkā, it is explained slightly differently and more extensively as follows.)

At the moment he thus strode, the Great Brahma followed, holding a white parasol three yojanas in size. Similarly, the Great Brahmas from the other world systems also followed, each holding a white parasol three yojanas in size, so that the entire world system was covered and filled with a garland of white parasols.

Likewise, ten thousand Suyama devas residing in the ten thousand world systems of the field of birth (jātikkhetta) each held yak-tail whisks, and ten thousand Santusita devas each held ruby fans, standing and waving them as far as the edge of the world system mountains.

Similarly, ten thousand Sakka Devas residing in the ten thousand world systems stood blowing ten thousand conch shells.
40:
Furthermore, other young devas stood holding golden flowers, some holding natural flowers, some holding mirror-like flowers (flowers that flash like mirrors), some holding banner-flowers, and some holding various jeweled offerings. Devas' daughters also stood holding various kinds of auspicious ceremonial offerings, covering and filling the entire world system.

While such abundant ceremonial offerings, which were like celestial medicine (cakkhurasāyana) for the eyes, were being made, while thousands of celestial and human conch shells were being blown gently, and while thousands of celestial and human musical instruments were being played, and while celestial maidens were dancing with joy, the noble Bodhisatta took seven strides towards the north and stood still.

At the moment the noble Bodhisatta stood still, all humans, devas, and Brahmas remained silent and still, without making any sound, listening intently and thinking, “What kind of words will this Great Man, the Bodhisatta, utter to us now?”

## Proclaiming the Bold Utterance

The noble Bodhisatta, having taken seven strides towards the north and standing still at the seventh step, said:
41:
(a) Aggo'hamasmi lokassa = I am the foremost in the world (of the three types of beings). (Alternatively) I am the most noble among the three worlds.
(b) Jeṭṭho'hamasmi lokassa = I am the eldest in the world. (Alternatively) I am the greatest among the three worlds.
(c) Seṭṭho'hamasmi lokassa = I am the most excellent in the world. (Alternatively) I am the most praiseworthy among the three worlds.
(d) Ayamantimā jāti = This present conception is my final conception.
(e) Natthi dāni punabbhavo = Now, there is no more new birth for me.

Thus, he proclaimed this bold utterance, making his voice heard simultaneously throughout the entire ten thousand world systems.

When the noble Bodhisatta proclaimed this bold utterance (āsabhibhācā), no Brahma, deva, or human was able to refute or contradict it, and thus all Brahmas, devas, and humans offered their acclamations to the noble Bodhisatta. 

## Significant Causes and Effects to Note

Among the great miracles that occurred during this birth of the noble Bodhisatta:
42:
(1) Standing firmly on the great earth with both feet placed evenly is the omen for attaining the four Bases of Power (Iddhipāda).
(2) Facing directly towards the north is the omen for being able to overcome and rule over all beings.
(3) Taking seven strides is the omen for attaining the seven Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅga), the treasure of Dhamma.
(4) Being shaded by the celestial white parasol is the omen for attaining the noble white parasol of the Fruition of Arahatship (Arahattaphala).
(5) Receiving the five royal regalia is the omen for liberation through the five types of deliverance (Vimutti): Tadanga-vimutti, Vikkhambhana-vimutti, Samuccheda-vimutti, Paṭippassaddhi-vimutti, and Nissaraṇa-vimutti.
(6) Being able to see all ten directions without obstruction is the omen for attaining the Unobstructed Knowledge (Anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa), which knows all things without hindrance or barrier.
(7) Proclaiming the bold utterance, “I am the foremost, the eldest, and the most excellent among the three worlds,” is the omen for being able to turn the noble Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka), which no Brahma, deva, or human has the right to stop or reverse.
43:
(8) Proclaiming the bold utterance, “This present conception is my final conception; now there is no more new birth,” is the omen for entering the peace of Nibbāna without remainder (Anupādisesa-parinibbāna).

## The Three Lives in which the Noble Bodhisatta Spoke at Birth

The noble Bodhisatta spoke at the moment of birth not only in this final life as Prince Siddhattha; he also spoke at birth in his lives as the wise Mahosadha and as King Vessantara. Thus, it should be understood that he spoke at the moment of birth in three lives, including this final (pacchima) life as Prince Siddhattha.

(1) To explain slightly further: In the life when the Bodhisatta was the wise Mahosadha, at the moment he was born pure from his mother's womb, Sakka, the king of devas, came and placed two pieces of sandalwood in the Bodhisatta's hand. When he was born holding those two pieces of sandalwood and his mother looked at him, seeing him clutching something in his hand, she asked, “Dear son, what object have you brought?” He replied, “O mother, it is medicine.”

Because of the fact that he was born clutching medicine, they first named that Bodhisatta Osadha-kumāra =
44:
the Medicine Youth. Later, that medicine was kept in a pot, and because it cured all the ailments of those who came, starting from the headache of the Bodhisatta's father, the wealthy merchant Sirivaḍḍhana, including the blind, the deaf, and all other diseased persons, the Bodhisatta youth, the master of that medicine, was called Mahosadha (the Great Medicine Master) in reference to the great power and efficacy of that medicine.

(2) In the life of King Vessantara, also at the moment of birth from his mother's womb, he extended his right hand and said, “Mother, is there any property in the royal palace? I wish to give charity.” At that time, the mother said to her son, “Dear son, you are born in a palace that has wealth,” and taking her son's extended hand in her own palm, she placed a bag of a thousand pieces of gold in his hand. In this way, the noble Bodhisatta also spoke at birth in his life as King Vessantara.

(3) As previously described, in this final life (as Prince Siddhattha), he also proclaimed the bold utterance at the moment of birth.

Thus, the noble Bodhisatta spoke at the moment of being born pure from his mother's womb in three lives.
46: (The significance of the Brahmas receiving him first was the omen for attaining the four Rūpāvacara Jhānas.) (4) After the Brahmas had received the Great Bodhisatta, humans received him. (The significance of humans receiving him after the Brahmas was the omen for attaining the four Arūpāvacara Jhānas.) (5) Lutes and harps strung with strings sounded of their own accord without being struck or played. (The significance of the lutes sounding of their own accord was the omen for attaining the nine successive meditative attainments, Anupubbavihāra Samāpatti, which include the four Rūpāvacara Samāpattis, the four Arūpāvacara Samāpattis, and Nirodha Samāpatti, to be entered in order.) (6) Large and small drums covered with leather sounded of their own accord without being struck. (The significance of the drums sounding of their own accord was the omen for the future beating of the Great Drum of Dhamma, making it heard by humans and Devas.) (7) The prisons and bonds that bound and fettered humans broke into pieces.
47: (The significance of such breaking was the omen for the future total eradication and abandonment of the conceit called 'I', māna.) (8) All diseases afflicting the sick were cured, just as acid washes away the grime attached to copper. (The significance of the curing of all diseases was the omen for the future realization of the Four Noble Truths, which is the cessation of the disease of all suffering in Saṃsāra for all people.) (9) Those who were blind from their mother's womb saw forms just like normal people. (The significance of their seeing was the omen for all people to attain the Divine Eye, Dibba-cakkhu.) (10) Those who were deaf from their mother's womb heard sounds just like normal people. (The significance of their hearing was the omen for all people to attain the Divine Ear, Dibba-sota.) (11) Those who were lame and unable to walk became strong and were able to walk. (The significance of their being able to walk was the omen for attaining the four Bases of Power, Iddhipāda.)
48: (12) Those who were mute from their mother's womb and unable to speak gained mindfulness and were able to speak. (The significance of the mute being able to speak was the omen for attaining the four Foundations of Mindfulness, Satipaṭṭhāna.) (13) Ships and vessels that were in dangerous places filled with terrifying perils reached their ports safely and without harm. (The significance of their reaching safely was the omen for attaining the four Analytical Knowledges, Paṭisambhidāñāṇa.) (14) Various jewels in the sky and various jewels on the earth shone with their own extremely bright radiance. (The significance of the jewels shining with their own radiance was the omen for attaining the light of the Dhamma. It was the omen for giving the light of Dhamma to those to be tamed and for the shining of the Buddha's own glory and power.) (15) Beings who were enemies towards each other gained a mind of loving-kindness, mettā. (The significance of gaining mettā was the omen for attaining the four Sublime States, Brahmavihāra.) (16) The fires of hell were extinguished.
49: (The significance of the extinguishing of hell fires was the omen for the extinguishing of the eleven types of fires, such as greed and hatred.) (17) Radiance and light appeared clearly in the Lokantarika hells, which are normally in total darkness. (The significance of this appearance was the omen for the ability to destroy the darkness of ignorance, avijjā, and to show and provide the light of wisdom, vijjā.) (18) The flowing currents of rivers stopped and did not flow. (The significance of this stopping was the omen for attaining the fourfold Intrepidity, Vesārajjañāṇa.) (19) All the water in the great ocean became sweet and pleasant in taste. (The significance of the ocean water becoming sweet was the omen for attaining the single sweet taste of the cessation of defilements.) (20) Harsh and violent winds did not blow; instead, only gentle, pleasant, and cool breezes blew. (The significance of the absence of violent winds was the omen for the disappearance and destruction of the sixty-two types of evil wrong views, micchādiṭṭhi.) (21) Birds that were in the sky, in trees, or on mountain peaks descended to the ground.
50: (The significance of their descending was the omen for all people to listen to the Buddha's instructions and take refuge in the Triple Gem for the rest of their lives.) (22) The moon shone more pleasantly and beautifully than ever before. (The significance of this beauty was the omen for the joy that all people would experience.) (23) The sun was neither too hot nor too cold, and being free from impurities, it was endowed with a pleasant temperature. (The significance of this was the omen for the attainment of physical and mental happiness.) (24) The Devas stood at the entrances of their respective celestial mansions and engaged in great celebrations, such as clapping their hands, whistling, and tossing their garments. (The significance of this celebration was the omen for the future inspired utterance, udāna, to be proclaimed upon becoming a Buddha.) (25) A heavy rain fell, covering all four continents. (The significance of this heavy rain was the omen for the future raining down of the rain of the Deathless Dhamma through the power of his great wisdom.)
51: (26) All people were free from hunger. (The significance of being free from hunger was the omen for attaining the Deathless Dhamma of Mindfulness of the Body, Kāyagatāsati; or, it was the omen for being free from the hunger of defilements by consuming the Deathless sustenance of Kāyagatāsati.) (27) All people were free from thirst. (The significance of being free from thirst was the omen for all people to be happy with the bliss of the Fruit of Arahantship, Arahattaphala.) (28) Doors that were closed and covered opened of their own accord. (The significance of the doors opening of their own accord was the omen for the opening of the great door to Nibbāna, which is the Eightfold Path.) (29) Flowering trees and fruit-bearing trees both bloomed and bore fruit. (The significance of this blooming and fruiting was the omen for all people to bloom with the flowers of Liberation, Vimutti, and to bear fruit with the four Noble Fruits, Ariyaphala.) (30) The entire ten thousand world systems were covered with a single flower of victory banners; the entire ten thousand world systems were completely covered with victory banners and flags.
53:
Because they came into existence at the same time, these seven are called the "Seven Co-natals" (Sahajāta). Among those seven:
1. Princess Bhaddakaccānā Yasodharā was born to King Suppabuddha, the ruler of Devadaha, and Queen Amitā.
2. Prince Ānanda was the son of Amitodana the Sakyan, the younger brother of King Suddhodana.
3. The Great Bodhi Tree grew at the central point of victory in the Uruvelā forest of the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), where Buddhas attain enlightenment.
4. The Four Great Pots of Gold appeared within the grounds of the golden palace in the royal city of Kapilavatthu.
(a) Among those four, one is named Saṅkha; the width of the mouth of this gold pot is one gāvuta.
(b) One is named Ela; its width is two gāvutas.
(c) One is named Uppala; its width is three gāvutas.
(d) One is named Puṇḍarīka; its width is four gāvutas, which equals one yojana.
When gold is taken out and used from these four great pots of gold, they do not appear depleted but return to being full as before. (The account of these four great pots of gold is mentioned in the commentary to the Caṅkī Sutta of the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, page 285, and in the commentary to the Soṇadaṇḍa Sutta of the Sīlakkhandhavagga, Dīgha Nikāya, page 253.)
54:
The sequence of names for these Seven Co-natals mentioned earlier is according to what appears in the Jātaka Commentary (Vol. 1, p. 63), the Buddhavamsa Commentary (p. 322), and the commentary to the Mahāpadāna Sutta of the Mahāvagga, Dīgha Nikāya (p. 18). Successive teachers have also presented them in this way, composing a mnemonic verse: "Ā-Bo-Kā-Ya, Nga-Shwe-Kan."

In the commentary to the Kāḷudāyī-vatthu in the Fourth Etadagga-vagga of the Aṅguttara Commentary (Vol. 1, p. 234), and in the commentary to the Rāhula-vatthu of the Mahākhandhaka in the Vinaya Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā (Vol. 3, p. 244), when counting these Seven Co-natals, the name of Prince Ānanda is not included. Instead, they are listed as: (1) The Bodhi Tree, (2) Yasodharā, (3) The Four Great Pots of Gold, (4) The State Elephant (Ārohaṇīya), (5) The State Horse Kaṇṭhaka, (6) Minister Channa, and (7) Minister Kāḷudāyī. This should be understood as an explanation according to the preference of various Reciter (Bhāṇaka) Elders.

## The Return of Queen Mahāmāyā to Kapilavatthu
The people of both Kapilavatthu and Devadaha took the Noble Bodhisatta Son along with Queen Mahāmāyā and traveled to the royal city of Kapilavatthu.

## The Account of the Hermit Kāḷadevila
On the very day the Bodhisatta and his mother arrived at the royal city of Kapilavatthu, the assembly of devas in Tāvatiṃsa, led by Sakka, the King of Devas, rejoiced, saying, "A noble son has been born to King Suddhodana in Kapilavatthu! This noble son will surely become a Buddha at the site of the Bodhi tree."
55:
Being filled with joy and delight, they celebrated by tossing their robes and scarves, clapping their hands, and playing joyfully.

At that time, the hermit Kāḷadevila, who possessed the five direct knowledges (abhiññā) and the eight attainments (samāpatti) and was a frequent visitor to King Suddhodana's palace, had finished his meal at the palace as on previous days. To rest during the day, he went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and sat upon a jeweled throne prepared inside a celestial mansion, enjoying the bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna-samāpatti). Upon arising, he stood at the entrance of the mansion and looked here and there. He saw the devas, led by Sakka, the King of Devas, on the sixty-yojana celestial highway, tossing their celestial turbans, praising the virtues of the Bodhisatta, and playing joyfully. He asked, "O devas, why are you so delighted, joyful, and playing with such great satisfaction? Tell me the reason."

Then the devas replied, "Noble Hermit, today a noble son has been born to King Suddhodana. This noble son, sitting upon the throne at the site of the Bodhi tree—the central pillar and supreme spot of the earth where all Buddhas attain enlightenment—will become a Buddha who fully knows all truths and will set in motion the wheel of the Dhamma (Dhammacakka).
56:
We shall have the great opportunity to behold the infinite and most excellent glory of that Buddha and to hear the clear and manifest Dhamma that he will preach. For this reason, we are so delighted, joyful, and playing with such great satisfaction."

Hearing the words spoken by the Tāvatiṃsa devas, the hermit Kāḷadevila quickly descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, entered King Suddhodana's palace, and sat on the prepared seat. After exchanging the usual friendly greetings with King Suddhodana, he said, "Great King, I have heard that a son has been born to you. I wish to see that son."

King Suddhodana then had the noble son, adorned with all ornaments, brought out and presented him to pay homage to the teacher, the hermit Kāḷadevila. At that very moment, the Bodhisatta Prince's feet rose up and rested majestically upon the tips of the hermit Kāḷadevila's matted hair, which were arranged like a flash of lightning shimmering against dark, black clouds.

It should be specially noted that for the Noble Bodhisatta in this, his final existence, there is no other person worthy of his homage. If those who did not know this fact had placed the head of the Bodhisatta in his final birth at the feet of the hermit, the hermit's head would have surely split into seven pieces.
57:
The hermit Kāḷadevila, truly seeing and reflecting upon such a wonderful and extraordinary display of the Bodhisatta's power, thought, "It is not proper for me to destroy myself," and decided to rise from his seat and pay homage to the Noble Bodhisatta with joined palms. Seeing such a wonder, the father, King Suddhodana, also paid homage to his own son.

## The Reason for Hermit Kāḷadevila's Smiling and Weeping
The hermit Kāḷadevila was a noble hermit who possessed the five direct knowledges and the eight attainments; he could recollect and see eighty aeons—forty aeons in the past and forty aeons in the future. (The detailed account of this hermit Kāḷadevila is presented in the Anudīpanī.)

While observing the major and minor marks of perfection on the Bodhisatta Prince, the hermit Kāḷadevila reflected, "Will he truly become a Buddha or not?" He then saw with his knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa), "This young prince will surely become a Buddha without a doubt." Delighted and joyful, thinking, "This prince is indeed a wonderful and supreme man," he smiled.

Then he reflected again, "Will I have the opportunity to behold this prince when he becomes a Buddha or not?" He realized, "I will not have the opportunity. I will pass away before this Bodhisatta becomes a Buddha and be reborn in the Formless Realm (Arūpa-bhūmi), where even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear, I would be unable to approach them to hear and understand the deathless Dhamma."
58:
Knowing this through his knowledge of the future, he wept with intense and sharp distress, thinking, "I will not get to behold such a wonderful man, endowed with the excellence of perfections and virtues, when he becomes a Buddha. Not being able to behold him as a Buddha is a great loss for me."

(In this context, the Formless Brahma Realm refers to a plane where there is no matter (rūpa) at all, but only mental phenomena (nāma), namely consciousness and mental factors. In that Formless Brahma Realm, worldlings (puthujjanas) with the three root-conditions (tihetu) who have attained formless absorptions, as well as Noble Ones (Ariyas)—Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners—who have attained those formless absorptions, are reborn. The Noble Ones who reach that realm do not descend to lower realms again. Having personally practiced the path to the Path and Fruit in previous lives in the lower Sensuous Blissful Realm or the Fine-material Brahma Realm, they are already clear about the practice of insight (vipassanā). Thus, even without hearing the Dhamma from others, they continue their practice in that Formless Realm, attaining the higher Paths and Fruits up to Arahatship, and thus end the cycle of suffering.

However, for those like the hermit Kāḷadevila, the hermit Āḷāra, and the hermit Udaka, who die as worldlings (tihetu-puthujjana) from the human world and are reborn in that Formless Realm, by the nature of that plane, there is no matter at all. Consequently, they lack the physical organs of the eye (cakkhu-pasāda) and the ear (sota-pasāda) to see the Buddha or hear the Dhamma.
59:
Even if Buddhas were to visit that Formless Realm to preach, they would be unable to see the Buddha or hear the Dhamma; therefore, Buddhas do not go to that Formless Realm to preach. Furthermore, worldlings cannot attain the Path and Fruit by any means if they do not receive the 'sound from another' (paratoghosa)—that is, hearing the Dhamma from others. Therefore, the hermit Kāḷadevila, the hermit Āḷāra, and the hermit Udaka, who were reborn in the Formless Realm as worldlings, are individuals who must drift in the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra). Kāḷadevila and Udaka reached the Realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, where they must remain for 84,000 great aeons, while the hermit Āḷāra reached the Realm of Nothingness, where he must remain for 60,000 great aeons. Even though a Buddha appears in the human world during this aeon, they have no opportunity for liberation.

In this regard, a question arises: "Could the hermit Kāḷadevila not have been reborn in a Fine-material Realm (Rūpa-bhūmi) if he had directed his mind toward it?" The answer is: Since the hermit Kāḷadevila was one who had fully attained all eight mundane absorptions (samāpatti), if he had the inclination to be reborn in a Fine-material Realm, he could have been reborn in any of the ten Fine-material Brahma realms up to Vehapphala, according to his wish.

If such a possibility existed, another question arises: "Why did he not direct his mind to one of the ten Fine-material realms that he preferred?" It should be said that he did not do so because he was not skilled in the procedure of directing the mind in that way. (The point is that a person who has attained all eight mundane absorptions...)
60:
(In the Rūpabhūmi and Arūpabhūmi, one can be reborn in the realm towards which one inclines one's mind. If the hermit Devala had also inclined his mind toward a lower Rūpabhūmi, he could have been reborn in that realm. In that case, he would have been able to see the Buddha as a Rūpa Brahma. However, it means that because he was not skilled or knowledgeable in the method of such inclination, he could not incline his mind to be reborn in a lower Rūpa realm.)

Even so, since the hermit Devala had suppressed his grief (domanassa) through meditative attainments (samāpatti), a question arises: why should he grieve and weep like this? The answer is that he grieved and wept precisely because the grief was only suppressed. To clarify further: only those defilements (kilesas) that have been completely eradicated by the Path (Magga) can no longer arise in an individual's mental continuum. Defilements that are merely suppressed by mundane meditative attainments can arise when they encounter a powerful cause. Therefore, the answer should be that the hermit Devala wept because his grief had not yet been eradicated by the Path, but only suppressed by meditative attainments.

Another question arises: since he felt grief and thus fell from his jhana while weeping, how could the hermit Devala attain rebirth in the Arūpa realm? The answer is that he could attain rebirth in the Arūpa realm because he regained it without much effort. To clarify further: when worldlings (puthujjanas) who have attained mundane meditative attainments encounter a powerful cause,
61:
the suppressed defilements arise and they fall from their meditative attainments. However, if they do not reach a state of grave transgression, they can regain those meditative attainments without much effort as soon as the momentum of the arisen defilements subsides. It is as if one could not even tell that "these people had fallen from jhana."

The point to note is: individuals like the hermit Devala who have attained the eight mundane meditative attainments can be reborn in any of the ten lower Rūpa Brahma realms or the four Arūpa Brahma realms toward which they incline their minds. If they do not incline their minds, they must be reborn in the realm corresponding to the highest of the mundane meditative attainments they have achieved, as that attainment takes the opportunity to produce its result. Furthermore, the knowledge that "if one inclines one's mind, one can be reborn in the desired realm of inclination" can only be known through the teachings of the Buddha within a Buddha's Dispensation (Sāsana). Outside the Dispensation, such penetrating insight is not possible. For this reason, the hermit Devala, not being a disciple of the Buddha within the Dispensation, did not know the method for such mental inclination. Had he known, he would have inclined his mind to be reborn in one of the ten Rūpa Brahma realms up to Vehapphala. If he had so inclined, he would have been reborn in that realm and had the opportunity to see the Buddha. Now, however, because he was neither knowledgeable nor skilled in that method, he failed to perform such mental inclination and was reborn in the highest Arūpa realm called Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana. Realizing he would lose the chance to see the Buddha, he felt anxious and distressed, and wept out of an impulse of anger (dosa-javana).
62:
(When he wept, the hermit Devala fell from his jhana. However, since he had not committed any grave misdeeds at all, as soon as the momentum of the defilement of anger subsided, he regained the eight mundane meditative attainments easily and without effort upon practicing the kasina preliminaries again, so much so that it was hardly noticeable that he had fallen from jhana. Therefore, it should be noted that when the great hermit Devala passed away, he was reborn in the Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana (Arūpa) Brahma realm, which is the result of the Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana jhana, the highest among the eight mundane meditative attainments.)

## The People's Inquiry

Seeing the great hermit Kāḷadevala laughing and then weeping, the people of the palace thought, "Our great hermit laughed just now and now he weeps again. How strange!" After considering this, they asked, "Noble hermit, is there any danger for our lord's son?" Then the hermit Devala replied, "There is no danger for this prince. This prince will certainly become a Buddha." When the people asked, "If that is so, why does the noble hermit weep?" the hermit Devala replied, "I will no longer have the opportunity to see such a Great Man endowed with these qualities when he becomes a Buddha. I weep out of personal sorrow and grief, thinking, 'What a great loss and misfortune it is for me!'"
63:
(In this regard, I have written according to the explanations in the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, Jātaka Commentary, and Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā. In some prose versions of the Buddhavaṃsa, it is written that when King Suddhodana asked, "At what age will the Bodhisatta renounce the world and become a Buddha?" the hermit Kāḷadevala replied, "He will become a Buddha at the age of thirty-five." This was written by taking the statement from the episode where the hermit Devala spoke to his nephew (his sister's son), the young Nālaka, saying, "Dear Nālaka, a son has been born in the palace of King Suddhodana; he is a sprout of a Buddha. He will become a Buddha after thirty-five years." King Suddhodana, however, could not even take pleasure in the answer that his son would become a Buddha. He did not wish to see his son become a Buddha; he only wished to see him become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). Therefore, he would by no means have asked, "At what age will the Bodhisatta renounce the world and become a Buddha?" For this reason, the ancient Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, Jātaka Commentary, and Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā did not write or explain this matter, and thus it is not written in this Buddhavaṃsa text either.)

## The Renunciation of the Young Nālaka

After giving this answer, the hermit Kāḷadevala reflected again, "Even if I myself will not see the Bodhisatta when he becomes a Buddha, will anyone among my relatives be able to see him or not?"
64:
He then saw that his nephew Nālaka, the son of his younger sister, would be able to see the Bodhisatta when he becomes a Buddha. He went to his sister's house, had the young Nālaka called, and said to Nālaka who came before him:

"Dear Nālaka, a son has been born in the palace of King Suddhodana; he is a sprout of a Buddha. When that son passes the age of thirty-five, he will become a Buddha, renowned in the world. You are one who is worthy of seeing that Buddha. Therefore, my nephew, renounce the world this very day!"

Thus he spoke and encouraged him.

Although the young Nālaka was a youth born into a family of parents possessing eighty-seven crores of wealth, he believed, reflected, and decided, "My maternal uncle would not encourage me in something that is not beneficial; he encourages me in this way only because it is truly beneficial." At that very moment, he had robes and an alms-bowl brought from the market, shaved his hair and beard, donned the robes, and said:

"My renunciation is dedicated to the Blessed One, the most excellent person in the world." (I renounce the world dedicated to the Blessed One who will surely be enlightened.)
65:
Uttering these words, he faced towards the palace of Kapilavatthu where the Bodhisatta resided, paid homage with the five-point prostration with joined palms, placed his bowl in its bag, slung it over his shoulder, and entered the Himalayan forest. There he awaited the Buddha, striving and exerting himself in the practice of a recluse.

(In connection with this episode of the Bodhisatta's birth, the lineage and history of the Bodhisatta, as well as the founding and development of Kapilavatthu, are described in the Anudīpanī.)

## The Ceremony of Head-Washing and Naming
## Reading the Marks and Signs

On the fifth day after the birth of the Bodhisatta, the father, King Suddhodana, had the ceremony of washing the Bodhisatta's head performed. Intending to name him, he had his palace smeared and perfumed with the powders of four types of perfumes: tagara, clove, saffron (kunkuma), and pann-nyo. He had five kinds of flowers scattered everywhere: nela-grass, rice-grains, mustard seeds, jasmine buds, and parched rice. He ordered the cooking of pure milk-rice unmixed with water. He invited one hundred and eight learned Brahmins who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas, seated them in excellent and clean places prepared within the palace, and served them delicious and excellent milk-rice.

(In this passage, the enumeration of the four types of perfumes is given according to the explanations in the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa-ṭīkā on the Sekha Sutta and the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta-ṭīkā. (a) In the Mahāsudassana Sutta-ṭīkā, kamyin perfume is included instead of kunkuma
66:
counted and shown. (b) In the old Jātaka-ṭīkā, the opening of the Avidūre-nidāna, etc., four types are shown: black sandalwood, tagara, camphor, and sandalwood essence. (c) In the Magadha Abhidhāna text, four types are shown: kunkuma, clove, tagara, and kamyin. (d) In the Saḷāyatana Saṃyutta-ṭīkā, the opening of the sixth sutta of the Āsīvisa-vagga, four types are shown: kunkuma, kamyin, clove, and pann-nyo. (e) In the Mālālaṅkāra-vatthu, four types are shown: sal, mahā-tagara, camphor essence, and sandalwood essence. (f) In the Jinatthapakāsanī, four types are shown: agaru, tagara, camphor, and sandalwood.)

After serving them thus, the King performed great and excellent offerings and honors. From among those one hundred and eight learned Brahmins, he selected eight Brahmins and had them read the marks of the Bodhisatta and predict what would happen.

Among those eight selected learned Brahmins—the Brahmin named Rāma, the Brahmin named Dhaja, the Brahmin named Lakkhaṇa, the Brahmin named Jotimanta, the Brahmin named Yañña, the Brahmin named Subhoja, and the Brahmin named Suyāma—these seven learned Brahmins, after examining the marks of the Bodhisatta, raised two fingers each and made a non-definitive prediction with two possibilities: "The lord's son who is endowed with these marks, if he lives the household life, will become a Universal Monarch, a ruler of the four continents; if he renounces the world, he will become a Buddha."

The Brahmin named Sudatta, of the Koṇḍañña clan, who was the youngest among those seven learned Brahmins, carefully and thoroughly examined the Bodhisatta's possession of all the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa) and thought, "For this lord's son to live the household life..."
67:
"There is no other possibility; he will certainly become a Buddha who breaks open the roof of defilements," he declared, raising only one finger and making a definitive decision with a single statement.
(In this regard, the young Brahmin Sudatta of the Koṇḍañña clan was a Pacchimabhavika—one in his final birth—who had cultivated perfections and meritorious deeds to reach the Fruit of Arahatship in this very life. Therefore, he surpassed the seven elder Brahmins in the power of wisdom and could decisively perceive the certain destiny of the Bodhisatta, saying, "This noble prince, endowed with these marks, will surely become a Buddha." Thus, he raised only one finger and interpreted the signs boldly and clearly.)
All the learned Brahmins accepted this interpretation made by the young Brahmin Sudatta of the Koṇḍañña clan, who raised one finger.
## The Treatise on the Marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa)
The ability of these Brahmins to recognize and interpret the marks of a Great Man, such as a Buddha, is because, during the eras when a Buddha is about to appear, the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas insert the details of the Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa (the marks of one who will become a Buddha) into the Vedic texts so that they can be recognized. They come to the human world in the guise of Brahmin teachers and, with the intention that "those with mature merit and wisdom will know these," they teach these Vedic texts containing the Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa to their disciples. Therefore, these Brahmins were able to clearly perceive, reflect upon, and interpret these marks of a Buddha.
68:
They were able to clearly perceive, reflect upon, and interpret these Marks of a Great Man.
## The Thirty-two Marks of a Great Man
There are thirty-two major marks by which a Great Man (a Bodhisatta) is recognized. These thirty-two are:
1. He has level feet, so that he sets his foot down evenly on the ground and lifts it up evenly.
2. On the soles of both his feet, there are wheels with a thousand spokes, with rims and hubs, complete in every respect with one hundred and eight auspicious signs.
3. He has long heels.
4. He has long fingers and toes.
5. He has soft and tender hands and feet.
6. He has net-like (jāla) fingers and toes, which are even and closely set like golden turned pillars at a palace gate.
7. He has high ankles that are not covered by dust.
69: 8. He has calves like those of an antelope (eṇī). 9. Standing, without bending his body, he can touch and rub both knees with both palms. 10. His male organ is concealed in a sheath, like that of a noble Chaddanta elephant. 11. He has a golden-hued complexion, like the color of pure gold. 12. He has smooth skin (so smooth that dust and dirt cannot adhere to it). 13. Each hair of his body grows singly, one in each pore. 14. His body hairs point upwards, their tips curling at the top as if looking up at his face. 15. He has a straight body, like that of a Brahma. 16. He has the seven convexities (fullness of flesh at the backs of the two hands, the backs of the two feet, the two shoulders, and the trunk/nape of the neck). 17. He has the front half of his body like that of a lion.
70: 18. He has a solid back, like a golden slab, full from the waist to the neck without any visible furrow. 19. His body is proportionate like a banyan tree; his height is equal to his arm span. 20. He has a neck that is both even and round. 21. He has seven thousand nerves of taste, with their tips meeting at the throat, capable of spreading even a tiny amount of flavor (the size of a sesame seed) throughout his entire body. 22. He has a jaw like that of a lion (as if about to smile). 23. He has forty teeth. 24. He has even teeth. 25. He has teeth without gaps, closely set. 26. He has four white canines that shine brilliantly like the morning star. 27. He has a tongue that is long, soft, and broad.
71:
28. He has a voice like that of Brahma, endowed with eight qualities.
29. He has eyes that are deep blue and clear.
30. He has eyelashes like those of a newborn calf, very soft and youthful.
31. Between his eyebrows, there grows a hair-tuft (uṇṇaloma), which is soft and white.
32. His forehead is like a golden turban (uṇhīsa-sīso), as if a golden frontlet were naturally placed upon it.
These are the thirty-two Marks of a Great Man. (Extracted from the Mahāpadāna Sutta and Lakkhaṇa Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya, and the Brahmāyu Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya.)
## The Meaning and Nature of the Thirty-two Marks
(1) Regarding the mark of having level feet that touch the ground evenly when stepping:
When other people place their feet on the ground, either the toes, the heel, or one side of the sole touches the ground first, while the middle part does not touch and remains separate. When they lift their feet from the ground, they also tend to lift either the toes, the heel, or one side of the sole first.
72: For the Great Man, the Bodhisatta, when he places his feet on the ground, they touch the ground evenly all at once, just as soft golden sandals would touch a level surface. When he lifts his feet, they also rise all at once. If the Great Bodhisatta wishes to step on uneven ground, such as pits, hollows, ravines, or cliffs, at that very moment, the uneven ground fills up like a leather bag filled with air, rising to become level like the face of a drum. Even if he wishes to step far away, even the King of Mountains, Mount Meru, comes under his sole in an instant. (2) Regarding the mark of having one hundred and eight auspicious signs on the soles of both feet along with the wheel (cakka) with a thousand spokes, rims, and hubs: The one hundred and eight signs are: (1) Spear, (2) Auspicious Mansion, (3) Jasmine flower, (4) Three folds of the neck, (5) Flower garland, (6) Tray of food, (7) Golden throne, (8) Goad, (9) Palace, (10) Archway. (11) White umbrella, (12) Sword, (13) Palm-leaf fan, (14) Peacock-feather fan, (15) Turban.
