74:
The verse (linga) for worshipping the Buddha's footprints containing the one hundred and eight marks was carefully examined and written in the first volume of the Guḷhatthadīpanī by the Taungkhwin Sāsanabaing Sayadaw as follows:
To the incomparable and virtuous Muni Sakya Gautama, on his famous and noble soles, the one hundred and eight marks appear clearly; let us examine and count them starting from... (1-2) The great spear and the noble house, (3) the three-petaled fragrant jasmine, (4) the three lines on the neck, (5) the shining head ornament, (6) the pure white turban and the prepared table, (7) the circular pedestal, (8-9) the goad and the palace, (10) the high gateway, (11-12) the bright white umbrella and the sword, (13) the palm-leaf fan, (14) the shining peacock-feather fan, (15) the golden frontlet, (16) the precious gems, (17) the shining alms bowl, (18) the jasmine flower garland, (19-23) the five kinds of beautiful lotuses, (24) the full pot, (25) the full bowl, (26) the great ocean, (27) the noble Cakkavāḷa mountains, (28) the Himavanta forest, (29) Mount Meru, (30-31) the bright Sun and Moon, (32) the constellations, (33-36) the four great islands and their surrounding small islands, (37) the glorious Universal Monarch, (38) the white conch with a right-hand spiral, (39) the pair of golden fish, (40) the wheel weapon, (41-47) the seven great rivers (Ganga), (48-54) the seven mountain ranges, (55-61) the seven great lakes, (62) the Garuda king, (63) the crocodile dwelling in the river, (64) the long banner, (65) the small banner, (66) the royal palanquin, (67) the golden yak-tail whisk, (68) the silver mountain Kelāsa, (69-70) the Lion and the Tiger, (71) the Valāhaka horse, (72) the noble Uposatha and Chaddanta elephants, (73) the Naga king named Vāsukī, (74) the golden hamsa, (75) the noble bull Usabha, (76) the Erāvaṇa elephant, (77) the golden Makara, (78) the shining golden boat, (79) the supreme Brahma, (80) the cow with her calf, (81) the beloved Kinnara and Kinnarī, (82) the sweet-voiced Karavīka bird, (83-84) the Peacock and the Crane, (85) the Cakravāka bird...
75:
(86) Pair of Jīvajīvaka birds, (87-92) Six Deva realms of the sensual sphere, (93-108) Sixteen Brahma realms; all these are present, surrounding the noble soles. Even if Sakka or Brahma from the highest heavens were to draw them, how could they compare? To the incomparable and supreme one of the three worlds, whose soles shine with the brilliance of gems, pure and red, with a thousand spokes, shining like gold, rimmed with coral, and radiant like dark gems—I pay homage with deep devotion. May this merit lead directly to the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna.

(3) Regarding the characteristic of having long heels (āyatapaṇhi):

This means having heels that are full and rounded. To clarify—in other people, the front part of the foot is long. The ankle bone, called the 'horse-head' (malleolus), is situated directly above the heel; thus, the heel appears as if it were shifted or jointed. In the Great Man, the Bodhisatta, it is not so. If the sole is divided into four parts, the first two parts are the front of the foot. The ankle bone is situated above the third part. In the fourth part at the rear, the heel is situated like a rounded marble on a red carpet, as if polished with a lathe. (In ordinary people, the ankle bone is at the top of the heel, making the heel joint look awkward and unattractive. In the Bodhisatta, the sole is divided into four parts, and the ankle bone is above the third part, so the heel appears rounded and prominent on the fourth part of the red-skinned sole, thus it is called 'long heels' and is beautiful.)
76:
(4) Regarding the characteristic of having long fingers and toes (dīghanguli):

In other people, some fingers and toes are long while others are short; they are uneven in thickness and length. In the Great Man, the Bodhisatta, it is not so. The fingers and toes are both long and even. They are thick at the base and gradually taper towards the tips. They are like rods of realgar (manosilā) that have been kneaded with oily resin and made perfectly round and straight.

(5) Regarding the characteristic of having soft and tender palms and soles (mudutalunahatthapāda):

Like a layer of cotton wool that has been carded a hundred times and dipped in clear ghee, the Bodhisatta's palms and soles are soft and tender. Just as in youth, they remain soft, tender, and youthful even in old age without changing.

(6) Regarding the characteristic of having fingers and toes that are even and closely spaced like golden lathed pillars (jālī) set in a palace window:

The four fingers (excluding the thumb) and the five toes of the Bodhisatta are not of unequal length but are of equal proportion. (If the reader holds up their right palm now, they will see that the fingers are of unequal length.)
77:
In the Bodhisatta prince, the eight fingers of both hands and the ten toes of both feet are equal in proportion. Therefore, the barley-grain marks (yava) at each joint are not high or low but are aligned as if they were connected through and through. The grain-like marks are also like lathed pillars set in perfect alignment. Thus, the Bodhisatta's fingers and toes resemble a golden lattice window crafted by master carpenters.

(7) Regarding the characteristic of having high ankles (ussankhapāda):

In other people, the ankles are situated close to the top of the foot. Because they are so closely connected, their feet are like they are bound with leeches, fish, or stumps, and they cannot rotate as they wish. Because they cannot rotate freely, the soles of their feet are not clearly visible when they walk.

In the Great Man, the Bodhisatta, it is not so. The ankle bones are situated about two or three finger-breadths above the top of the foot, like the neck of a water pot. Therefore, the upper part of the Bodhisatta's body from the navel upwards remains steady like a golden statue placed on a boat, while only the lower part moves. The soles of the feet rotate easily. People standing and watching from the front, back, left, or right can clearly see the surface of the soles.
78:
(When elephants walk, the soles can only be seen from behind; when the Bodhisatta walks, the soles can be seen from all four directions: front, back, left, and right.)

(8) Regarding the characteristic of having calves like those of an antelope (eṇijaṅgha):

(The reader should feel their own calf. They will find the bone hard in the front and the muscles hanging to one side in the back.) In the Great Man, the Bodhisatta, it is not so. Like the husks of rice or barley, the muscles are evenly distributed all around, surrounding the calf bone, and the calves are rounded and beautiful. They are like the calves of the antelope called Eṇī.

(9) Regarding the characteristic of being able to touch both kneecaps with both palms while standing without bending the body (thitako va anonamanto...):

Other people may be hunched, or they may be bow-legged, or both. In hunched people, the upper body is shorter than the lower body, so their limbs are not well-proportioned. In bow-legged people, the lower body is shorter than the upper body,
79:
so their limbs are not well-proportioned. (Hunched people are short in the upper part, and bow-legged people are short in the lower part.) Because of such disproportionate limbs, they cannot touch their knees without bending.

In the Great Man, the Bodhisatta, it is not so. The upper body is not hunched, and the lower body is not short; both the upper and lower parts of the body are well-proportioned and perfectly balanced. Therefore, even while standing, he can touch and rub both kneecaps with both palms without bending his body.

(10) Regarding the characteristic of having the male organ concealed in a sheath like that of a noble Chaddanta elephant (kosohitavatthaguyha):

Like the male organs of a noble bull or a noble elephant, the Bodhisatta's male organ is covered by a sheath resembling a golden lotus petal. It means the organ is well-secured and covered, as if placed in a perfectly tailored bag of wool, velvet, or broadcloth.

(11) Regarding the characteristic of having skin the color of pure Singī gold (suvaṇṇavaṇṇa):

Like a golden statue that has been kneaded with vermilion powder, polished with a wooden tusk, and smoothed with red lacquer, his skin is of a solid, smooth, and delicate natural golden hue.
80:
(In this characteristic, although the Pali and Commentaries use the words 'suvaṇṇa' and 'kañcana' which mean ordinary gold, the noble teachers translate it as 'like Singī gold' because in the verses recited by Sakka disguised as a youth when the Buddha entered Rājagaha for alms, it is mentioned as 'singīnikkhasuvaṇṇo' (having the color of pure Singī gold). Furthermore, among the types of gold used by humans, Rasaviddha gold is superior to Yuttika gold; Ākaruppanna gold is superior to that; the gold used by Devas is superior to that; among Deva gold, Sātakumbha gold is superior to Cāmīkara gold; Jambunada gold is superior to that; and Singī gold is superior to that (as mentioned in the Vimānavatthu Commentary, the explanation of the first Pīṭhavimāna, the Terasakaṇḍa Ṭīkā, the Mahāvagga Mahākhandhaka Bimbisārasamāgama section, etc.). Therefore, it is translated using the most precious gold.)

(12) Regarding the characteristic of having smooth and delicate skin (sukhumacchavi):

Because the skin of the Blessed One is so delicate and smooth, neither fine dust nor coarse dust can adhere to his body. Just as a drop of water falling on a lotus leaf cannot remain there but must slide off, so any dust that reaches the body of the Blessed One falls away.
81:
81
All dust and impurities simply slide off and fall away from His body.

If it is asked why, despite being so clean and free from dust, the Blessed One still performs the washing of His hands and feet and the bathing of His body: the Buddha performs these acts of washing and bathing to regulate the bodily elements of heat and cold, to increase the merit and benefits for those who offer the water, and to set a standard of discipline and practice for His disciples, the bhikkhus, so that they may respectfully follow the conduct of entering the monastery only after cleaning their hands and feet as He does.

(13) Regarding the characteristic of having only one hair growing in each pore (Ekekaloma-lakkhaሗa):
While other people may have two or three hairs growing from a single pore, it is not so for the Bodhisatta. In each and every pore, only a single hair grows.

(14) Regarding the characteristic of having body hairs that point upwards, as if looking up to pay homage to His face (Uddhaggaloma-lakkhaሗa):
The hairs growing singly from each pore over the entire body of the Great Being are blue-black in color, like the hue of dark collyrium (a!jana).
82:
82
Those body hairs are curled to the right in three turns. They stand pointing upwards, facing the golden countenance which possesses a glory as beautiful as a newly blossomed lotus flower.

(15) Regarding the characteristic of having a body as straight as that of a Mahābrahmā (Brahmujugatta-lakkhaሗa):
The body of a Mahābrahmā does not lean or tilt even slightly to the front, back, or either side, but rises straight upwards. Similarly, the body of the Bodhisatta rises straight and upright. It is a body that rises straight and smooth, like a statue cast from pure refined gold.

Ordinary people, for the most part, tend to lean or bend at three places: the nape of the neck, the waist, or the knees. Among these three, if they bend at the waist, they tend to protrude. If they bend at the neck and knees, they tend to stoop forward. Some very tall people tend to lean to either the left or right side. Because of such leaning or bending at one of these three places, some people naturally lean backwards and have faces tilted upwards as if they were observing and counting the stars in the sky. Others lean forward and have downward-looking faces, as if they were contemplating the characteristics of the great earth.
83:
83
Some people, due to a lack of flesh and blood, are as thin and gaunt as a stake or a rod.

The Great Being, however, is not like that. Because His body rises straight upwards, He is like a golden gatepost (toraሗa) erected at the entrance of a celestial city.

In this matter, certain marks of a Great Man, such as having a body as straight and tall as a Brahmā, are not yet fully and clearly visible to ordinary people during His infancy immediately after birth from His mother's womb. In truth, it is by seeing these signs, features, and conditions at the time of birth that the court Brahmins, who are highly proficient in the Suddhāvāsa Brahma mantras and Vedic lore, use their wisdom to predict: "When He reaches maturity, these characteristics, such as the straight and tall body like a Brahmā, will become clearly manifest for all to see." They calculate and interpret the signs as if they were already fully apparent. (Similarly, the marks such as having forty teeth and the teeth being without gaps
84:
84
are not yet actually visible in the newborn Bodhisatta, but the Brahmins, through their Vedic knowledge of the Suddhāvāsa Brahma mantras, know for certain they will appear in due time and thus make their predictions.)

(16) Regarding the characteristic of having the seven surfaces full and rounded (Sattussada-lakkhaሗa), namely: the backs of the two feet, the backs of the two hands, the two shoulders, and the trunk of the neck:
In other people, the veins on the backs of the feet and hands appear prominently like a net. The joints of the bones are visible at the shoulders and the neck. Therefore, when others see such people, they appear like petas (hungry ghosts) living in cemeteries, with bony shoulders, protruding neck bones, and prominent veins, looking unsightly.

The Great Being, however, is not like that. He has full flesh in the seven mentioned places. Although called "full," it is not an unsightly swelling of flesh; it is full only to the extent that veins are not prominent, bone joints do not protrude, and it is aesthetically pleasing. Thus, the Bodhisatta has no protruding veins on the backs of His hands and feet, nor are the bones prominent at His shoulders and neck. He has a neck that is like a well-polished golden muruja drum. Because of the fullness and beauty of these seven places, to the eyes of those who behold Him, He appears
85:
85
like a well-carved stone statue or a wonderfully designed painting.

(17) Regarding the characteristic of having a torso like the front half of a lion (Sġhapubbaddhakāya-lakkhaሗa):
The front part of a lion king's body is full and broad, but the hind part is not. Since the hind part of a lion is not full, it is not intended for comparison here. Only the front part of the body is taken as a metaphor because of its fullness and breadth. Therefore, both the upper and lower parts of the Great Being's torso are as full and broad as the front part of a lion king. Even though this comparison is made, the Bodhisatta's body does not have the ungraceful shapes found in a lion's body, such as certain parts being bent, raised, sunken, or having lumps of flesh. In fact, the various parts of His body are long where they should be long, short where they should be short, plump where they should be plump, slender where they should be slender, broad where they should be broad, and rounded where they should be rounded, being most graceful and magnificent. No artist of any science nor any powerful being can create or fashion a physical form equal to that of this Great Being.

(18) Regarding the characteristic of having a back that is full and flat like a golden slab, with no furrow visible from the waist up to the neck (Citantaraቃsa-lakkhaሗa):
86:
86
In short, this means the back is exceptionally full and beautiful. The flesh over the ribs, the flesh on both sides of the back, and the flesh in the middle of the back—these three areas of flesh are well-filled and beautiful from the waist up to the neck.

The backs of other people appear as if divided into two halves. The central spine and the flesh around it are sunken or hollowed. Or they may be crooked, or they may protrude and be humped. The flesh on either side of the spine appears like the halves of a split bamboo placed face down. The flesh over the ribs at the edges of the back is also thin.

The Great Being, however, is not like that. The flesh over the ribs on both sides, the flesh below the shoulder blades, and the flesh over the central spine are all well-filled from the waist to the neck, with no visible furrow or indentation. Therefore, He has a back that is full with layers of flesh, like a golden slab set upright.

(19) Regarding the characteristic of having a body as perfectly proportioned as a banyan tree, where the height is equal to the arm span (Nigrodhaparimaሗሇala-lakkhaሗa):
87:
87
Just as a banyan tree with a trunk and branches of fifty or a hundred cubits has a height equal to its lateral spread, so too the Bodhisatta's height and His arm span are equal in measure (each being four cubits of His own). (For others, the arm span and height are mostly unequal.)

(20) Regarding the characteristic of having a neck that is both even and well-rounded (Vaሗሇakkhandha-lakkhaሗa):
Some people have long necks like a crane. Some have crooked necks like a heron. Some have thick, swollen, and large necks like a pig. When such people speak, the veins in their necks stand out like a net. Their voices come out weak and thin.

The neck of the Great Being is like a well-rounded golden muruja drum. When He speaks, the network of veins does not stand out or appear. His voice is great and resonant, like the sound of thunder or the booming of a muruja drum.

(21) Regarding the characteristic of having seven thousand taste nerves (rasaharaሗĩ) which can spread even a tiny amount of flavor, the size of a sesame seed, throughout the entire body, with their ends meeting and encircling the throat (Rasaggasaggĩ-lakkhaሗa):
88: The seven thousand taste nerves (rasaharaṇī) of the Great Being are well-situated, with their tips turned upwards and converging at the throat, as if waiting to distribute the essence of any food consumed throughout the entire body. Even a tiny amount of food, the size of a sesame seed, once placed on the tip of the tongue and swallowed, spreads and permeates the whole body. This is why, during the six years of his great austerities (dukkharacariyā), the Great Being was able to sustain his physical body with just a single grain of rice or a handful of broth from boiled black grams. In other people, this is not the case; the nutritional essence of the food they eat cannot spread throughout the whole body, and thus they are prone to many diseases. (22) Regarding the characteristic of having a jaw like that of a lion (sīhahanu), which seems to hint at a smile: This comparison is intended only for the lower part of a lion's jaw. A lion's jaw is full only in the lower part, not the upper. However, the Great Being's jaw is full and fleshy in both the upper and lower parts, like the lower jaw of a lion. It resembles the shape of the moon on the twelfth day of the waxing fortnight. (23) Regarding the characteristic of having exactly forty teeth (cattālīsadanta)...
89: This means he has exactly forty teeth, twenty in the upper jaw and twenty in the lower jaw. Even among other people who are said to have a full set of teeth, there are only thirty-two teeth in total, upper and lower combined. The Great Being, however, possesses forty teeth, with twenty in the upper and twenty in the lower jaw, surpassing the usual thirty-two. (24) The characteristic of having even teeth (samadanta). (25) The characteristic of having teeth without gaps (avivara/aviraḷadanta). (26) The characteristic of having four fangs (dāṭha) that are extremely pure and white, shining like the morning star (osadhī-tārakā). Regarding these: In other people, some teeth are high and some are low, making them uneven. The Great Being, however, has teeth as even as a conch shell sliced with a saw. In other people, the teeth are separated and gapped like those of a crocodile. Therefore, when they eat fish or meat, fragments of food get stuck and packed between their teeth. The Great Being's teeth are not like that; they are set closely together like a row of diamonds (vajira) on a gold or coral plate.
90: They stand closely and perfectly aligned like a row of diamonds. In other people, some fangs may be decayed, and thus some are black or discolored. The four fangs of the Great Being, however, are exceedingly pure and white; they possess a particularly beautiful and radiant luster that outshines even the light of the morning star. (In this regard, one might ask: Since the newborn Great Being did not yet have teeth, how did the wise Brahmins know about these characteristics related to the teeth? The answer is: The wise Brahmins who read the marks observed the positions and features where the teeth would appear according to their Buddhamanta Brahmanical Vedas, and they predicted them as if they were already present, knowing they would certainly appear when he reached maturity.) (To provide some understanding of the Mahāpurisa Lakkhaṇa texts, I shall quote from the Ambaṭṭha Sutta Commentary and others: When the time for a Buddha's appearance draws near, the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās insert the knowledge of the Great Being's characteristics into the Vedas. They teach these Vedas in the guise of Great Brahmin teachers, saying, 'These are called the Buddha-Vedas.')
91: In those Buddha-Vedas (Buddhamanta), the Mahāpurisa Lakkhaṇa texts fully describe the marks of one who will become a Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, the Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Disciples, the Buddha's mother, the Buddha's father, the noble attendant, and a Cakkavatti King. Therefore, in ancient times, the Great Man's characteristics were clearly and directly present in the Vedas. In the period after the Buddha's Parinibbāna, just as the light from the sun gradually disappears after sunset, these Mahāpurisa Lakkhaṇa texts, which arose due to the glory and power of the Buddhas, also gradually disappeared, starting from one or two verses. (27) Regarding the characteristic of having a long, soft, and broad tongue (pahūtajivha): In other people, the tongue may be thick, small, short, rough, or uneven. The Great Being's tongue is not like that. It is extremely soft, long, broad, and beautiful in color. To make this clear: When the Great Being became the Buddha, since the tongue remained inside the mouth, its characteristics could not be easily seen. To remove the doubts of those like the youth Ambaṭṭha and the youth Uttara who came to examine this mark...
92: ...so that they might be free from doubt, because his tongue was so soft, he rolled and curled it like a hard needle (or like a rolled-up lottery slip) and showed them by touching both his nostrils with his tongue. Because it was very long, he showed them by touching both his ear canals with his tongue. Because it was broad, he showed them by covering his entire forehead up to the hairline with his tongue. (One can know by practical experiment that an ordinary person's tongue cannot extend more than an inch outside the mouth.) (28) Regarding the characteristic of having a voice like that of the Brahmā (brahmassara), endowed with eight qualities: Other people have broken voices, cracked voices, or unpleasant voices like that of a crow. The Great Being is not like that; he is endowed with a voice like that of the Great Brahmā. To make this clear: The voice of the Brahmā is pure because it is not mixed with or oppressed by bile or phlegm. For the Great Being, the meritorious deeds he fulfilled and accumulated purified the vocal organs such as the throat and palate. Because the vocal organs are pure, the voice that arises from the navel is pure. It arises endowed with eight qualities. These eight qualities are: 1. Being clear, 2. Being intelligible, 3. Being sweet, 4. Being pleasant to hear,
93: 5. Being full (resonant), 6. Being indistinct (not scattering outside the audience), 7. Being deep (not shallow, with strong resonance), 8. Being resonant—these are the eight. The extraordinary and wonderful nature of this voice is that it is hundreds and thousands of times sweeter and more melodious than the voice of the Karavīka bird. To make this clear: The voice of the Karavīka bird is very smooth, deep, long, gentle, and melodious. It is full and delightful. When these Karavīka birds perch on an upper branch of a tree and sing, and then move to a lower branch, they can listen to the echo of the song they sang while on the upper branch. It is that gentle, melodious, and full. When the Karavīka bird-king pecks a sweet ripe mango with its beak, drinks the flowing juice, flaps its wings, and sings, the four-legged animals become as if intoxicated by the Karavīka bird-king's voice (like those who lose consciousness from alcohol) and strive to frolic with great joy. Even four-legged animals that have reached their grazing grounds and are in the middle of chewing grass in their mouths forget the food and drop it...
94: ...and remain standing still, listening only to the song of the Karavīka bird-king. Small animals like deer, which are running in fear of death from predators like lions, leopards, and tigers, do not lift the feet they have put down, nor do they put down the feet they have lifted; they do not even remember the danger of death and remain standing still, listening only to the song of the Karavīka bird-king. The predators like lions, leopards, and tigers that were chasing them to catch and eat them likewise do not remember their prey and remain standing still, listening only to the song of the Karavīka bird-king. Birds flying in the sky also stop with their wings spread and listen. Fish dwelling in the water stay still without moving their fins and listen only to the song of the Karavīka bird-king. (From the Buddhavamsa Commentary, page 82.) (The story of Queen Asandhimittā and the voice of the Karavīka bird-king should be looked for in the Anudīpanī.) (29) Regarding the characteristic of having deep blue eyes (abhinīlanetta): This does not mean that every part of the Great Being's eyes is dark blue. It is said he has deep blue eyes based on the primary color. In fact, the eyes of the Great Being have a very pure blue color, like the color of the flax flower (ummapuppha), in the parts that should be blue. In the parts that should be golden, they have a golden color like the mahāleghā flower. In the parts that should be red...
95:
In certain areas, they are endowed with a crimson hue, similar to the color of the Bandhujīvaka flower. In areas where they should be white, they are endowed with a brilliant white color, like the radiance of the morning star. In areas where they should be black, they are endowed with a deep black color, like the color of black beads. The eyes of the Great Being are like ruby-encrusted lion-windows (lattice windows) opened in a golden mansion. (According to the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā, they are like ruby-encrusted lion-windows set into a golden wall.)

(30) Regarding the mark of having eyelashes as soft and delicate as those of a newborn calf:
In the Pāḷi Canon, this mark is preached as “Gopakhuma-lakkhaṇa.” The Pāḷi term “Gopakhuma” refers to the entire eye, including the eyelids. Among various types of cattle, the eyes of black calves tend to be thick and dull, whereas the eyes of red calves are particularly clear and bright. Here, in the context of the Gopakhuma mark, it means having eyes like those of a newborn red calf. The eyes of other people are often imperfect; some have bulging eyes like those of an elephant, a rat, or a crow, while others have sunken eyes with dark circles. The eyes of the Great Being are not like that; they are like well-polished rubies, smooth and elegant, with delicate, fresh, and dark eyelashes growing in neat rows.
96:
They exist in such a manner. (This mark uses the eyelashes as a part to represent the entire eye; it means having eyes and eye-sockets that are clear and beautiful like well-polished rubies, neither bulging nor sunken, with dark, fresh, and delicate eyelashes growing in neat rows, just like those of a newborn red calf.)

(31) Regarding the mark of the Uṇṇaloma hair-tuft growing in the middle of the two eyebrows:
This sacred hair-tuft is gracefully situated in the very center between the two eyebrows, directly above the bridge of the nose, in the middle of the forehead. It is as pure all around as the morning star. It is exceedingly soft, like a tuft of cotton that has been carded a hundred times and dipped in clear clarified butter. It is as white as the silk-cotton or the white climber. When this sacred hair is pulled from the tip and stretched, it is about two cubits long; when released, it naturally curls to the right, with its tip pointing upwards. It is as beautiful as a silver star set on a golden plate, or a stream of milk flowing from a golden pot, or the morning star in the sky reflecting the dawn light, possessing a splendor that can attract and inspire faith in the hearts of those who behold it.

(32) Regarding the mark of having a fleshy protuberance (Uṇhīsa) on the forehead, as if a golden diadem were naturally arranged there:
97:
This means having a perfect forehead and a perfect head. To elaborate:

## The Forehead
In the Great Being, a layer of flesh rises from the edge of the right ear, covers the entire forehead, and descends to end at the edge of the left ear. This fleshy diadem (Uṇhīsa) is exceedingly beautiful, being delicate, golden in color, radiant, and spreading across the forehead, much like the diadem plates worn by kings on their foreheads. It is because they saw this mark of the fleshy diadem on the Great Being's forehead that kings (who do not naturally possess such a fleshy layer) created and used the royal ornament known as the diadem (Uṇhīsa). (This is the explanation of the perfection of the forehead.)

## The Head
The head of the Great Being is perfect and beautiful from all sides. Other people do not possess a head mark as complete as that of the Great Being. Some people have heads that are split into two like a monkey's head. Some have heads that appear to have cracks or fissures. Some, because they have very little flesh on their heads,
98:
have heads that look like bone covered only by skin. Some have uneven heads like a gourd. Some have heads that hook backward or protrude at the back (occipital protrusion). The Great Being is not like that; His head is perfect all around, like a golden sphere turned on a lathe, crafted beautifully and proportionately.

(This 32nd mark is preached in the Pāḷi as “Uṇhīsasīso.” This Pāḷi can be interpreted in two ways: (a) having a head as if entwined and encircled by a fleshy diadem, and (b) having a head as round and beautiful as a turban arranged by a very skillful person. Therefore, the meaning is described in two ways: the perfection and beauty of the forehead, and the perfection and beauty of the head.)

(The kamma and other causes for obtaining these thirty-two major marks are specifically described in the Anudīpanī.)

## The explanation of the thirty-two major marks is finished.
99:
## The Eighty Minor Marks
The Great Being, the Superior Man, also obtained the eighty minor marks called the Asīti-anubyañjana, which are the attendants to the thirty-two major marks of a Great Man already mentioned. ## The Satapuñña Marks
The various major and minor marks that have been described are also called the Satapuñña marks (Marks of a Hundred Merits). In the infinite world-systems of the universe, all beings perform various kinds of wholesome deeds many times; even one such kind of accumulated wholesome deed, the Great Bodhisatta alone performed a hundred times over. The merit of that Bodhisatta is called 'Satapuñña', and it is meant that because of those Satapuñña merits, he obtained the results consisting of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks previously described.
## Naming as Siddhattha
In this manner, the learned Brahmins, after thoroughly examining and contemplating the major and minor marks of the Great Bodhisatta, predicted and reported that "He will surely become a Buddha." Thereafter, when they consulted and deliberated on the name to be given to the young Bodhisatta, they considered the omen and etymological reason that he would fulfill and accomplish the welfare and interests of the entire world.
108:
Based on that, they conferred the name "Siddhattha."
## About the Group of Five Monks (Pañcavaggī)
(In this matter, regarding the account of the five monks of the Group of Five headed by the Venerable Koṇḍañña, the explanation in the Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā and the explanations in the Jātaka Commentary and Buddhavamsa Commentary are not the same. Therefore, I shall first present the account of the five monks of the Group of Five by interpolating the explanations from those Ṭīkā and Commentaries.)
## The Account from the Sāratthadīpanī Vinaya-ṭīkā
At the time the young Bodhisatta was born, among the eight selected learned Brahmins who were experts in reading marks—namely, Rāma the Brahmin, Dhaja the Brahmin, Lakkhaṇa the Brahmin, Manti the Brahmin, Koṇḍañña the Brahmin, Bhoja the Brahmin, Suyāma the Brahmin, and Sudatta the Brahmin—the five learned Brahmins headed by Koṇḍañña predicted, "The young Bodhisatta will surely and definitely become a Buddha." After giving the rewards they received from the ceremony of reading marks to their relatives, they decided without doubt, "This Great Man, the young Bodhisatta, will not remain in the household life; he will surely become a Buddha." Accordingly, they went forth and ordained in advance, dedicating themselves to the Bodhisatta. These Brahmins had mastered many Vedic texts since their youth. Therefore, even from a young age, these Brahmins were treated as teachers by other Brahmins. Those five learned Brahmin youths,
109:
consulted and agreed, "If it is after we have established families, we will not be able to cut off the entanglements of wife and children to ordain. Let us ordain in advance early on." Thus, shortly after interpreting the signs of the young Bodhisatta while he was still at a young age, they ordained in dedication to the Bodhisatta. They lived in pleasant forest monasteries and occasionally asked the people, "Friends, has the young Bodhisatta renounced the world yet?" When the people replied, "How could you see the young Bodhisatta renouncing the world? The young Bodhisatta is enjoying great royal splendor like a celestial being in the three palaces, amidst a company of dancers and female attendants," those five monks of the Group of Five (Pañcavaggī) reflected, "The Bodhisatta's wisdom is not yet mature," and they remained unconcerned (appossukka), merely waiting for the time the Bodhisatta would renounce the world. (This is the explanation in the Vinaya Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Volume 3, page 162.)
## The Account from the Buddhavamsa and Jātaka Commentaries
After the young Bodhisatta was given the name Siddhattha, those eight selected learned Brahmins returned to their homes, called their sons to them, and said, "Dear sons, we are now old and advanced in years. Now, Prince Siddhattha, the son of our King Suddhodana, will surely become a Buddha. Whether we will live to see Prince Siddhattha
110:
attaining the state of an Omniscient Buddha, we do not know for certain. Dear sons, when that Prince Siddhattha becomes a Buddha, you should ordain in the Dispensation (Sāsana) of that Blessed One."
Among those eight learned Brahmins, all except Koṇḍañña lived out their lifespan and passed away before the Bodhisatta's renunciation, according to their kamma. Only the youth Koṇḍañña remained free from illness. When the Bodhisatta reached maturity and renounced the world, he went to the Uruvela forest and thought, "This ground is indeed pleasant; it is very suitable for a man of good family who wishes to strive in the practice of meditation to develop and practice the Dhamma." While the Great Bodhisatta was practicing austere efforts (dukkaracariyā) in that Uruvela forest, Koṇḍañña heard the news that "The young Bodhisatta has ordained." He then went to the sons of those seven deceased Brahmins and said, "Friends, it is said that Prince Siddhattha has ordained. That Prince Siddhattha will surely and definitely become a Buddha. If your fathers were still alive today, they would have renounced the world and ordained this very day. If you wish to ordain, come; I shall follow that Great Man, the Bodhisatta, and ordain." Among those seven sons of the Brahmins,

The womb that has been occupied by a Bodhisatta is like the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī) of a pagoda; it is not fit to be used by others. Furthermore, while the mother of a Bodhisatta is still alive, it is not appropriate to set aside the mother of the Bodhisatta and appoint another woman to the position of Chief Queen. Therefore, it is the natural law (dhammatā) that the mother of a Bodhisatta has only seven days of life remaining after giving birth to the Bodhisatta. Thus, at that time, the Queen Mother passed away.

## The Age at which Queen Māyā Passed Away

At what age did Queen Māyā pass away? She passed away in her middle age (majjhima-vaya). To elaborate: in the first stage of life, the desire and passion (chanda-rāga) in the bodies of beings are very strong, and therefore a woman who conceives during this first stage cannot look after the womb well. Consequently, the child conceived at that time tends to have many ailments. When the middle age is divided into three parts, and the time reaches the third part after passing the first two, the physical house of the mother’s womb is clean. Children born in such a clean physical house are free from ailments. Therefore, the mother of the Bodhisatta, after enjoying royal pleasures in the first stage of life, gave birth to the Bodhisatta and passed away when she reached the third part of the middle age. (From the commentary on Bodhisatta-dhammatā, Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, Vol. 2, page 29.)

Calculating this commentary's explanation precisely, ancient teachers composed: 'Fifty-six years and five months, minus three days, without error, is the lifespan of the Mother'—meaning Queen Māyā passed away at the age of 56 years, 4 months, and 27 days. Furthermore—
114:
'In years and days, subtract one; in months, add two; this is the age at conception'—meaning Queen Māyā conceived the Bodhisatta when she was 55 years, 6 months, and 20 days old.

To briefly explain the meaning: If the 100-year human lifespan of Queen Māyā is divided into three parts, the first stage is 33 years and 4 months, the middle stage is 33 years and 4 months, and the last stage is 33 years and 4 months. Having enjoyed pleasures in the first stage of 33 years and 4 months, and then dividing the middle stage of 33 years and 4 months into three parts, each part is 11 years, 1 month, and 10 days. Adding the first and second parts of the middle stage together gives 22 years, 2 months, and 20 days. Adding this to the first stage of 33 years and 4 months results in 55 years, 6 months, and 20 days. At that time, the Queen Mother conceived the Bodhisatta. Therefore, it was composed as 'In years and days, subtract one; in months, add two; this is the age at conception.'

To this 55 years, 6 months, and 20 days, if the ten months (of the Bodhisatta’s gestation) are added, and the seven days after birth are also added, the age (at which Queen Māyā passed away) is 56 years, 4 months, and 27 days. Referring to this, it was composed as: 'Fifty-six years and five months, minus three days, without error, is the lifespan of the Mother.' (The detailed meaning of this matter should be sought in the Samantacakkhu Dīpanī, Vol. 1, Sudhammavatī Edition, pages 113-114.)

## Explanation on Whether Queen Māyā Became a Goddess or a God

Regarding the doubt and speculation as to whether Queen Māyā became a god (devaputta) or a goddess (devī) in Tusita heaven, it should be understood without doubt that she became a god (devaputta).

In this matter, although some teachers, based on a superficial reading of scriptural phrases such as 'mātaraṃ pamukhaṃ katvā' (placing the mother at the head), say and write that 'Queen Māyā became a female deity,' authoritative texts such as the Theragāthā Commentary and others explain that 'Queen Māyā became only a male deity (devaputta) in Tusita heaven.' The explanation is as follows:

In the commentary on the verses of Elder Kāḷudāyī in the Dasakanipāta, Theragāthā Commentary, Vol. 2, page 172: 'Devūpappatti pana purisabhāveneva jātā = The rebirth in Tusita heaven occurred only in the form of a male.'

In the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā, Sudhammavatī Edition, pages 166-167, in the section on the Birth Festival: 'Yasmā ca bodhisattena vasitakucchi nāma cetiyagabbhasadisā hoti, na sakkā aññena sattena āvasituṃ vā paribhuñjituṃ vā, tasmā bodhisattamātā gabbhavuṭṭhānato sattame divase kālaṃ katvā tusitapure devaputto hutvā nibbattī = Because the womb chamber where a Bodhisatta has resided is like the chamber of a shrine and is not fit to be inhabited or used by any other being, the mother of the Bodhisatta, seven days after giving birth,
116:
passed away and was reborn specifically as a male deity (devaputta) in Tusita heaven.'

Also in the Maṇidīpa-ṭīkā, Vol. 1, Sudhammavatī Edition, pages 205-206, in the commentary on the Twenty Verses: 'Sirīmahāmāyā hi bodhisattaṃ vijāyitvā sattāhamattaṃ ṭhatvā ito cavitvā tusitabhavane purisabhāveneva nibbattā, na itthibhāvenāti- etc. = Queen Sirīmahāmāyā, after giving birth to the Bodhisatta, remained in the human world for only seven days, and after passing away from here, was reborn in Tusita heaven only as a male (as a devaputta), not as a female. It is indeed the natural law (dhammatā) for all Bodhisatta mothers that after giving birth to a Bodhisatta, they remain in the human state for only seven days, and after passing away from this human world, they are reborn as male deities in Tusita heaven and not as goddesses.' Therefore, it should be understood without doubt that 'Queen Māyā became only a male deity (devaputta) in Tusita heaven.'

## Appointment of Nurses for the Bodhisatta Prince

For the sake of his son, Prince Siddhattha, the royal father King Suddhodana selected and appointed two hundred and forty (240) female nurses who were beautiful, clean in appearance, and skilled in their respective duties of providing sweet milk free from defects such as saltiness or bitterness, bathing, nursing and fondling, and carrying or moving the child.

He further appointed sixty (60) male attendants for those nurses, and sixty (60) ministers to oversee and record
117:
whether those male and female attendants were performing their respective assigned duties.

Among those two hundred and forty (240) female nurses, sixty nurses were responsible for breastfeeding the Bodhisatta Prince. Another sixty women were responsible for bathing the Bodhisatta Prince with scented water and dressing him. Another sixty women were responsible for nursing, embracing, and fondling the Bodhisatta Prince for long periods on their chests, arms, and laps. Another sixty women were responsible for receiving the Bodhisatta Prince from the hands of those who had been holding him, transferring him from one bosom to another and from one pair of hands to another. Thus, there were two hundred and forty (240) female nurses who performed these divided duties. Together with the sixty male attendants and the sixty ministers who oversaw them, there were three hundred and sixty (360) persons in total for the purpose of nursing and care.

This current description is in accordance with the Sutta Mahāvagga Pali Commentary, paragraph 37, page 43. In those Pali commentaries, it is directly and explicitly taught and explained that King Bandhuma appointed nurses for the (Bodhisatta) Prince Vipassī. Based on that, this Great Chronicle of Buddhas records that King Suddhodana appointed nurses for the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha.
118:
In the *Sway Zon Kyaw Htin* (Volume I, Question No. 33), regarding the question: "How could more than two hundred and forty wet nurses have suckled [the prince]?"—the answer on page 45 of that same text states: A day and a night consist of 60 Burmese hours. Since four wet nurses had to take turns caring for and protecting him every hour, 60 multiplied by 4 equals two hundred and forty. This was the answer given by the Kyee Thay Lay Htat Sayadaw to the question posed by the famous novice Shin Nandadhaja of Kyee Kan Village.

According to the statement in the *Sway Zon Kyaw Htin* that "four wet nurses had to take turns caring for and protecting him every hour," if we consider that one nurse was responsible for breastfeeding, one for bathing and adorning him with perfumes and flowers, one for holding and carrying him on her chest, arms, and lap for long periods, and one for moving and carrying him about, then this would be consistent with the *Mahāpadāna Sutta* Commentary of the *Dīgha Nikāya* mentioned earlier.

## The Selection of Wet Nurses in the Temiya Jātaka
In the *Temiya Jātaka* Commentary, when the father, King Kāsī, selected and appointed two hundred and forty (240) wet nurses for his son, Prince Temiya (the Bodhisatta):
(1) If a child suckles while resting on the lap of a very tall woman, the child's neck tends to stretch and become elongated; therefore, a very tall woman was not appointed as a wet nurse.
119:
(2) If a child suckles while resting on the lap of a very short woman, the child's neck tends to become hunched and short; therefore, a very short woman was also not appointed as a wet nurse.

(3) If a child suckles while resting on the lap of an extremely thin or emaciated woman, the child's limbs, such as the thighs, tend to become painful; therefore, an extremely thin woman was also not appointed as a wet nurse.

(4) If a child suckles while resting on the lap of an excessively stout or obese woman, the child tends to become lame (because the thighs, knees, and feet may not develop smoothly); therefore, an excessively stout woman was also not appointed as a wet nurse.

(5) If a child suckles from a woman with very long breasts, those long breasts may press against the child's nose, causing the nose to become flat; therefore, a woman with very long breasts was also not appointed as a wet nurse.

(6) The milk of an extremely dark-skinned woman is very cold, which is not suitable for a child over a long period...

(7) The milk of an extremely fair-skinned woman is very hot, which is not suitable for a child over a long period...

(8) The milk of a woman with a cough is very sour, which is not suitable for a child...

(9) The milk of a woman with skin diseases (such as scabies or leprosy) has defects such as being very acrid or bitter, and is thus not suitable for a child...
120:
...for these reasons, such women were not appointed as wet nurses; only women free from all such defects were appointed, as explained in the commentary.

Based on the aforementioned commentary, the Venerable Manle Sayadaw also wrote and composed the following (in the *Mahāsutakārī Maghadeva Laṅkā Thit*, Nemicariya Section, Verse No. 498):

When the Great Bodhisatta Maghadeva,
That noble being, descended from the Brahma realm
With a radiant presence to the mother's womb,
And was born pure after the full term,
The father, the leader of men, for his firstborn son,
Carefully considered with his golden wisdom:
If suckled by women who are excessively tall,
The child, stretching upward, develops a long, thin neck—
A significant defect. In one who is short,
The neck becomes stunted. If too thin,
The little one suffers pain. If too stout,
He may become lame. Long breasts
Will flatten the nose. A dark-skinned mother
Has milk that is cold; if extremely fair,
It is known to be hot. The milk of one with a cough
Is sour, and from one with skin disease,
It is acrid and bitter. Having discarded
Those with such defects and who are unsuitable,
Two hundred and forty wet nurses,
Endowed with the sixty-four qualities,
Of noble birth and graceful form,
Like the eggs of a golden crane,
Whose milk is sweet and pleasant,
Were gathered in the shade of the golden palace.
Without leaving his side, day and night,
Without weariness, they embraced him in turn;
Four nurses per hour, one for each quarter,
To tenderly care for and suckle him—
Thus were the wet nurses chosen,
For the one with the beauty of a celestial being.

## How the Foster Mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī
## Nursed and Cared for the Bodhisatta Prince
Although wet nurses were arranged and appointed for Prince Siddhattha the Bodhisatta as described, it was mostly the foster mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī herself who personally breastfed, raised, and cared for the Bodhisatta. To make it clearer: after Mother Māyā Devī
121:
passed away, King Suddhodana elevated the foster mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī to the position of Chief Queen. Two or three days after Mother Māyā gave birth to the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha, the foster mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī gave birth to Prince Nanda. When Queen Mahā Māyā Devī passed away seven days after the Bodhisatta's birth, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī entrusted her own biological son, Prince Nanda (who was only three or four days old), to wet nurses to be suckled and cared for. She herself personally breastfed and looked after the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha. The Bodhisatta spent most of his time in the lap of his foster mother. (From the Commentary on the *Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta* of the *Uparipaṇṇāsa*.)

In this way, the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha grew up comfortably and prosperously, surrounded by many attendants and tender care, and endowed with great and noble glory.

## Chapter 2
## The Royal Plowing Festival
## King Suddhodana’s Plowing Festival and
## The Second Act of Homage to the Bodhisatta
One day, it was the time for King Suddhodana’s annual Royal Plowing Festival, which was held according to the season. On that day, the entire royal city of Kapilavatthu was decorated like a celestial abode. All the citizens, including the laborers, wore new clothes,
122:
anointed themselves with perfumes, wore flowers, and gathered at the palace courtyard. At the site where the Royal Plowing Festival was to be held, one thousand plows were prepared. Among those one thousand plows, eight hundred (800) were for the King and his ministers. The seven hundred and ninety-nine (799) plows to be used by the ministers were adorned with silver, including the plowshares, yokes, ropes, reins, the oxen, and the goads. The auspicious royal plow to be used by King Suddhodana was entirely adorned with red gold.

When King Suddhodana departed from the capital of Kapilavatthu with a large retinue of ministers, attendants, and bodyguards, he also took his son, the Bodhisatta Prince, to the site of the plowing festival. Near the festival grounds, beneath a rose-apple (Jambu) tree that was exceptionally delightful, thick with leaves, and provided cool shade, a couch was well-prepared with a woolen rug. After placing his son there, a red woolen canopy decorated with gold and silver stars was fastened above, and curtains were drawn around the sides. Having stationed guards for security, King Suddhodana, dressed in the royal auspicious attire usually worn on the day of the plowing festival, proceeded to the auspicious royal field accompanied by his ministers to participate in the festival.
123:
Upon arriving at the royal field, King Suddhodana drove the golden plow prepared for him. The seven hundred and ninety-nine (799) ministers participating in the ceremony also drove their respective silver plows. The remaining two hundred (200) plows were driven by the farmers. These two hundred farmers plowed back and forth across the entire field. King Suddhodana, however, plowed only one round for the sake of the auspicious ceremony, from one side of the field to the other (or vice versa). The auspicious plowing ceremony was extremely grand and crowded.

Therefore, the nurses and guards who were protecting the Bodhisatta Prince said, "Let us go and see the glory of the King celebrating the Royal Plowing Festival," and they went outside from within the curtains.

## The Bodhisatta Attaining the First Ānāpāna Jhāna
At that moment, the Bodhisatta Prince looked here and there, and seeing no one near him, he quickly rose from his place. Sitting down cross-legged in a calm and composed manner, he practiced the *Ānāpānasati Bhāvanā Kammaṭṭhāna* (meditation on mindfulness of breathing), focusing on the outgoing and incoming breath. By doing so, he attained the first *Rūpāvacara Jhāna*. (In this matter, it should be understood without doubt that the Noble Bodhisatta attained the first *Rūpāvacara Jhāna* in a mere moment because of the powerful habit of practicing *Ānāpānasati* meditation throughout many past lives and world-cycles.)
124:
The nurses who had gone outside wandered among the various foods, drinks, and snacks, and thus a considerable amount of time passed. The shadows of all the trees, except for the rose-apple tree where the Bodhisatta Prince was staying, moved and shifted according to the natural movement of the sun. In the afternoon, the shadows of the trees fell toward the east. However, the shadow of the rose-apple tree where the Bodhisatta Prince was staying did not shift even though it was past noon; it remained uniquely circular, just as it had been when the Bodhisatta was first placed there.

The nurses suddenly remembered, "Oh, our master's son is staying all alone!" and they returned quickly. When they opened the curtains and entered, they saw the Bodhisatta Prince sitting calmly cross-legged on the magnificent couch, and they witnessed the miraculous phenomenon of the rose-apple tree's shadow remaining stationary and circular. Amazed by what they saw with their own eyes, they went quickly to King Suddhodana and reported, "Your Majesty, the Prince is sitting in such an amazing, calm, and composed manner. While the shadows of other trees have shifted with the sun, the shadow of the rose-apple tree where the Prince is staying remains circular and has not moved, even though it is past noon."

King Suddhodana came quickly and looked, and seeing those two wonderful and extraordinary miracles with his own eyes, he said, "O noble dear son..."
126:
"What kind of ponds do you wish for?" Sakka replied, "The ponds you create must be free of mud, scattered with rubies, pearls, and corals, and surrounded by walls made of the seven kinds of jewels. The staircases descending into the ponds must be laid with slabs of gold, silver, and rubies, and the tops of the ruby railings and pillars must be capped with coral. Within those divine ponds, you must create gold boats with silver thrones, silver boats with gold thrones, ruby boats with coral thrones, and coral boats with ruby thrones, along with gold, silver, ruby, and coral water-splashing cups for the Bodhisatta to play with. Those ponds must be beautiful, covered with the five kinds of lotuses."

Vissakamma agreed, saying "Very well," and descended to the human world that very night. At the sites designated by King Suddhodana for the auspicious lakes, he created the ponds exactly as Sakka had instructed. (Here, one might ask: How do the five kinds of lotuses grow and bloom in a pond free of mud? The answer is: Within those mud-free ponds, Vissakamma created small boats of gold, silver, ruby, and coral in various places and resolved, "Let these small boats be filled with thick mud; let the five kinds of lotuses bloom in these small boats." By Vissakamma's creation and resolution, the five kinds of lotuses bloomed—
127:
and flourished). From those lotus clusters, the pollen was scattered and spread across the water's surface, moving with the gentle breeze and soft ripples. Bees of five colors and five lineages swarmed and buzzed beautifully. Having created the auspicious lakes according to Sakka's instructions, Vissakamma returned to the celestial realm.

When morning dawned, many people saw those divine ponds, which were extraordinarily magnificent and wonderful. Joyfully, they went to King Suddhodana and reported, "These must surely be ponds created by Sakka, the King of Devas, for the Great Man, the Bodhisatta." King Suddhodana, surrounded by a large retinue, went to the site and saw the ponds, which were indeed magnificent, beautiful, and wonderful. He rejoiced, thinking, "The devas and Sakka must have created these ponds due to the power and merit of my son."

From then on, the Bodhisatta Siddhattha went to play in those auspicious lakes, which were of divine quality. (This passage is extracted from the commentary to the Sukhumāla Sutta, Devadūta Vagga, Tika Nipāta, Sixth Council Edition, Aṅguttara Commentary, Volume 2, pages 124-125.)

## Building Palaces for the Bodhisatta to Reside

The noble Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha grew up with great happiness, playing in the divine ponds covered with the five kinds of lotuses mentioned above, wearing brand new, extremely delicate and soft robes made in the Kāsī kingdom, and always being sheltered by divine and human white umbrellas so that heat, cold, dust, and dew would not touch him. When he reached the age of sixteen, his father, King Suddhodana, thought, "I shall have palaces built for my son to reside in." He summoned and gathered the most skilled and famous architects, carpenters, masons, sculptors, and painters in the capital. At an auspicious astrological moment, after completing all preliminary rites such as laying the foundation, he had three grand palaces built—Ramma, Suramma, and Subha—suitable for the three seasons: winter, summer, and the rainy season.

These three palaces were equal in length, width, and height; they differed only in the number of stories.

(The details of these three palaces are not extensively explained in the Buddhavamsa Commentary or the Jātaka Commentary. However, they are explained in detail in the commentary to the Sukhumāla Sutta of the Devadūta Vagga in the Tika Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Commentary, the commentary to the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta of the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, and the Agārikasampatti section of the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā. I shall present a summary of what is explained in those texts here.)

(1) The Ramma Palace was built for residence during the winter season.
128:
...playing in the divine ponds, wearing brand-new, delicate Kāsī silk robes, and always being sheltered by divine and human white umbrellas to protect him from heat, cold, dust, and dew, he grew up in immense luxury. When he reached the age of sixteen, King Suddhodana thought, "I shall build palaces for my son to reside in." He summoned the most skilled architects, carpenters, masons, sculptors, and painters in the capital. At an auspicious astrological moment, after completing the preliminary rites such as laying the foundation, he ordered the construction of three palaces suitable for the three seasons: the Ramma Palace, the Suramma Palace, and the Subha Palace.
These three palaces were equal in length, width, and height, differing only in the number of stories.
(The details of these three palaces are not extensively explained in the Buddhavamsa or Jātaka Commentaries. However, they are detailed in the Anguttara Commentary on the Sukhumāla Sutta, the Majjhima Commentary on the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, and the Agārikasampatti section of the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā. Those details are summarized here.)
(1) The Ramma Palace was built for residence during the winter season.
129:
## (2) Suramma Palace (Summer Residence)

The palace named Suramma had five stories. To capture a cool atmosphere, the stories were built high, and the halls and windows were made spacious. The main doors and windows were not made too tight, so that as much cool breeze as possible could be obtained from outside; some door leaves were perforated with holes, and others were fitted with lattices (of iron, gold, or silver). On the walls, pillars, and roof of that palace, painters had to paint blue lotuses, red lotuses, and white lotuses so that the mere sight of them would relieve heat and exhaustion. Near the windows, brand new pots were placed, filled with water, and planted with aquatic flowers and plants such as blue, red, and white lotuses. In various suitable places, water fountains and mechanical sprays were installed to spray water in all directions, creating a lush and green environment as if it were raining during the monsoon. Inside the palace, flower pots and water barrels filled with fragrant mud were placed, and lotuses of five colors were grown in them. Furthermore, to provide an extremely delicate and cool atmosphere—
130:
...robes were also prepared. Delicate, seasonal food with spicy flavors was well-provided. The windows were opened during the day to let in warmth and closed at night.
## (2) The Suramma (Summer) Palace
The Suramma Palace had five stories. To capture cool air, the rooms were designed with high ceilings and wide windows. The main doors and windows were not tightly sealed but were designed with palace-style openings or fitted with lattices (of gold, silver, or iron) to allow as much cool breeze as needed. On the walls, pillars, and ceilings, paintings of blue, red, and white lotuses were depicted to soothe the heat upon sight. Near the windows, new pots filled with water were placed, containing various water flowers like blue, red, and white lotuses. In suitable places, mechanical fountains were installed to spray water, creating a lush and cool atmosphere like a rainy day. Scented mud was placed in pots and tubs throughout the palace, where five-colored lotuses were planted. Furthermore, to provide a very soft and cool atmosphere...
131:
Chariot-style canopies and ceilings were also intricately fitted and installed in appropriate places. Gold-adorned walls and screens, beautifully decorated, were set up along with fine, delicate curtains and white woolen rugs that could generate a cool atmosphere. For the summer season (Gimmana-utu), sets of fine white garments and robes suitable for the season were prepared and kept ready. Food and nourishment possessing sweet and cool properties (sīta-vīriya) were also well-prepared.

On the roofs of the palace, networks of golden bells were properly installed, which produced melodious and pleasant sounds that surpassed even the five kinds of celestial musical instruments.

In that Suramma palace, golden plate ceilings with extremely fine and small perforations were suspended. When water was drawn and pumped up by mechanical water-lifting machines from the ponds located in the four directions of the palace (to be described later) to the space above those golden ceilings, the water would flow down through the fine holes of the golden plates like raindrops during a rainstorm.

Above the golden plate ceilings, dried buffalo hides were spread out. When gravel stones were lifted to the roof by mechanical devices and thrown onto the buffalo hides, the sound of those falling stones resembled the rumbling of thunder during the rainy season.
132:
For the Bodhisatta Prince, one hundred and eight gold and silver pots were filled with scented water, and networks of blue lotuses were made to surround his sleeping quarters. To maintain a cool and pleasant climate, large bronze water-storage jars were filled with scented mud, and blue, red, and white lotuses were planted and placed in various locations. These lotuses would bloom by the light of the sun. Various swarms of bees would enter the palace, suck the nectar from those lotus blossoms, and fly to and fro. Thus, the Suramma palace, constructed for the Bodhisatta Prince’s summer residence, was always filled with an exquisite fragrance. The main gates and the casement windows of this summer palace were kept closed during the day and opened at night (to allow the cool air to enter).

Later, when the Great Being (Bodhisatta) resided in this summer palace and the time for water-play arrived, the gravel stones were thrown onto the buffalo hides as previously described to mimic the sound of thunder. When water was pumped onto the golden ceilings by mechanical devices, the water dripping through the lattice holes of the golden ceilings resembled falling rain. At that time, the Great Being would don dark garments and dark ornaments. Surrounded by forty thousand female attendants who were also dressed in dark garments, adorned with dark ornaments, and anointed with dark-colored perfumes, he would engage in water-play during the day and enjoy the comfort of the cool season.

In the four directions of that Suramma (summer) palace, four ponds were created, which were free from impurities and covered with the five kinds of lotuses.
133:
The four ponds were filled with water that was as clear, emerald-green, and cool as precious gems. Various species of water birds, such as hamsas (swans), ducks, and cakkavākas (ruddy shelducks), would fly up from the pond on the eastern side of the palace, chirping melodiously, and fly through the sky above the palace to descend and rest in the pond on the western side. Similarly, they would fly from the western pond to the eastern pond, from the northern pond to the southern pond, and from the southern pond to the northern pond. Thus, even though it was the summer season, it was as pleasant as the rainy season in that summer palace.

## (3) The Subha (Rainy Season) Palace
The palace named Subha, intended for the rainy season, had seven stories. The layout, including the opening of chambers and the tiered roofs, was designed to be moderate—neither too low nor too high, neither too wide nor too narrow—so as to accommodate both heat and cold. The main gates and the casement windows were also constructed to suit the two seasons; some were fitted with solid wooden door-leaves, while others were fitted with lattice or perforated door-leaves. Painted murals were also created, depicting scenes of flames and fire in some places, and scenes of lakes and ponds in others. Clothing, robes, and floor coverings were also prepared in two varieties, mixing those shown in the previous two palaces to suit the two seasons. Some doors were kept open during the day and closed at night, while others...
134:
...were kept closed during the day and opened at night. (The splendor and completeness of this rainy season palace were similar to those of the winter and summer palaces.)

## The Chapter on Stringing the Bow
## The Bodhisatta Prince Demonstrating Archery Skills
After King Suddhodana had thus ordered the construction of these three magnificent, extraordinary, and beautiful palaces—the likes of which no previous royal lineage had ever resided in—for his son's residence, he thought: "My son has now reached the age of sixteen. I shall now crown him with the white umbrella, elevate him to kingship, and behold him enjoying the royal glory." He then sent messages to the eighty thousand Sakyan relatives, saying: "O Sakyan kings, my son has now reached the age of sixteen. I intend to establish him in the kingship. Let all Sakyan kings send their daughters who have reached marriageable age to my palace."

When the Sakyan kings heard the news in the message, they sent back disparaging and defiant words, saying: "Prince Siddhattha is merely handsome to look at, but he lacks wisdom and skill. Since he does not know any arts or sciences (sippa), he will not be able to fulfill the responsibility of supporting and maintaining a wife and children. Therefore, we cannot give our daughters as requested by King Suddhodana."
135:
(This sequence of events is according to the commentaries of the Buddhavamsa, the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā. However, in the Buddhavamsa section of the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā-nidāna, it is stated that the disparaging remarks by the Sakyan relatives occurred only after the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha was already residing in the three palaces with forty thousand attendants, led by Chief Queen Yasodharā Devī.)

When King Suddhodana heard the reply from the Sakyan kings, who were the fathers of the maidens, he went to the Bodhisatta Prince and informed him of the matter. The Bodhisatta Prince then asked: "Great Father, I have no need to learn any arts. What skill do you wish me to show the great relatives now? What skill should I demonstrate?" When the King replied: "Dear son, you should now demonstrate the skill of the thousand-strength bow (Sahassathāmadhanu) to the great relatives," the Prince said: "Great Father, if that is so, I shall demonstrate the archery skill on the seventh day from today. Let it be proclaimed by drum throughout the golden city that I will demonstrate the skill of the bow." Accordingly, the King had the drum sounded throughout the entire city of Kapilavatthu so that everyone would know.

(Regarding the term 'Sahassathāmadhanu' in the Pali, it should be interpreted as a bow that requires the strength of a thousand men to string or draw, according to the Aṅguttara Tika-nipāta Commentary, its sub-commentary, and the Buddhavamsa Commentary. If it refers to weight...)
136:
...it is likely that 'Sahassathāmadhanu' refers to a bow that can withstand a weight of one thousand units (pol), as explained in detail on page 33 of the first volume of the Samantacakkhu-dīpanī; one may refer to that text if desired.

One 'pol' is equal to four ticals (kyat). Therefore, one thousand pol equals four thousand ticals, which is forty viss (peittha). The opinion that a bow is called a 'thousand-strength bow' if its string is drawn by hanging a weight of forty viss from the middle of the bowstring and lifting it off the ground by shouldering the bow-staff is a very moderate and reasonable explanation. Therefore, it has been recorded as such in this work.

According to the commentaries on the Saṃyutta Nikāya and others, which explain the 'Daḷhadhanu' (the strong bow used by masters), one 'bhāra' is equal to two thousand pol. Thus, if a weight of two thousand pol (eight thousand ticals or eighty viss) is tied to the middle of the bowstring and the bow-staff is shouldered such that the weight is lifted from the ground and the string reaches the position for firing an arrow, that bow is called a 'Daḷhadhanu' (a master's strong bow). This interpretation may also be accepted.

(The following is a poetic description from the Candakinnarī Pyo, verse 83, regarding the twelve types of archery skills, including Saravedhī, Akkhaṇavedhī, and Vālavadhī, and the immense strength of the Daḷhadhanu bow, which can withstand two thousand pol, and the Prince's peerless display of these twelve skills, reminiscent of the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka, which left no rival equal to him.)
137:
Calculating truly, for twelve whole years, the practice of the art was mastered. Known as Daḷhadhanu, the bow was firm and hard. In the world of men, five yway make one pè, sixteen pè make one kyat, and four kyat make one pol (pala). A thousand such pol were the weight of the bow. With the teacher's bow, in twelve ways of archery, both great and small, he drew and shot. With the strength of five rutting bull elephants, like a flash of lightning in the sky, he shot seven or eight times in succession, his hands moving with incredible speed. (From Maghadevalaṅkāra Thit, Verse 446)

After having the city prepared, arrangements were made for the Prince to demonstrate his skill in archery. Seats and ceremonies were fully prepared for the ministers, royal attendants, the harem, the retinue, the soldiers, and the great royal relatives to witness. When the seventh day arrived and the King, ministers, and the vast assembly had gathered in their respective places, the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha took the bow that required the strength of a thousand men to string (alternatively, a bow weighing a thousand pala, or two thousand pala). While remaining seated in the cross-legged posture upon the jeweled throne, he caught the bowstring with one of his big toes and drew it to string the bow. Then, holding the bow-staff with his left hand and plucking the bowstring with his right hand, he produced a series of thunderous sounds. The sound was so intense that it echoed throughout the entire city of Kapilavatthu, as if it would soar up into the sky.

At that time, some people asked, "What is this sound?" and some replied, "It is the sound of a thunderclap." Then,
138:
other people said, "Friends, you do not know. This sound is not a thunderclap. It is the sound produced by the Supreme Sakyan, Prince Siddhattha, who is endowed with a beautiful form and a radiant body, as he strings the bow that requires the strength of a thousand men (or a weight of two thousand pala) and plucks the bowstring."

All eighty thousand Sakyan royal relatives felt great joy and satisfaction as soon as the Bodhisatta demonstrated the plucking of the bowstring.

## Demonstration of the 12 Minor Feats of Archery

The Bodhisatta summoned four great master archers in the city of Kapilavatthu, known as Akkhaṇavedhī, Vālavedhī, Saravedhī, and Saddavedhī, and had them assemble in the royal courtyard. As for the Bodhisatta himself (just as in his previous life as the youth Jotipāla in the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka of the Cattālīsanipāta), he donned a dark suit of armor adorned with spotted rubies, both short and long tunics, and placed upon his head a diadem set with the nine kinds of gems. He wore a belt made of the seven precious jewels and carried a bow made of horn shaped like a crescent moon, strung with a coral-colored string. He slung an emerald-colored quiver over his shoulder. Standing gracefully in the midst of the fourfold assembly like a young Naga emerging from the earth or like Sakka, the King of Devas, entering a battle assembly, he positioned the four aforementioned master archers at the four corners of a square. Those who would hand him arrows
139:
were given thirty thousand arrows each. The Bodhisatta himself held an arrow tipped with a diamond point (vajira). He then commanded the master archers, "All of you, shoot at me simultaneously and in unison."

(1) The master archers replied, "O Prince, we are Akkhaṇavedhī masters who can shoot many times in a single flash of lightning; we are Vālavedhī masters who can split a hair or a small fruit in half; we are Saravedhī masters who can hit a previously shot arrow with a subsequent one; we are Saddavedhī masters who can hit a target by sound alone without looking. Your Highness is young and tender of age; we do not wish to shoot at you."

The Bodhisatta Prince said, "Do not be concerned. If you can hit the mark, then shoot at me." He stood fearlessly like a golden lion in the middle of the vast royal courtyard. The four master archers, exerting all their skill, simultaneously discharged hundreds and thousands of arrows in a single flash. The Prince, using only a single diamond-tipped arrow, parried all the incoming arrows. He did not let them fall randomly; instead, he made them fall arrow-head to arrow-head, tail to tail, shaft to shaft, and fletching to fletching, so precisely that they formed a great arrow-chamber called Saragabbha. The thirty thousand arrows from each of the master archers were thus exhausted. The Prince, knowing well that the masters had run out of arrows,
140:
leapt out of the great arrow-chamber without destroying it.

When he demonstrated this feat of parrying incoming arrows, known as (1) Sarapaṭibāhana, the sound of the assembly—including princes, Brahmins, and wealthy merchants—clapping their chests and shouting in praise echoed through the sky like thunder, and the earth seemed to tremble.

(This is the feat of (1) Sarapaṭibāhana, parrying many arrows shot by enemies with a single arrow of one's own.)

(2) Then, King Suddhodana asked the Bodhisatta, "Dear son, what is the name of this archery skill you have just shown?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, this archery skill of parrying the enemy's incoming arrows with one's own arrow is called Sarapaṭibāhana." When King Suddhodana asked, "Dear son, are there others besides you who know this archery skill?", the Prince replied, "Great King, in the whole of Jambudīpa, there is no one else who knows this archery skill except for me." King Suddhodana then said, "Dear son, please demonstrate other archery feats besides this one." The Prince said, "Great King, these four master archers standing at the four corners could not hit me, who was alone. As for me, I shall demonstrate hitting all four of these master archers standing at the four corners with a single arrow."

When the Bodhisatta said this, the four master archers were greatly terrified and trembled, unable to remain still.
141:
Thereafter, the Bodhisatta had four banana trees planted at the four corners where the four master archers had stood. He tied a red silk thread to the tail of a diamond-tipped arrow and aimed at one of the banana trees. When he shot, the arrow pierced the first banana tree it was aimed at, and without stopping, it proceeded to pierce the second, then the third, and then the fourth banana tree. Finally, it pierced the first banana tree again and returned to the Prince's hand. The four banana trees stood encircled by the red silk thread in the form of a circle. The multitude of people shouted and cheered so loudly that it echoed everywhere.

Then, King Suddhodana asked the Bodhisatta, "Dear son, what is the name of this archery skill you have just shown?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, this archery skill of hitting the intended targets in a circular path with a single shot and having the arrow return to one's hand is called Cakkavedhī."

(This is the feat of (2) Cakkavedhī, hitting intended targets in a circular path with a single shot and having the arrow return to one's hand.)
142:
Furthermore, King Suddhodana said, "Dear son, please demonstrate other archery skills as well." Thus, the Bodhisatta demonstrated:

(3) The archery skill of shooting arrows continuously like a creeping vine, known as Saralaṭṭhi.
(4) The archery skill of shooting arrows like a continuous rope, known as Sararajju.
(5) The archery skill of shooting arrows to appear like a palace, known as Sarapāsāda.
(6) The archery skill of shooting arrows to appear like a staircase, known as Sarasopāna.
(7) The archery skill of shooting arrows to appear like a pavilion, known as Saramaṇḍapa.
(8) The archery skill of shooting arrows to appear like a surrounding wall, known as Sarapākāra.
(9) The archery skill of shooting arrows to appear like a square lotus pond, known as Sarapokkharaṇī.
143:
(10) The archery skill of shooting arrows in successive layers like the petals of a Paduma lotus, known as Sarapaduma.
(11) The archery skill of hitting a previously shot arrow with a subsequent arrow, known as Saravedhī.
(12) The archery skill of shooting arrows to resemble a falling rain of arrows, known as Saravassa.

He demonstrated these one after another. These are the twelve minor feats of archery.

## Demonstration of the 4 Major Feats of Archery

Furthermore, the Bodhisatta demonstrated to the assembly led by King Suddhodana the following four major feats of archery:

(1) Akkhaṇavedhī: the skill of hitting many targets accurately in a single flash of lightning.
(2) Vālavedhī: the skill of splitting a hair or a small fruit in half by aiming at it.
(3) Saravedhī: the skill of hitting a succession of previously shot arrows with a succession of subsequent arrows with perfect accuracy.
(4) Saddavedhī: the skill of hitting a target accurately by listening to the sound alone without looking with the eyes.
