He demonstrated these four major feats of archery as described.
144:
## Demonstrating the Piercing of the Seven Great Masses

Not only this, but the Bodhisatta Prince also demonstrated his archery skills, known as *Sattama-mahākāya-padālana*, by piercing through seven great masses before the assembly led by his father, King Suddhodana.

The seven types of masses are: (1) *Cammakāya*—a mass of hide, (2) *Dārukāya*—a mass of wood, (3) *Lohakāya*—a mass of copper plate, (4) *Ayokāya*—a mass of iron plate, (5) *Vālikakāya*—a mass of sand, (6) *Udakakāya*—a mass of water, and (7) *Phalakakāya*—a mass of wooden planks. Among these seven masses:

(1) While other archers capable of piercing hide could at most pierce through a single thickness of buffalo hide, the Bodhisatta Prince demonstrated piercing through a stack of one hundred buffalo hides.

(2-7) While other archery masters could only pierce through a single plank of fig wood eight finger-breadths thick, or a single plank of padauk wood four finger-breadths thick, the Bodhisatta Prince demonstrated piercing through a stack of one hundred such planks. Similarly, while other archery masters could only pierce through copper plates two finger-breadths thick or iron plates one finger-breadth thick, the Bodhisatta Prince...
146:
...sixteen, he mastered the three Vedas and the eighteen branches of knowledge under a world-renowned teacher (*Disāpāmokkha*) in the city of Takkasilā. He particularly excelled in archery beyond compare. Upon his return to Bārāṇasī, although King Brahmadatta, when near death, had instructed that his eldest son, the Bodhisatta Prince Asadisa, be crowned king, the Bodhisatta would not accept the kingship. Therefore, the ministers crowned the younger brother, Prince Brahmadatta.

While the Bodhisatta Prince Asadisa lived as he normally did, slanderers who served at the king's feet spoke divisive words to the sovereign to alienate him from the Bodhisatta, saying, "Prince Asadisa is aiming for and coveting the throne." Believing them, the younger brother, the King, issued an order to arrest his elder brother, Prince Asadisa.

At that time, a servant who wished for the Bodhisatta's welfare informed him of the matter. The Bodhisatta, feeling aggrieved, left Bārāṇasī for another country. He sent word to the king of that land that an archery master had arrived and was waiting at the palace gate for an audience. When the king summoned him and inquired about his salary, they agreed on a service for a salary of one hundred thousand per year. From then on...
147:
...the Bodhisatta Prince Asadisa served the King in the capacity of an archer. The old, established archers were envious and spoke disparagingly because the new archer was being paid a salary of one hundred thousand per year.

One day, the King saw a cluster of mangoes at the very top of a large mango tree near the royal stone slab in the park. Considering that no one could climb up to pick them, he summoned the old archers and asked, "Can you sever this mango cluster with an arrow and bring it down?" The old archers replied in unison, "O King, this is not a heavy burden for us. However, Your Majesty has seen our work many times. The newly arrived archery master receives a much higher salary than we do. Let that new master shoot it down."

The King summoned the Bodhisatta Prince Asadisa and asked, "Dear son, can you shoot down that mango cluster with an arrow?" The Bodhisatta Prince replied, "O King, I can shoot it down if I may have the place where you are currently reclining." (He requested that spot because the King's reclining position was directly beneath the stem of the mango cluster.) The King then...
148: ...moved aside and gave the Bodhisatta Prince permission to shoot from that spot. The Bodhisatta Prince was not one who carried his bow openly like other archers; he carried it concealed within his garments. He requested a curtain to be drawn around him. Entering within, he removed his white outer garment and put on a red garment. After tucking in his lower cloth firmly, he tied a red cloth tightly around his chest. He drew his sword from its sheath and slung it on his left side, donned a golden tunic, and slung his quiver on his back. He then took up his great bow made of goat-horn, joined at its segments, and strung it with a bowstring as red as coral. Placing a jeweled headband on his head, he twirled a very sharp arrow with his nails like a wheel. Emerging from the curtain like a Naga youth rising from the earth, he went to the shooting position and asked, "O King, shall I bring it down with an upward-flying arrow or with a downward-falling arrow?" The King replied, "Dear son, I have seen many archers who bring things down with an upward-flying arrow. I have never seen archers who can bring things down with a downward-falling arrow. Dear son, bring it down with a downward-falling arrow."
149:
The Bodhisatta Prince said, "Great King, this first arrow I am about to shoot will travel far, up to the Realm of the Four Great Kings. Your Majesty should wait patiently until this arrow returns from the Realm of the Four Great Kings." The King agreed, saying, "Very well."

Then the Bodhisatta Prince said again, "Great King, as this first arrow I shoot ascends, it will cut through half of the mango stem. When this arrow descends from the sky, without deviating by even a hair's breadth, it will perfectly sever the remaining half of the mango stem and bring the cluster down with it. Great King, please watch." Having made this bold declaration, he released the arrow with great force.

As the Bodhisatta had said, the arrow ascended, cutting through half of the mango stem. Knowing that the arrow would have reached the Realm of the Four Great Kings by then, the Bodhisatta released a second arrow, even swifter and more powerful than the first. This second arrow ascended, struck the feathers of the first arrow, and caused the first arrow to turn and fall back down, while...
150:
...it continued its ascent to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. The devas of Tāvatiṃsa caught that second arrow.

The sound of the first arrow descending, cutting through the air with great force, was like a thunderclap, making the earth seem to tremble. When the people asked, "What is this sound?" the Bodhisatta Prince replied, "This is the sound of the first arrow returning." Seeing the people terrified that the arrow might fall on them, he comforted them, saying, "Do not be afraid." He reassured them, saying, "I will not let the arrow fall to the ground, nor will I let it hit anyone; I myself will catch it."

As the arrow descended, without deviating by even a hair's breadth, and while the multitude watched, it perfectly severed the remaining half of the mango stem that had been half-cut during its ascent, and it came down along with the mango cluster. The Bodhisatta Prince Asadisa did not allow the mango cluster or the arrow to fall to the ground; reaching out into the air, he caught the mango cluster with one hand and the arrow with the other.

The King and the entire multitude, seeing such an extraordinary and wonderful feat, exclaimed, "We have never seen such a marvel before!"
151:
They praised the Bodhisatta, shouted cheers of victory, slapped their arms in triumph, and snapped their fingers. Thousands of turbans were tossed into the air. The king's assembly, filled with immense joy, offered wealth amounting to one crore as a reward to the Bodhisatta. The reigning king also bestowed upon the Bodhisatta, the archer Prince Asadisa, a great amount of wealth and a large retinue, like a heavy downpour of rain.
(This concludes the account of the extraordinary archery skills of the Bodhisatta as Prince Asadisa.)
Thus, even when the Bodhisatta was Prince Asadisa, he had displayed marvelous and wondrous archery skills. In this final existence as Prince Siddhattha, he demonstrated the twelve minor archery feats, the four major archery feats, and the seven feats of piercing through massive objects, as previously mentioned. Besides these archery skills, he also displayed all other arts and sciences that a prince should master in that assembly. Upon seeing this, the eighty thousand great Sakyan relatives were cleared of their doubts as to whether the Prince was proficient in the arts of men.
153:
This Yasodharā Devī was one of the seven co-natals (sahajāta) mentioned earlier. She was the daughter born of the union between the Sakyan King Suppabuddha, son of King Añjana of Devadaha, and Princess Amittā, the younger sister of King Suddhodana. She received the name "Yasodharā" because she possessed great and beautiful retinue, fame, and virtues. (Yasodharā means the princess who bears (dharā) great retinue and fame (yaso).)
Her complexion was of a beautiful golden hue, appearing as if cast from pure Bimbā gold, always pleasing to the sight. Her physical form was exceptionally graceful and elegant, standing out like a victory banner planted in the celestial assembly hall, the playground of Māra known as Manobhū. Her body radiated a brilliance like that of a celestial nymph (devaccharā), capable of illuminating the entire dark chamber of the palace. She was endowed with the five beauties (Pañcakalyāṇa) of noble women: (1) beauty of skin (chavi-kalyāṇa), (2) beauty of flesh (maṃsa-kalyāṇa), (3) beauty of sinews (nhāru-kalyāṇa), (4) beauty of bones (aṭṭhi-kalyāṇa) or teeth (danta-kalyāṇa), and (5) beauty of hair (kese-kalyāṇa). Alternatively, these are counted as the beauty of bones, skin, hair, flesh, and youth. Her touch was as soft and pleasant as a hundred-times-beaten cotton wool,
154:
possessing the element of pleasant touch (sukhasamphassa). She was free from the six physical defects: being too dark, too fair, too fat, too thin, too short, or too tall. From her graceful body, the fragrance of sandalwood always wafted. From her mouth, which was as red as coral, the scent of blue lotuses always emanated. Bhaddakaccānā Yasodharā Devī was a noble woman (itthi-ratana) worthy of being possessed by a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti).
This description is given by way of illustration (upalakkhaṇa). In truth, this Yasodharā Devī was a noble woman endowed with extraordinary beauty and virtues that surpassed humans and rivaled goddesses, as the result of her supreme perfections (pāramī) and past merits reaching their final fruition, making her a sight one could never tire of.
## The Handing Over of the Kingdom
The eighty thousand Sakyan relatives of Kapilavatthu, led by King Suddhodana, held a grand and magnificent assembly. They raised the white parasol over the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha, performed the royal consecration (Abhiseka) by pouring ceremonial water, and formally handed over the kingship. They then completed the royal ceremony of his ascension to the golden palace.
155:
Among the forty thousand maidens presented by the Sakyan kings, ten thousand were constant attendants who lived with Yasodharā Devī. The remaining thirty thousand maidens resided in the three palaces, ten thousand in each.
The Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha, surrounded by these noble Sakyan maidens like a young celestial being or like Sakka, the King of Devas, enjoyed the grand and magnificent royal splendor, comparable to that of a Universal Monarch. He was entertained by the melodious music played solely by women, without any men. He resided happily in the three magnificent palaces—Ramma, Subha, and Suramma—which were suited to the three seasons.
**********
## Chapter 3
## The Vision of the Four Great Omens
## Going to the Auspicious Garden
Thus, the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha, having ascended the throne of Kapilavatthu at the age of sixteen, enjoyed royal splendor similar to that of a Universal Monarch for thirteen years, being attended to and entertained by the forty thousand court ladies led by Queen Yasodharā.
156:
Having enjoyed the royal pleasures happily until he reached the age of twenty-nine, one day, desiring to go to the auspicious garden, he called his charioteer and said, "Friend charioteer, harness the chariot. I shall go out to see the garden." The charioteer replied, "Very well," and adorned the noble royal chariot, fit only for the exalted, with all kinds of ornaments. He harnessed four noble Sindh horses, which were as white as the full moon or the Kumuda lotus and as swift as the wind or the king of Garuḍas. He then informed the Bodhisatta that the chariot was ready. The Bodhisatta mounted the chariot, which was as magnificent as a celestial mansion, and set out towards the garden in great state.
## (1) Seeing the Omen of an Old Man
As the Bodhisatta was proceeding to the garden and reached a point on the road, the devas consulted among themselves, "The time for Prince Siddhattha to become a Buddha is drawing near. Let us show him the preliminary omens (pubbanimitta) that lead to his renunciation." Then, one deva manifested himself in the form of an old man with white hair, broken teeth, a bent back, leaning on a staff, and trembling. Only the Bodhisatta and the charioteer saw this omen of the old man created by the devas; others did not see it.
157:
When the Bodhisatta saw the omen of the old man, he asked the charioteer, "Friend charioteer, that man's hair is not like others'; it is white. His body is also not like others'; his teeth are gone, his flesh is withered, his back is bent, and he is trembling. What is that man called?" The charioteer replied, "Your Majesty, that man is called an 'old man'."
The Bodhisatta, who had never seen an old man before, nor even heard the word "old man," asked again, "Friend charioteer, I have never before seen a person with white hair, broken teeth, withered flesh, a bent back, and trembling. What does this 'old man' mean?" The charioteer replied, "Your Majesty, an 'old man' is one who cannot live much longer; it means one whose remaining life is short."
Then the Bodhisatta asked, "Friend charioteer, how is it? Am I also subject to old age? Have I not transcended the nature of aging?" The charioteer replied, "Your Majesty, all of us, including Your Majesty, are subject to old age; we have not transcended the nature of aging." When the charioteer replied thus, the Bodhisatta said, "Friend charioteer, if all people, including myself, are subject to old age..."
158:
“If everyone is indeed unable to overcome the nature of aging, then I, who cannot overcome aging, no longer desire to go to the auspicious park to enjoy myself. Turn the chariot back to the golden palace from this very spot where the old man was seen,” he commanded. The charioteer replied, “Very well, your Majesty,” and instead of proceeding to the park, he turned the chariot back to the palace from that spot.

## The Spiritual Urgency (Saṃvega) of the Bodhisatta Prince

Lions, when hit by an arrow, do not focus on removing the arrow, which is the effect, but seek out and eliminate the hunter, who is the cause of the arrow's flight. Similarly, when faced with both cause and effect, the Buddhas do not focus on removing the arrow-like effect, but use wisdom to find and eliminate the hunter-like cause. Thus, the Buddhas are like lion kings. Therefore, the Bodhisatta, as one who would become a Buddha, even though the charioteer spoke of the worldly nature of aging (jarā) as he knew it, clearly contemplated and realized that the root cause of aging is the taking of rebirth (jāti). Upon reaching the palace, he thought, “Oh, the nature of birth (jāti) is truly loathsome and disgusting...”
159:
“...For anyone in whom this birth (jāti) is manifest, the decay of old age (jarā) must also manifest.” Reflecting thus with the wheel of spiritual urgency (saṃvega-ñāṇa), he remained brooding, his face neither bright nor clear.

## King Suddhodana Increasing the Guards

King Suddhodana summoned the charioteer and asked, “Friend charioteer, for what reason did my son return so quickly without reaching the park?” The charioteer replied, “Your Majesty, the Prince returned quickly because he saw an old man.” King Suddhodana thought, “My son must only rule the kingdom. He must not renounce the world and become a monk. The words of the brahmin fortune-tellers who said he would renounce and become a Buddha must be proven wrong.” He then said, “Friends, why are you ruining me? Quickly appoint more female attendants and dancers for my son than before. If more attendants and dancers are provided, he will enjoy the five cords of sensual pleasure and will not remember to become a monk.” He then ordered guards to be stationed within a radius of half a league (two gāvutas) in all four directions.
160:
(Note: This sign of an old man was shown by the Arahant Brahmas of the Suddhāvāsa realm through their psychic power in front of the chariot, while the Prince was traveling surrounded by a vast army. Only the Prince and the charioteer saw it. The Brahmas thought, “The Bodhisatta is sinking into the mire of the five cords of sensual pleasure like a great elephant in a swamp. Let us rouse his mindfulness.” The subsequent signs should be understood in the same way. From the Mahāpadāna Sutta Commentary, page 46.)

## (2) Seeing the Sign of a Sick Man

Due to the deception and concealment of the five cords of sensual pleasure provided by King Suddhodana to prevent renunciation, the Bodhisatta's sense of urgency (saṃvega) regarding birth and old age diminished slightly, and he lived again enjoying sensual pleasures. After four months had passed, the Prince set out for the park again in a chariot drawn by noble horses. On the way, he saw for the second time a sign created by the devas: a man severely afflicted by disease, suffering greatly, who could only rise or lie down with the help of others, lying in his own excrement.
161:
Seeing him, he asked, “Friend charioteer, that man's eyes are not like those of others; they are dull and trembling. His voice is not like others'; he is crying out in unbearable pain. His body is not like others'; he looks extremely exhausted. What kind of man is he?” The charioteer replied, “Your Majesty, he is called a sick man.”

The Bodhisatta, who had never seen a sick man nor heard the word “sick” before, asked again, “Friend charioteer, I have never seen such a person who can only rise or lie down with help and lies in his own excrement, crying out in pain. What does this ‘sick man’ mean? Explain the nature of this sick man to me.” The charioteer replied, “Your Majesty, this ‘sick man’ is one of whom it is not known whether he will recover from his current illness or not.”

Then the Bodhisatta asked, “Friend charioteer, how is it? Am I also subject to sickness? Am I one who cannot overcome the nature of sickness?” The charioteer replied, “Your Majesty, you, we, and all people are subject to sickness; we are all unable to overcome the nature of sickness.”
162:
“Friend charioteer, if all people, including myself, are unable to overcome the nature of sickness, then I, who cannot overcome sickness, no longer desire to go to the park to enjoy myself. Turn the chariot back to the palace from this very spot where the sick man was seen,” he commanded. The charioteer replied, “Very well, your Majesty,” and turned the chariot back to the palace.

## The Spiritual Urgency (Saṃvega) of the Bodhisatta Prince

As mentioned before, the Bodhisatta, who is like a lion king, even though the charioteer spoke of the worldly nature of disease (byādhi) as he knew it, clearly realized that the root cause of both disease and the previously seen old age is birth (jāti). Upon reaching the palace, he reflected with the wheel of spiritual urgency: “Oh, the nature of birth (jāti) is truly loathsome... For anyone in whom birth is manifest, old age (jarā) must manifest, and sickness (byādhi) must manifest.” He remained brooding, his face unhappy.
163:
## King Suddhodana Increasing the Guards

King Suddhodana summoned the charioteer as before. The charioteer reported, “Your Majesty, the Prince returned quickly because he saw a sick man.” The King, after thinking and speaking as before, ordered guards to be stationed within a radius of three-quarters of a league (three gāvutas) and increased the number of female attendants and dancers.

## (3) Seeing the Sign of a Dead Man

Due to the deception and concealment of the five cords of sensual pleasure provided by King Suddhodana to prevent renunciation, the Bodhisatta's sense of urgency (saṃvega) regarding birth, old age, and sickness diminished slightly, and he lived again enjoying sensual pleasures. After four months had passed, the Prince set out for the park again in a chariot drawn by noble horses. On the way, for the third time, he saw a sign created by the devas: a large crowd gathered and a bier (funeral litter) decorated with various dyed cloths.
164:
“Friend charioteer, why is that crowd gathered? Why have they prepared a bier decorated with various dyed cloths?” the Prince asked. The charioteer replied, “Your Majesty, the crowd is gathered and the bier is prepared because someone has died.”

(Note: Since he had never seen a funeral bier before, he asked about it.)

The Bodhisatta, who had never seen a dead person nor heard the word “dead” before, said, “Friend charioteer, if that is because someone has died, drive the chariot to where the dead person is.” The charioteer complied. Seeing the corpse, the Prince asked, “Friend charioteer, what is the nature of this ‘dead person’?” The charioteer replied, “Your Majesty, this ‘dead person’ is one whom parents and relatives will never see again, and who will never see his parents and relatives again.” The Prince then asked, “Friend charioteer, how is it? Am I also subject to death like that person? Am I one who cannot overcome the nature of death? Will I also...”
165:
"Will my mother, father, and relatives one day not see me? And will I myself one day not see my mother, father, and relatives?" the Prince asked. The charioteer replied, "O Great King, both Your Highness and we ourselves, indeed all beings, are of the nature to pass away and die like this person. Everyone is unable to transcend the nature of death. It is certain that one day Your Highness's mother, father, and relatives will not see you, and it is certain that one day Your Highness will not see your mother, father, and relatives." (In this context, 'mother' refers to the Great Foster-Mother Mahāpajāpatigotamī.)

Then the Bodhisatta Prince said, "Friend charioteer, if indeed all people, including oneself and others, are unable to transcend the nature of death, then for me, who cannot transcend death, there is no longer any desire to go to the auspicious garden to enjoy and delight myself. Turn the chariot back from this very place where I have seen the dead body and drive back to the golden palace." The charioteer replied, "Very well, Great King," and acknowledging the command, he did not proceed to the auspicious garden but turned the chariot back from the place where the corpse was seen and drove back to the golden palace.

## The Bodhisatta Prince's Spiritual Urgency (Saṃvega)

As previously mentioned, the Bodhisatta Prince, who was like a lion king and destined to become a Buddha, even though the charioteer had explained the worldly nature of death as he knew it—saying, "Regarding a dead person, the remaining relatives will not see them again, and the deceased will not see the remaining relatives again"—
166:
the Prince clearly contemplated and realized the nature of birth (jāti), which is the root cause of this death (maraṇa), as well as the previously encountered old age (jarā) and sickness (vyādhi). Upon reaching the golden palace, he reflected with the wheel of spiritual urgency (saṃvega-ñāṇa): "O, the nature of birth, which is the establishment of a new existence, is truly loathsome and disgusting! For anyone in whom this birth (jāti) is manifest, old age (jarā) must manifest; sickness (vyādhi) must manifest; and the falling away and death (maraṇa) must manifest." Thus, he remained in deep thought, his face neither bright nor joyful.

## King Suddhodana Increasing the Guards

King Suddhodana, the father, summoned the charioteer as before and questioned him. When the charioteer reported, "O Great King, your son returned quickly because he saw a dead man," King Suddhodana planned and spoke as before. He then ordered an increase in guards in all four directions within a radius of one yojana.
167:
He also arranged for an increased number of female attendants and dancers compared to before.

## (4) Seeing the Omen of a Recluse

As King Suddhodana increased the arrangements of the five cords of sensual pleasure to prevent the Prince from renouncing the world and becoming a monk, the Prince's spiritual urgency—the sense of dread and weariness regarding birth, old age, sickness, and death—diminished slightly, and he returned to enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure.

When four months had passed while living in this manner, the Bodhisatta Prince again set out for the garden, riding in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses as before. On the way, he saw for the fourth time a man created by the devas who had entered the state of a recluse, having shaved his hair and beard and wearing saffron-dyed robes. The Prince asked, "Friend charioteer, that person's head is not like the heads of others; it is shaven of hair and beard. His clothes are also not like those of others; they are dyed with saffron. What is such a person called?" The charioteer replied, "O Great King, that person is called a recluse (pabbajita)."

Again, the Bodhisatta Prince asked, "Friend charioteer, what is meant by the name 'recluse'?"
168:
"Please explain the nature of that 'recluse'," he requested. The charioteer replied, "O Great King, this person called a recluse is one who has emerged from the human state and life, wearing saffron-dyed robes, with the thought: 'Practicing the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakamma-patha) such as generosity (dāna) is excellent.' This recluse is one who has emerged from the human state and life, wearing saffron-dyed robes, with the thought: 'Practicing the ten wholesome courses of action that are consistent with the Dhamma, the ten wholesome courses of action that are blameless, and the ten wholesome courses of action that are very pure is excellent.' This recluse is one who has emerged from the human state and life, wearing saffron-dyed robes, with the thought: 'Non-violence toward beings and protecting beings for their welfare is excellent.'"

[In this context, because it was not the time of a Buddha's dispensation, the charioteer did not know of recluses or their virtues. However, through the power of the devas, he identified the person as a recluse and explained the virtues of a recluse. (From the Buddhavamsa-aṭṭhakathā, page 327, and the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā, page 184.)

Bodhisattas with long lifespans see each of the four great omens only after intervals of a hundred years. However, because our Bodhisatta appeared at a time of short lifespans, he saw each of the great omens in succession every four months while going to the garden. The masters who memorized the Dīgha Nikāya say that he saw all four great omens on the very same day. (From the Buddhavamsa-aṭṭhakathā, page 328.)]
169:
Then the Bodhisatta Prince said, "Friend charioteer, that person who has entered the state of a recluse with the thought, 'Practicing the ten wholesome courses of action, practicing the ten wholesome courses of action consistent with the Dhamma, practicing the ten wholesome courses of action that are blameless, and practicing the ten wholesome courses of action that are pure is excellent,' is indeed praiseworthy and excellent. That person who has entered the state of a recluse with the thought, 'Non-violence toward beings and protecting beings for their welfare is excellent,' is indeed praiseworthy and excellent. Because it is so praiseworthy and excellent, friend charioteer, drive the chariot to the place where that recluse is." The charioteer replied, "Very well, Great King," and drove the chariot to where the recluse was. Upon reaching that place, the Bodhisatta Prince asked the recluse created by the devas, "Friend, what are you doing? Your head is not like the heads of others, and your clothes are not like the clothes of others."

When the recluse, a form created by psychic power (iddhirūpa) by the devas, replied, "O Great King, I am called a recluse," the Bodhisatta Prince asked again, "Friend, what is meant by you being a 'recluse'?" The recluse of psychic form replied, "O Great King, I am a recluse who, with the thought that it is excellent to practice the ten wholesome courses of action such as generosity—which are characterized by the four special qualities of Dhamma (righteousness), Sama (tranquility), Kusala (wholesomeness), and Puṇya (merit)—
170:
has shaved hair and beard, donned saffron-dyed robes, and emerged to practice for liberation from the household life and the human realm. I believe that non-violence toward beings and protecting beings for their welfare is excellent." When he said this, the Bodhisatta Prince acknowledged and praised him, saying, "Friend, you who have shaved hair and beard, donned saffron-dyed robes, and emerged to practice for liberation from the household life and the human realm with the thought that it is excellent to practice the ten wholesome courses of action characterized by the four special qualities of Dhamma, Sama, Kusala, and Puṇya, and that non-violence and protecting beings is excellent—you are indeed a praiseworthy and excellent person."

## Recording the Years and Months of the Renunciation

In the section on the Bodhisatta Prince's renunciation, regarding his four trips to the garden before leaving: In the year 96 of the Great Era (Mahā-sakkarāj), on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, he set out for the garden in a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses and saw the first omen, an old man, on the way. Having seen the omen of the old man, he abandoned the pride of youth (yobbana-māda), which is the elation of mind based on being young.

Then, on the full moon day of Kattika in that same year, he set out for the garden as before and saw the second omen, a sick man, on the way. Having seen
171:
the omen of the sick man, he abandoned the pride of health (ārogya-māda), which is the elation of mind based on being free from disease. 

Then, on the full moon day of Phagguna in that same year, he set out for the garden as before and saw the third omen, a dead man, on the way. Having seen the omen of the dead man, he abandoned the pride of life (jīvita-māda), which is the elation of mind based on being long-lived.

Then, in the year 97 of the Great Era (Mahā-sakkarāj), on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, he set out for the garden as before and saw the omen of a recluse on the way. Because he saw the omen of the recluse, the Bodhisatta Prince took delight in the state of a recluse and made the resolution, "I shall become a monk this very day," and then proceeded to the garden on that same day.

(In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, Dhammasaṅgaṇī Pāḷi, Nikkhepakaṇḍa, page 264, the Buddha taught that the knowledge that fears birth (jāti)—or the knowledge that birth is a great and fearful danger—is called jāti-bhaya. The knowledge that fears old age (jarā) is called jarā-bhaya. The knowledge that fears sickness (vyādhi) is called vyādhi-bhaya. The knowledge that fears death (maraṇa) is called maraṇa-bhaya. This collection of four types of knowledge is called spiritual urgency (saṃvega).

Among the four great omens mentioned, the first three omens appear if the nature of birth (jāti) is manifest.)
172:
As surely as striking the ground with one's hand, the truths of aging (jarā), sickness (byādhi), and death (maraṇa) are indeed manifest. Because of the manifestation of birth (jāti), the truths of aging, sickness, and death also manifest. For one who has birth, there is no escape from the perils of suffering—aging, sickness, and death; they are truly terrifying and harsh. To one who contemplates thus, the knowledge of spiritual urgency (saṃvega-ñāṇa) arises intensely; therefore, these are called the Great Signs of Spiritual Urgency (Saṃvega-nimitta). The final sign, the sign of the monk, is the causal sign shown so that one may practice the Dhamma to escape from those perils of aging, sickness, and death; it should be specifically noted here as the Primary Sign (Padhāna-nimitta).

## Sakka Sending Vissakamma Deva
## to Adorn the Bodhisatta

On that day, the Bodhisatta enjoyed himself in the auspicious garden, partaking in its delights. After bathing in the auspicious pond, he sat gracefully upon the auspicious stone slab at the time of sunset. At that moment, the Great Being felt a desire to adorn himself. Knowing this, Sakka, the King of Devas, sent Vissakamma Deva. Vissakamma approached the Bodhisatta, disguised himself as the Bodhisatta’s royal barber, and adorned the Bodhisatta with celestial ornaments. (In this instance, one should visualize the Great Being’s extreme beauty when adorned with celestial garments.)

For the Bodhisatta, who was thus adorned with all celestial ornaments,
173:
while musicians played their five kinds of musical instruments, danced, and sang, and while Brahmins offered various auspicious words pleasant to the ear, saying, “May the Great King be free from all dangers, harms, and enemies; may he be filled with all auspicious blessings and be satisfied,” the Bodhisatta mounted the noble chariot, adorned with all ornaments, to return to the golden palace.

## The Birth of Son Rāhula

At that time, King Suddhodana, having heard that the Chief Queen Yasodharā had given birth to a son, sent royal messengers to the Bodhisatta, saying, “Go and report this joyful news to my son.” As soon as the Bodhisatta heard the news of his son’s birth, he spoke with the heart of one established in spiritual urgency, “Rāhu the Asura, who will seize me, has been born; a great bond has been created.”

King Suddhodana asked the messengers, “What did my son say?” The messengers reported the words spoken by the Bodhisatta. Upon hearing those words, King Suddhodana declared, “From this time forth, let my grandson be named Prince Rāhula.”
174:
The grandson was thus named and addressed.

## The Sakyan Princess Named Kisāgotamī
## Chanting the Paean of Peace (Nibbuti)

The Bodhisatta, riding the chariot with a large retinue and with the utmost grace of most delightful glory, entered the royal city of Kapilavatthu. As the Bodhisatta entered the city in his noble chariot, the Sakyan princess named Kisāgotamī—who was great and noble in attributes such as beauty, glory, and lineage—was staying on the upper terrace of her noble palace. Seeing the beauty of the Bodhisatta’s physical form as he entered the city, she was filled with joy and sang:

Nibbutā nūna sā mātā,
Nibbuto nūna so pitā.
Nibbutā nūna sā nārī,
yassāyaṃ īdiso patī.

(Truly at peace is that mother, truly at peace is that father, truly at peace is that woman, who has such a one as her husband.)

“Yassa mātuyā = Of which glorious and fortunate mother. Īdiso = Having such a nature, whose glory is as radiant as the rising sun, whom one can never tire of looking at. Ayaṃ suto = This extraordinary son, worthy of being called 'Atijāta' (surpassing the parents), the pinnacle of beauty, the crown of elegance, the foremost in wisdom. Jāto = Has been born, truly making her worthy of being called the mother of a noble son. Sā mātā = That glorious and fortunate mother.”
175: ...cooled (nibbutā). (Contemplating the qualities and physical appearance of her own son, her heart will be constantly filled with joy and peace.) Of whichever fortunate father this son—who is so glorious like the rising sun, prominent and never-tiring to behold, the pinnacle of beauty, the crown of elegance, and the foremost in wisdom, truly worthy of being called an atijāta son—is born, that father is indeed cooled (nibbuto). (Contemplating the qualities and physical appearance of his own son, his heart will be constantly filled with joy and peace.) Of whichever fortunate woman this husband—who is a true man of quality, the pinnacle of beauty, the crown of elegance, and the foremost in wisdom, this extraordinary lord—is born (as her husband), appearing in this world as a blessing to be remembered, that woman is indeed cooled (nibbutā). (Contemplating the qualities and physical appearance of her lord, her heart will be constantly...
176: ...filled with joy and peace. Thus she uttered this inspired verse of peace (nibbuti-udāna). (Just as oil overflows from a pot when it is full, when a person experiences intense joy (pīti-somanassa) for a certain reason, that joy overflows from within, and the verse or prose that arises from that joy is called an Udāna.) The Bodhisatta, hearing this inspired verse uttered by the Sakyan princess Kisāgotamī, thought: "This princess Kisāgotamī, my sister, utters this verse of peace, saying that the hearts of the mother, father, and wife who see such a person will be peaceful and cooled. But when what things are extinguished is the heart truly cooled?" As he was one whose mind was detached from the defilements, the thought arose in the Bodhisatta's mind: "When the fire of lust (rāga) is extinguished, it is truly cooled; when the fire of hatred (dosa) is extinguished, it is truly cooled; when the fire of delusion (moha) is extinguished, it is truly cooled. When all the heat of defilements such as conceit (māna) and wrong view (diṭṭhi) is cooled, it is truly called peace. This princess Kisāgotamī has spoken pleasant words to me concerning the element of peace (nibbuti-dhātu). Indeed, I am one who is searching for the ultimate truth of Nibbāna, where all suffering is extinguished..."
177: ...this very day, I should renounce the household life, go forth into the forest, become a monk, and seek to attain the great ultimate truth of Nibbāna." Thoughts of renunciation arose repeatedly. He said, "Let this pearl necklace be a teacher's fee for this princess Kisāgotamī, who has reminded me to seek the element of peace (nibbuti)." He then took off a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand from his neck and sent it to Kisāgotamī. Princess Kisāgotamī thought, "Prince Siddhattha has a mind inclined towards me, which is why he sends this gift," and she was greatly pleased. The Bodhisatta, with great and vast glory, ascended his magnificent and delightful palace and lay down on his splendid couch. As soon as the Bodhisatta lay down on the couch, a group of female attendants and dancers, as beautiful as celestial nymphs and skilled in dancing, singing, and music, surrounded him with their five kinds of sweet-sounding instruments. They played, danced, and sang to entertain the Bodhisatta so that he might enjoy the five sensual pleasures. Although they entertained him thus, the Bodhisatta, whose mind was disgusted with things that increase the fires of defilement...
178:
Therefore, not delighting or enjoying the dancing, singing, and music at all, he fell into a brief sleep for a moment.

The group of female dancers and attendants, seeing that the Bodhisatta had fallen into a brief sleep, thought, “We have been performing dancing, singing, and music for the sake of this prince. Now that the prince has fallen asleep, why should we continue to tire ourselves?” Thinking thus, they lay down, clutching their respective instruments, and fell asleep. The scented oil lamps lit within the golden palace continued to burn brightly.

## The Bodhisatta Gaining Great Spiritual Urgency
## and Renouncing the World

The Bodhisatta awoke from his sleep and sat cross-legged upon the couch. Looking around, he saw some dancers sleeping with saliva trickling out, with dirty cheeks and dirty bodies, clutching their instruments; some were sleeping while grinding their teeth; some were snoring; some were muttering and talking in their sleep; some had their mouths wide open; some were partially unclothed; some had their hair disheveled and messy. They appeared like corpses in a cemetery, sleeping in a repulsive manner.
179:
When the Bodhisatta Prince saw the repulsive and distorted state of the dancers, his mind became even more detached from sensual pleasures than before. His thoughts were as follows:

(1) Appassādā kāmā = Sensual pleasures provide little gratification; they are full of suffering and despair. The faults and dangers in these sensual pleasures are indeed many.

(2) Aṭṭhikaṅkalūpamā kāmā = Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton. To illustrate: just as a hungry and emaciated dog, finding a bare bone that has been scraped clean of meat and discarded, might gnaw on it with saliva flowing, yet find no satisfaction or fullness. It cannot reach a state of contentment. Because of the lingering smell of the bone, the dog cannot abandon it and go elsewhere; instead, with great expectation that it might find some taste or satisfaction, it turns the bone around, biting the tip, the base, and the middle. It dies before ever finding any real taste. In the same way, many beings, both men and women, are like the hungry dog. They enjoy the bone-like sensual objects—gold, silver, wealth, fields, property, children, spouses, and masters, whether animate or inanimate—clinging to them for a long time. Yet they can never find satisfaction or contentment. With great expectation that they might find some taste or happiness, they continue to live in this manner.
180:
They continue to live in this way. Because the element of sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā) within beings binds and pulls them toward these sensual objects, they are unable to abandon them. Without being able to contemplate thoughts of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) to escape from sensual pleasures, they remain obsessed and attached, eventually meeting death at the feet of their spouses, children, or masters. Therefore, the five strands of sensual pleasure are indeed like a skeleton; they bring only much suffering and despair. In these sensual pleasures, there is no refuge, only many faults and dangers.

(3) Maṃsapesūpamā kāmā = Sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat. To illustrate: just as a hawk carrying a piece of meat in its beak is pursued and pecked at by many other birds. As long as it does not let go of the meat, that hawk encounters great suffering. The moment it discards the meat, it is freed from those dangers. If another bird then snatches that meat and flies away, it too is pursued and pecked at by the flock of birds. Thus, for the sake of a single piece of meat, every bird that clings to it and flies with it encounters danger. In the same way, one who possesses various sensual objects, which are like a piece of meat, and holds onto them with craving as 'my property' or 'my wealth,' will be constantly sought out by the five enemies—water, fire, kings, thieves, and those who are unloved—who look for an opportunity to plunder, extort, or seize them.
181:
When encountering these enemies because of those possessions, if one tries to protect them with all one's might but fails, one may even face the loss of life. As long as one cannot renounce those sensual pleasures, one remains surrounded by all kinds of dangers and lives in a state of distress and confinement. Only when one renounces those sensual pleasures can one obtain the opportunity to live in peace and coolness. Therefore, the five strands of sensual pleasure, whether animate or inanimate, are indeed like a piece of meat; they bring only much suffering and despair. In these sensual pleasures, there is no refuge, only many faults and dangers.

(4) Tiṇukkūpamā kāmā = Sensual pleasures are like a grass torch. To illustrate: when a person carries a large grass torch that has been set on fire and walks against the wind, the fire burns down from the tip. If that person does not discard the grass torch, the fire will burn their hands, feet, and other limbs. Because of such burning, that person might die, or if they do not die, they will encounter death-like suffering. In the same way, sensual objects grasped and embraced with the hand of craving as 'I own this,' 'this is mine,' or 'this is my wealth,' cause the fires of suffering—such as worry, anxiety, and the burden of protection—to increase and burn within the one who finds pleasure in possessing them. Even while cherishing and keeping them, if they perish or are depleted according to their nature, they cause the great flames of grief and other sufferings to increase and burn. Sometimes, because of these sensual objects,
182:
because of the fire of sensual pleasures, one may even suffer the burning of the fire of death (maraṇa). Thus, possessing the various animate and inanimate objects of desire—such as spouses, children, homes, fields, and lands—is like possessing blazing flames. Therefore, the five strands of sensual pleasure are indeed like a grass torch; they bring only much suffering and despair. In these sensual pleasures, there is no refuge, only many faults and dangers.

(5) Aṅgārakāsūpamā kāmā = Sensual pleasures are like a pit of glowing coals. To illustrate: a pit of acacia coals covered with ash on top does not appear to be fire because no smoke or flames are visible. Lacking the perception of fire, one who descends or falls into that pit of coals will be burned and scorched even more than by a flaming fire, leading to the loss of life. In the same way, sensual objects appear superficially pleasant through the sight of the eye, the sound of the ear, the smell of the nose, the taste of the tongue, and the touch of the body; thus, they do not even seem to be hot. When one descends into the coal-pit of sensual pleasures by taking delight in them, craving them, and possessing them, they cause intense suffering and distress. Burning by flames is obvious and clear to everyone's sight. However, the burning of objects like taro or sweet potatoes buried within a heap of coals is not obvious. Even though it is not obvious,
183:
the intensity of the burning and heat is greater than that of flaming fire. Similarly, those who are submerged in the coal-pit of sensual pleasures do not show external heat visible to others, but they burn with internal heat. They suffer from various internal burnings and distresses—such as various sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka), the various sufferings of seeking wealth (pariyesana), and the concerns of children, housing, and livelihood—just as taro and sweet potatoes buried in a coal-pit are burned until they are cooked or charred. They suffer great heat internally, unknown to others. This great realm of sensual desire (kāmabhava), which is overflowing with countless sensual objects, is like a great pit of glowing coals. The more sensual objects there are, the thicker the mass of coals becomes. Beings in the sensual realm are like the taro and sweet potatoes buried in the coal-pit. Therefore, the five strands of sensual pleasure are indeed like a pit of glowing coals; they bring only much suffering and despair. In these sensual pleasures, there is no refuge, only many faults and dangers.

(6) Supinakūpamā kāmā = Sensual pleasures are like a dream. To illustrate: a person while sleeping might dream of becoming a wealthy man, a local lord, or a sovereign king. In the dream, they enjoy all desired sensual pleasures to their heart's content and remain as happy as they wish. While dreaming, it seems as if it is
184:
actually real. The pleasure from those riches and comforts seems endless. But before the delight and attachment in the dream can end, they suddenly wake up, and everything they encountered in the dream becomes vain and cannot be found even if searched for. In the same way, humans and devas in this sensual realm are led by the factor of craving (taṇhā) which takes the lead. While they are enjoying human and celestial pleasures, they perceive them as joyful, happy, and stable. They live possessing and clinging to them through the three factors of craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and wrong view (diṭṭhi); they are, in effect, dreaming. In the very short duration of the present life, they enjoy and take delight in them as if in a dream. Before their attachment can end, they must abandon all those clung-to sensual objects, pass away, and move to another life. As soon as they die, just as everything seen in a dream vanishes completely for the one who wakes up, all the sensual objects they possessed and clung to as 'I own this,' 'this is mine,' or 'this is my wealth' during the short time of the present life become entirely unrelated to them, without exception. Therefore, the five strands of sensual pleasure are indeed like a dream; they bring only much suffering and despair. In these sensual pleasures, there is no refuge, only many faults and dangers.

(7) Yācitakūpamā kāmā = Sensual pleasures are like
185: borrowed goods that are used only for a short time. To illustrate: in this world, a person who has no property of their own might borrow items such as diamonds, gems, gold, and silver to wear and enjoy for a festival. Before they have to return them to the owner, they can wear and use them with a joyful and smiling face as if they were their own property. However, when the time for the loan expires and they must return them, or when the owner comes to take them back, they are left with nothing of those borrowed goods in their hands and remain brooding with a dejected face. In the same way, many people in this world enjoy and experience the sensual pleasures that arise for them according to the results of their wholesome kamma. When they experience them, they tend to perceive those sensual pleasures as if they were permanent. When those sensual objects are destroyed by the oppression of some unwholesome kamma, or when the person dies, those sensual pleasures become entirely unrelated to them. The person who once thought of themselves as the owner of those pleasures is left with empty hands and must face the consequences accordingly. Therefore, the five strands of sensual pleasure are indeed like borrowed goods used for a short time; they bring only much suffering and despair. In these sensual pleasures, there is no refuge, only many faults and dangers.
186: (8) Rukkhaphalūpamā kāmā = Sensual pleasures are like a tree laden with fruit. The comparison is as follows: In a forest not far from a village or town, there might be a large tree laden with sweet fruit. A man seeking fruit enters the forest, wanders about, and seeing that tree, thinks: 'This tree is full of sweet fruit. There are no fruits fallen on the ground, but I am skilled in climbing trees. I shall climb this tree, eat my fill, and also gather fruit in the folds of my garment.' Having thought so, he climbs the tree, eats his fill, and gathers fruit in the folds of his garment. Then, a second man comes along carrying an axe, also seeking fruit. Seeing the same tree, he thinks: 'This tree is full of sweet fruit. There are no fruits fallen on the ground, and I am not skilled in climbing trees. I shall cut this tree down from the root, eat my fill, and gather fruit in the folds of my garment.' He then cuts the tree down from the root. If the first man who had already climbed the tree does not descend quickly before the tree falls, he might break his arms or legs as the tree crashes down. He might suffer lethal pain, or even meet his death.
187:
In the same way, while a person is enjoying and consuming a wealth of sensual objects, another person might approach and attack, strike, or shoot him to plunder those sensual objects. If the first possessor of sensual pleasures cannot quickly abandon those objects before the attack, striking, or shooting occurs, he might suffer broken limbs due to the assault over those objects, or reach lethal suffering, or even die. If he dies with a lingering attachment to sensual pleasures, he will experience various sufferings, such as falling into the woeful states (apāya). Therefore, sensual pleasures are indeed like a tree laden with fruit; they bring much suffering and despair. In these sensual pleasures, there is no refuge, and faults are many.

(Alternatively) Sensual pleasures are like a ripe poisonous fruit. The comparison is as follows: The ripe poisonous fruit called Kiṃpakka (or Kimphala) resembles a very delightful ripe sweet mango. It is perfect in color, scent, and taste, appearing delicious to those who see it. However, it causes suffering even unto death for those who eat it. Those who eat that poisonous fruit, lured only by its fine color, scent, and taste, will have their intestines and liver shredded; they will writhe in agony like one who has drunk a mixture of diamond dust and lime juice, suffering great exhaustion and—
188:
—meeting their end in death and destruction. Similarly, sensual pleasures appear in various attractive ways to those who lack the eye of wisdom, putting on an outward show of delight. Those who, being attached and captivated by such outward appearances of pleasure, consume and possess these sensual pleasures, will find the unwholesome poisons of greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha) surging through their entire bodies. They will writhe in various dangers such as burning and grief, eventually dying a helpless death. After death, having been poisoned by sensual pleasures, they do not reach a happy destination (sugati) but must face dangers such as falling into the woeful states (apāya). Therefore, sensual pleasures are indeed like a ripe poisonous fruit; they bring much suffering and despair. In these sensual pleasures, there is no refuge, and faults are many.

(9) Asisūnūpamā kāmā = Sensual pleasures are like a butcher's chopping block where things are cut with swords and knives. The comparison is as follows: In the world, criminals, deer, and other animals are slaughtered upon a chopping block. Their meat is also minced and chopped on that very block. The chopping block is the place where beings are killed and meat is minced. Similarly, sensual pleasures mince all those who are attached to them with the swords of sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā) and—
189:
—lead them to destruction. All those who have placed their necks upon the chopping block of sensual pleasures (those who are attached to them) are unable to establish the element of renunciation (nekkhamma-dhātu) which leads to the broad open paths of tranquility meditation (samatha-bhāvanā) and insight meditation (vipassanā-bhāvanā). Instead, they are hacked and sliced by the swords of sensual craving on that very chopping block of sensual pleasures, meeting a miserable death and destruction. Therefore, sensual pleasures are indeed like a butcher's chopping block where one is minced by swords; they bring much suffering and despair. In these sensual pleasures, there is no refuge, and faults are many.

(10) Sattisūlūpamā kāmā = Sensual pleasures are like the sharp blade of a sword or the point of a spear. The comparison is as follows: An extremely sharp sword-blade or spear-point cuts and pierces whatever it touches. A sword or spear is meant only for stabbing, killing, or hacking enemies. Similarly, sensual pleasures, having extremely sharp power, pierce and wound all those who come into contact or become entangled with them. For example, a person pierced by the sword-blade or spear-point of visual objects (rūpārammaṇa) is like a fish caught on a hook; unable to quickly extract the piercing of that visual object, he remains submissive to its will. Because of the wound—
190:
—inflicted by that spear, he can no longer remember or care for the virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā) he previously guarded and cultivated, leading to his ruin and loss. (The same applies to sounds and other sense objects.) The five spears of the five strands of sensual pleasure are meant only to stab and destroy beings. All beings who have not yet abandoned sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā) live like prisoners or criminals, caught between the sword-blades and spear-points of the five sense objects aimed directly at them in whatever destination (gati) they reach. These five sense objects pierce any being they encounter without mercy, according to their nature. Therefore, sensual pleasures are indeed like the sharp blade of a sword or the point of a spear; they bring much suffering and despair. In these sensual pleasures, there is no refuge, and faults are many.

(11) Sappasirūpamā kāmā = Sensual pleasures are like the head of a venomous snake. The comparison is as follows: The head of a venomous snake is full of harsh and potent venom, making it loathsome and terrifying. Just as the head of a venomous snake brings various dangers to those who touch it, so too are sensual pleasures loathsome and terrifying, for they are filled with the 'poison' of defilements (kilesa) that causes the bad blood of corruption to arise in all those they touch or bite.
191:
Just as the head of a venomous snake provides no benefit in the world but only causes harm, so too do sensual pleasures cause only various fears and dangers for the people of the world. Just as a person who touches or steps on the head of a venomous snake meets with great peril, so too does a person who touches or steps on the snake's head of sensual pleasures meet with great peril. Therefore, sensual pleasures are indeed like the head of a venomous snake; they bring much suffering and despair. In these sensual pleasures, there is no refuge, and faults are many.

(This collection of teachings on the disadvantages of sensual pleasures is written based on the Potaliya Sutta of the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, page 27.)

'Great terrifying danger' is a name for the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Suffering' is a name for the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Disease' is a name for the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'A great tumor' is a name for the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Entanglement and bonding' is a name for the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'A great swamp difficult to cross' is a name for the five strands of sensual pleasure. (From the Chakka Nipāta, Aṅguttara Nikāya, page 274.)

Even this great throne and royal luxury, like the Vejayanta palace of Sakka, the King of Devas, is like a—
192:
—cemetery where corpses are buried. The three realms of existence—the sensual realm (kāma-bhava), the fine-material realm (rūpa-bhava), and the immaterial realm (arūpa-bhava)—are like a great house engulfed in blazing flames. All beings—humans, devas, and brahmās—must undergo conception, aging, sickness, and death. After death, they must undergo conception again. After conception, they must again face aging, sickness, and death. They are greatly exhausted and distressed by conception, aging, sickness, and death. Being so, they do not know the way to escape from the dangers of aging, sickness, and death. When will they ever know?

Having contemplated and realized the terrifying nature of birth (jāti), aging (jarā), sickness (byādhi), and death (maraṇa), and seeing how the two types of sensual pleasure—objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective defilement (kilesa-kāma)—and the three realms of existence offer little satisfaction but are full of faults, the Great Bodhisatta's mind became free from excessive attachment to the five strands of sensual pleasure. He uttered the solemn exclamation: 'Upaddutaṃ vata bho = Oh, how oppressed! Upassaṭṭhaṃ vata bho = Oh, how afflicted!' His mind inclined strongly toward renouncing the world to become a monk.

The Bodhisatta Prince thought, 'I should renounce the world this very day.' Rising from his magnificent couch, he went near the door and asked, 'Who is there?' The minister Channa, who was sleeping with his head against the threshold, replied, 'My Lord, it is I, Channa.' The Bodhisatta—
193:
The Prince commanded, “I wish to renounce the world today. Go now and quickly prepare a noble Sindh horse of great speed, without informing anyone.” The minister Channa replied, “Very well, my Lord,” and taking the horse’s trappings, went to the stable. There, under a canopy of jasmine flowers where scented lamps were burning brightly, he saw the noble horse Kanthaka standing on a delightful ground, a horse capable of conquering all enemies. He thought, “Tonight, I must prepare this very auspicious horse named Kanthaka for my Lord’s renunciation,” and he fully equipped Kanthaka with all the necessary trappings.

As soon as Kanthaka was harnessed and adorned, he thought, “This harnessing and adorning today is very firm and tight. It is not like on other days when we go to play in the royal gardens. Without a doubt, tonight my Lord will mount me and depart on the Great Renunciation to become a monk.” Knowing this, with a heart full of great joy and delight, he neighed loudly. The sound of Kanthaka’s joyful neighing could have filled and echoed throughout the entire city of Kapilavatthu; however, the deities prevented anyone from hearing the horse’s neighing.
194:
While his companion Channa was going to prepare Kanthaka, the Bodhisatta thought, “I will look upon my son before I depart.” He rose from where he was and went to the chamber of Princess Yasodharā, the mother of Rāhula, and opened the door. At that time, scented lamps were still burning brightly within the chamber. Princess Yasodharā, the mother of Rāhula, was sleeping on a noble bed strewn with about a basketful of jasmine and Arabian jasmine flowers, with her hand resting upon the head of her son.

Standing with his foot on the threshold, the Bodhisatta looked in and thought, “If I move the Princess’s hand and take my son in my arms, Yasodharā will wake up. If she wakes up, it will be an obstacle to my renunciation, as I am about to depart right now. Let it be... I will not look at my son now. Only after I have become a Buddha will I come back to see my son.” Having thought thus, he descended from the golden palace and went near the horse Kanthaka, saying:

“My dear companion Kanthaka, please help and protect me for just this one night. Depending on you, after I have become a Buddha, I shall deliver the world of beings, including the devas, from the current of Saṃsāra to the dry land of Nibbāna.”

After saying this, he leaped up and mounted the back of the horse Kanthaka.
195:
The royal horse Kanthaka was eighteen cubits in length from the neck onwards; he was endowed with proportions suitable to that length, and possessed great speed and immense strength. His entire body was pure white, with a beautiful color like a freshly polished conch shell. Then, the Bodhisatta mounted the horse Kanthaka, positioning himself in the middle of the horse’s back, and had his companion-by-birth, the minister Channa, hold onto the horse’s tail. At the stroke of midnight on Monday, the full moon day of Āsāḷha in the year 97 of the Great Era, he departed from the golden palace and reached the main gate of the royal city. (When he departed from the golden palace riding the horse Kanthaka, the devas held the horse’s hooves with their hands every time they touched the ground so that the people would not hear the sound of the hooves.)

## The Intentions of the Bodhisatta, Minister Channa,
## and the Royal Horse Kanthaka

At that time, King Suddhodana had previously made arrangements, thinking, “If I arrange it in this way, my son the Bodhisatta will not be able to open the city gate and leave at any unexpected time.” To prevent the renunciation, he had reinforced the two leaves of the main city gate so that each leaf could only be opened by the strength of a thousand men.

The Bodhisatta was naturally endowed with great strength, possessing the strength of a thousand crores of Kālāvaka elephants.
196:
and he possessed the strength of ten billion average men (majjhima-purisa). Thus, the Great Being thought, “If the city gate does not open, today I will use my own strength. While remaining seated on Kanthaka’s back, I will squeeze the horse Kanthaka with my thighs, along with Channa who is holding the tail, and leap over the eighteen-cubit high wall of the city of Kapilavatthu.”

Channa also thought, “If the city gate does not open, I will have my Lord sit on my shoulders, tuck the horse Kanthaka under my right arm, and carrying them with my right hand, I will leap over the eighteen-cubit high wall of the city of Kapilavatthu.”

The state horse Kanthaka also thought, “If the city gate does not open, I will leap over the eighteen-cubit high wall of the city of Kapilavatthu with my Master sitting on my back as usual, along with my companion Channa who is holding my tail.”

## The Physical Strength of the Bodhisatta

(One elephant of the Kālāwaka breed has the strength of ten average men. One Gaṅgeyya elephant has the strength of ten Kālāwaka elephants (the strength of 100 men). One Paṇḍara elephant has the strength of ten Gaṅgeyya elephants (the strength of 1,000 men). One Tamba elephant has the strength of ten Paṇḍara elephants (the strength of 10,000 men). One Piṅgala elephant
197:
has the strength of ten Tamba elephants (the strength of 100,000 men). One Gandha elephant has the strength of ten Piṅgala elephants (the strength of 1,000,000 men). One Maṅgala elephant has the strength of ten Gandha elephants (the strength of 10,000,000 men). One Hema elephant has the strength of ten Maṅgala elephants (the strength of 100,000,000 men). One Uposatha elephant has the strength of ten Hema elephants (the strength of 1,000,000,000 men). One Chaddanta elephant has the strength of ten Uposatha elephants (the strength of 10,000,000,000 men). Bodhisattas possess the strength of ten Chaddanta elephants (the strength of 100,000,000,000 men). — From Aṅguttara Commentary, Vol. 3, page 293, etc.)

## The Obstruction by Vasavattī Māra

Thus, the intentions of the three were very similar. If the palace city gate had not opened, any one of the three would have fulfilled their intention. However, due to the power of the Great Being’s merit and perfections, the deities guarding the city gate were joyful and opened the main gate in advance, ready for the Bodhisatta’s departure.

As soon as the Bodhisatta, riding Kanthaka and accompanied by Channa, emerged from the city gate, Vasavattī Māra—who never delights in the liberation of beings from Saṃsāra and always opposes and obstructs—descended from his abode in the Paranimmita-vasavattī heaven. In an instant, as quickly as a strong man might stretch his bent arm or bend his stretched arm,
198:
he arrived before the Bodhisatta to prevent and obstruct him by using deceptive and enticing words, pretending to be concerned for his welfare. Standing in the air, he said:

*Mā nikkhamā mahāvīra, ito te sattame dine.*
*Dibbaṃ tu cakkaratanaṃ, addhā pātu bhavissati.*
(From the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary)

“O Great Hero, Prince of great effort! Do not depart to become a monk. For this reason: on the seventh day from today, the divine Wheel Treasure (Cakkaratana) will surely and certainly appear to you.”

“You shall become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) ruling over the four great islands and their two thousand surrounding small islands. Turn back, O Prince!” Thus he spoke to stop him. Then the Bodhisatta asked, “Who are you that speaks thus to stop me?” Māra replied, “O Prince, I am the King of Māras, Vasavattī.” Then the Bodhisatta said:

*Jānāmahaṃ mahārāja, mayhaṃ cakkassa sambhavaṃ.*
*Anatthikohaṃ rajjena, gaccha tvaṃ māra mā idha.*

“O Māra of great power! Regarding the fact that the divine Wheel Treasure
199:
endowed with celestial majesty will surely arrive for me, I already knew this long before you. As for me, I have not the slightest desire for the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch. O Māra! Go away now to another place. Do not stand here in front of me to oppose and obstruct my purpose.”

*Sakalaṃ dasasahassampi, lokadhātumahaṃ pana.*
*Unnādetvā bhavissāmi, buddho loke vināyako.*

“As for me, I shall strive to become a Buddha, the Knower of all Truths (Sacca-ñeyya-dhamma), who, after making the entire ten thousand world systems shake and echo like a potter’s wheel on its axis, will lead and deliver the multitude of beings to the sanctuary of Nibbāna, the land of victory.”

After he spoke these bold and fiery words, Māra said, “Friend Siddhattha, mark my words well. From this moment on, whenever a thought of sensuality (kāma-vitakka), a thought of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka), or a thought of cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka) arises in your mind, I shall make you know who I am.” From that time onwards, he followed him like a shadow.
200:
For seven years, Māra followed the Bodhisatta closely like a shadow, constantly watching for any opportunity where defilements might arise in the Bodhisatta's mind. (He followed the Bodhisatta's every step for seven years with the intent that if any defilement were to arise in the Bodhisatta's mind, he would kill him right then and there.)

## The Devas and Brahmas Escorting the Bodhisatta to the Anomā River with Great Ceremony

When the Bodhisatta was twenty-nine years old, he resolutely renounced the glory of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), which was almost within his reach, as if it were a drop of spittle. Leaving behind a palace as magnificent as that of a Universal Monarch, he departed at midnight on Monday, the full moon day of the month of Āsāḷha, in the year 97 of the Great Era (Mahā-sakkarāj), while the moon was in the Āsāḷhī constellation. Riding the royal horse Kanthaka and accompanied by his courtier Channa, who was born on the same day as he, a desire arose within the Bodhisatta to look back once more at the royal city of Kapilavatthu.

Immediately after this thought occurred to the Bodhisatta, the earth in that place turned around like a potter's wheel, as if to say, "O Great Being, you have not performed deeds that require you to turn back and look. You have only performed deeds that will spontaneously bring what you wish to see before your eyes without you having to turn around." Thus, without having to turn back intentionally, the Great Being was able to look upon the city of Kapilavatthu while remaining in his original position.
201:
That spot of earth became the place where the royal horse Kanthaka stopped, marked as the site of the Kanthaka-nivattana Stupa. With a vast and magnificent array of offerings and honors, the Bodhisatta proceeded on his journey, riding the horse Kanthaka. At that time, along the path where the Bodhisatta traveled, groups of Devas and Brahmas from the four directions—front, back, left, and right—followed him, each group carrying sixty thousand torches (according to the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, it was six million torches each). Other Devas and Brahmas followed, surrounding and honoring him with fragrant flower garlands, sandalwood powder, yak-tail whisks, banners, flags, and jasmine bouquets. They sang celestial songs and played various divine musical instruments.

Traveling with this magnificent glory, the Great Being crossed three kingdoms—Sakiya, Koliya, and Malla—in a single night, covering a distance of thirty yojanas, and arrived at the banks of the Anomā River.

(Special Note: The royal horse Kanthaka possessed the speed and power to run around the edge of the universe and return to eat its prepared breakfast within the morning hours. However, at that time, Devas, Brahmas, Nagas, and Garudas stood in the sky and showered offerings such as fragrant flowers, which covered the ground up to the horse's navel. Because the horse had to struggle through these flowers as if wading through mud, it took the entire night to travel only thirty yojanas.)
202:
## Chapter 4
## The Renunciation and Cutting of the Hair
## Crossing to the Other Bank of the Anomā River and Cutting the Hair

Upon reaching the bank of the Anomā River, the Great Being stopped the horse at the water's edge and asked the courtier Channa, "What is the name of this river?" When Channa replied, "Your Majesty, this river is named Anomā," the Great Being took it as an auspicious omen, thinking, "My monkhood shall also be not inferior (anomā), but noble and excellent." (The word 'Anomā' signifies 'not inferior' or 'superior'.) Giving a signal to the horse by touching it with his heel to cross the river, Kanthaka leaped from this bank and landed on the other side of the Anomā River, which was eight usabhas wide.

The Great Being dismounted from the horse's back, stood on the sandy beach which resembled a heap of pearls, and said to Channa, "Friend Channa, take my ornaments and the horse Kanthaka and return to the kingdom. I shall become a monk."

When Channa requested, "Your Majesty, I too wish to become a monk," the Great Being refused him three times, saying, "Friend Channa, you do not have the opportunity to become a monk now; you must return to the kingdom." He then handed over his ornaments and the horse Kanthaka to his companion Channa.
203:
Then the Great Being thought, “This hair of mine is not suitable for a monk; I shall cut it with a sword.” Holding the sword in his right hand and the topknot together with the crown in his left hand, he cut it off. The remaining hair, two finger-breadths in length, curled to the right and remained close to his head. Throughout his life, his hair remained at that length of two finger-breadths without needing to be shaved or cut again. His beard and mustache also remained for the rest of his life in a manner that was beautiful and dignified, just like his hair. For the Bodhisatta, there was no further need to shave the hair, beard, or mustache.

## Making an Act of Truth and Tossing
## the Shorn Hair into the Sky

The Bodhisatta, holding the topknot together with the crown, made an act of truth (adhiṭṭhāna), saying, “If I am indeed to become a Buddha, let this topknot remain in the sky. If I am not to become a Buddha, let it fall to the ground.” He then tossed it into the sky. The topknot with the crown rose one yojana into the air and remained there miraculously, like a floral garland suspended in the sky.

## Sakka Receiving it with a Golden Casket
## and Establishing the “Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya” in Tāvatiṃsa

Then Sakka, the lord of devas, saw the hair with his celestial eye. He received the topknot and crown with a jeweled casket one yojana in size and took it to his abode,
204:
the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. There, he enshrined it and built the Cūḷāmaṇi Stupa, three yojanas high and adorned with the seven kinds of gems, for worship.

## Becoming a Monk with the Requisites Offered by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma

Next, the Bodhisatta reflected, "These royal garments of mine, made of Kāsī cloth, are very costly. They are not suitable for one who is a monk." At that time, the Great Brahma Ghaṭīkāra, who had been a close friend since the time of Kassapa Buddha, thought with pure and true metta that had remained unchanged throughout a Buddhantara Kappa: "Ah, today my friend, the Bodhisatta Prince, has seen the dangers of birth and other fears, and has departed on the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana). I shall go and bring the monk's requisites for my dear friend."

He brought the eight requisites (parikkhāra) used by monks and offered them to the Bodhisatta: (1) the double robe (saṅghāṭī), (2) the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), (3) the under robe (antaravāsaka), (4) the girdle (kāyabandhana)—these four are the inner requisites; (5) needle and thread, (6) a razor/knife, (7) an alms bowl with its bag, and (8) a water filter—these four are the outer requisites.

The Bodhisatta then donned the robes, which are the banner of Arahatship, offered by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma. Having assumed the noble appearance of a monk, he tossed his royal garments into the sky.
205:
(The interval between one Buddha and another is called a Buddhantara Kappa. In this section regarding the offering of the Brahma robes, the Buddhantara Kappa refers to the interval from the time of Kassapa Buddha to the time of the current Gotama Buddha. This interval is very long, spanning more than one Antara Kappa, because after Kassapa Buddha appeared when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the lifespan decreased to ten years, then increased again to an incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) period, and then decreased again until it reached one hundred years, at which point Gotama Buddha appeared. Here, although there was no teacher to instruct the Bodhisatta on how to wear and wrap the robes, it should be noted that he was able to wear the requisites properly because he had been a monk under previous Buddhas and was accustomed to it, and also because of his great wisdom.)

## The Enshrinement of the Bodhisatta’s Royal Garments
## in the “Dussa Cetiya” in the Akaniṭṭha Brahma Realm

At that time, Ghaṭikāra Brahma took the royal garments that the Bodhisatta had tossed into the sky and built a cetiya twelve yojanas high made of various jewels, enshrining the garments within it for worship. That cetiya is called the Dussa Cetiya because it is the place where the garments (dussa) are enshrined.

(Regarding this, the location and height of the Dussa Cetiya are mentioned on page 223 of the second volume of the Samantacakkhu-dīpanī: “Since Ghaṭikāra Brahma took the robes, and Ghaṭikāra Brahma is from the Akaniṭṭha realm, it should be noted that the Dussa Cetiya is in the Akaniṭṭha realm.” Also in the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā...)
206:
...referencing these, the Mon-yway Zetawun Sayadaw wrote in detail: "It should be noted that in the Suddhāvāsa Akanittha Brahma realm, there is the Dussa Ceti, twelve leagues in height." (A separate point.)

Regarding the eight requisites offered by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma, the Apadāna Commentary, Volume 1, page 128, explains uniquely: "Having received the eight requisites that appeared within the bud of a Paduma lotus at the site of the Mahābodhi terrace at the beginning of the aeon as a sign of the world, brought by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma, which arose through the power of the Bodhisatta's merit and perfections, he went forth as a monk." Relying on this explanation from the Apadāna Commentary, it is composed in the Saṃvara Pyo: "In the cycle of rebirth, when the auspicious signs appeared at the beginning of the Bhadda-kappa, at the center of all lands, the golden terrace of the Bodhi tree, within the swelling buds of the five branches, the forty requisites of the Buddha were present, while the Brahma bowed his head with a joyful heart," and so on. The Jinatthapakāsanī also states: "These eight requisites were included in the lotus that grew as a preliminary sign at the beginning of the aeon."

However, in the Mahāpadāna Sutta Commentary of the Dīgha Nikāya, page 5, it says: "The site of the Mahābodhi is the last to be destroyed when the world perishes and the first to be established when the world is formed. At the beginning of the aeon, a Paduma lotus grove grows there as a sign. If a Buddha is to arise in that aeon, flowers bloom in that grove. If no Buddha arises, no lotus blooms. If one Buddha is to arise, one flower blooms. If two Buddhas are to arise, two flowers bloom; if three, three flowers; if four, four flowers; and if five Buddhas are to arise, five flowers bloom on a single stalk." Thus, only the blooming or non-blooming of the lotus is mentioned; it does not mention the eight requisites being present in the lotus.
207:
Regarding the robes offered by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma, although the Apadāna Commentary explains them as "iddhimaya-parikkhāra" (requisites created by the power of the Bodhisatta's merit), the Sutta Nipāta Commentary, Volume 2, page 111, in the chapter where the Bodhisatta enters Rājagaha for alms after renouncing, states: "Having donned the devadattiya paṃsukūla robes offered by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma and taking the earthen bowl, he entered the city through the eastern gate and wandered for alms from house to house."
