Considering this explanation by the Great Elder Mahābuddhaghosa, it should be understood that in his view, the robes offered by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma were not "iddhimaya" but "devadattiya" (given by a deity). This is presented for consideration as to whether the requisites offered by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma were indeed those that appeared in the lotus at the Mahābodhi terrace at the beginning of the aeon.

## Sending Minister Channa Back to the Royal Capital

After renouncing, the Bodhisatta sent Minister Channa back, saying, "Friend Channa, go and report to my mother (referring to his foster mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī) and my father that I am free from illness and well." Channa paid respectful homage to the Bodhisatta, circumambulated him to the right, and taking the bundle of ornaments worn by the Bodhisatta and leading the royal horse Kanthaka, he departed from the Bodhisatta in sorrow.
208:
## The Death of the Horse Kanthaka and Rebirth as a Deity in Heaven

From the moment the royal horse Kanthaka heard the words spoken by the Great Being to Minister Channa, he thought with longing, "From now on, there is no more opportunity to see my master again." As soon as he passed beyond the range of the Great Being's sight, he could not bear the sorrow (soka) arising from the suffering of separation from his beloved master (piyehi vippayoga dukkha). His heart burst, and he died, becoming a deity named Kanthaka in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. As for Minister Channa, who was already grieving over the separation from the Great Being, he was now doubly afflicted by the intense sorrow of Kanthaka's death, and he returned to the capital of Kapilavatthu weeping and lamenting.

(The Vimānavatthu Commentary, starting from page 293, explains that after Kanthaka died, he became a deity named "Kanthaka" endowed with great celestial splendor in Tāvatiṃsa. It states that because Kanthaka had served the Bodhisatta faithfully over many lifetimes, he could not endure the suffering of separation and died of a broken heart. However, he did not become a deity because of that sorrow. Rather, when the Bodhisatta was about to mount Kanthaka for the Great Renunciation, he heard the Bodhisatta say, "Kanthaka, I am renouncing to attain the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience." Hearing these words, great joy and rapture (pīti-somanassa) associated with renunciation (nekkhamma) and free from sensual desires arose, along with clarity of mind led by faith (pasāda-saddhā). Due to the power of that merit, he was reborn as a deity in Tāvatiṃsa.)
210:
wander for alms." Having made this resolution, he donned the paṃsukūla robes offered by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma, held the earthen bowl in his golden hands, entered the city through the eastern gate, and wandered for alms from house to house.

In Rājagaha, seven days prior to the Bodhisatta's arrival, a great festival had been celebrated with much joy. On the day the Bodhisatta entered for alms, King Bimbisāra had ordered the drum to be beaten to announce to the citizens: "The festival is over; everyone must return to their respective duties." Thus, a great multitude of people was still gathered at the royal courtyard. King Bimbisāra, while opening the lion-supported palace window to manage various affairs and looking out at the crowd, saw the Bodhisatta entering Rājagaha for alms with extremely calm and composed faculties.

When the citizens of Rājagaha beheld the peerless and supreme beauty of the Bodhisatta, the whole city was thrown into a stir and commotion, just as when the elephant king Dhanapāla (also known as Nālāgiri) entered Rājagaha, or as when the Asura King Vepacitti entered the celestial city of Tāvatiṃsa. As the Great Being wandered for alms from house to house in Rājagaha with the grace of a Chaddanta elephant king, the city dwellers...
211:
beheld the peerless and supreme beauty of the Bodhisatta and were filled with intense joy and amazement, their minds focused solely on gazing at his form.

Among those people, one person said to another, "O friend, what is this? Has the great Moon Mansion, fearing the Asura Rāhu, hidden its rays and descended to this world of men?"

Hearing this, a second person said mockingly to the first, "O friend, what are you saying? When have you ever seen the full moon descend to the human world? In truth, this is the God of Love (Kāma) who, having taken another form, has come to play and enjoy himself with us, having seen the supreme splendor and glory of our King and the citizens."

Hearing this, a third person likewise said mockingly to the second, "O friend, have you gone mad? The God of Love is one whose body is scorched and blackened by the fire of anger arising from his pride of power. In reality, this is none other than the thousand-eyed King of Devas, Sakka, who has entered our city of Rājagaha, perhaps mistaking it for the Tāvatiṃsa heaven."
212:
A fourth person, smiling slightly, said to the third person, “O friend, what are you saying? Your words are quite contradictory. If you say he is Sakka, the King of Devas, where are his thousand eyes? Where is his Vajira weapon? Where is his royal elephant, Erāvaṇa? (If he were truly Sakka, he would possess the thousand eyes, the Vajira weapon, and the elephant Erāvaṇa. Now, none of these are present.) In truth, he is the Great Brahma who, seeing the negligence of the brahmins, has come to urge them to follow the Vedas and other practices without negligence.”

Rebuking all four of them, another wise man said, “This person is neither the full moon, nor the god of love (Kāma), nor Sakka the King of Devas who possesses a thousand eyes, nor the Great Brahma. In fact, he is a marvelous and extraordinary person, a supreme leader and teacher who is the forerunner of the three worlds.”

While the citizens of Rājagaha were thus conversing among themselves in various ways, the king's men went to King Bimbisāra and reported, “Your Majesty, a marvelous person—whom we cannot distinguish as a celestial king from the upper realms, a Gandhabba, a Naga king, or a Yakkha—is wandering for alms within our city of Rājagaha.” Upon hearing their words, King Bimbisāra stood on the upper terrace of his palace and...
213:
Upon seeing the Noble Bodhisatta, King Bimbisāra was filled with an unprecedented sense of wonder. He addressed his ministers and attendants, saying, “Friends, go and observe that marvelous person closely. If he is a Yakkha, he will vanish upon reaching the outskirts of the city. If he is a deity, he will travel through the sky. If he is a Naga king, he will dive into the earth and disappear. If he is a true human being, he will eat the alms-food he has received in some place.” With these instructions, he sent them forth.

The Bodhisatta, with peaceful faculties and a peaceful mind, as if drawing the eyes of the citizens of Rājagaha who gazed upon the incomparable beauty of his form, looked only a yoke’s length (about four cubits) ahead. He accepted only enough mixed alms-food (missaka-piṇḍapāta)—a mixture of red, white, speckled, coarse, and fine food—for his sustenance. He then asked the townspeople, “Where do the monks who arrive in this city usually reside?” When the people informed him, “Monks who arrive in this city usually reside in the cave facing east at the summit of Paṇḍava Hill,” the Noble Bodhisatta departed from the city through the same eastern gate by which he had entered. He went to the cave facing east on the summit of Paṇḍava Hill, sat down facing east, and prepared to consume the mixed coarse and fine alms-food he had collected.

Having enjoyed royal luxury as great as that of a Cakkavatti king only a few days prior, he now faced this extremely coarse food of various colors and textures...
214:
As he prepared to eat a morsel of that mixed alms-food and was about to put it into his mouth, he felt an intense revulsion, as he had never even seen such food in this lifetime. His intestines seemed to turn upside down, and he suffered such distress that he felt like vomiting. At that moment, the Noble Bodhisatta admonished himself: “Friend Siddhattha, although you were a ruler in the golden palace, where you could easily obtain pleasant food and drink and consume scented Shali rice stored for three years with various exquisite flavors as you desired, did you not go forth and become a monk after seeing a monk clad in rag-robes (pāṃsukūla)? Did you not then think, ‘When shall I, having become a monk like this one, wander from house to house for alms and eat whatever food I receive? When will such a time come for me?’ Now that you have reached this time when your wish is fulfilled, why do you act in such a distorted manner?” Thus, he disciplined himself and, without any further wavering, consumed that very coarse food.

The three royal messengers sent by King Bimbisāra approached the Bodhisatta and observed all his actions. Two of them remained near the Bodhisatta, while one messenger returned to King Bimbisāra and reported, “Your Majesty, that monk who went for alms is now sitting comfortably at the cave facing east on the summit of Paṇḍava Hill, eating the alms-food he received without any hesitation...
215:
...just like a lion king, a tiger king, or a noble bull, without any fear.” Upon hearing the messenger's words, King Bimbisāra did not delay. He set out for Paṇḍava Hill, where the Bodhisatta was, in a noble chariot. He traveled by chariot as far as the ground permitted, then dismounted and approached the Bodhisatta on foot. With the Bodhisatta's permission, he sat on a cool stone slab. Greatly inspired by the Bodhisatta's posture and demeanor, he spoke pleasant words of greeting and said, “Friend, you are still young and in the prime of youth. You are endowed with a perfect stature and complexion. I perceive you to be a pure Khattiya of noble birth. I offer you the sovereignty over both the Anga and Magadha kingdoms, which I rule, according to your desire. Please rule the kingdom. Also, please tell me of your lineage and family.” Thus, he invited him with the offer of royal power.

Then the Bodhisatta thought, “If I desired kingship, even the four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika) and other celestial rulers would invite me with the luxuries of their respective realms. Or, if I had continued to rule in my palace, I would certainly have become a Cakkavatti king. This King Bimbisāra, not knowing this, speaks to me thus and invites me with royal power.
216:
I shall now let King Bimbisāra know clearly that I am indeed a king.” Having considered this, he raised his arm, pointed in the direction from which he had come, and said:

(1) Ujuṃ janapado rāja, himavantassa passato.
Dhanavīriyena sampanno, kosalesu niketino.

“O King, who pleases the citizens with the four ways of showing favor (saṅgaha-dhamma) and loves them with metta! In the Kosala country, there is a region belonging to my father, the Great Suddhodana, who is of the Solar lineage (Ādicca) and whose royal line has been preserved since the beginning of the world. That kingdom of Kapilavatthu lies straight from here, to the north, near the Himalaya mountains. It is a land abundant in grain and food, flourishing with glory like the celestial city of Amaravatī. It is endowed with the seven treasures of wealth and is filled with eighty-two thousand brave warriors who are so courageous that they could even pluck a star from the sky. It is so complete that the one hundred and one other kings do not dare to challenge or show pride against it.”

(2) Ādiccā nāma gottena, sākiyā nāma jātiyā.
Tamhā kulā pabbajitomhi, na kāme abhipatthayaṃ.

“O King! By lineage (gotta), I belong to the pure race known as Ādicca, which is not different from the Sun God.
217:
By birth (jāti), I belong to the powerful Sakyan race, whose name was established by King Okkāka with the words ‘Sakya vata bho kumārā’. From that pure Ādicca lineage and Sakyan royal family, I have gone forth as a monk with the aspiration to become a Buddha. I have not gone forth because I long for or desire the objects of sensual pleasure (kāma).

(3) Kāmesvādīnavaṃ disvā, nekkhaṃmaṃ daṭṭhu khemato.
Padhānāya gamissāmi, ettha me rañjatī mano.

“O King! Having clearly seen with wisdom the danger (ādīnava) in sensual pleasures—that they provide little satisfaction and much suffering—and having clearly seen with wisdom that renunciation (nekkhamma), the departure from both the objects and the defilements of pleasure, is a state of safety (khema), I have gone forth as a monk with the aspiration to become a Buddha. I shall now go to strive (padhāna) to attain Nibbāna, which is called Padhāna because it is superior to all other phenomena (dhamma) due to its quality of peace and true renunciation. In that Nibbāna, which is superior to all phenomena, my mind finds delight and constantly yearns to attain it.”
218: With these three verses, the Noble Bodhisatta declared that he had gone forth from the Sakyan royal family, that he had no desire for sensual pleasures, and that as one who had gone forth solely for the sake of Nibbāna (Padhāna), he would now go to the forest to practice austerities (dukkharacariya) to swiftly attain that Nibbāna. When he had spoken, King Bimbisāra said to the Noble Bodhisatta, “Venerable Sir, I have heard long ago the news that ‘Prince Siddhattha, the son of King Suddhodana, after seeing the four great omens, will go forth, become a monk, and certainly become a Sammāsambuddha, the Supreme One of the three worlds.’ Now that I have personally witnessed Your Reverence's great foundation of renunciation (nekkhamma) and your firm intention (adhimutta-chanda) which seeks only Nibbāna, I believe without a doubt that you will certainly become a Buddha. Venerable Sir, I have one request to make: after you have attained Buddhahood, please visit my kingdom first.” Having made this solemn invitation, King Bimbisāra returned to the city of Rājagaha.
220:
220
was entering the city of Rājagaha, the Bodhisatta also set out on his journey to seek the bliss of Nibbāna, known as Santi-vara (the Supreme Peace). Traveling stage by stage, he reached the great teacher named Āḷāra, who was of the Kālāma clan.

(The section on seeking guidance and discussion with the great teachers Āḷāra and Uddaka is directly and extensively taught in the Pāḷi Canon. Although the Buddhavamsa Commentary, Jātaka Commentary, and others explain it very briefly, it is not easy for the readers of the Buddha's life story to access those Pāḷi texts. Therefore, in this Chronicle of the Buddha, the section on meeting these two great teachers will be presented with some elaboration. Here, one might ask: Why did the Bodhisatta not go to the great heretical teachers (who claimed to be Buddhas) such as Pūraṇa Kassapa, but instead went to Āḷāra and Uddaka? The practices of those heretical teachers were paths without any essence. The Great Being had personally practiced those paths ninety-one aeons ago to investigate whether they had essence or not. Through his own practice, he knew very well that they were essence-less. Therefore, instead of going to those heretical teachers, he went to the famous great teachers who were practicing the Dhamma in a forest, surrounded by many disciples.)

When the Bodhisatta reached the great teacher Āḷāra, he addressed him, saying, "O friend of the Kālāma clan, I wish to lead the holy life in this, your dispensation." The great teacher Āḷāra replied straightforwardly and encouragingly, "O Great One, you may stay in this dispensation of ours. The Dhamma
221:
221
that we are currently striving to practice is such that a wise person can, in no long time, personally realize the teacher's doctrine through their own higher knowledge, attain it, and dwell in it happily."

With the permission of the great teacher Āḷāra, the Bodhisatta learned and practiced their system of practice within a few days. Being a person of great wisdom, he mastered the doctrine and the path of practice taught by the teacher so easily that he reached the stage where he could say, "I know this practice," merely by moving his lips and repeating what the teacher had said. He personally claimed, "I know, I see," and this was acknowledged by the teacher and the disciples as well.

When the Bodhisatta reflected on how the great teacher Āḷāra explained their path of practice thoroughly up to the attainment of the (mundane) meditative absorption of the Sphere of Nothingness (Ākiñcaññāyatana), he realized: "It is not likely that the great teacher Āḷāra has merely learned this Dhamma up to the Sphere of Nothingness by rote through mere faith without the involvement of wisdom realized by himself. Surely, this teacher must be one who has personally attained and known the seven mundane meditative attainments (samāpatti)." Therefore, the Great Being approached Āḷāra again and asked directly,
222:
222
"O friend of the Kālāma clan, to what extent do you say that you have personally reached, realized, and dwell in this doctrine and path of practice?"

As he had personally realized it, Āḷāra explained in full the seven meditative attainments up to the Sphere of Nothingness, speaking not as one who merely recites from books, but as one who personally enters into those attainments.

Then, this thought arose in the Bodhisatta's mind: "Not only the great teacher Āḷāra has faith firm enough to reach these absorptions; I too have faith firm enough to reach them. Not only the great teacher Āḷāra has the energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom firm enough to reach the meditative attainments (appanā-jhāna); I too have the energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom firm enough to reach them. Since the teacher Āḷāra declares that he has personally reached, realized, and dwells happily in these seven mundane meditative attainments up to the Sphere of Nothingness through his own higher knowledge, it would be well if I were to strive and practice to personally reach and realize those seven mundane meditative attainments just as the teacher Āḷāra has."

With this thought, he practiced the preliminary exercises (parikamma) for the kasina meditations. Within a short time, in just two or three days, he personally realized and reached the seven mundane meditative attainments up to the Sphere of Nothingness, which the teacher Āḷāra had reached, and he dwelt in the bliss of those attainments.

The Great Being went to the teacher Āḷāra again and asked, "Friend Kālāma, is it to this extent
223:
223

"By this path of practice, friend, do you say that you have personally realized and dwell in these seven mundane meditative attainments (jhāna) through your own higher knowledge?" When he asked this, the Great Teacher Āḷāra confirmed that it was so. Then the Great Bodhisatta said, "Friend, I too, by this much path of practice, have personally realized, attained, and dwell happily in the seven mundane meditative attainments up to the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) through my own higher knowledge."

At that time, the Great Teacher Āḷāra, being a virtuous person free from the stains of envy and stinginess (issā-macchariya), spoke joyfully and heartily: "Friend, we have seen face-to-face such a sharp and wise fellow practitioner like your noble self. It is a great gain for us, friend!"

Issābhibhūta lokamhi,
āḷāro yo anissukī.
vaṇṇavādī sudhīrassa,
aho uḷārachandatā.

Issābhibhūta lokamhi = In this world overwhelmed by the evil trait of envy (issā), where people are unwilling to see others prosper. Yo āḷāro = that Great Teacher Āḷāra. Anissukī = being truly a virtuous person free from envy. Sudhīrassa = of the Great Bodhisatta, who possessed incomparable and sharp wisdom. Vaṇṇavādī = spoke words of praise openly. Sudhīrassa = of that faultless and wise one...
226:
Because of this, when he considered the current state and the future benefits to be gained in the next life from those seven mundane meditative attainments (lokiya samāpatti), he clearly saw the nature of those seven mundane attainments up to the Sphere of Nothingness (Ākiñcaññāyatana) in the present life, and how they would yield rebirth in the Brahma realm of Ākiñcaññāyatana in the next life. At that time, he came to the conclusion that these seven mundane meditative attainments were only things included within the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha). He reflected deeply: "This group of seven mundane meditative attainments does not lead to weariness with the round of rebirths; it does not lead to detachment; it does not lead to the cessation of defilements such as lust; it does not lead to the total calming of all defilements. It does not lead to the direct knowledge of all things that should be known; it does not lead to the attainment of the four Path-knowledges (magga-ñāṇa); it does not lead to the realization of Nibbāna. Indeed, even if these seven mundane meditative attainments yield the highest and most supreme result, they will only lead to the Brahma realm of Ākiñcaññāyatana, where the lifespan is sixty thousand great aeons (mahākappa). They cannot provide a benefit beyond that. Even that Brahma realm of Ākiñcaññāyatana, which is the result of such jhāna, is a place that is not yet free from the dangers of birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa). It is already surrounded by the snare of the King of Death."

Just as a man who is severely oppressed by hunger might obtain a delightful feast and eat it with great pleasure in the first part, but later, whether due to an upset of bile or phlegm, or because a fly has fallen into that feast, he becomes...
228:
...learned the doctrine and the path of practice of the teacher Uddaka's sect. Just as when he was learning under the great teacher Āḷāra, because he was a person of great wisdom, he was able to master the doctrine and path of practice taught by the teacher Uddaka very easily. Merely by moving his lips and repeating what the teacher said, he reached the stage where he could say, "I know this path of practice." He himself claimed, "I know, I see this doctrine," and the sect leader (Uddaka) and the disciples also acknowledged it.

When the Bodhisatta reflected on how the teacher Uddaka explained their path of practice according to the traditional teaching up to the attainment of the (mundane) jhāna of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), he realized: "It is not likely that Uddaka's father, the late great teacher Rāma, merely learned this path of practice up to the jhāna of Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana by rote through mere faith in what others said. Certainly, Uddaka's father, the teacher Rāma, must have been one who personally attained and knew the eight mundane meditative attainments."

(In this regard, at the time the teacher Uddaka was discussing this with the Bodhisatta, he himself had not yet attained the eight meditative attainments. He was only telling the Bodhisatta what his father, the teacher Rāma, had taught. As for the teacher Uddaka himself, after the Bodhisatta had learned the path of practice from him and attained the peak of the eight mundane meditative attainments (up to Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) within two or three days, and after the Bodhisatta had departed from him, he was moved by a great sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Since he was already one who practiced meditation, he strove and attained up to the jhāna of Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana...
229:
...as directly explained in the second volume of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa-ṭīkā, pages 139 and 140. Therefore, when the Bodhisatta reflected for himself, he considered only Uddaka's father, the teacher Rāma. When he asked questions in response to the teacher Uddaka, he also asked only about his father, the teacher Rāma. This point is mentioned so that the readers of the Buddha's life story may be aware of it beforehand.)

The Great Bodhisatta approached the teacher Uddaka again and asked directly, "O Friend, to what extent did your father, the teacher Rāma, say that he had personally reached, realized, and abided in this doctrine and path of practice?" The teacher Uddaka replied to the Bodhisatta regarding the attainment up to the jhāna of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). At that time, this thought arose in the Bodhisatta's mind: "It is not only Uddaka's father, the teacher Rāma, who has firm faith (saddhā) to reach the jhāna of Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana; I also have firm faith to reach the jhāna of Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana. It is not only Uddaka's father, the teacher Rāma, who has firm energy (viriya), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā) to reach the jhāna of Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana; I also have firm energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom to reach the jhāna of Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana. Regarding those eight mundane meditative attainments up to the jhāna of Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana, which Uddaka's father, the teacher Rāma, said he had personally reached and realized through direct knowledge and abided in happily; I too...
232: During that time, because he had practiced those jhānas in previous lives and possessed great analytical wisdom, he reflected on the current tendencies and future benefits of those eight mundane attainments (lokiya samāpatti) up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). He clearly perceived that these eight mundane attainments would lead to rebirth in the highest Brahma realm, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, in the next life. At that time, he reached a conclusion, thinking, "These eight mundane attainments are only phenomena included within the suffering of the cycle (vaṭṭa). This group of eight mundane attainments is not conducive to disenchantment with the suffering of the cycle. It is not conducive to dispassion. It is not conducive to the cessation of defilements such as lust. It is not conducive to the complete tranquility of all defilements. It is not conducive to the direct knowledge of all things that should be known. It is not conducive to the attainment of the four Path-knowledges (magga-ñāṇa). It is not conducive to the realization of Nibbāna. Indeed, at their highest and most supreme result, these eight mundane attainments will only lead to the Brahma realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, where life lasts eighty-four thousand great aeons (mahākappa). They cannot provide any benefit beyond that. Even that Brahma realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the result of such jhāna, is a place not yet free from the dangers of birth, aging, and death; it is still surrounded by the snare of the King of Death." Thus, he reflected and considered deeply.
233:
Just as a man oppressed by intense hunger might receive a delightful meal and eat it with great satisfaction at first, but later, due to an upset of bile or phlegm, or because a fly has fallen into the meal, he becomes disgusted and repulsed by it, abandons it, and no longer has any desire to eat even a single mouthful; in the same way, the Great Bodhisatta easily attained those eight mundane attainments within two or three days and enjoyed entering those attainments at first. However, from the moment he saw the faults mentioned before, such as their inclusion within the suffering of the cycle, he had no desire at all to practice or use those eight attainments through any of the five masteries (vasībhāva). Thinking repeatedly, "There is no benefit in these eight attainments; there is no benefit in these eight attainments," he became weary of them and soon departed from the presence of the great teacher Udaka.

## Chapter 6
## The Practice of Austerities
## Journeying to the Uruvelā Forest
## Practicing Austerities for Six Years
After departing from the presence of the teacher Udaka, the Bodhisatta, seeking Nibbāna, wandered through the Magadha country and eventually arrived at Senānigama. Near Senānigama was the Uruvelā forest. In that Uruvelā forest, he saw a ground and landscape suitable for the delight of noble ones,
234:
a forest that was pleasing to the mind, and the Nerañjarā River with its clear water flowing steadily, filled with playful fish and turtles, and having beautiful sandy banks like a spread of silver, with excellent landing places that were clean and free of mud. He also saw small villages nearby where forest-dwelling monks could easily obtain alms-food. A thought arose in the Bodhisatta's mind: "Oh, the ground is indeed delightful for noble ones! The forest is indeed pleasing to the mind! The Nerañjarā River is pure, with easy landing places and clear, emerald-like water flowing steadily. There are also small villages nearby where forest-dwelling monks can easily obtain alms-food. This place is indeed suitable for a son of good family who desires Nibbāna to strive in the practice of meditation." Having had this good thought, he built a simple leaf-hut with whatever dry wood and leaves he could find and sat down in that Uruvelā forest to begin his great striving (padhāna).
## The Appearance of Three Similes in the Bodhisatta's Wisdom
At that time, three similes appeared in the wisdom of the Bodhisatta. These three similes are:
(1) Just as a man desiring fire might take a piece of wet wood (a large piece of wet fig wood) that has been soaked in water and rub it with a fire-stick, yet he would not get fire and would only experience exhaustion; in the same way, in this world,
235:
those who are called recluses and brahmins, if they themselves are not dry of the moisture and sap of sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā) and do not live apart from sensual objects and pleasures, no matter how painfully they strive and exert themselves to exhaust defilements, they will not attain the Path and Fruit (magga-phala) and will only experience exhaustion. This simile appeared first in the wisdom of the Great Bodhisatta.
(In this simile, the large piece of wet fig wood is like a person whose sap of defilement and craving is not yet dry. Placing the wet fig wood in water is like those whose sap of defilement is not dry placing themselves in the water of sensual objects. Just as rubbing the wet fig wood soaked in water results only in exhaustion without obtaining fire, so too those who do not abandon sensual objects, no matter how much they strive, cannot obtain the fire of Path-knowledge. This simile appeared regarding the renunciation of those called Saputtabhariyapabbajjā, who go forth together with their wives and children.)
(2) Just as a man desiring fire might take a large piece of wet fig wood that has been placed on dry land far from water, yet because it is inherently wet, no matter how much he rubs it with a fire-stick, he would not get fire and would only experience exhaustion; in the same way, in this world, those who are called recluses and brahmins, even if they physically and mentally depart far from the water of sensual objects, if they themselves are not dry of the moisture and sap of sensual craving, no matter how greatly they strive with hardship, they will not attain the Path and Fruit and will only experience exhaustion.
236:
This simile appeared second in the wisdom of the Great Bodhisatta.
(In this simile, the large piece of wet fig wood is like a person whose sap of defilement and craving is not yet dry. Even though the wet fig wood is placed on dry land far from water, because it is inherently wet, fire cannot be produced no matter how much it is rubbed; this is like those whose sap of defilement is not yet dry, even if they live far away from sensual objects in body and mind and strive with great hardship, because they themselves are still wet with the sap of defilement, the fire of Path-knowledge cannot be produced. This simile appeared regarding the renunciation of those called Brāhmaṇadhammikapabbajjā, brahmins who abandon their wives and children but follow wrong sectarian practices.)
(3) Furthermore, just as a man desiring fire might take a large piece of dry fig wood placed on dry land far from water, and when he rubs it with a fire-stick, because it is far from water and inherently dry, fire is easily produced; in the same way, in this world, those who are called recluses and brahmins, if they themselves are dry of the moisture and sap of sensual craving and live far apart from sensual objects in body and mind, whether they strive for the true recluse-dharma with great hardship or strive with ease and comfort, they can attain the Path and Fruit. This simile appeared third in the wisdom of the Great Bodhisatta. (Apply the comparison as in the previous methods. This simile appeared regarding the Lord himself.)
237:
## The Group of Five Monks Arriving and Serving the Bodhisatta
As mentioned before, the five monks of the Group of Five (Pañcavaggiya), who had gone forth since the time the Bodhisatta was born, were listening for news of whether the Prince Bodhisatta had gone forth. Upon hearing that he had indeed renounced the world, they wandered through villages and towns searching for him and eventually found him in the Uruvelā forest. Then, with great expectation that "He will become a Buddha right now, he will become a Buddha right now," they served the Bodhisatta as he strove in his great work for six years. They performed duties such as sweeping the precinct of his leaf-hut and offering him hot and cold water, and they remained nearby him.
## Practicing the Great Work of Austerities
The kind of persistent effort and energy characterized by the four factors: (1) let only skin remain, (2) let only sinews remain, (3) let only bones remain, (4) let flesh and blood dry up as they will, but I will perform this work until successful, is called "Padhāna-vīriya" (Great Effort). The practices to be described now are called the Great Work because they were performed with such Padhāna-vīriya. These practices are called "Dukkharacariyā" (Austerities) because they are difficult for ordinary people to practice.
(a) The Bodhisatta entered Senānigama to collect alms, practiced the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā),
238:
and after many days had passed, he progressed to a higher level, reflecting: "What benefit is there for me in consuming this coarse food that must be chewed and swallowed? By eating my fill of such food and merely developing loving-kindness, I will not be able to attain the sought-after Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)." Thus, he abandoned the practice of collecting alms and subsisted only on large and small fruits that fell naturally in the Uruvelā forest. Since he still could not attain Omniscience by that method, he reflected: "Even these naturally fallen fruits are still coarse food. Searching for fruits is also a kind of impediment (palibodha)." He then subsisted only on the fruits that fell naturally from the tree under which he resided.
(b) The Bodhisatta thought: "It would be good if I could prevent the arising of unwholesome thoughts, such as sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka), by clenching my teeth and pressing my tongue against my palate, and by suppressing the unwholesome mind with a wholesome mind associated with powerful right thought (sammā-vitakka). It would be good if I could remove those unwholesome thoughts with the heat of my energy." He then clenched his teeth and pressed his tongue, suppressing the unwholesome mind with the wholesome mind; he did not allow them to arise and removed them with the heat of his energy. At that time, sweat poured from his armpits. It was just as if a strong man were to take a weak man by the head or shoulders and crush him. At that time, the Bodhisatta's energy was extremely
239:
His energy was extremely fierce. There was no regression whatsoever. His mindfulness was also very clear and firmly established, without any forgetfulness. However, because the painful exertion was as if piercing his entire body, the Bodhisatta's whole body was burning and smarting, and he did not attain any tranquility. Even though he reached such great suffering, his will to strive did not diminish or become exhausted.

(c) The Bodhisatta thought, "What if I were to develop the Appāṇaka Jhāna (breathless meditation) by restraining both the inhalation and exhalation?" With undiminished effort, he restrained and held his breath so that the in-breaths and out-breaths could not enter or exit through the mouth and nose. At that time, since the air had no way to exit through the mouth and nose, it gathered and escaped through the ear-holes. The sound of the air escaping in this way was extremely fierce, like the sound of air coming from a blacksmith's bellows. At that time, the Bodhisatta's energy was extremely fierce. There was no regression whatsoever. His mindfulness was also very clear and firmly established, without any forgetfulness. However, because the painful exertion was as if piercing his entire body, the Bodhisatta's whole body was burning and smarting, and he did not attain any tranquility. Even though he reached such great suffering, his will to strive did not diminish or become exhausted.

(d) Again, the Bodhisatta thought, "What if I were to further develop that same Appāṇaka Jhāna?" With undiminished effort, he restrained and held his breath so that the in-breaths and out-breaths could not enter or exit through the mouth, the nose, and the ear-holes. At that time, since the air had no way to exit through the mouth, nose, or ear-holes,
240:
the air ascended to the head and began to push and pierce it. For example, it was as if a strong man were boring into the head with a very sharp and pointed drill. At that time, the Bodhisatta's energy remained as fierce as ever; there was no regression whatsoever. His mindfulness also remained as clear and firmly established as ever; there was no forgetfulness. However, because the painful exertion was as if piercing his entire body, the Bodhisatta's whole body was burning and smarting, and he did not attain any tranquility. Even though he reached such great suffering, his will to strive did not diminish or become exhausted.

(e) Again, the Bodhisatta thought, "What if I were to further develop that same Appāṇaka Jhāna?" With undiminished effort, he continued to restrain and hold his breath so that the in-breaths and out-breaths could not enter or exit through the mouth, nose, and ear-holes. At that time, because the extremely fierce winds struck the head, very intense headaches and pains arose. For example, it was like the great suffering experienced when a strong man wraps a leather strap around the head and pulls it tight. (Let the reader imagine a strong man placing a sturdy leather loop over the head, inserting a stick, and twisting it to tighten it. It was just like that.) At that time, the Bodhisatta's energy remained as fierce as ever; there was no regression whatsoever. His mindfulness also remained as clear and firmly established as ever; there was no forgetfulness. However, because of the painful
241:
impact of the exertion, which was as if piercing his entire body, the Bodhisatta's whole body was burning and smarting, and he did not attain any tranquility. Even though he reached such great suffering, his will to strive did not diminish, regress, or become exhausted.

(f) Again, the Noble Bodhisatta thought, "What if I were to further develop that same Appāṇaka Jhāna?" As before, with undiminished effort, he continued to restrain and hold his breath so that the in-breaths and out-breaths could not enter or exit through the mouth, nose, and ear-holes. At that time, the extremely fierce winds pierced his abdomen as if cutting it open. For example, it was as if a skilled butcher (or a butcher's apprentice) were carving the abdomen with a sharp butcher's knife. At that time, the Bodhisatta's energy remained as fierce as ever; there was no regression whatsoever. His mindfulness also remained as clear and firmly established as ever; there was no forgetfulness. However, because the painful impact of the exertion was as if piercing his entire body, the Bodhisatta's whole body was burning and smarting, and he did not attain any tranquility. Even though he reached such great suffering, his will to strive did not diminish, regress, or become exhausted.

(g) Again, the Noble Bodhisatta thought, "What if I were to further develop that same Appāṇaka Jhāna?" As before, with undiminished effort, he continued to restrain and hold his breath so that the in-breaths and out-breaths could not enter or exit through the mouth, nose, and ear-holes. At that time, in the Bodhisatta's entire body, an intense
242:
burning sensation (dāha-roga) arose. For example, it was like the intense burning experienced when two strong men grab a weaker man by each arm and roast him over a large pit of coals. At that time, the Bodhisatta's entire body was scorching hot. Even then, as before, his effort and energy were fierce without regression. His mindfulness was also very clear and firmly established without forgetfulness. Due to the painful impact of the exertion in his primary task, he did not attain tranquility. Nevertheless, his will to strive did not diminish, regress, or become exhausted.

Note: [The passage (a) is from the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā; the passages from (b) to (g) are from the Mahāsaccaka Sutta.]

## Fainting while Sitting in the Cloister
When such extreme bodily heat occurred in the Noble Bodhisatta, he became dizzy and fainted right there in the cloister, toppling over while in a sitting position. (He did not fall in an unsightly manner, such as lying flat or face-down; because he was one of great mindfulness, he simply toppled over while sitting during his walk in the cloister.) When the Noble Bodhisatta thus toppled over while sitting, the deities near the cloister had three different opinions:

(1) Some deities said, "The ascetic Gotama is dead."
(2) Some deities said, "The ascetic Gotama is not dead yet, but he is in the process of dying right now."
(3) Some deities said, "The ascetic Gotama is not dead,
243:
nor is he in the process of dying. The ascetic Gotama has become an Arahant; this state is the way an Arahant dwells."

Among the three groups of deities who spoke thus, those who said "He is dead" went to King Suddhodana and said, "Your son, O King, is dead." When King Suddhodana asked, "Did my son die after becoming a Buddha, or before becoming a Buddha?", those deities replied, "Your son was unable to achieve Buddhahood and died by toppling over right in the cloister grounds while engaged in his primary exertion." King Suddhodana then spoke very firmly, saying, "I do not believe your words at all. For my son, the phenomenon of dying without reaching Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is simply impossible."

## Eating a Reduced Amount of Food
When the Bodhisatta regained consciousness from his fainting spell, he thought, "What if I were to practice by completely abstaining from food?" Then the deities said, "O virtuous Noble Bodhisatta, please do not completely cut off food. O virtuous Noble Bodhisatta, if you practice by completely cutting off food, we will infuse divine nutritive essence (ojā) into your body through the pores of your skin. By that divine essence, you will be sustained." Then the thought occurred to the Noble Bodhisatta: "If I claim that I do not eat any food at all, and yet these deities
244:
infuse divine essence through my pores, and I am sustained by that divine essence, then while claiming to eat no food at all, being sustained by divine essence would be a contradiction and a falsehood for me." Thus he thought, "O deities, do not perform this act of infusing divine essence through my pores. I will consume just enough food to sustain myself."

From then on, the Bodhisatta did not completely cut off food but consumed only a very small amount. For his daily sustenance, he sometimes subsisted on a single handful (palmful) of green gram soup. Sometimes he subsisted on a single handful of black gram soup. Sometimes he subsisted on a single handful of chickpea soup. Sometimes he subsisted on a single handful of pea soup.

Because he subsisted on only a single handful of bean soup, the Bodhisatta's physical body (rūpakāya) became extremely exhausted and emaciated.

Because the Bodhisatta consumed only a very small amount of food, his limbs and joints became like the nodes of the āsītika or kāḷa vines; the joints protruded and bulged, while the parts that were not joints were thin and sunken.
245:
The Bodhisatta's buttocks were shriveled all around like a camel's hoof, and the rectum (vicchamagga) was sunken inward.

The Bodhisatta's spine was like a string of large beads threaded together, sunken in the middle with the bones protruding prominently.

Like the rafters of an old rest-house, an old monastery, or an old house, his ribs were sunken where the flesh had wasted away between them, appearing unsightly, disordered, and uneven.

His eyes within their sockets were seen to be deep-set, like the bubbles of water at the bottom of a very deep well.

The skin of his head was shriveled, wrinkled, and withered, like a young bitter gourd that has been picked and dried in the sun.

Because the skin of his belly clung to his spine, if one felt the belly skin, one would also be touching the spine; if one felt the spine, one would also be touching the belly skin.

When he sat down to evacuate his bowels or bladder, because there was no nutritional fluid in his stomach to produce urine, no urine came out at all, and his stool consisted of only one or two hard, dry pieces like betel nuts, which were passed with great difficulty. Sweat poured from his entire body, and he toppled over face-down right in that spot.
246:
When he rubbed his body with his hand, hoping to find even a little relief, the hair, whose roots were rotten (due to the lack of blood and flesh to support them), fell away from his body and stuck to his hand.

The natural complexion of the Bodhisatta was as bright and golden as pure Singī gold. However, during that time of intense practice, those who saw him said, "The ascetic Gotama is black-skinned." Others said, "The ascetic Gotama is not black-skinned, he is brown-skinned." Yet others said, "The ascetic Gotama is neither black nor brown; he has a dark blue-grey complexion like the skin of a catfish."

(Let the reader of this Chronicle of the Buddha pause here for a moment and reflect: the Bodhisatta did not practice this conduct, which is difficult for ordinary people to endure, for just a short period of days or months, but for six long years. Even after suffering such hardship for six years, the thought never occurred to the Bodhisatta: "Though I have practiced with such difficulty for six years, I have not attained Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Well then, I shall return to the golden palace and live comfortably, receiving the care and attention of the forty thousand court ladies led by Queen Yasodharā, and looking after my father, my mother (referring to his foster mother, Gotamī), and the eighty thousand kinsmen who are still alive." Nor did he think, "I shall consume excellent food like the food of the devas and sleep comfortably on a bed of exquisite touch." He did not seek such ease.
247:
He did not have even a grain of desire to pamper his body. An ordinary person would not even dare to imagine such a thing, let alone practice it in reality. Therefore, this practice is called Dukkharacariyā (the practice that is difficult for ordinary people to perform).

## Māra Approaches to Forbid Him with Deceptive Words of Benefit

Even when the Bodhisatta first renounced the world, Māra the deity had forbidden him, saying, "O Prince Siddhattha, on the seventh day from now, the Celestial Wheel Treasure will appear for you. Do not renounce the world." However, the Bodhisatta had replied boldly, "O Māra, I know the Wheel Treasure will come to me. But I have no desire for the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). You must go; do not stand here. I will strive to become a Buddha, making the ten thousand world systems echo with my effort."

From that time on, Māra followed the Bodhisatta for six years, watching for a lapse or an opportunity, thinking, "If a thought of sensual desire (kāma-vitakka), a thought of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka), or a thought of harm (vihiṃsā-vitakka) arises in Prince Siddhattha's mind, I will destroy him right then and there." But now, after six years, he found no opportunity at all for such wrong thoughts to arise in the Bodhisatta's continuum.
248:
When six years had passed, Māra thought to himself: "Prince Siddhattha's energy is great, and his difficult practice is intense. He might become a Buddha at any moment. It would be good if I approach Prince Siddhattha, give him some advice, and make him stop this Dukkharacariyā." Having thought so, he approached the Bodhisatta and spoke his intended words. (The manner in which Māra came and spoke deceptive words as if wishing for his benefit, and how the Bodhisatta replied boldly, was later taught by the Buddha to the monks in the discourse named the "Padhāna Sutta." I shall now present the dialogue between Māra and the Bodhisatta from that Padhāna Sutta in easy-to-understand Burmese.)

In the Uruvelā forest near the Nerañjarā River, while the Bodhisatta was dwelling with a mind solely intent on Nibbāna, repeatedly developing the Appānaka Jhāna, Māra approached him and said:

"O friend, Prince Siddhattha, you are now emaciated, having lost your flesh and blood. Your appearance and complexion are ruined and unsightly. Your death is very near. If one were to divide death into a thousand parts, only one part of your life remains; nine hundred and ninety-nine parts are already dead. O Prince Siddhattha, take care of your life. To remain alive is a very noble and praiseworthy thing. If you live long, you will be able to perform many meritorious deeds."
249:
"If you practice the Uposatha observances or perform fire sacrifices, many merits can arise for you, Prince Siddhattha. What is the use of your striving in this Padhāna work, living in the forest like this, not knowing whether you will live or die, and being oppressed by great hardship and exhaustion? (It will be of no use.) The ancient path of practice to reach the Nibbāna you aim for is very difficult to travel, very painful to undertake, and very hard to enter and follow."

In this way, he spoke with a voice of feigned compassion, as if wishing for the Bodhisatta's benefit. (To an ordinary person, his words would seem worth listening to.)

To Māra, who spoke with such feigned compassion, the Bodhisatta replied with these bold words:

"O Māra, you who are the kinsman of the heedless, who bind devas, humans, and Brahmas so they cannot escape from Saṃsāra! You have come to me only for your own benefit, hoping to cause obstacles and disturbances to others. (With these words, the Great Being refuted Māra's claim of coming out of concern for his benefit.)

I have not even an atom's worth of desire for the kind of merit that leads to further rebirth (vaṭṭagāmi-kusala) of which you speak. You should speak such words only to those who hope for and desire such vaṭṭagāmi-kusala."
250: "O Māra, you should only encourage and inquire about the life of those who have no faith (saddhā) in the Peace of Nibbāna, or those who, even if they have faith, are weak and lazy in energy (viriya), or those who, even if they have faith and energy, lack wisdom (paññā). As for me, I have clear faith that 'if I strive, I will surely reach Nibbāna where the aggregates cease in this very life.' I have ardent energy that burns the grass and rubbish of defilements into ashes. I have wisdom as sharp and powerful as Indra's thunderbolt to shatter the mountain of ignorance. I also have mindfulness (sati) that forgets nothing of what has been done or said long ago, which is sufficient to reach Buddhahood, and concentration (samādhi) as firm as a stone pillar that does not waver even when the storms of worldly conditions blow. Since I possess these five factors completely, enabling me to easily ascend toward Nibbāna, and since I am striving by sacrificing my life and body without hesitation, why do you, Māra, encourage and inquire about my staying alive? In truth,
251:
is it not better to live for even a single day in the human world for one who strives with firm energy and persistence, whose wisdom is sharp through Appanā Samādhi, and who clearly perceives the arising and passing away of the mental and physical aggregates? (With these words, the Bodhisatta in turn intimidated Māra, who had tried to frighten him by saying, 'If one divides death into a thousand parts, only one part of your life remains.')

O Māra, the wind generated by the force of my energy in practicing Appānaka Jhāna is capable of drying up even the currents of rivers like the Ganges and Yamunā. Why then should it not be able to dry up the mere blood of me, whose mind is directed toward Nibbāna? It is intense enough to dry it up. Because of my striving in meditation toward Nibbāna, if the four measures of blood in my body dry up due to the force of the wind, then the bile (both bound and unbound), the four measures of phlegm that cover the food consumed so that no foul odor escapes, and the four measures of urine and nutrients will also surely dry up. When the blood, bile, phlegm, urine, and nutrients gradually dry up, the flesh will also surely waste away. When the blood, bile, phlegm,
252:
urine, nutrients, and flesh waste away, my mind becomes even clearer. (It will by no means retreat because of that wasting away. It is only because you do not know my mind, which is so intense, that you speak these words of attachment to life, such as 'O Prince Siddhattha, you have lost your flesh and blood and are emaciated.') Not only is the mind clear, but when this happens, the group of qualities—mindfulness which is like the treasurer of a Universal Monarch, wisdom which is like a vajra weapon or a thunderbolt, and concentration which is like Mount Meru—remains unshaken and increases even more.

Even though my body's blood and flesh waste away, my mind remains noble and becomes even clearer. Though I have reached a state of incomparable and supreme pain, which is endured with great patience by the Great Men (Mahāpurisa), the banners of men, my mind does not look back even for a moment at the palace, the kingdom, Yasodharā, the forty thousand court ladies, or any such objects of sensuality (vatthu-kāma). O Māra, observe and analyze the purity and uprightness of my heart, the heart of a man who has fulfilled the extraordinary Perfections (Pāramīs)." (With these words, the Bodhisatta demonstrated the great firmness of his mental state.)
253:
## The Ten Armies of Māra
(1) O Māra! For those living the household life, the objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) consisting of animate and inanimate objects, and the defilement sensuality (kilesa-kāma) consisting of the craving and greed that clings to those objects—these two types of sensuality cause such bewilderment that the true and sublime Dhamma cannot be known. Therefore, these two, vatthu-kāma and kilesa-kāma, constitute your first great army. (For monks, the collection of robes, alms-bowls, requisites, buildings, monasteries, parks, gardens, beds, couches, and all types of coverings that are delightful through craving also constitute their sphere of vatthu-kāma. Although they know the rarity of a Buddha's appearance (Buddhuppāda-dullabha) and the rarity of becoming a monk (pabbajita-dullabha), those who cannot renounce lay possessions (gihi-bhoga) and die as worldlings (puthujjana) in the midst of those possessions, as well as those monks who, despite hearing about the four supports—dwelling at the root of a tree, wearing rag-robes, eating alms-food, and using fermented urine as medicine—at the time of their ordination, cannot renounce the monasteries, robes, food, and medicine donated by householders and die as worldlings in the midst of these four requisites which are the sensual objects of monks—these laypeople and monks are those who have encountered Māra's first great army of sensuality and died an ignoble death. From Ledi Sayadaw's Padhāna Sutta Nissaya.)
(2) Even if one has beautifully renounced all lay possessions and attained monkhood, some monks may be troubled, disturbed, and destroyed by discontent (arati) and dissatisfaction (ukkaṇṭhita)—that is, not delighting in the monkhood, not delighting in the works of scripture (pariyatti) or practice (paṭipatti), not delighting in secluded forest or mountain dwellings, and not delighting in the practice of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) meditation. Thus, the aforementioned arati and ukkaṇṭhita are your second great army, O Māra! (Some monks sink and perish right within this second great army.)
254:
Even if one can overcome that second great army, some monks, when the practice of the ascetic dhutaṅga becomes extremely difficult and they face hunger and exhaustion—like a thirsty cow unable to find water or when they must subsist on whatever mixed food is available—may experience the arising of hunger and thirst (khuppipāsa), which causes the mind to be utterly ruined and filled with burning thoughts and intense passion, like a worm writhing when touched by salt. This khuppipāsa is your third great army, O Māra! (Some monks sink and perish right within this third army.)
(4) When oppressed by such intense hunger and thirst, some monks may experience the arising of languor (tandī)—a state of being dispirited and weary, where both mental and physical strength decline, intentions retreat, and one becomes reluctant and lazy toward the primary task of the monk's practice. This tandī is your fourth great army, O Māra! (Some monks sink and perish right within this fourth army.)
(5) When work does not progress and laziness sets in, leading to a dispirited and weary state, from that day forward, one becomes dazed and forgetful,
255:
and the state of sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) arises, characterized by repeatedly turning over and tossing about in the monastery, sleeping excessively. This thīna-middha is your fifth great army, O Māra! (Some monks sink and perish right within this fifth army.)
(6) When one sleeps excessively due to a lazy mind, the Dhamma does not progress and the mind lacks sharpness. With weak strength and trailing passions, one becomes confused and agitated in thought, and fear (bhīru) arises, causing one to tremble and startle at the sight of even a tree stump, mistaking it for an elephant, a tiger, or an ogre. This bhīru is your sixth great army, O Māra! (Some monks sink and perish right within this sixth army.)
(7) If one overcomes fear through practice and becomes courageous, continuing the work of meditation, the path to jhāna and the Path (Magga) may remain hidden and submerged. Then, doubt (vicikicchā) arises in the form of a divided mind, wondering, "Will I actually hit the right track in my work and intentions, or will I likely miss it?" This vicikicchā is your seventh great army, O Māra! (Some monks sink and perish right within this seventh army.)
(8) While continuing to strive day and night without reduction, having cleared away the doubt of vicikicchā, if one sees special signs (nimitta) in meditation and develops a strong perception of them, there may arise contempt (makkha) and obstinacy (thambha)—the failure to recognize others as worthy and the destruction of their reputation, as well as the failure to show humility and the presence of arrogance toward those of great age, virtue, and seniority.
256:
These states of makkha and thambha are your eighth great army, O Māra! (Some monks sink and perish right within this eighth army.)
(9) When one continues the work of Dhamma after abandoning makkha and thambha, and when extraordinary signs appear and one reaches a significant stage in the journey, there may arise craving and conceit (taṇhā-māna) characterized by: excitement and delight in abundant gains and offerings; excitement and delight in widespread fame in all four directions; excitement and delight in receiving extraordinary gains that others have never received; and craving and conceit that delights in ill-gotten retinue, fame, and reputation, achieved through showing false or counterfeit Dhamma to increase gains, associated with evil desire (pāpicchatā) and practicing deceit and boastfulness. This collection of states is your ninth great army, O Māra! (Some monks sink within this ninth army.)
(10) Some monks who abide in the states of the ninth group practice self-exaltation (attukkaṃsana) and the disparaging of others (paravambhana). These two states, attukkaṃsana and paravambhana, are your tenth great army, O Māra!
257:
O Māra! You who strive to prevent humans, devas, and brahmās from escaping the suffering of the round of rebirth (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa), these ten groups of states starting with sensuality (kāma) and discontent (arati) are your military forces and the collection of passions. O Māra, you of great passion and dark heart! These are also the firearms, cannons, and diamond bombs that shoot and kill every monk and hermit they encounter. Poor worldlings and cowards who lack sharp faith, desire, energy, and wisdom cannot repel and destroy these ten armies of yours to escape. Only noble heroes (ājānīya) who are extremely courageous and possess sharp and great faith, desire, energy, and wisdom are able to quickly repel and destroy them and escape, without regarding even a single blade of grass. Only by being able to repel and destroy them and escape can one properly and fully attain the bliss of the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna, which is free from the danger of the swords, spears, and weapons of the numerous soldiers of your ten evil armies, O Māra.
O Māra! I want you to regard me thus: "This Prince Siddhattha is truly a noble hero; once he reaches the battlefield, he never retreats a single step. He is a great leader (Kettaung Bo-gyi) who has planted the true banner of victory on his head and wears the flower of courage, the white muñja grass."
(Soldiers who do not retreat in battle traditionally tie muñja grass to their heads, their banners, or the weapons they hold to signify that they are heroes who will not retreat. Such a
258:
military leader was called a 'Kettaung Bo-gyi' in ancient times.) I want you to regard me as one who is firm in heart, thinking: "If I were to live in this world after retreating from the battlefield and falling back under your power, it would be shameful, useless, ignoble, and a source of ill-repute—utterly loathsome. Therefore, it is much nobler for me to die right here on the battlefield than to suffer defeat by your army. Living in defeat and failure is not noble at all."
The reason is: in this world, some monks and brahmins who lack strength but come forth disguised in the yellow robe and full requisites as commanders on the front lines of the battlefield of defilement-thorns, sink completely into your great army of ten divisions. They are like those who enter into darkness, where the light of virtues such as morality (sīla) does not shine. Because those people are being oppressed by your ten great armies, they can in no way know the great jeweled highway of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅga), which is the path to Nibbāna traveled by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Ones (Ariyas). (Therefore, I want you to regard me as one who will gallantly plant the banner of victory and defeat your ten armies.)
When he heard these fiery words spoken by the Bodhisatta, the son of Māra
259:
was unable to say anything in return and turned away, leaving that place.
## Questions to be Asked
A question that arises in this chapter on the practice of austerities (dukkharacariyā) is: If the Bodhisatta had not practiced austerities, would he have been unable to become a Buddha? (The essence of the question is: Is it only by practicing austerities that one can become a Buddha, and if one does not practice them, can one not become a Buddha?)
Answer: Whether he practiced austerities or not, he could have become a Buddha because he had already fully practiced the causes, namely the Perfections (Pāramī), Sacrifices (Cāga), and Conduct (Cariya).
If he could have become a Buddha without practicing austerities, why did he undergo such hardship to practice them?
He underwent the hardship of practicing austerities because he wished to clearly demonstrate his incomparable and intense energy (vīriya) to the multitude of beings including devas and brahmās, and because he reflected that later, after becoming Buddha, when he reconsidered the merit of that energy, it would cause his heart to be joyful and delighted. To illustrate this with an example: A king who attains kingship according to ancient tradition while sitting in a palace, without having to wage war or fight anyone, [might not feel the same pride as one who] assembles an army and [wins] in battle...
260:
A king who attains kingship after conquering enemies in two or three battles does not experience as great a joy as [the Buddha]. Indeed, when a king who has achieved victory and attained kingship after fighting two or three battles reflects on his own effort while enjoying royal splendor and looking at his subjects, he thinks: “In such a place, I performed such a task; having struck and fought such and such enemies in this way, I have now attained this royal splendor.” Every time he reflects thus, great joy arises. Similarly, the Buddha practiced these austerities (dukkharacariya) because He wished to clearly demonstrate His incomparable and intense effort to all beings, including devas and Brahmās, and because He reflected that the merit of this effort would bring joy and delight to His heart when He would look back upon it after attaining Buddhahood.

Alternatively, He practiced austerities out of compassion, to provide a model for future disciples (sāvakas). To clarify: future disciples who hear about the Buddha’s practice of austerities will reflect: “Even the Buddha, after fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand world-cycles, had to exert Himself in the practice of austerities to attain the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). What need is there to mention us? Only by exerting ourselves in the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) will we
261:
attain the Knowledge of the Path (magga-ñāṇa).” Thus, gaining the right view through such reflection, they will realize that they should exert great effort (padhāna-vīriya, the effort of practicing meditation). By reflecting and acting in this way, they will be able to reach the end of rebirth, aging, and death (Nibbāna). Thus, He practiced austerities out of compassion to provide a model for future disciples. (From Majjhima-nikāya Aṭṭhakathā, Vol. 2, p. 189.)

It is the natural law (dhammatā) for every Bodhisatta in his final existence to practice austerities for at least seven days. Similarly, our Buddha was one capable of practicing austerities. Being so capable, He practiced in this manner for six years. However, He did not become a Buddha because of those austerities; rather, He became a Buddha only through the Middle Way (majjhima-paṭipadā). He practiced austerities because He wished to show the world, including the devas, by way of contrast (vyatireka), that the practice of austerities is not the path to attaining the Knowledge of the Path.

While other Bodhisattas practiced austerities for a short period, such as seven days or at most one month, our Bodhisatta had to practice for six years due to the result of verbal karma (vacī-kamma-vipāka). This occurred during the time of Kassapa Buddha, when he was the Brahmin Jotipāla, who, out of pride in his birth, spoke harshly: “Where could this shaven-headed one (u-pyī) possibly attain the Knowledge of the Path and Omniscience? Enlightenment (bodhi-ñāṇa) is
262:
extremely difficult to attain.” (From Majjhima-nikāya Ṭīkā, Vol. 2, p. 213.)
