## Chapter 7
## The Attainment of Buddhahood
## Changing the Practice
As mentioned previously, after the Bodhisatta had practiced austerities for six years, the time reached approximately the first day of the waxing moon of Kason (Vesākha), following the end of the month of Tagu in the year 103 of the Great Era (Mahā-sakarāj). At that time, a thought arose in the Bodhisatta’s mind:

“Whatever ascetics or Brahmins in the past have experienced painful, racking, piercing feelings due to their exertion, this is the utmost; there is none beyond this. Whatever ascetics or Brahmins in the future will experience painful, racking, piercing feelings due to their exertion, this is the utmost; there will be none beyond this. Whatever ascetics or Brahmins in the present experience painful, racking, piercing feelings due to their exertion, this is the utmost; there is none beyond this. (I have practiced the austerities for six years with such exertion that it is equal to or even exceeds the suffering experienced by any ascetic or Brahmin in the three periods of time.)
263:
Yet, despite this great exertion, I have not attained the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience through this practice of austerities. I have not become a Buddha. There must be another path to the attainment of the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience and Buddhahood.” Then, reflecting further, He remembered: “I recall when my father, King Suddhodana, was performing the ceremonial plowing, I sat in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree and entered and dwelt in the first absorption (paṭhama-jhāna) born of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna). Could that path of the first absorption of ānāpāna be the true path to the attainment of the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience and Buddhahood?” Following this realization, He thought: “Why should I fear that pleasure of the ānāpāna-samādhi jhāna, which is a pleasure apart from sensual desires (vatthu-kāma) and unwholesome states (kilesa-kāma), and is associated with renunciation (nekkhamma)? I do not fear that pleasure of ānāpāna-samādhi jhāna.”

Then He reflected again: “It is not easy to attain that ānāpāna-samādhi jhāna with a body so excessively emaciated. It would be good if I were to take some solid food—rice and gruel—to restore strength and vitality to this withered body, and then strive to attain that ānāpāna-samādhi jhāna.” After reflecting thus, the Great Being took His alms-bowl from where it was kept, went for alms in the village of Senānigama, and partook of whatever solid food, rice, and gruel He received, thereby sustaining His emaciated body.
264:
Within two or three days, His strength was restored, and the marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa), which had disappeared during the painful practice of austerities, reappeared in their original state. At that time, the Bodhisatta’s physical body became radiant and golden in hue.

(Note: When the Bodhisatta abandoned the practice of austerities and reflected on the true path to Buddhahood and Omniscience, He realized that the eight mundane attainments (samāpattis) He had achieved while with the teachers Āḷāra and Udaka were only bases for continued existence (vaṭṭa-pādaka). However, the ānāpāna-samādhi He attained under the rose-apple tree during His father King Suddhodana’s plowing ceremony was included in mindfulness occupied with the body (kāyagatāsati) and served as the basis for insight (vipassanā) for all Bodhisattas. Therefore, it should be specially noted that He correctly reflected on this ānāpāna-samādhi as the true path to the attainment of the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience and Buddhahood. From Mūlapannāsa-ṭīkā, Vol. 1, p. 215.)

## The Five Attendant Monks (Pañcavaggiya)
## Abandoning the Bodhisatta
It is a natural law (dhammatā) that when Bodhisattas have completed their austerities and are nearing Buddhahood, either the attendant monks abandon them for some reason, or the Bodhisatta leaves the attendant monks. Accordingly, when the Great Bodhisatta partook of the solid food and rice He received to sustain His body, the five attendant monks (pañcavaggiya) mentioned earlier said: “The ascetic Gotama
265:
has become one who strives for abundance; he has given up the struggle and reverted to a life of abundance.” Having said this, they abandoned the Bodhisatta and, prompted by the force of natural law, departed for the Isipatana Migadāya (Deer Park) near Bārāṇasī, where all Buddhas preach their first sermon, the Dhammacakka. (It is the natural law that just before becoming a Buddha, the attendant monks abandon the Bodhisatta and go to the Migadāya forest, the place where every Buddha must preach the first sermon, the Dhammacakka.)

The five monks abandoned the Bodhisatta and moved to the Migadāya forest around the day of the new moon of Tagu. (That was the time when the Bodhisatta’s work of austerities reached its conclusion.) When the five monks had departed, the Bodhisatta, being alone, attained a special state of seclusion, and His concentration (samādhi) became exceptionally powerful and progressive in His practice. Having thus spent about fifteen days in seclusion and meditation, His concentration increased, and as the night of the 14th day of the waxing moon of Kason reached the period after midnight towards dawn, He saw five great dreams. Those five great dreams were:

## The Five Great Dreams of the Bodhisatta
(1) He dreamt that He was lying with the great earth as His bed, the Himālaya mountains as His pillow, His left hand resting in the eastern ocean, His right hand in the western ocean, and His two feet in the southern ocean.
266:
This first dream He saw signified that He would attain the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience and truly become a Buddha in the three worlds.

(2) He dreamt that a type of grass called tiriyā grew out of His navel with a reddish stalk as thick as a yoke, and as He watched, it grew higher and higher—a span, a cubit, a fathom, a pole, a quarter-league, half a league, a league—and so on, until it stood touching the firmament of the sky, thousands of leagues high. This second dream He saw signified that He would be able to preach the Eightfold Path (aṭṭhaṅgika-magga), which is the Middle Way, to devas and humans.

(3) He dreamt that a host of white worms with black heads crawled up from His feet to His knees, covering them. This third dream He saw signified that a great number of people (black-headed ones) wearing white garments would seek refuge in the Buddha and take the Great Threefold Refuge (saraṇagamana).

(4) He dreamt that four birds of different colors—blue, golden, red, and grey—flew from the four quarters and, upon alighting at His feet, all four types of birds became perfectly white. This fourth dream He saw signified that members of the four castes—warriors, brahmins, merchants, and laborers—would enter the dispensation (sāsana) of the Buddha, become monks, and
267:
267

It was a vision signifying that they would reach the Fruition of Arahantship.

(5) He dreamed that he was walking back and forth on a great mountain of filth without being smeared by that filth. Seeing this fifth dream signified that when he became a Buddha, he would receive an abundance of the four requisites—robes, alms-food, dwellings, and medicines—and that he would use these four requisites without being attached, craving, or clinging to them.

## Notable Points

## Four Causes of Dreaming

A person dreams due to these four causes: (1) due to the disturbance of bodily elements, (2) due to habitual experience or past impressions, (3) due to the influence or deception of devas, or (4) due to pre-signs (pubbanimitta).

Among these, (1) when dreaming due to the disturbance of elements such as bile and so on, one may have terrifying dreams such as feeling as if rolling down from a mountain, traveling through the sky with a pounding heart, or being closely pursued by wild animals like fierce elephants, wild horses, lions, leopards, and tigers, or by wicked people.

(2) When dreaming due to habitual experience or past impressions, one may dream of seeing, hearing, or enjoying objects that one has seen, heard, or...
268:
268

enjoyed in the past, as if they were happening again.

(3) When dreaming due to the deception of devas, the devas may present various objects to the dreamer, either wishing for their benefit or their harm, to bring about gain or loss; the person then dreams of those various objects through the power of the devas.

(4) When dreaming due to pre-signs, the person dreams of a pre-sign that foreshadows the coming of good or bad results based on the power of good or bad deeds (kamma). Examples include Queen Mahāmāyā dreaming of obtaining a son, King Kosala dreaming the sixteen great dreams, and the present Bodhisatta dreaming the five great dreams; these are types of dreams that occur to signal the arising of good or bad results.

Mnemonic Verse: Disturbed elements, past habits, deception by devas, and pre-signs—these are the four causes of seeing dreams.

Among these four types of dreams: (1) dreams due to the disturbance of elements and (2) dreams due to past habits are generally not true. (3) Dreams due to the deception of devas may be true or may be false. They are false when devas, being angry, use a trick to show deceptive and wrong dreams to cause ruin.
269:
269

## The Story of Devas Showing False Dreams Due to Anger

In the great Nāga Monastery in the Rohana region of Sri Lanka, a senior Elder (Thera) had a large ironwood (kaṅkhā) tree cut down without informing the Saṅgha. The tree-deity (rukkha-devatā) living in that tree first gave the Elder true dreams to gain his trust, and once trusted, later told him in a dream: "Seven days from today, your lay supporter, the Great King, will pass away." The Elder, believing these words, told the ladies of the palace. The palace ladies all wept bitterly at once. When the King asked for the reason, they reported what the Elder had said. The King counted the days, and when seven days had passed (and he had not died, thinking how the Elder could say such false and terrifying things), he ordered the Elder's hands and feet to be cut off. (This story is found in the Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Volume II, page 312.) (4) Dreams due to pre-signs, however, are certainly true.

These four types of dreams are experienced only by worldlings (puthujjana) and trainees (sekha)—Sotāpannas, Sakadāgāmīs, and Anāgāmīs—because they have not yet abandoned the distortions (vipallāsa). Arahants do not dream because they have abandoned the distortions. Regarding time, dreams seen during the day, in the first watch of the night, or at midnight usually do not come true.
270:
270

In the early morning near dawn, when the food and drink consumed have been digested and the essence (ojā) is established in the body, dreams seen at the time of daybreak tend to come true. If one sees a dream of a pleasant sign (iṭṭhanimitta), good results tend to follow; if one sees a dream of an unpleasant sign (aniṭṭhanimitta), bad results tend to follow. These notable points are extracted from the Aṅguttara Commentary, Volume III, Explanation of the Pañcakanipāta, Catuttha-paṇṇāsaka, 5-Brāhmaṇavagga, Explanation of the Mahāsupina Sutta, pages 71-72.

The five great dreams mentioned earlier are not seen by ordinary worldly people, nor by kings, nor by Cakkavatti kings, nor by Chief Disciples, nor by Paccekabuddhas, nor even by the Omniscient Buddhas themselves. Only a person who is a Bodhisatta (a Buddha-to-be) sees them. Our Bodhisatta saw these five great dreams in the year 103 of the Great Era (Mahā Sakkarāj), on the 14th day of the waxing moon of Kason, after midnight and near dawn.

## Interpreting the Great Dreams Himself

After the Bodhisatta saw these five great dreams, he rose from his bed, sat cross-legged, and reflected: "If I had seen these five great dreams while living in the royal city of Kapilavatthu, I would have told my father, King Suddhodana. If my mother were still alive, I would have told her. But here in this great Uruvelā forest,
271:
271

there is not a single person who can receive and listen to these great dreams and interpret their signs. I myself shall receive, listen to, and interpret my own great dreams." Having thus reflected, he interpreted the five great dreams himself, as previously described: "This first dream is a pre-sign for obtaining such-and-such a benefit; this second dream is a pre-sign for obtaining such-and-such a benefit."

## Sujātā Offering Thick Milk-Rice

Thus, after the Bodhisatta saw these five great dreams and interpreted the signs himself, he made the resolution: "Today, I shall certainly and without fail become a Buddha." When the night had passed and morning came (the morning of the full moon day), he cleansed himself and left that place. He then went to the foot of the banyan tree where the merchant's daughter Sujātā made annual offerings, and while waiting for the time to go for alms, he sat facing the east, making the entire banyan tree radiant and brilliant with his own bodily aura.

At that time, in the market town of Senāni in the Uruvelā region, Sujātā, the daughter of a merchant named Senānī, had made a prayer at the foot of that banyan tree when she reached maturity: "O Lord Banyan Tree Deity, if I reach a merchant's house of equal status and obtain a son during my first pregnancy, I shall make an offering of milk-rice to you, my Lord Deity." That prayer of Sujātā had been fulfilled exactly as requested. Therefore, that merchant's daughter Sujātā...
272:
272

had performed the duty of making an offering of milk-rice to that banyan tree deity every year on the full moon day of Kason.

(Note: When reading the section on Sujātā offering milk-rice, if one does not pay careful attention, one might generally assume that Sujātā's prayer was fulfilled for the very first time on that full moon day of Kason when the Bodhisatta was to become Buddha, and that she offered the milk-rice then. In truth, her prayer had been fulfilled about twenty years before that year, and she had been offering milk-rice to the tree deity since then. The reason is that Sujātā's son was Yasa, the merchant's son. By the year the Buddha attained enlightenment, Yasa was already married and enjoying the wealth of a merchant. Considering this fact, it should be understood that Sujātā had been making the annual offering of milk-rice to the banyan tree deity on the full moon day of Kason for over twenty years, starting from when her prayer for a son was fulfilled.)

On the full moon day of Kason, marking the completion of the six years of the Great Bodhisatta's practice of austerities (dukkara-cariyā), Sujātā, the merchant's wife, wishing to make an offering to the tree deity: (1) First, she had a thousand milk cows grazed in a forest of licorice (sweet vines) and fed the milk from those thousand cows to another five hundred milk cows. (2) She fed the milk from those five hundred cows to another two hundred and fifty milk cows. (3) She fed the milk from those two hundred and fifty cows to another one hundred and twenty-five milk cows. (4) She fed the milk from those one hundred and twenty-five cows to another...
273:
273

sixty-four milk cows. (5) She fed the milk obtained from those sixty-four cows to another thirty-two milk cows. (6) She fed the milk obtained from those thirty-two cows to another sixteen milk cows. (7) She fed the milk obtained from those sixteen cows to another eight milk cows. In this way, Sujātā, the merchant's wife, performed the successive transfer of milk with the intention of making the milk thick, sweet, and full of essence (ojā). (This is the account found in the Jātaka Commentary.)

According to the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā: Sujātā, the merchant's wife, first had one hundred milk cows grazed in a forest of licorice. She then had the one hundred milk cows born from those first hundred cows grazed in the same way in the licorice forest. She then had the one hundred milk cows born from those second hundred cows grazed in the same way in the licorice forest. She then had the one hundred milk cows born from those third hundred cows grazed in the same way in the licorice forest. She then had the one hundred milk cows born from those fourth hundred cows grazed in the same way in the licorice forest. She then had the one hundred milk cows born from those fifth hundred cows grazed in the same way in the licorice forest. She then had the one hundred milk cows born from those sixth hundred cows grazed in the same way in the licorice forest. In this manner, she extracted the milk from the seventh generation of one hundred milk cows and prepared to cook the thick milk-rice.

On the full moon day of Kason, Sujātā, the merchant's wife, thinking, "I shall perform the offering of milk-rice early in the morning..."
274:
Early on the morning of that full moon day, when she caused the eight cows mentioned earlier to be milked, the young calves (without being tied or restrained) did not approach the udders of their mothers. Remarkably, as soon as the milk vessels were placed near the udders, the milk began to flow in a steady stream by itself, naturally, without even being milked. Seeing such a miracle, Sujātā, the merchant's wife, unlike in previous years, took the milk that had flowed out spontaneously with her own hands, put it into a new pot, and personally kindled the fire to prepare the milk-rice (pāyāsa).

## Assistance from Devas and Brahmās

While the milk-rice was being cooked: (1) Large, large bubbles arose and swirled only in a clockwise direction; not even a single drop fell outside. (2) Not even a bit of smoke rose above the hearth. (3) At that time, the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājā) came and stood guard at the hearth. (4) Mahābrahmā held an umbrella over the pot of milk-rice. (5) Sakka adjusted the firewood and brands to keep the fire burning evenly. (6) Devas gathered the divine essence (ojā), suitable for both devas and humans from the four continents with their two thousand surrounding islands, and infused it into the pot of milk-rice, just as one might squeeze honey from a honeycomb formed on a branch.

A special note: On other occasions, when the devas prepare the essence for the Buddha to consume as alms-food,
275:
they add the aforementioned essence suitable for humans and devas to each morsel. However, on the day he becomes a Buddha and the day he attains Parinibbāna, they infuse the essence directly into the pot.

Sujātā, the merchant's wife, having personally witnessed many such miracles at the place where the milk-rice was being cooked on that single day, called her servant named Puṇṇā and said, "Dear Puṇṇā, today our guardian deity of the banyan tree seems very pleased. In more than twenty years, I have never seen such miracles. Go quickly and clean the area around the banyan tree, the deity's dwelling." The servant named Puṇṇā replied, "Very well, mistress," and went quickly to the banyan tree. There, she saw the Bodhisatta sitting and looking towards the eastern quarter, and the entire banyan tree was glowing with a golden hue from the radiance emitting from his body. She thought, "Today, our tree deity has descended from the tree and is sitting there to personally receive the offerings and oblations." Trembling with awe, she hurried back home and told Sujātā about it.

Upon hearing the servant's words, Sujātā was filled with great joy and said, "From today onwards, you shall hold the position of my eldest daughter," and gave her all the ornaments suitable for a daughter.
276:
It is a natural occurrence for Bodhisattas to consume milk-rice on the day they attain Buddhahood. Since it was appropriate for her to obtain a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand on the day he would become a Buddha, Sujātā thought, "I shall put the milk-rice in a golden bowl." She had a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand brought out from the storehouse. When she tilted the pot of cooked milk-rice to pour it into the golden bowl, all the milk-rice slid into the bowl like water drops sliding off a Paduma lotus leaf, leaving not a single drop behind. The entire amount of milk-rice exactly filled the golden bowl, neither more nor less.

Sujātā covered the golden bowl filled with milk-rice with another golden bowl, wrapped it in a pure white cloth, and adorned herself with all her ornaments. Carrying the golden bowl on her head, she went to the banyan tree with great ceremony and grandeur. Upon seeing the Bodhisatta, she was filled with immense joy. Mistaking him for the tree deity, she approached him, bowing repeatedly from the moment she saw him. She lowered the golden bowl from her head, opened it, took scented water infused with various flowers from a golden ewer, and stood near the Bodhisatta.

The earthen bowl offered to the Bodhisatta by Ghaṭīkāra Brahmā at the time of his Great Renunciation had never left him during the six years of his ascetic practices (dukkaracariya). However, at that moment when Sujātā came to offer the milk-rice,
277:
it vanished instantly and completely. Not seeing his bowl, the Bodhisatta stretched out his right hand to receive the water. Sujātā then placed the milk-rice along with the golden bowl into the Bodhisatta's hand. The Bodhisatta looked at Sujātā. Sujātā, understanding the meaning of his gaze, said, "Venerable Sir, I have offered this milk-rice together with the golden bowl. Please accept it with the bowl and go wherever you wish." After paying homage, she made a wish: "Just as my heart's desire has been fulfilled and successful, may your heart's desire also be fulfilled and successful." Then, without the slightest lingering attachment to the golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, as if it were a mere dry leaf, she departed.

The Bodhisatta rose from his seat, circumambulated the banyan tree clockwise, and taking the golden bowl of milk-rice, proceeded to the banks of the Nerañjarā River. At that river, there is a bathing place named Suppatiṭṭhita where many Bodhisattas bathe on the day they attain Buddhahood. Having placed the golden bowl down and bathed, he came up from the bank and sat under the cool shade of a tree facing the east. He made the entire amount of milk-rice, which contained no water, into exactly forty-nine morsels, each about the size of a ripe palmyra nut seed (not the whole fruit), and consumed them.
278:
That very milk-rice, consumed in forty-nine morsels, became the nourishment for forty-nine days for the Blessed One as he stayed near the Bodhi tree for the seven-week period (Satta-sattāha) after attaining Buddhahood. During these forty-nine days, there was no other food. There was no bathing, washing of the face, or cleaning of the body; he spent the time only in the bliss of Jhana and the bliss of Fruition (Phala).

After consuming the milk-rice offered by Sujātā, the Bodhisatta took the golden bowl and made a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna): "If I am able to become a Buddha today, may this golden bowl float upstream. If I am not able to become a Buddha, may it float downstream." Then he floated the golden bowl onto the Nerañjarā River. The golden bowl cut across the current, went straight to the middle of the river, and then, from the very center of the river, it sped upstream for about eighty cubits like a swift horse. It then sank into a whirlpool and reached the palace of Kāla, the Naga King. There, it struck the three golden bowls used (on the day of their Enlightenment) by the three previous Buddhas—Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa—making a "kili kili" sound, and settled beneath those three bowls.

Hearing that sound, Kāla the Naga King rose, saying, "Only yesterday a Buddha appeared, and today another Buddha has appeared again!" and uttered many verses of praise. (For Kāla the Naga, the long period of time during which the great earth rose by one yojana and three gāvutas between the time of Kassapa Buddha and our Buddha
279:
seemed as short as if it were only between yesterday and today.)

Then, the Bodhisatta spent the day in a Sāla grove on the bank of the Nerañjarā River, which was adorned with highly fragrant flowers and was lush and dark green, delighting the hearts of all who saw it. There, he practiced the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-kammaṭṭhāna) and attained the eight mundane meditative attainments (samāpatti) and the five mundane supernormal powers (abhiññā). In the evening, at twilight, he proceeded along a path decorated by devas and brahmās. He descended into the Nerañjarā River to bathe and then, along the path created by the devas, he headed straight towards the Mahābodhi tree. At that time, devas, nagas, yakkhas, and gandhabbas worshipped him with divine flowers and perfumes. They sang sweet divine songs. The entire ten thousand world systems were almost covered with divine flowers and perfumes, and the sounds of devas and brahmās shouting and cheering in praise.

At that time, a grass-cutter named Sotthiya was coming from the opposite direction carrying grass. Understanding the Bodhisatta's intention (his need for grass), he offered eight handfuls of grass to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta took the eight handfuls of grass, ascended the mound of the Mahābodhi tree, and stood on the southern side of the Mahābodhi tree, facing the north. At that moment—
280: The southern part of the universe sank down as if to touch the Great Avīci, while the northern part rose up as if to reach the Highest Plane of Existence (Bhavagga). Seeing this, the Great Bodhisatta reflected, "This place is not the location for attaining the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (Arahattamagga-ñāṇa) and the Knowledge of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)." After this reflection, he circumambulated the Mahābodhi tree, keeping it to his right, and went to the western side, standing there facing the East. At that moment, the western part of the universe sank down as if to touch the Great Avīci, while the eastern part rose up as if to reach Bhavagga. Seeing this, the Great Bodhisatta reflected as before, "This place also is not the location for attaining the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and the Knowledge of Omniscience." He then circumambulated the Mahābodhi tree to his right, went to the northern side, and stood there facing the South. At that moment, the northern part of the universe sank down as if to touch the Great Avīci, while the southern part rose up as if to reach Bhavagga. (The state of the great earth at the spots where the Great Bodhisatta stood—the South, West, and North—was like a cartwheel placed flat on the ground; when one treads on the rim, it wobbles at the axle. Similarly, the earth sank at the side he turned his back to and rose at the side he faced.) Seeing this, the Great Bodhisatta reflected, "This place also is not the location for attaining the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and the Knowledge of Omniscience."
281:
Reflecting as before, he circumambulated the Mahābodhi tree to his right, went to the eastern side, and stood there facing the West.

(In this regard, the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary states: "The Great Bodhisatta arrived at the Mahābodhi tree, circumambulated it three times to the right, and stood at the northeastern corner to scatter the eight handfuls of grass." It does not mention the tilting of the earth when he stood at the South, West, and North. However, the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā states that when he stood at the South, West, and North, the great earth trembled like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, and that he stood at the northeastern corner to scatter the eight handfuls of grass.)

The area on the eastern side of the Mahābodhi tree where the Aparājita Throne (the Unconquered Throne) arises remained firm and unshakable (because it is the Avijahitaṭṭhāna, the spot never abandoned by any of the Buddhas). The Great Bodhisatta, realizing, "This is indeed the victorious ground where all Buddhas destroy the defilements," held the eight handfuls of grass by their tips and scattered them.

At the very moment they were scattered, those eight handfuls of grass lost their appearance as grass and became a great jeweled throne, fourteen cubits in size, so exquisitely crafted that no painter or sculptor could ever replicate it, standing there in a most wondrous form.
283:
Santusita, the King of Devas, stood fanning him with a jeweled circular fan. Sahampati, the King of Brahmas, stood honoring him by holding a white umbrella three yojanas in size. Kāla, the Naga King, stood honoring and worshipping the Great Bodhisatta by reciting hundreds of verses of praise, surrounded by eighty thousand Naga dancers. The devas and brahmas from the ten thousand universes stood honoring him with extremely fragrant flower garlands, perfumes, scented powders, incense, and aromatic sticks, raising thousands of cheers.

At that time, Māra, a resident of the Vasavatti deva realm, had abandoned his celestial luxury and followed the Bodhisatta closely for six years while he was practicing the difficult austerities (dukkharacariya). He had been waiting and investigating for any moment the Bodhisatta might have sensual thoughts or other wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka), but he had not seen even a slight slip. He then thought, "Now Prince Siddhattha has reached the Mahābodhi seat to become a Buddha. Now this Prince Siddhattha is striving to transcend my domain (the three planes of existence). I cannot, by any means, allow Prince Siddhattha this opportunity to transcend my domain of the three planes." Thinking thus, he went to the Vasavatti deva realm, assembled his army of Māra, and commanded them: "Friends, create various terrifying and hideous forms, each carrying a different weapon, and go quickly to where Prince Siddhattha is, like a great flood overwhelming everything!" After giving this command, he himself
284:
mounted the elephant Girimekhala, which was one hundred and fifty yojanas in size, created a thousand arms, and followed them, carrying a thousand different types of weapons in each hand.

(In this context, this Māra is not the official Great King who rightfully rules the Paranimmita-vasavatti deva realm; there is another King Vasavatti who rightfully rules that realm. This Māra is merely a powerful rebel leader among the devas of that Paranimmita-vasavatti realm, who, like a rebel leader in the human world who plunders and revolts with many followers, surrounds himself with many foolish devas and greatly obstructs the meritorious deeds of humans, devas, and brahmas.)

The great army of Māra that marched toward the Bodhisatta was 12 yojanas wide in front of Māra, 12 yojanas to the right, 12 yojanas to the left, and 9 yojanas in height, while to the rear, it was so vast that it reached the edge of the universe. The sound of the shouting and roaring of this great army of Māra could be heard from a distance of a thousand yojanas, sounding as terrifying as the earth splitting apart. Māra himself, having created a thousand arms and carrying a thousand kinds of weapons, and his numerous soldiers, each carrying a weapon and assuming various terrifying forms and faces, marched forward to overwhelm, oppress, and destroy the Bodhisatta.

When the great army of Māra marched directly toward the Bodhi seat in this manner, among those who were previously honoring the Bodhisatta,
286:
286
At the time when the son of Māra appeared and arrived, the Bodhisatta sat bravely without any fear, like the king of Garuḍas among birds or the king of lions among beasts.

While those great ill omens were clearly appearing, the son of Māra arrived but was unable to enter the perimeter of the Mahābodhi-maṇḍala and stood still. The great army of Māra also did not dare to approach closely and surrounded the Great Being from all sides. Māra, looking at his army, could only give orders such as "Come! Seize him!", but just as a fly cannot approach a red-hot iron ball, they were unable to enter near the Mahābodhi tree. He then spoke to his army again: "Friends, there is no one equal to this Prince Siddhattha, the son of King Suddhodana. We are unable to fight him face-to-face. Let us attack this Prince Siddhattha from behind (the back)."

When the Bodhisatta looked towards the front and the two sides, he saw that all the devas and Brahmās had fled far away, and the place was empty and silent. Then, seeing the troops of Māra's army advancing and overwhelming from the northern side, he thought: "This vast number of Māra's soldiers are making a great effort directed at me alone. In this place, neither my mother, nor my father, nor my brothers, nor any other relatives..."
287:
287
"...are present. Only the ten Pāramīs (Perfections) that I have fulfilled are like my retinue and followers whom I have nurtured for a long time. Therefore, it is proper that I should rely only on my soldiers, the ten Pāramīs, and destroy this army of Māra by striking and attacking with these weapons of Pāramī." Thus, he remained contemplating only his own wholesome dhammas, the ten Pāramīs.

## The Launching of the Nine Weapons by the Son of Māra
While the Great Being was thus contemplating the wholesome Pāramīs, the son of Māra thought: "I will make this Prince Siddhattha flee by hurling the nine great weapons at him."

(1) First, he caused a whirlwind to blow. At that moment, the east wind, west wind, north wind, and south wind arose, capable of breaking and piercing mountain peaks half a league, one league, two leagues, or three leagues in size, uprooting forests and bushes, and grinding villages and towns to powder. However, due to the power of the Bodhisatta's merit and glory, their influence vanished, and when they reached the vicinity of the Great Being, they were unable to even rustle the hem of his robe.

(2) Then Māra thought: "The ascetic Gotama must have been crushed to pieces by hitting Mount Cakkavāḷa due to the storm weapon I hurled." Thinking thus...
288:
288
...and looking, he saw the Great Being sitting as unmoved as a firmly planted gatepost. Feeling displeased, he thought: "I will kill him by drowning him in a great torrent of water," and instantly caused dark clouds to rise and a heavy rain to fall. Due to the force of the rain caused by Māra, the earth became full of holes and hollows. That torrent of water came flowing, overwhelming the tops of forests, mountains, and trees, but when it reached the vicinity of the Bodhisatta, it could not even wet a single thread of his robe; it avoided him and flowed away.

(3) Seeing this, the son of Māra thought: "I will grind this Prince Siddhattha to powder with stones," and caused a rain of stones to fall. Huge stones, like mountain peaks, came rolling through the sky emitting smoke and flames, but when they reached the vicinity of the Bodhisatta, they turned into celestial garlands and bouquets of flowers.

(4) After that, he thought: "I will mince this Prince Siddhattha and make him die; I will kill him," and caused a rain of weapons to fall. Various weapons such as single-edged and double-edged spears and swords came from the sky emitting smoke and flames, but upon reaching the perimeter of the Mahābodhi-maṇḍala, they turned into jasmine flowers and fell.
289:
289
(5) After that, the son of Māra thought: "Prince Siddhattha will surely become like a heap of minced meat," and looking, he saw the Great Being sitting as unshaken as a mountain of diamond. Reaching a state of wonder, he again caused a rain of live coals to fall. Those live coals also came towards the Bodhisatta emitting smoke and flames, but their form as live coals vanished and they turned into jasmine flowers and fell.

(6) Then, he caused a rain of hot ashes to fall. The heap of ashes, as hot as fire, came from the sky, and when it reached the feet of the Bodhisatta, it fell as celestial sandalwood powder.

(7) Then, he caused a rain of hot sand to fall. The very fine and soft sand particles came from the sky and fell as celestial flowers at the feet of the Bodhisatta.

(8) Then, he caused a rain of hot mud to fall. That mud also came from the sky emitting smoke and flames and fell at the feet of the Bodhisatta as celestial scented paste.

(9) After that, thinking "I will frighten this Prince Siddhattha with darkness and make him flee," he caused a great darkness. The darkness created by Māra was like the darkness of the four factors: the new moon, thick clouds, midnight, and the middle of the forest.
290:
290
When it reached the presence of the Bodhisatta, it vanished like darkness meeting sunlight. (In this regard, it should be noted that the Bodhisatta, knowing that the son of Māra had created a great darkness, emitted a net of radiance from his pores. That net of radiance destroyed the great darkness created by the son of Māra and caused a great light to shine.)

## The Launching of the Discus Weapon by the Son of Māra
Although the son of Māra hurled the aforementioned nine great weapons to destroy him, they were ineffective and unsuccessful. Therefore, he further caused meteors to fall. Because of the falling meteors, the entire world-system was covered in smoke. The whole sky thundered without any clouds. Thousands of terrifying thunderbolts fell. Since Māra could not cause any harm to the Bodhisatta even with all this, he thought: "I will make the head of this Siddhattha break into pieces and fall to the ground," and hurled the Discus Weapon (Cakkāvudha). The power of that Discus Weapon was such that: if hurled at the ground, no grass could grow for twelve years. If hurled into the sky, there would be a drought for twelve years without a single drop of rain. If hurled at the peak of Mount Meru, it could split the mountain in two and slide down. Such was the power of that Discus Weapon. The Discus Weapon hurled by the son of Māra came like a thunderclap from the sky, but acting to humble the pride of Māra, it fell at the feet of the Bodhisatta, coiled like a foot-wiping cloth.
291:
291
The son of Māra, not knowing what to grasp (being at his wit's end), became extremely angry and commanded: "Why are you standing still? Act so that this Prince Siddhattha does not achieve the Buddhahood he hopes for! Seize him! Kill him! Cut him! Split him! Do not let him escape!" He himself, sitting on the back of the elephant Girimekhala and brandishing an arrow with one hand, approached the Bodhisatta and said: "O Prince Siddhattha, leave this jeweled throne immediately!" Then, the army of Māra also displayed and performed many terrifying things. The Bodhisatta, through the power of loving-kindness (mettā), warded off and prevented all the perversions and offenses committed by Māra and his army.

(In this matter, regarding the Bodhisatta's victory over the nine weapons hurled by Māra, I shall further present the verse of worship for the victory over the nine weapons written by Taungdwin Sayadaw Khingyi Phyaw, together with its word-by-word meaning.)

## Victory Vandanā over the Nine Weapons of Māra with Aspiration
## Verse and Nissaya
Vātaṃ vassañca pāsāṇaṃ, āvudhaṃ vāḷukaṃ tathā.
Kukkuḷaṃ kalalaṅgāraṃ, andhakāranti me nava.
Satthe mārena vissaṭṭhe, vijayantaṃ jinaṃ name.
Ahampi tena puṇṇena, vijeyya sabbamāyudhe.
292:
292
Vātaṃ = The weapon of the foul storm and whirlwind from the eight directions, which Māra, with evil intent, created to crush our Buddha, the Supreme of the World, while He sat upon the throne at the foot of the five Māras, intending to grind Him into fine dust like flower refuse by striking Him with the mountains of the Cakkavāḷa, causing the sky to roar and the earth to echo, and destroying trees, rocks, and houses. Vassañca = The weapon of the violent rain and foul water, which he created to drown Him in a vast expanse of water without any refuge, reaching the height of palm trees and mountain peaks, overflowing the eight directions. Pāsāṇaṃ = The rain of stones and rocks, which he created to crush Him to powder, accompanied by the sound of thunder and lightning filling the sky with flames. Āvudhaṃ = The rain of weapons of various names such as spears and swords, single-edged and double-edged, flashing like lightning across the sky, created to kill Him without delay by cutting through skin, flesh, and bone. Vāဠukaṃ tathā = The rain of sand, created to kill Him by smothering Him with sand so that no breath could go out or in. Kukkuḷaṃ = The rain of hot ashes, created with the intent to kill Him with simmering heat. Kalalaṃ = The rain of hot mud, boiling and steaming. Aṅgāraṃ = The rain of live coals, created to kill Him with intense heat in an instant. Andhakāraṃ = The darkness, created to kill Him quickly by inducing fear where nothing can be seen or felt.

Iti = Thus. Mārena vissaṭṭhe = Hurled with repeated threats by the wicked Māra. Ime nava satthe = These nine weapons: wind, rain, stone, sand...
293:
The nine kinds of dangerous weapons—mud, glowing coals, ashes, darkness, and various brilliant, flashing weapons—were all overcome. Vijayantaṃ: Although he could lead tens of millions of troops, he remained like a young child playing at his father's feet, even if he were to be struck or beaten. With a heart as clear and cool as the moon, he bore witness to the earth itself, achieving the Great Victory. (Or) Because he achieved victory. Jinaṃ: To the Exalted Buddha, the Lord of Victory, famously known by the title and seal of 'Jina' (The Conqueror). Name-namāmi: I pay homage and bow down with body, speech, and mind, humbling my pride before the Exalted Buddha. Ahampi: I, too, a combination of mind and matter produced by the four causes (kamma, citta, utu, āhāra). Tena puññena: By the power of this noble merit of praising and worshipping the virtues of the Buddha who crushed and conquered all weapons. Sabbāmāyudhe: All kinds of weapons, whether guns, bows, arrows, spears, swords, fire-locks, cannons, or diamond bombs—summarized as those that are launched and those that are not—all such weapons. Vijeyyaṃ: From this day until I attain Nibbāna, throughout the rounds of saṃsāra, may I be one who conquers and overcomes them from afar, without even seeing or hearing them, O Lord Buddha.

## The Compassion of the Bodhisatta
(Since the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā explains the scene of the victory over Devaputta Māra more extensively and inspiringly than the Jātaka Commentary or the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, I shall mostly extract and write from that Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā.)

(1) Sa pādamūle kīḷantaṃ, passaṃto taruṇaṃ sutaṃ.
Pitāvudikkhi taṃ māraṃ, mettāyanto dayāparo.
294:
Just as a father, full of intense compassion and gratitude, watches his young son playing at his feet; even if the child strikes him with hands or feet or behaves erratically, the father is far from anger. Out of love for his son, he embraces him with joy, lets him sleep in his bosom, and bears no grudge whatsoever. In the same way, the Great Bodhisatta endured everything that the wicked Māra did and all his offenses. Without the slightest displeasure and devoid of fear, he looked upon Māra while raining down the rain of loving-kindness and compassion.

(2) Tadā so āsabhiṃ vācaṃ, sīhanādaṃ nadī muni.
Na jānāti sayaṃ mayhaṃ, dāsabhāvampayaṃ khalo.
(3) Yena kenaci kammena, jāto devapure vare.
Sakaṃ gatiṃ ajānanto, lokajeṭṭhomhi maññati.

When Māra thus came with his great army to harass him, the Bodhisatta uttered these bold and brilliant words. He spoke thus: "This wicked Māra does not even know that he himself is a servant of mine. Having been born in the Vasavatti heaven due to some small amount of merit, he knows nothing of his own life-span, the time of his death, or the miserable destination (duggati) in the lower realms where he will fall after death. Thinking himself to be permanent, he considers himself the sole ruler of the whole world. He does not realize or consider the danger of falling into the lower realms after his death. It is precisely because he does not know this that he dares to commit such offenses."
295:
(4) Anantalokadhātumi,
Sattānaṃ hi kataṃ subhaṃ.
Mayhekapāramitāyāpi,
Kalaṃ nāgghati soḷasiṃ.
(5) Tiracchāno saso hutvā,
Disvā yācakumāgataṃ.
Pacitvāna sakaṃ maṃsaṃ,
Patitoggimhi dātave.

If one were to place the collective merit performed by all beings in the infinite universes on one side of the scale of wisdom, and the collective merit of my perfections (pāramī) on the other side, the merit of all beings would not equal even one two-hundred-and-fifty-sixth (1/256) part of just one of my ten perfections. Indeed, even when I was born as a small hare (sasa), upon seeing a beggar approach me, I joyfully jumped into the blazing fire to offer my own roasted flesh.

(Note: The Bodhisatta's bold statement that the collective merit of all beings in the infinite universes cannot match even 1/256th of just one of his ten perfections might seem like an exaggeration to an ordinary thinker. However, it is not an exaggeration. It is a very natural and true statement.)
296:
To make it clearer: most people, other than the Bodhisatta, perform meritorious deeds while longing for the happiness of humans or devas. (In today's Sasana, even Buddhists who know that 'vaṭṭanissita-dāna'—giving while longing for existence and wealth—is not as great or noble as 'vivaṭṭanissita-dāna'—giving while longing for Nibbāna—still harbor a desire for such worldly wealth in their hearts, even if they do not pray for it aloud.) Because such merit performed by others is done while longing for the cycle of birth (vaṭṭa), it yields the fruits of suffering within that cycle. Just as a person who spends every bit of money they earn to buy goods never accumulates wealth, those beings other than the Bodhisatta, who are 'vaṭṭābhirata' (delighting in the cycle of birth and worldly wealth), do not accumulate the wealth of merit and remain spiritually poor.

The Bodhisatta, however, whenever he performed a perfection, did so only while praying for the Golden Wisdom of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Therefore, as long as his meritorious deeds have not yet yielded the fruit of Omniscience, they remain continuously present within his continuum as 'kamma-samaṅgī' (kamma-endowment). Thus, just like a person who saves money without spending it...
297:
...finds their wealth increasing day by day, the Bodhisatta's wealth of merit increased from one life to the next, making him a person of immense spiritual riches.

Just as many poor people would surely lose if they tried to compete in wealth with a multi-millionaire, so too would the 'poor' beings of the infinite universes—who are spiritually destitute because they spend their merit as soon as they get it to buy the temporary use of worldly and celestial attainments—surely lose if they competed in the 'business' of merit with the Great Bodhisatta, the 'merit-millionaire' who possesses incalculable wealth of perfections. Therefore, the Bodhisatta's bold statement (mentioned earlier) is not an overstatement; it is a very natural and true statement.

(6) Evaṃ anantapuññehi,
Siddhaṃ dehamimaṃ pana.
Yathābhūtaṃ ajānanto,
Manussoti hi maññati.

Māra does not know the truth about this body of mine, which has arisen from such infinite merit, and he mistakenly thinks of me as just an ordinary man.
298:
(7) Nāhaṃ manusso nāmanusso, na brahmā na ca devatā.
Jarāmaraṇaṃ lokassa, dassetuṃ paniḍhāgato.

I am not an ordinary human being. I am not a yakkha (amanussa). I am not a Brahma, nor a deva. (If one asks why I was born in a human woman's womb if I am not an ordinary human, it is this:) I have come to be born in the womb of a human woman in this world to clearly demonstrate the suffering of the cycle of birth—aging, sickness, and death—to all beings.

(To clarify: One cannot definitively say the Bodhisatta is just a man, a yakkha, a deva, a Māra, or a Brahma. This is because those humans, yakkhas, devas, Māras, and Brahmas do not possess the kind of work [attainments] the Bodhisatta has.

If one asks why he was born from the womb of a human woman [Queen Māyā], the answer is that he came to be born in this world from a human woman's womb to clearly demonstrate the suffering of aging, sickness, and death to all humans, devas, and Brahmas.

To elaborate further: There is no Deva, Māra, Brahma, or 'Atta' (Self) who creates or brings beings into existence. In reality, it is only the craving (taṇhā) within each individual's own continuum of aggregates that repeatedly brings about rebirth. Wholesome and unwholesome kammas also arise through the power of craving. To make it clearer:)
299:
Kamma is like a field. Consciousness (viññāṇa), which arises together with kamma, is like a seed. Craving (taṇhā-lobha) is like water. Just as a plant sprouts due to the combination of the field, the seed, and water, a being arises due to the combination of the field of kamma, the seed of consciousness associated with kamma, and the moisture of craving. If the moisture of craving is absent, even if the field of kamma and the seed of consciousness exist, the sprout of a new life will not grow. For this reason, the Arahants, having abandoned the moisture of craving, are not reborn in a new existence.

Thus, for a being who arises from the combination of these three causes—the field of kamma, the seed of consciousness, and the moisture of craving—many sufferings such as birth (jāti) overwhelm and oppress them like a flood. The Bodhisatta is one who wishes to remove those many dangers and sufferings of beings, starting with birth. The root cause of all suffering, such as birth, is craving. When that craving is abandoned, birth no longer occurs. When birth does not occur, aging, death, and so on also do not occur. Therefore, craving is the most fundamental thing that must be eradicated. That craving arises from the perception (saññā) that the six sense objects, such as visible forms, are permanent, pleasant, beautiful, and stable—namely, nicca-saññā, sukha-saññā, subha-saññā...
300:
300
(The perception of self) arises through the power of delusion (moha) in beings who desire pleasure. Therefore, craving (taṇhā) can only be abandoned by showing the faults in the six sense objects, which are the causes of that craving. The faults in the six sense objects are the characteristics of impermanence (anicca) and so forth that occur within them. These characteristics of impermanence can only be realized by seeing aging and death (jarā-maraṇa). (Only by seeing aging and death can one see the faults, such as the nature of impermanence, in the six sense objects. Only by seeing the faults in the six sense objects can one abandon the greed of craving that clings to them. Only by abandoning the greed of craving can the sufferings of saṃsāra, such as birth (jāti), be extinguished.) Thus, the realization of aging and death is the fundamental and primary task for the cooling of the suffering of saṃsāra. Therefore, for the sake of revealing and teaching the nature of aging and death, which is the primary root for the complete cessation of the sufferings of saṃsāra such as birth, the Bodhisatta came to be conceived and born in the womb of Mother Māyā in this human world.

To clarify further: if the Bodhisatta were to teach the Dhamma or perform miracles while appearing as a Deva or a Brahma, others would not believe him. They would think, 'This King of Devas or King of Brahmas is himself happy, permanent, and stable, yet he comes to teach us about impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta).'
301:
301
Thinking, 'What kind of words are these?', they would not believe him, nor would they listen respectfully. They would think, 'What is there that a Deva or Brahma cannot say or teach? They can certainly say and teach anything. What kind of miracle can they not perform or create? They can certainly perform and create them. This teaching and performance of miracles by this Deva or Brahma is not surprising.'

However, when he is born from a mother's womb while all people are watching, and upon reaching maturity, enjoys sensual pleasures, and after having a son, renounces that son to enter the forest and become a monk, practices the great austerities (dukkara-cariyā), attains the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) (i.e., attains Buddhahood), and then teaches the Dhamma, reveals aging and death, and teaches the Three Characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), people will think: 'Even this Great Man, though possessed of such great power and wisdom, and knowing all phenomena without exception, cannot escape the nature of aging, sickness, and death. For us, there is no question.' Thinking thus, they will listen to the Dhamma respectfully. They will think, 'Our Blessed Buddha, who teaches the Dhamma to remove sufferings such as birth, indeed knows all things analytically. That Nibbāna, where there is no suffering such as birth, is truly peaceful.'
302:
302
Having gained faith in the Buddha and the Dhamma, and following the teaching, they will direct their wisdom into the Dhamma. They will see this personality, which is purely the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā), as suffering and as the cause of suffering. Then they will clearly see the fault of the greed of craving (taṇhā-lobha) that gives rise to this personality of the five aggregates of clinging. Seeing this, they will become frightened, ashamed, and disgusted by the Truth of the Cause (samudaya-sacca), which is craving, and the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca), which is the five aggregates of clinging arising from that craving. Then they will cause craving to cease completely. When it is thus ceased, they will be worthy of entering the Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbāna) and ending the cycle of suffering. Therefore, it is said, 'He came to be born in the womb of Mother Māyā in this human world for the purpose of revealing and teaching the dangers of the suffering of saṃsāra, such as aging, sickness, and death, to all beings.'

(8) Anupalitto lokena,
jāto'nantajino ahaṃ.
Buddho bodhitale hutvā,
tāremi janataṃ bahuṃ.

O Māra! Although I was born in this human world, I have remained entirely unstained and unattached to any being or formation (saṅkhāra). Because I have conquered infinite beings and infinite defilements, I have received the name 'Anantajina' (Infinite Conqueror). Right now, while sitting on this Aparājita Throne,
303:
303
without even breaking this cross-legged posture, I shall cremate and abandon all defilements and, having truly become a Buddha in the three worlds, I shall rescue the multitude of beings—humans, devas, and brahmas—from the flood of saṃsāra and bring them to the dry land of Nibbāna. You are in no way able to hinder me; this is not your domain.

(9) Samantā dhajiniṃ disvā,
yuddhaṃ māraṃ savāhanaṃ.
Yuddhāya paccugacchāmi,
mā maṃ ဌာနာ acāvayi.

(10) Yaṃ te taṃ nappasahati,
seṇaṃ loko sadevako.
Taṃ te paññāya bhecchāmi,
āmaṃ pakkaṃva asmanā.

O Māra! Seeing your great army advancing from all sides with banners flying, and seeing you together with the elephant Girimekhala, I advance directly toward you with wisdom to bravely do battle. (This does not mean the Buddha physically rose and advanced, but that he advanced with wisdom.) You shall in no way be able to make me rise or move from this Aparājita Throne; I shall act so that I cannot be moved.

O Māra! Just as a strong man might crush all the pots made by a potter—whether baked or unbaked—with a large stone, leaving none unbroken, so shall I
304:
304
crush your army of ten defilements, such as sensual lust, which the entire world surrenders to and finds loathsome. (Alternatively) Your great army, which extends twelve yojanas to the front and to the left and right, and is nine yojanas in height, and reaches back to the Cakkavāḷa wall—I, being alone, without even moving from this spot where I sit, shall repel and crush every single one of them by the power of wisdom. I shall soon make you and your troops flee, just as one scatters a flock of crows by throwing a stone.

(These verses 9 and 10 are verses taught by the Blessed One in the Padhāna Sutta. Verses 1 to 8, and the verses to be shown hereafter, were composed by the Elder Buddharakkhita, the author of the Jinālaṅkāra, based on various Suttas according to the Buddha's intention.)

(11) Icchanto sāsape gabbhe, caṅkamāmi ito cito.
Icchanto lokadhātumi, attabhāvena chādayi.

O Māra! If I wish (to be small), I can walk back and forth within a mustard seed. If I wish (to be large), I can cover the entire universe (lokadhātu) with my own body.

(12) Ete sabbe gahetvāna, cuṇṇetuṃ accharāyapi.
Atthi thāmabalaṃ mayhaṃ, pāṇaghāto na ruccati.

O Māra! I have the strength and power to seize you and all your troops and crush you to powder with just a snap of my fingers. Nevertheless, I
305:
305
do not take even an atom's weight of pleasure in the misconduct of taking life (pāṇātipāta).

(13) Imassa gaṇḍuppādassa, āvudhena balena kiṃ.
Mayhaṃ hi tena pāpena, sallāpopi na ruccati.

What use is there for me to use weapons or physical strength against this Māra, who is merely the size of an earthworm? Indeed, I do not even take pleasure in having this conversation with this wicked Māra.

(Before the Bodhisatta spoke these bold words, Māra had said, 'O Prince Siddhattha! Why are you sitting on this Aparājita Throne, which is my property?' The Bodhisatta then asked, 'Who is the witness that the throne is your property?' Māra replied, 'What is the use of bringing others as witnesses? This entire army of Māra, which is present before your eyes, is my witness.' When he stretched out his hand, Māra's followers cried out all at once, 'I am a witness! I am a witness!', appearing in hundreds of millions. It was as noisy as the earth sliding. Therefore, to stop Māra's followers and reveal his own witness, the Buddha recited this verse:)

(14) Pallaṅkaṃ mama bhāvāya,
kimatthaññena sakkhinā.
Kampitā maddiyā dānā,
sakkhi hoti ayaṃ mahī.
306:
306
O Māra! In my desire for this Aparājita Throne, there is no gift (dāna) I have not given, no virtue (sīla) I have not observed, and no austerity (dukkara) I have not practiced throughout many lives and aeons. O Māra! Setting aside the perfections of giving and so forth performed in many past aeons, in the single life of Vessantara alone, when I gave the great gifts culminating in the gift of Queen Maddī, this great earth (mahāpathavī) shook seven times. Now, while I sit on this Aparājita Throne to conquer the entire world, why does this great earth remain silent and motionless as your great army of Māra advances to do battle? O Māra! You have made your followers bear false witness. This earth is impartial to both you and me; it has no volition. Even so, this great earth, which is impartial to us and entirely without volition, shall be my witness right now.' Saying this, the Bodhisatta withdrew his right hand, which was as graceful as a flash of lightning from the edge of a cloud, from within his robe and pointed it toward the great earth.

At that very moment, the great earth spun rapidly like a potter's wheel and roared intensely. With the sound of the earth, the entire sky resounded with a thunderous noise. The seven mountain ranges surrounding Mount Meru, as well as the Himalayas and others, roared intensely. The entire universe made a harsh and terrifying sound, crackling and snapping like a burning bamboo forest.
307:
The thunder roared; just as popcorn pops in a scorching pan, the entire cloudless sky resounded with terrifying thunderclaps. Sparks of fire, like a rain of glowing embers, scattered everywhere, and thunderbolts fell repeatedly with crashing sounds. Māra, the celestial son, caught between the earth and the sky filled with incessant, tumultuous noise, was overcome with extreme terror, having no refuge to rely upon. He lowered his great battle-standard, abandoned his thousand weapons right there, and fled headlong in whatever direction he faced, unable even to look back at his great elephant, Girimekhala. As soon as the King Māra fled, the great army of Māra also broke apart in disarray and ruin. Like dust scattered by a whirlwind, they fled in every direction they faced and returned only to the Vasavatti deva realm.

Thus, the Bodhisatta achieved victory over Devaputta Māra (Vasavatti Māra) before sunset on the full moon day of Kason in the year 103 of the Great Era (Mahā Sakkarit). Having attained victory over the entire world of sentient beings (Satta-loka), he reached a state of fearlessness, freedom from enemies, and absence of trepidation. At that very moment, the devas and brahmas, who had fled in fear when Māra arrived, had been watching to see who would win and who would lose. Seeing the great army of Māra’s followers broken and destroyed, they simultaneously shouted fourfold praises, beginning with "Jayo hi Buddhassa sirīmato ayaṃ."

"Māra the celestial son has lost! Prince Siddhattha has won! Let us perform a victory celebration!" Thus, Nagas with Nagas, Garudas with Garudas, Devas with Devas, and Brahmas with Brahmas shouted in acclaim.
308:
Carrying perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, they gathered in unison at the Mahābodhi Throne where the Bodhisatta was seated.

Jayo hi Buddhassa sirīmato ayaṃ.
Mārassa ca pāpimato parājayo.
Ugghosayuṃ bodhimaṇḍe pamoditā,
Jayaṃ tadā nāgagaṇā mahesino. (1)

Ayaṃ = This extraordinary victory, which resounds through the earth and sky as if they were animate, though they are inanimate.
Sirīmato = Of Him who is the repository of all glorious attributes, incomparable to any that exist in this universe (Cakkavāḷa).
Buddhassa hi = Only of the Lord Buddha, who truly knows all that should be known (Ñeyya-dhamma) through His Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) without exception.
Jayo = Is the victory celebration acclaimed by human kings, deva kings, and brahma kings.
Pāpimato = Of the one who is truly blind and ignorant, being wicked and depraved.
Mārassa ca = Of Māra, the celestial son, who marched with a great army to seize the glorious Bodhi Throne, attacking with such force that the earth tilted across the eight directions.
Parājayo = Is the defeat in battle, falling prostrate, unable to retaliate against the enemy, and retreating with his army in fear of the Buddha's majestic power.
Iti = Thus.
Tadā = On that full moon day of Kason in the year 103 of the Great Era, the day of the victory over Māra.
Bodhimaṇḍe = At the seat of victory, the Unconquered Place (Aparājita-ṭhāna), where Omniscient Wisdom matures and clarifies.
Pamoditā = The hosts of Nagas, who were joyful, delighted, and exuberant,
Nāgagaṇā = The hosts of celestial Nagas,
Mahesino = Of the Buddha, who has sought, practiced, and acquired special qualities such as the aggregate of virtue (Sīlakkhandha).
309:
Jayaṃ = Shouted the sound of the glorious victory acclamation.
Ugghosayuṃ = They proclaimed it loudly, resounding throughout the ten thousand world systems.
