All the devas and brahmas residing in the ten thousand world systems beyond this one also came to gather and pay homage to the Great Being (Bodhisatta), offering flowers, perfumes, and scented pastes, and uttering various auspicious words of praise and eulogy.

(This concludes the chapter on the victory over Devaputta Māra [Vasavatti Māra].)

Special Note: In describing the itinerary and activities of the Bodhisatta on the full moon day of Kason, 103 Great Era, other accounts in the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary, the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā-nidāna, and the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā are similar in meaning, differing only in the level of detail. Regarding the chapter on staying for the day in the Sal grove, the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary and the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā-nidāna do not mention the attainment of any meditative attainments (Samāpatti) or supernormal knowledges (Abhiññā) while staying there. However, the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā explains that while staying for the day in that Sal grove, he attained the eight mundane meditative attainments and the five supernormal knowledges. It further states that when the Great Being approached the Mahābodhi tree, he was already endowed with the physical strength (Kāya-bala) equivalent to ten billion average men (Majjhima-purisa) and the power of supernormal knowledges (Abhiññā-bala). This explanation by the author of the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā is consistent with the words spoken by the Great Being when Māra’s army marched forth: "If I wish, I can walk to and fro within a mustard seed. If I wish, I can cover the entire universe with my body," as well as with the account of the Vessantara birth, which is the domain of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (Pubbenivāsānussati-abhiññā)...
313:
This is consistent with the statement "pointing to the great gifts as witness" etc., and is not blameworthy. According to the view of the author of the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā, the Bodhisatta had already attained the five mundane absorptions (jhāna) and mundane supernormal powers (abhiññā) while meeting the great teachers Āḷāra and Uddaka. Since he did not use them throughout the six years of practicing austerities (dukkharacariya), they became like gold bowls that gather grime when left unused. He purified them at the Sal grove (just as one would polish them to be clean again). It is implied that after overcoming Māra, he used his previously attained Pubbenivāsa-abhiññā and Dibbacakkhu-abhiññā beautifully to reach the stage of penetrating the Vijjā-ñāṇa (just as one would beautifully use a gold bowl one possesses). This is specifically highlighted because it is extraordinary and noteworthy.

## Attaining the Three Vijjā: Pubbe, Di, Ā

In this way, the Bodhisatta, having conquered Vasavatti Māra, also known as Devaputta Māra, before sunset on the full moon day of Kason in the year 103 of the Great Era (Mahā-sakkarāj), attained the three Vijjā-ñāṇa in succession: Pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa in the first watch of the night, Dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa in the middle watch, and Āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa in the last watch. Thus, he reached Buddhahood in the last watch of the full moon day of Kason. The detailed account of this is as follows:

## Attaining the Pubbenivāsānussati-abhiññā

The collection of things consisting of the past sequence of aggregates (khandha), the Dhamma of Nibbāna to be known through that sequence, and the concepts (paññatti) such as names and lineages, is called "Pubbenivāsa" in Pali.
314:
The special supernormal power associated with mindfulness that recollects that past life (pubbenivāsa) is called "Pubbenivāsānussati-abhiññā." The Buddha taught this very knowledge as the first Vijjā-ñāṇa. Ancient scholars designated it with the initial symbol "Pu" (the method of naming by the first letter). The detailed account of how he attained this first Vijjā-ñāṇa is as follows:

While the Great Bodhisatta, having conquered Vasavatti Māra, sat smiling and serene on the Aparājita Throne, the vast multitude of devas and brahmās, starting from the earth-dwelling devas (bhūmmazo) residing in the ten thousand world systems, shouted and proclaimed: "O many devas and brahmās, come! The victory of the Great Bodhisatta and the defeat of Māra have become clearly evident. Let us celebrate together the auspicious festival of victory and the auspicious festival of the impending Buddhahood for the Great Bodhisatta." Thus, they gathered and approached the Great Bodhisatta simultaneously.

At that time, the sun, beautiful with its thousand rays and fifty yojanas in size, was about to set like a great golden wheel being held at its rim and submerged into the whirlpool of the great ocean. The moon-chariot, forty-nine yojanas in size, emitting cool and brilliant rays, illuminating the entire world system, was about to rise in the eastern direction from the ocean of milk like a silver chariot wheel being held at its rim and thrown up into the sky by someone.
315:
(Imagine the great world system in the form of a great golden palace.) In the center of the golden palace of the world system, the Great Bodhisatta was exceedingly beautiful, as if submerging the Mahābodhi terrace and all surrounding animate and inanimate objects in a flow of liquid gold with his body's radiance, which was like the color of gold. The Bodhisatta, thus beautiful, sat cross-legged on the Aparājita Throne at the foot of the Mahābodhi tree, which was like an umbrella of sapphire (indanilā), and reflected upon the Dhamma. (The details of how the Great Bodhisatta reflected on the Dhamma will be clear later.)

## The Great Offerings by Devas and Brahmās

At that time, Sakka, the king of devas, stood in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and blew the Vijayuttara conch, which was one hundred and twenty (120) yojanas in size, to assemble the devas and brahmās. The sound of that conch spread and was heard throughout the entire deva realm, which is ten thousand yojanas wide. While blowing the conch, he quickly ran and reached the Mahābodhi terrace. (Not only the Sakka of this world system, but all the Sakkas within the ten thousand world systems of the field of birth (jāti-khetta) also came to the presence of the Bodhisatta, blowing their conchs.)

Mahābrahmā came to worship, holding the white umbrella he had left on the peak of the world-system mountain, shading it over the Bodhisatta. (The Mahābrahmās within the ten thousand world systems of the field of birth also...
316:
...came and stood, holding white umbrellas so that they were joined edge to edge without any gap throughout this world system.)

Suyama, the king of the Yāma deva realm, also came to worship, standing near the Bodhisatta and fanning him with a yak-tail whisk (cāmari) three gāvutas in size. (The Suyama kings within the ten thousand world systems of the field of birth also came to worship, each holding a yak-tail whisk, filling this world system.)

Santusita, the king of the Tusita deva realm, came to worship, standing and fanning with a ruby fan-circle three gāvutas in size. (All the Santusita kings ruling in the other ten thousand world systems of the field of birth also came to worship, each holding a ruby fan-circle, filling this world system.)

Pañcasikha, the son of devas, came to worship, standing and playing the Beluva lute, which was three gāvutas in size, surrounded by a host of celestial dancers, performing dance, song, and music. (All the celestial dancers living in the other ten thousand world systems of the field of birth also came to worship, dancing, singing, and playing music.)

Furthermore, the hosts of devas and goddesses living within the ten thousand world systems of the field of birth gathered in this world system; some stood surrounding and worshipping, each holding a jeweled archway (toraṇa) post.
317:
Some held offerings made of the seven kinds of gems in rows; some held golden banana trees in rows; some held auspicious houses made of the seven gems in rows; some held yak-tail whisks in rows; some held goads; some held pairs of carp; some held jasmine flowers; some held golden circular pedestals; some held full bowls; some held full pots; some held conchs; some held fire-stirring ladles; some held ruby lamps; some held large golden mirrors; some held large jeweled mirrors; some held large mirrors decorated with the seven gems; some held ruby lights; some held banners and streamers; some held wish-fulfilling trees (padesā-bin) in rows, surrounding and worshipping in their respective groups. All the devas living in the ten thousand world systems took the form of dancers, performing celestial dances and songs, and worshipped with celestial flowers, celestial perfumes, and celestial scented powders. At that time, the entire sky was filled without any gap with rains of celestial flowers and perfumes, as if the surroundings were filled with the flow of heavy raindrops from a torrential rain.

The reason why the hosts of devas and brahmās worshipped so loudly and magnificently was because they were filled with faith, hope, and joy, thinking: "When this Great Bodhisatta becomes Buddha, we will hear the Dhamma and attain the supramundane deathless Dhamma of the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna. We will surely obtain from this Buddha the joy and rapture (pīti) born of focusing on those nine supramundane Dhammas. We will also see various miracles that are a deathless nectar for the eyes.
318:
That Great Buddha, preaching the deathless Dhamma to us, will liberate and save us from the difficult journey of birth (jāti), the difficult journey of old age (jarā), the difficult journey of sickness (vyādhi), the difficult journey of death (maraṇa), and the collection of difficult journeys of sorrow (soka), lamentation (parideva), pain (dukkha), grief (domanassa), and despair (upāyāsa)."

Although the Great Bodhisatta was worshipped by the devas and brahmās filling the world system for the reasons mentioned, and although he clearly saw and heard such vast and special offerings, he did not have any attachment or delight in those special offerings at all. Without even paying attention to them, he remained reflecting, contemplating, and considering only the Dhamma which was his refuge and reliance.

The situation of the Great Bodhisatta as he remained thus was like this: the Great Cakkavāḷa mountains were like curtains surrounding him; the sky above was like a canopy ceiling decorated with gold and silver stars of the constellations; the great world system was like a great royal palace with seven stories, representing the seven celestial realms of the happy destination (sugati). Within that great palace of the world system, the site of the Mahābodhi terrace was like a great audience hall; the Aparājita Throne was like a great royal throne for the audience; and the Mahābodhi tree was like a great royal umbrella made of emerald gems.

Inside that great audience hall of the victorious ground of the Mahābodhi terrace, from the base to the top...
319:
...the Mahābodhi tree, which was one hundred cubits in height and one hundred cubits in circumference, shaded him like a great emerald umbrella. The Great Bodhisatta, sitting on the royal throne of the Aparājita Throne, did not look at or listen to the devas and brahmās who were worshipping him from all around the world system. By reflecting and recollecting only the Dhamma, his energy (vīriya) was unflagging and extremely intense, his mindfulness (sati) was unforgetting and extremely clear, and both his body and mind were unperturbed and extremely peaceful. Thus, he again attained and entered the first Rūpāvacara jhāna.

In the mental continuum of the Bodhisatta entering that first Rūpāvacara jhāna, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) were extremely pure and absent. Because of being secluded from sensual desires (vatthu-kāma) and defilements (kilesa-kāma), rapture and happiness (pīti-sukha) were arising repeatedly.

Then, when he again entered the second Rūpāvacara jhāna, in the Bodhisatta's mental continuum, the movements and disturbances of initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra) were absent; he was extremely clear with pure faith (saddhā) within his internal nature, and his concentration (samādhi) was incomparably firm. Because of that concentration, rapture and happiness (pīti-sukha) increased more and more.

Then, when he again attained and entered the third Rūpāvacara jhāna, in the Bodhisatta's mental continuum, even the prominent rapture (pīti) disappeared, and he remained clearly peaceful with pure pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā). Furthermore, even in that supreme pleasant feeling...
320:
He was endowed with the mental factor of tatramajjhattatā, known as jhānūpekkhā, which is unattached and capable of equal equanimity; his mindfulness was extremely clear and his wisdom was exceptionally sharp.

Furthermore, when he again attained and entered the fourth rūpāvacara jhāna, the Great Bodhisatta's mental continuum, having already abandoned the physical and mental suffering and happiness, remained steady, experiencing the object only with the neutral feeling of equanimity (upekkhā vedanā). Due to the influence of this upekkhā vedanā and the mental factor of tatramajjhattatā, the associated states such as mindfulness present in that fourth jhāna became exceedingly pure, like the moonlight.

## The Bodhisatta's Mental Continuum Being Endowed with Eight Qualities

Now, if one were to reflect upon and examine the Great Bodhisatta's mental continuum with devotion, even during the six years of practicing austerities (dukkharacariyā), one would find and admire a mental continuum so pure that it was not mixed with the three types of wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka)—namely, sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka), thoughts of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka), and thoughts of cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka)—to the extent that Māra the Evil One could find no opportunity. Again, on the full moon day of Kason, the day he would become the Buddha, while resting during the day in the Sal grove, one would find his mental continuum admirable and extremely pure through the eight mundane attainments (samāpatti). Even more so now, as he sat on the Unconquered Golden Throne (Aparājita Pallanka) at the foot of the Mahābodhi tree, having conquered Māra the son of a deva (Devaputta Māra), he did not pay attention to the assembly of devas and brahmas from the ten thousand world systems who had gathered to honor him. Instead, he focused only on his own practice of the Dhamma, and as previously mentioned, he again attained and entered the four rūpāvacara
321:
jhānas (pertaining to individuals of sharp wisdom). The mental continuum of the Bodhisatta, possessing immense strength of concentration through the fourth jhāna, was as follows:

(1) Due to the influence of the extremely pure fourth jhāna consciousness (cittuppāda), it was pure from beginning to end and all around.

(2) Because it was so pure, it was brilliant and radiant, like pure gold that has been recently smelted and polished, almost as if it were emitting flashes of light.

(3) Having abandoned and removed pleasant feelings (sukha-somanassa), which are the cause of greed, and painful feelings (dukkha-domanassa), which are the cause of hatred, it was free from the mental stains of greed and hatred.

(4) Because it was free from such mental stains and impurities, it was also free from the defilements (upakkilesa) that tarnish and oppress the mind.

(5) Because he had mastered his mind through the five masteries (vasībhāva), and because it was well-tamed and disciplined through the fourteen modes, his mental continuum was malleable (mudu), like leather that has been well-kneaded to follow one's desire, or like a block of lac that has been well-refined.
322:
(6) Because it was malleable, just as pure and refined gold is easy and excellent for making any desired ornament, being responsive to every pull and draw, so too was his mind excellent and ready (kammañña) to easily and beautifully accomplish various tasks, such as recollecting past lives and deeds, and seeing distant, hidden, or subtle forms as if with a divine eye.

(7) Because he had well-developed and practiced so that the aforementioned qualities would not fade away, his mental continuum remained firm and steady (ṭhita) in those qualities (not loosely, but resolutely).

(8) Because it was so firm and steady, it was completely imperturbable (āneñjappatta).

(Alternatively)

(7) Because it was malleable and excellent for easily and beautifully accomplishing various tasks, his mental continuum remained according to his will. (8) Such a mental continuum, being established with the great strength of the light of faith (saddhā), energy (vīriya), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā), was completely imperturbable by the darkness of defilements such as faithlessness, laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, and ignorance; (or) not even a trace of faithlessness and so forth could enter his mental continuum.
323:
In another way:

(1) The Bodhisatta's mental continuum was well-concentrated (samāhita) through the fourth jhāna concentration. (2) It was pure (parisuddha) all around, being far from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). (3) Having transcended the coarse jhāna factors such as initial thought (vitakka) which agitate the mind, it was bright and clear (pariyodāta), almost as if emitting radiance. (4) It was free from blemishes (anaṅgaṇa) because of the absence of conceit (māna), deceit (māyā), and hypocrisy (sāṭheyya) that can arise based on the attainment of jhāna. (5) It was free from defilements (vigatūpakkilesa) such as covetousness (abhijjhā) which tarnish the mind. (6) It was malleable (mudubhūta) because he had mastered the five masteries (vasībhāva). (7) It was wieldy and ready for work (kammañña), serving as the foundation for various psychic powers (iddhi), to perform tasks related to the Dhamma as desired. (8) It was steady and imperturbable (ṭhita āneñjappatta) because his meditative development (bhāvanā) was complete and sufficient.

The mind of the Great Bodhisatta, endowed with these eight qualities, was extremely easy to direct toward the realization of those things that must be known through higher knowledge (abhiññā). If the mind was directed toward the object of an abhiññā, the abhiññā-javana (impulse of higher knowledge) could arise with great ease.
325:
The Great Bodhisatta, reflecting on and knowing his successive lives through this true knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati vijjā-ñāṇa), realized:

"In these various successive rounds of rebirth (saṃsāra) without a discoverable beginning, only mind and matter (nāma-rūpa) have arisen. At the moment of rebirth-linking, during the course of existence, and at the moment of death—at all these three times—only mind and matter have arisen. In all planes of existence and at all times, these mind and matter phenomena have arisen in an uninterrupted continuum, like the flame of a lamp or the current of a river, through the succession of cause and effect. Only successive mind and matter have performed their respective functions, such as seeing forms at the eye-door and hearing sounds at the ear-door, through the six doors of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and have brought about various expressions (viññatti) such as bodily and vocal movements. (In reality) there is no person, being, 'I', 'another', man, or woman at all. There is no single Deva, Māra, or Brahma who creates or makes such a person or being."

Thus, through penetrating insight, he also attained special knowledges that are certain for the attainment of the supramundane paths and fruits (lokuttara magga-phala). Consequently, the Great Bodhisatta, through the knowledge of recollecting past lives, abandoned the four types of self-view (attā-diṭṭhi = sakkāya-diṭṭhi) related to the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha)—namely, that form is self, that self possesses form, that form is in self, or that self is in form. Similarly, he abandoned the four types of self-view related to the aggregate of feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), mental formations (saṅkhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇa),
327:
He saw those who were low-born and high-born, those who were beautiful and ugly, those who reached happy destinations and those who reached miserable destinations. (Alternatively) He saw those who were wealthy due to the results of wholesome kamma rooted in non-greed, and those who were poor due to the results of unwholesome kamma rooted in greed.

With the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu), having seen the beings in the woeful states suffering, He reflected: "What kind of kamma did these beings in the woeful states perform to suffer such terrifying misery?" Then, the special knowledge of yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa, which knows the unwholesome kamma of those beings, arose. Likewise, having seen with the Divine Eye the many beings in the human realm, deva realms, and brahma realms enjoying great happiness in ascending levels, He reflected: "What kind of kamma did these human, deva, and brahma beings perform to enjoy such (successively) grand human, deva, and brahma bliss?" Then, the special knowledge of yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa, which knows the wholesome kamma of those beings, arose.

Through that special knowledge of yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa, He knew: "These beings in the woeful states committed wrong bodily, verbal, and mental conduct in previous lives. They spoke words of accusation, abuse, and blame against the Noble Ones (ariyas). They held wrong views, and with those wrong views, they themselves undertook and committed various unwholesome deeds, and also caused others to undertake and commit them."
328:
"These beings, after the breaking up of the body and death, have been reborn in the four woeful states: hell, the animal realm, the peta realm, and the asura realm." And He knew: "These beings in the happy destinations performed well their bodily, verbal, and mental conduct. They did not accuse, abuse, or blame the Noble Ones; they held right views. With those right views, they themselves undertook and developed various wholesome deeds, and also caused others to undertake and develop them. Because of those wholesome deeds, after the breaking up of the body and death, they have been reborn in the happy destinations of the human realm, the deva realms, and the twenty brahma realms." Thus, He saw and understood according to reality, in detail, the wholesome and unwholesome kamma previously performed by beings.

The Great Bodhisatta attained this Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu = Second Knowledge) during the middle watch of that night. Through this Divine Eye, the element of ignorance (avijjā) and delusion (moha), which covers the passing away and rebirth of beings, was eliminated from the Great Bodhisatta's mental continuum. Since He saw and understood with clarity the true causes of beings' past kamma through the yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa based on that Divine Eye, and because the sixteen types of doubt had been abandoned, the Great Bodhisatta reached the stage of kankhāvitaraṇavisuddhi (Purification by Overcoming Doubt).

## (3) Attaining the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints (Āsavakkhaya = Third Knowledge)
## and Becoming the Buddha

(Since there are many very important points and notes to be understood regarding this āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa, I shall write and present them in two ways: briefly and in detail.)
329:
Briefly:

In the last watch (pacchima-yāma) of the night, the Great Bodhisatta reached the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa) called āsavakkhaya, and while obtaining Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), in order to truly become the Buddha in the three worlds, He inclined His mental continuum, which was endowed with the eight qualities mentioned earlier, toward the attainment of the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship. Then, He applied His knowledge to the Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) consisting of twelve factors: ignorance (avijjā), volitional formations (saṅkhāra), consciousness (viññāṇa), mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa), the six sense bases (saḷāyatana), contact (phassa), feeling (vedanā), craving (taṇhā), clinging (upādāna), becoming (bhava), birth (jāti), and aging-and-death (jarā-maraṇa). Reviewing and reflecting repeatedly on the factors of Dependent Origination in forward and reverse order, He reached the Noble Path called yathābhūtañāṇadassana (Knowledge and Vision according to reality). (This is the brief account.)

In detail:

These four Path Knowledges called yathābhūtañāṇadassana do not arise in the mental continuums of those with great power in the world, such as Sakka, the King of Devas, the Great Brahma, or virtuous hermits like Kaladevila and Nārada who possess great meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti) and psychic powers (abhiññā). Why did these four Path Knowledges—which are extremely subtle and profound, never before seen or realized even in a dream throughout the beginningless round of rebirths (saṃsāra)—arise only in the mental continuum of the Great Bodhisatta, who attained monkhood by Himself without a teacher? The answer is...
330:
## The Great Beneficence of the Perfections

The Great Bodhisatta, throughout the period of four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, which is so vast that the number of lives cannot be counted in hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands, did not care for or withhold even His own life. Based on the four types of meditation (to be described in the miscellaneous section below), He performed various meritorious deeds of the Perfection of Generosity (dāna-pāramī). In every life, He abandoned the defilement of greed (lobha) whenever it arose toward various objects, practicing until it was so minimal that others would say, "Does the defilement of greed even exist in this Great Being's mental continuum?"

Likewise, through the Perfections of Virtue (sīla-pāramī), Patience (khanti-pāramī), and Loving-kindness (mettā-pāramī) cultivated for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, He restrained anger (kodha) and ill-will (dosa). By sprinkling the cool water of loving-kindness for a very long time, He extinguished the fire of anger, as well as its companions: envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), and remorse (kukkucca).

Through the Great Perfection of Wisdom (paññā-pāramī) well-cultivated over many lives and aeons, He cut off the darkness of ignorance (moha) and abandoned wrong views (micchā-diṭṭhi), becoming an exceedingly pure wise man. Furthermore, He approached the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples (ariya-sāvakas) He encountered, as well as other wise persons, and inquired: "What is blameless and what is blameworthy? What is dark and what is bright?" By thus investigating, He removed doubt (vicikicchā) regarding the Dhamma and caused His wisdom to grow and increase from one life to the next.
331:
By paying respect, honoring, worshipping, giving up His seat, rising to welcome, and greeting His elders such as parents and uncles in His family, and by respecting wise persons endowed with virtue, He abandoned conceit (māna) and restlessness (uddhacca). He Himself was free from pride, like a snake with its fangs removed, a bull with its horns broken, or a foot-wiping cloth. He was accustomed to speaking only words of praise regarding patience, seeking the welfare of others, and compassionate protection.

The Great Bodhisatta, through Renunciation (nekkhamma), abandoned royal wealth and became a monk, attaining meditative absorptions (jhāna-samāpatti) in the forest and removing the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). In every life, He dispelled sensual lust (kāma-rāga) and delight in women (itthi-rati). Through the Perfection of Truth (sacca-pāramī), He abandoned false speech (micchā-vācā) that causes the world to go astray. Through the Perfection of Energy (vīriya-pāramī), He dispelled dissatisfaction (arati) and laziness (kosajja) in the practice of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) meditations, which are superior wholesome deeds, and always kept His mind active and energetic in wholesome actions.
332:
In this manner, He practiced to make His mental continuum purer and purer from one life to the next.

The Great Bodhisatta, who thus abandoned various defilements through the collection of perfections such as generosity, would find that defilements He had purified in one life might arise again (since they had not yet been abandoned by the Path Knowledge of Eradication, samuccheda-pahāna). He would then purify those defilements again. Without giving up or surrendering, He would abandon and cleanse those defilements through great wholesome deeds and lofty wholesome deeds (by way of temporary abandonment, tadaṅga-pahāna, and abandonment by suppression, vikkhambhana-pahāna). In this way, for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, He cleansed the defilements that are the impurities of the mind. He cleared away the general of defilements, ignorance (avijjā-moha), along with its army of attendant defilements. He caused the five faculties—faith (saddhā), energy (vīriya), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā)—to mature and grow from one life to the next. Having crossed the difficult journey of rebirth by intensely developing the perfections, He completed the practices that enable one to become a Buddha by giving away Queen Maddī in His life as King Vessantara. Then, He resided in the Tusita heaven enjoying celestial bliss, merely waiting for the time to become the Buddha.

Thus, by abandoning and cleansing various factors of defilements such as greed and hatred through the collection of perfections like generosity,
333:
and because He was one who had reached the pinnacle of wisdom and had fully developed it, the four Path Knowledges, which are extremely subtle, delicate, and profound, arose in the Great Bodhisatta's mental continuum (without the help of a teacher).

Furthermore, from the time He was at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, the Bodhisatta performed, collected, and developed the perfections such as generosity, which are very difficult for ordinary people to do. Yet, He never made an aspiration for any kind of worldly pleasure in any life in exchange for those wholesome deeds. For all the wholesome deeds He performed, such as generosity, He only made the aspiration: "May this collection of merit be a strong supporting condition (upanissaya) for the attainment of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)." Others, after performing various wholesome deeds, aspire for celestial or human pleasures, and according to those aspirations, they receive and enjoy the results of human and celestial bliss, like those who consume and waste the collection of wholesome wealth they have acquired. The Great Bodhisatta did not do so; like a person who fills a granary with grain and keeps it carefully without using it, He made the aspiration for every wholesome deed He performed: "May it be a supporting condition only for the four Path Knowledges crowned by Omniscience," and stored them well. Thus, all the perfections and wholesome deeds the Bodhisatta collected for the long duration of four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons were ready to give their results in this final life as Siddhāttha, leading to Buddhahood.
334:
334
As the opportunity had arrived, the merits that were to bear fruit were so numerous that the single life seemed extremely crowded and narrow. 

Because of the power of his aspiration (patthanā), which had been directed solely toward attaining Buddhahood, the merits that were to bear fruit in this final life crowded together with such great force that the four stages of profound and subtle Path Knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) arose within the Great Bodhisatta without the help of a teacher. (In this section on the attainment of Buddhahood, many inspiring points from the Jinālaṅkāra text are presented.)

## The Bodhisatta Developing Three Million Six Hundred Thousand 
## Mahāvajira-vipassanā Meditations

As mentioned before, the Bodhisatta had already discarded and cleansed the factors of defilements such as greed (lobha) and hatred (dosa) through the accumulation of merits like the perfections (pāramī). Having also cleared the chief of defilements, ignorance (moha), which obstructs and veils the path to Nibbāna, along with its retinue, the Bodhisatta practiced Mahāvajira-vipassanā (Great Diamond Insight) during the dawn (the last watch of the night) on that full moon day of Kason (Vesākha). A brief summary of his practice is as follows:

When he contemplated the true essence of the Dhamma that actually occurs in the three periods of time for humans, devas, and brahmās within each of the one hundred thousand crores of world systems (cakkavāḷa) known as the field of authority (āṇā-khetta), he clearly perceived the ultimate reality (paramattha-sabhāva). No matter how many humans, devas, and brahmās there were in each world system, he saw the twelve factors of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda): ignorance (avijjā) and formations (saṅkhāra) [as causes from the past]; consciousness (viññāṇa), mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa), the six sense bases (saḷāyatana), contact (phassa), and feeling (vedanā) [as...
335:
335
...effects in the present]; craving (taṇhā), clinging (upādāna), and the process of becoming (kammabhava) [as causes in the present]; and birth (jāti), aging and death (jarā-maraṇa) [as effects in the future]. He clearly perceived these twelve factors of Dependent Origination as the true essence of the Dhamma.

When he contemplated the ultimate reality of the Dhamma that truly exists in the three periods of time for humans, devas, and brahmās in this world system, he clearly perceived the twelve factors of Dependent Origination as the core of the Dhamma (the group of phenomena to be subjected to insight). Similarly, he contemplated the ultimate reality of the Dhamma for humans, devas, and brahmās in the remaining world systems. In doing so, he clearly perceived the group of phenomena to be subjected to insight, consisting of the twelve factors of Dependent Origination for each world system, just as he had for this world system.

Thus, through the wisdom of the Great Bodhisatta contemplating the ultimate reality of the Dhamma occurring in the three periods of time within the continuity of the aggregates (khandha) of humans, devas, and brahmās in the one hundred thousand crores of world systems within the field of authority, the groups of phenomena to be subjected to insight were: one hundred thousand crores of ignorance (avijjā), one hundred thousand crores of formations (saṅkhāra), and one hundred thousand crores each of consciousness, mind-and-matter, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and aging and death.
336:
336
(When these 12 factors are combined), the objects of insight (vipassanā-cāra) for the Great Bodhisatta amounted to one million two hundred thousand crores.

Just as a man clearing a very dense and difficult forest would repeatedly sharpen his sword on a whetstone and then clear the thicket with his sharp blade, the Great Bodhisatta, in order to clear the thicket of the one thousand five hundred defilements (kilesa), sharpened the blade of his personal weapon—the Mahāvajira-vipassanā wisdom—on the whetstone of the fourth ānāpāna-jhāna attainment. After repeatedly entering the fourth ānāpāna-jhāna, he contemplated each of the aforementioned one million two hundred thousand crore factors of Dependent Origination by applying the mark of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa), the mark of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa), and the mark of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa).

Consequently, since there were three types of insight—insight into impermanence, insight into suffering, and insight into non-self—for each of the one million two hundred thousand crore factors of Dependent Origination, the total number of Mahāvajira-vipassanā knowledges was three million six hundred thousand crores (1,200,000 crores multiplied by 3).

(This brief account of Mahāvajira-vipassanā knowledge is found on page 275 of the Uparipaṇṇāsa-ṭīkā in the commentary on the Anupada Sutta, and on page 229 of the third volume of the Vinaya Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā in the commentary on the Mahākhandhaka Sāriputta-Moggallāna Pabbajjā Kathā.)
337:
337
It is the natural law (dhammatā) for every Bodhisatta to contemplate Dependent Origination in both forward (anuloma) and backward (paṭiloma) order just before becoming a Buddha. Our Great Bodhisatta, following the way of previous Bodhisattas, also contemplated Dependent Origination in forward and backward order. At that time, the entire ten thousand world systems of the birth-field (jāti-khetta) shook to the very depths of the waters.

After the Great Bodhisatta had generated the three million six hundred thousand crores of Mahāvajira-vipassanā Sammasana-ñāṇa (Comprehension Knowledge) regarding the twelve factors of Dependent Origination, as is the custom of all Buddhas, he again entered the fourth ānāpāna-jhāna. (This re-entry was to sharpen the blade of higher insight knowledges, such as the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-ñāṇa), on the excellent whetstone of the fourth ānāpāna-jhāna attainment.) Having re-entered the fourth ānāpāna-jhāna and sharpened the blade of higher insight, he emerged from that jhāna and easily developed higher and higher insight knowledges, starting with udayabbaya-ñāṇa, regarding the group of the five aggregates.

(In this regard, it should be faithfully noted that the Great Bodhisatta attained these higher insight knowledges easily because he had practiced insight meditation up to the stages of udayabbaya-ñāṇa, bhaṅga-ñāṇa, bhaya-ñāṇa, ādīnava-ñāṇa, nibbidā-ñāṇa, muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa, paṭisaṅkhā-ñāṇa, and saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa after becoming a monk and mastering the Tipiṭaka under previous Buddhas, and because his power of wisdom was immensely strengthened by the three million six hundred thousand crores of Mahāvajira-vipassanā Sammasana-ñāṇa mentioned earlier.

Thus, the Great Bodhisatta easily ascended to higher and higher insight knowledges. When he finally reached the Knowledge of Conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa), just as a man returning from a long journey who enters his house through the eaves does not stop at the threshold of the open house but enters directly inside, the Great Bodhisatta, having ascended through the eight stages of insight knowledge starting with udayabbaya-ñāṇa, did not stop at the Knowledge of Conformity to the Truth (saccānuloma-ñāṇa), which is like the threshold (to the city of Nibbāna). Instead, through the three moments of saccānuloma-ñāṇa—known as preparation (parikamma), access (upacāra), and conformity (anuloma)—which are part of the Path cognitive process (magga-vīthi), he dispelled the clouds and darkness of ignorance (avijjā-moha) that veil the Four Noble Truths: the Truth of Suffering, the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Truth of the Path. Then, like seeing the moon clearly in a cloudless sky, he clearly and vividly realized the great light of Nibbāna through the Path Knowledge of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) which arises immediately after the Change-of-lineage Knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). (After the consciousness of the Path of Stream-entry arises and ceases once, in accordance with the attribute of the Dhamma being 'akalika'—yielding results without delay—the Fruition of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) occurs for three thought-moments and then ceases, followed by the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousness.)

Because he had reached the Path of Stream-entry, the three defilements—self-view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), skeptical doubt (vicikicchā), and attachment to rites and rituals (sīlabbata-parāmāsa)—were eradicated from the Great Bodhisatta's continuity. These defilements could never arise in him again.

## Attaining Higher Paths and Fruitions and Becoming a Buddha

After the Great Bodhisatta attained the Path and Fruition of Stream-entry:

"The Path, the Fruition, Nibbāna, the abandoned defilements, and the remaining defilements—these five are reviewed in sequence."

In accordance with this, (1) he first reviewed the Path of Stream-entry; (2) then he reviewed the Fruition of Stream-entry, which is the result of that Path; (3) then he reviewed Nibbāna, which is the object of that Path and Fruition; (4) then he reviewed the defilements abandoned by that Path of Stream-entry; (5) then he reviewed the defilements that were not yet abandoned and remained after that Path of Stream-entry. (These five types of reviewing knowledge are called the five paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa.)

After reviewing these five things—the Path of Stream-entry, the Fruition of Stream-entry, Nibbāna as their object, the abandoned defilements, and the remaining defilements—with the five reviewing knowledges, the Great Bodhisatta again developed and practiced the stages of insight knowledge, such as udayabbaya-ñāṇa...
340:
340
...and before long, he reached the second stage, the Path and Fruition of Once-returner (sakadāgāmi-magga and phala). Through that Path of Once-returner, he eradicated coarse sensual desire (kāmarāga) and coarse ill-will (byāpāda). From that moment on, the latent tendencies (anusaya) of coarse sensual desire and coarse ill-will were completely cut off from the Great Bodhisatta's continuity (like seeds burnt by fire).

After the Great Bodhisatta attained the Path and Fruition of Once-returner, he reviewed the five things—the Path of Once-returner, the Fruition of Once-returner, Nibbāna as their object, the abandoned defilements, and the remaining defilements—using the five types of reviewing knowledge as before. Then, he again developed and practiced the stages of insight knowledge, such as udayabbaya-ñāṇa, and before long, he reached the third stage, the Path and Fruition of Non-returner (anāgāmi-magga and phala). Through that Path of Non-returner, he eradicated subtle sensual desire and subtle ill-will. From that moment on, the latent tendencies of subtle sensual desire and subtle ill-will, along with their habitual tendencies (vāsanā), were completely cut off from the Great Bodhisatta's continuity.

After the Great Bodhisatta attained the Path and Fruition of Non-returner, he reviewed the Path of Non-returner and the Fruition of Non-returner using the five types of reviewing knowledge as before...
341:
After reviewing Nibbāna, which is the object of those Paths and Fruitions, the defilements abandoned by the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-magga), and the remaining defilements not yet abandoned by that Path, the Bodhisatta again developed and practiced the stages of insight (Vipassanā-ñāṇa), starting with the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away (Udayabbaya-ñāṇa). Before long, he reached the fourth stage, the Path and Fruition of Arahatship (Arahatta-magga and Arahatta-phala). By that Path of Arahatship, he completely uprooted the remaining defilements—lust for fine-material existence (rūparāga), lust for immaterial existence (arūparāga), conceit (māna), restlessness (uddhacca), and ignorance (avijjā)—leaving no trace of habitual tendencies (vāsanā). From that moment on, the 1,500 defilements along with the habitual tendencies and the seven latent tendencies (anusaya) were entirely cut off within the Great Being.

(After attaining this Path and Fruition of Arahatship, there arose four impulsion processes (javana-vāra) of Reviewing Knowledge (Paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), which respectively review the Path of Arahatship, the Fruition of Arahatship, Nibbāna as the object of those, and the abandoned defilements. When these Reviewing Knowledges are combined, there are five after attaining the Path and Fruition of Stream-entry, five after the Path and Fruition of Once-returning, five after the Path and Fruition of Non-returning, and four after the Path and Fruition of Arahatship—making nineteen in total. These nineteen Reviewing Knowledges are also called the attribute of Knowledge and Vision of Liberation (Vimutti-ñāṇadassana). In the case of Reviewing Knowledge after attaining the Path of Arahatship, since there are no remaining defilements, the Reviewing Knowledge that reviews remaining defilements does not arise; thus, only four Reviewing Knowledges are attained.)

## Becoming the Buddha in the Three Worlds
As soon as the Great Bodhisatta reached the Fruition of Arahatship (Arahatta-phala), which immediately follows the Path of Arahatship, he possessed a perfectly pure mental continuum. He attained and reached the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) along with the attributes of the Buddhas, such as the four Knowledges of Analytical Insight (Paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), the six Unshared Knowledges (Asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), the fourteen Buddha-knowledges (Buddha-ñāṇa), the eighteen Unique Qualities (Āveṇika-guṇa), and the four Knowledges of Fearlessness (Vesārajja-ñāṇa), thus becoming the Sammāsambuddha, the Supreme Head of the Three Worlds. Simultaneously with the attainment of the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience, the dawn broke. (The attainment of the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience itself is called becoming the Buddha.)

## The Seven Purifications of the Buddha
At this point, I shall briefly pause the narrative of the Buddha's lineage to enumerate and explain the Buddha's Seven Purifications (Visuddhi), which are like seven great chariots leading to Nibbāna.

## (1) Purification of Virtue (Sīla-visuddhi)
After the Bodhisatta stopped at the bank of the Anomā River and became a monk, he undertook the practice of restraint from misconduct (Saṃvara-sīla). That restraint of virtue consists of the eightfold morality with livelihood as the eighth (Ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla): abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from stealing or taking what is not given by the owner through body or speech, abstaining from sexual misconduct (abstaining from all forms of unchaste behavior), abstaining from false speech, abstaining from slandering,
345:
In the last watch of the night, the Great Bodhisatta applied his knowledge to the twelve links of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda). Starting from the Knowledge of Comprehension (Kalāpa-sammasana-ñāṇa) and based on the seven types of contemplation such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), suffering (dukkhānupassanā), and non-self (anattānupassanā), he gave rise to the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away (Udayabbaya-ñāṇa), which perceives the arising and passing of mental and material phenomena. At that time, the imperfections of insight (vipassanupakkilesa), such as aura and light, arose within the Great Bodhisatta.

The aura and light of the Buddha did not shine only in one spot or one part like the light of others. Indeed, through the extremely sharp Great Diamond-like Insight (Mahāvajira-vipassanā-ñāṇa) mentioned earlier, he took the mass of phenomena belonging to the three periods of time (tekālika) occurring within himself and in infinite beings, summarized them as the twelve links of Dependent Origination, and then divided those twelve links into two groups: mind and matter. As the Great Bodhisatta contemplated these mind and matter phenomena with the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away, his energy (vīriya) was extremely powerful, his mindfulness (sati) was extremely clear, and his mind was extremely concentrated. Therefore, his wisdom (paññā) was extremely sharp, and his faith (saddhā) was very strong. Bliss (sukha) and tranquility (passaddhi) of body and mind occurred repeatedly. The mental factor of equanimity (tatramajjhattatā), known as equanimity of insight (vipassanupekkha), which is indifferent toward all conditioned things, was also very powerful. In the continuum of the Great Bodhisatta, whose mind was thus supported and uplifted by such factors as bliss and tranquility,
346:
the five types of rapture (pīti) occurred vibrantly: (1) Minor rapture (khuddikā-pīti) which can cause the hair to stand on end; (2) Momentary rapture (khaṇikā-pīti) which arises like flashes of lightning; (3) Showering rapture (okkantikā-pīti) which breaks over the body again and again like waves hitting the shore; (4) Uplifting rapture (ubbegā-pīti) which is powerful enough to make the body float in the air; and (5) Pervading rapture (pharaṇā-pīti) which stays pervading the whole body like fine cotton soaked in oil. His heart, blood, and sense faculties such as eyes, ears, and nose were also extremely clear.

Therefore, rays of light emanated from his body, turning the earth, water, and air elements below into a bright golden hue, and they rushed down into the open space of the lower universe. Above, they turned everything up to the highest heaven (Bhavagga) into a bright golden hue and rushed into the open space of the upper sky. Horizontally, they illuminated ten thousand world systems and spread throughout the infinite universe. (When such imperfections of insight arise, unskilled practitioners tend to mistake these imperfections for the Path or Fruition, abandon their original meditation subject, and remain attached to and delighted by these imperfections.) When these imperfections of insight arose in his continuum, the Great Bodhisatta reflected and realized: "These phenomena are not the path to attaining the Path of Arahatship and Omniscience; they are merely imperfections of insight. Only the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away,
347:
and other knowledges that I am practicing, are truly the right path to attaining the Path of Arahatship and Omniscience." Having realized this, he did not allow his mind to linger or become attached to the imperfections of insight, but directed it straight toward the object of insight.

Thus, when the imperfections of insight arose in the Great Bodhisatta's continuum as they do for others, he did not allow the subtle craving called attachment (nikanti) to arise. The pure and special knowledge that clearly distinguished, "This group of phenomena is not the right path to Enlightenment; they are merely imperfections of insight. Only the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away and the subsequent knowledges are truly the right path to Enlightenment," is called the Bodhisatta's Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and What Is Not the Path (Maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi).

## (6) Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way and
## (7) Purification by Knowledge and Vision
The nine stages of insight knowledge, starting from the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away up to the Knowledge of Adaptation (Anuloma-ñāṇa) occurring in the Great Bodhisatta's continuum, are called the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way (Paṭipada-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi). The four Noble Paths attained by the Great Bodhisatta are called the Purification by Knowledge and Vision (Ñāṇadassana-visuddhi).

(In this context, it should also be specifically noted that the Buddha's Path of Stream-entry is a first-jhana path with five jhana factors: initial application, sustained application, rapture, bliss, and one-pointedness. The Path of Once-returning is a second-jhana path with three jhana factors: rapture, bliss, and one-pointedness. The Path of Non-returning is a third-jhana path with two jhana factors: bliss and one-pointedness. The Path of Arahatship is a fourth-jhana path with two jhana factors: equanimity and one-pointedness. From the commentary to the Upakkilesa Sutta, Uparipaṇṇāsa, page 149.)
348:
348
Thus, the aforementioned seven stages of the Noble Path of Purification are the true and correct way to reach Nibbāna. The Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples (Ariya-sāvakas) of the three periods of time—those who have appeared, those who are appearing, and those who will appear—as well as those noble persons who attained the Noble Path (Ariya-magga) by practicing the meditation on the fivefold skin-group (taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna) as a minimum, and those noble persons who attained the Noble Path by hearing the verse of light (obhāsa-gāthā) preached by the Buddha through the projection of his radiant image while remaining in his monastery—all these noble beings realized Nibbāna only through these successive seven stages of the Noble Path of Purification.

A question may arise: If all the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples who have appeared throughout the three periods of time realized Nibbāna only through these successive seven stages of the Noble Path of Purification, should they not all be identical? Why then is there a distinction such as: this person is a Buddha, this person is a Paccekabuddha, this person is a Chief Disciple (Aggasāvaka), this person is a Great Disciple (Mahāsāvaka), and this person is an Ordinary Disciple (Pakati-sāvaka)?

The answer is: Although they all realize Nibbāna only through the successive seven stages of the Noble Path of Purification, there are differences in the fundamental causes, namely: differences in wisdom (paññā), differences in practice (paṭipadā), differences in faith (saddhā), and differences in inclination (ajjhāsaya). Therefore, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for a duration of one hundred thousand aeons (kappas), or more, or less, according to their own
349:
349
strength of faith and strength of wisdom, those noble ones who reach the fruition of Arahatship (arahatta-phala) through the knowledge consisting of what is heard (sutamaya-ñāṇa), i.e., by hearing the Dhamma from others, are called Ordinary Disciples and Great Disciples.

Those noble ones who fulfill the perfections for one incalculable (asaṅkheyya) and one hundred thousand aeons (or slightly more or slightly less) and reach the fruition of Arahatship through the knowledge consisting of what is heard are called Chief Disciples (Aggasāvakas).

Those noble ones who fulfill the perfections for two incalculables and one hundred thousand aeons, and reach the fruition of Arahatship through self-evolved knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa) known by themselves (without being a disciple of another), yet lack the power to preach the Dhamma to lead others to the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna, are called Paccekabuddhas.

Those incomparable persons who fulfill the perfections for at least four incalculables and one hundred thousand aeons, performing the five great sacrifices (mahā-pariccāga) which are beyond the capacity of future Paccekabuddhas and future Disciples, and reach the fruition of Arahatship crowned by Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) through self-evolved knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa) without the help of a teacher, and who are uniquely skilled in various terminologies, preaching the Dhamma endowed with the four depths—depth of the text (Pāḷi), depth of meaning (attha), depth of teaching (desanā), and depth of penetration (paṭivedha)—in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings, thereby leading the veneyyas (those ready to be taught) to the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna, and becoming a refuge and reliance for them,
351:
351
In the ten thousand world systems, all kinds of flowering trees bloomed simultaneously out of season, and all kinds of fruiting trees bore fruit in clusters and bunches simultaneously out of season. Flowers on trunks, branches, and vines bloomed miraculously. From the sky, clusters of flowers hung down without any visible plant. Breaking through the great stone slabs of the lower earth, lotus flowers (paduma) without leaves but with stalks appeared miraculously, blooming in seven layers each. Thus, the ten thousand world systems of the field of birth (jāti-khetta) were trembling gently at that time, appearing like a great ball of flowers tossed about, or like a vast, orderly bed of flowers.

Furthermore, the thirty-two great omens described in the section on the birth of the Bodhisatta (page 45) also clearly appeared.

## The Utterance of the Paean of Joy (Udāna)

Having thus fully attained Omniscience along with all the glorious attributes of a Buddha, the Blessed One reflected:

"I have indeed been liberated from the great suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa). I have indeed attained the most noble state of the Sammāsambuddha, the Lord of the Three Worlds. A great victory has indeed been celebrated. I am also capable of preaching the Dhamma to all beings—humans, devas, and Brahmas—to free them
352:
352
from the bonds of the three worlds."

As he reflected thus, intense and repeated rapture (pīti) arose within the Blessed One's mind. With the force of that repeated rapture, the Blessed One uttered these two verses of joy (udāna), which is the natural custom of all Omniscient Buddhas to utter upon attaining Buddhahood:

(1) Anekajāti saṃsāraṃ, sandhāvissaṃ anibbisaṃ.
Gahakāraṃ gavesanto, dukkhā jāti punappunaṃ.
(2) Gahakāraka diṭṭhosi, puna gehaṃ na kāhasi.
Sabbā te phāsukā bhaggā, gahakūṭaṃ visaṅkhataṃ.
Visaṅkhāraṃ gataṃ cittaṃ, taṇhānaṃ khayamajjhagā.

(1) Punappunaṃ = Repeatedly through the round of rebirths, without being able to cut the root of the cycle of the aggregates. Jāti = Having to be conceived and born, wandering through the four modes of birth. Dukkhā = If there is the birth of the aggregates, it is not pure happiness but is extremely wearying and painful, being oppressed by disease, old age, and death which follow closely. (Tasmā = Therefore). Ahaṃ = I, the Bodhisatta. Gahakāraṃ = Searching for the carpenter, the man of craving (taṇhā), who is the base cause, the Truth of Suffering (samudaya-sacca), who repeatedly builds this house of the aggregates entwined with suffering. Gavesanto = Investigating and searching for who the real builder is. (Or) I, the Bodhisatta, while searching. Anibbisaṃ - Anibbisanto = Because I had not yet attained the great Omniscient Knowledge which clearly and brightly perceives the carpenter, the man of craving.
353:
353
Anekajāti saṃsāraṃ = Throughout the long period of saṃsāra with many births. Sandhāvissaṃ = Even while fearing the wheel of suffering of the five aggregates, without being fond of it, I have had to run and wander incessantly in the cycle of rebirth.

(2) Gahakāraka = O carpenter, you wretched man of craving, the Truth of Suffering, who repeatedly builds this house of the aggregates entwined with suffering! Idāni = Now that I have become Buddha. Tvaṃ = You, the carpenter craving. Diṭṭho = I have seen you clearly by attaining Omniscience. Asi = You are seen. Tvaṃ = You, the carpenter craving. Gehaṃ = The house which is the physical body and personality entwined with suffering. Puna na kāhasi = You will no longer be able to build it again, because your feet, your hands, and your life have been cut four times by the axe of knowledge with the radiance of the four Paths, and you have truly become like a stump with its roots pulled out. Te = Of you, the carpenter craving. Sabbā = All, without exception. Phāsukā = The rafters and ribs of the house of the aggregates, which are the defilements (kilesas). Bhaggā = I have shattered them into pieces so that no trace of latent tendencies (anusaya) remains. Gahakūṭaṃ = The ridge-pole of the house, which is ignorance (avijjā), that blocks the view of the Four Truths and Nibbāna and keeps them far away. Visaṅkhataṃ = I have destroyed and ground it into powder. Cittaṃ = My mind, which is pure and free from the dust and stains of defilements. Visaṅkhāraṃ = To the palace of Nibbāna, which is the true escape from the cycle of formations and all suffering. Gataṃ = Has reached and entered, having realized the state of peace (santi-dhātu)
354:
354
through the attainment of success. Ahaṃ = I, the Lord of the Three Worlds. Taṇhānaṃ khayaṃ = To the fourth Path and Fruition, the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya), where the one hundred and eight types of craving are extinguished. Gato = I have arrived with joy and clarity, while the hosts of devas and Brahmas from the ten thousand world systems proclaim my praise.

Note: There are two types of Udāna: the mental utterance (manasā-udāna) made only with the mind, and the verbal utterance (vacasā-udāna) made by speaking aloud. This Udāna verse beginning with "Anekajāti saṃsāraṃ" was uttered by the Buddha only with his mind; therefore, this Udāna should be noted as a mental utterance. The Udānas found in the Udāna Pāḷi text beginning with "Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā" were uttered by the Buddha aloud; therefore, those Udānas in the Pāḷi text should be firmly noted as verbal utterances.

(The details concerning the Law of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), the four Analytical Knowledges (Paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), the six Uncommon Knowledges (Asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), the ten Powers (Dasabala-ñāṇa), the fourteen Buddha-knowledges (Cuddasa-buddha-ñāṇa), the eighteen Unique Qualities (Āveṇika-guṇa), and the four types of Intrepidity (Vesārajja-ñāṇa) mentioned in this chapter on becoming Buddha will be described in a moderately detailed manner upon reaching the chapter on the Dhamma Ratana.)
