## Chapter 8
## The Seven Stations (Sattatṭhāna)
## (1) Pallanka Sattāha
Thus, after becoming the Buddha, at the beginning of the 1st day of the waning moon of Kason (Vesak), the Blessed One, having uttered an inspired utterance of joy, remained seated in a cross-legged posture on that very Aparājita Throne (Unconquered Throne).

He reflected: "To attain this Aparājita Throne, I have fulfilled and accumulated the ten Perfections (Pāramīs) to an incomparable degree for a period of four incalculables (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa). For this long duration, to attain this Aparājita Throne, I have sacrificed my adorned head many times; I have sacrificed both my eyes and my heart many times. I have given away sons like Prince Jāli, daughters like Princess Kaṇhājinā, and wives like Queen Maddī to those who requested them, to be used as servants. This throne is the place where I have conquered the five Maras without remainder; it is a throne of glory, auspiciousness, and supreme nobility. While sitting on this Aparājita Throne, all my aspirations and desires to become a Buddha have been fulfilled. I shall not rise from this throne which has bestowed such immense benefits."

Having thus reflected, He entered into millions of attainments of the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala Samāpatti) and the fourth jhāna, and remained on that Aparājita
356:
Throne for seven days.

Throughout the 1st day of the waning moon of Kason, the Blessed One enjoyed the bliss of liberation (Vimutti-sukha) by entering into millions of attainments of the Fruit of Arahantship and the fourth jhāna. In the first watch of the night (the first part of the night) of that same day, He contemplated the Law of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) in the forward order (anuloma), as the process of the suffering of the round of rebirth: "Avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā" = "With ignorance as condition, the three types of volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra, apuññābhisaṅkhāra, āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) arise," and so forth. He also contemplated it in the reverse order (paṭiloma), as the process of the cessation of the suffering of the round of rebirth: "Avijjāyateva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho" = "With the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance through the Path of Arahantship, the three types of volitional formations cease," and so forth.

(In this regard, it should be noted: Although all phenomena were already clear in all aspects to the Buddha's Golden Knowledge, He specifically contemplated Dependent Origination in forward and reverse order because He had used Dependent Origination as the primary object during His practice of Insight (Vipassanā), and because this Law of Dependent Origination is extremely subtle, profound, and difficult to see.)

While thus repeatedly reviewing and contemplating Dependent Origination in forward and reverse order, in the Buddha's Golden Knowledge,
357:
the forward meaning of the process of suffering in the round of rebirth—the incessant arising of effects such as volitional formations due to causes such as ignorance—and the reverse meaning of the cessation of suffering in the round of rebirth—the cessation of effects such as volitional formations due to the cessation (non-arising) of causes such as ignorance—became clearer and clearer. Consequently, a continuous stream of Great Functional (Mahākiriyā) consciousness, accompanied by joy (somanassa), associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta), and unprompted (asaṅkhārika), led by the factor of rapture (pīti), arose within the Buddha's heart-base (hadayavatthu).

Just as when butter or oil is poured into a vessel, and once the vessel is full, the excess butter or oil overflows, so too, the butter and oil of rapture (pīti) preceded by wisdom (paññā), which arose based on the ever-increasing clarity of the Dhamma within the vessel of the Buddha's heart-base, could not be contained within and overflowed. Based on that rapture preceded by wisdom, He uttered this inspired verse (Udāna):

Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā,
Ātāpino jhāyato brāhmaṇassa.
Athassa kaṅkhā vapayanti sabbā,
Yato pajānāti sahetudhammaṃ.

Ātāpino = Possessing the ardent effort of Right Exertion (Sammappadhāna) which greatly suppresses and burns away the 1,500 defilements. Jhāyato = Because of being intensely and firmly established in meditation, reaching the Jhanic Path during the moment of absorption (appanā) upon the objects of Samatha such as mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), and upon the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self of all mental and physical phenomena.
358:
Brāhmaṇassa = In the continuum of the Arahant who has discarded all evil. Yadā = When. Dhammā = The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma). Have = Truly. Pātubhavanti = Become manifest and arise. Yato = Because of the manifestation of these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Sahetudhammaṃ = The mass of suffering, which is the group of effects such as volitional formations, together with their causes such as ignorance. Pajānāti = He clearly understands through discernment. Atha = Then, when he clearly and brightly sees the nature of Dependent Origination. Assa = In the continuum of that Arahant. Sabbā = All, without exception. Kaṅkhā = The sixteen types of doubt concerning mental and physical phenomena occurring in the three periods of time, which arise due to ignorance and lack of vision regarding the Law of Dependent Origination. Vapayanti (Vi-apayanti) = They vanish and cease, like dewdrops disappearing under the heat of the sun.

Then, when the middle watch of the night (majjhima-yāma) arrived, the Blessed One repeatedly reviewed and contemplated that same Law of Dependent Origination, the causal connection of causes and effects, in forward and reverse order throughout that middle watch. While so contemplating, Nibbāna, the end of all causes, became clearer and clearer to the Buddha's Golden Knowledge. Consequently, a stream of Great Functional consciousness accompanied by joy,
359:
associated with knowledge, and unprompted, led by wisdom and rapture, arose continuously. Unable to contain that momentum of rapture within, it spread and overflowed as if it could not be held inside. Based on that rapture preceded by wisdom, He uttered the inspired verse (Udāna) again:

Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā,
Ātāpino jhāyato brāhmaṇassa.
Athassa kaṅkhā vapayanti sabbā,
Yato khayaṃ paccayānaṃ avedi.

Ātāpino = Possessing the ardent effort of Right Exertion which greatly suppresses and burns away the 1,500 defilements. Jhāyato = Because of being intensely and firmly established in meditation, reaching the Jhanic Path during the moment of absorption upon the objects of Samatha such as mindfulness of breathing, and upon the characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self of all mental and physical phenomena. Brāhmaṇassa = In the continuum of the Arahant who has discarded all evil. Yadā = When. Dhammā = The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Have = Truly. Pātubhavanti = Become manifest and arise. Yato = Because of the manifestation of these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Paccayānaṃ = Of the causes such as ignorance. Khayaṃ = The Unconditioned Nibbāna, which is the true end. Avedi = He has clearly understood through penetration. Atha = Then, when he clearly and brightly sees the ultimate Unconditioned Nibbāna, known as the destruction of causes. Assa = In the continuum of that Arahant,
360:
Sabbā = All, without exception. Kaṅkhā = The collection of doubts that would have arisen within himself due to not penetrating Nibbāna. Vapayanti (Vi-apayanti) = They vanish and cease, like dewdrops disappearing under the heat of the sun.

Then, when the last watch of the night (pacchima-yāma) arrived, the Blessed One again repeatedly reviewed and contemplated that same Law of Dependent Origination, the causal connection of causes and effects, in forward and reverse order throughout that last watch. While so contemplating, the factors of the Noble Path (Ariya-magga), which clearly see the constant rotation and the cessation of the wheel of suffering of Dependent Origination, became clearer and clearer to the Buddha's Golden Knowledge. Consequently, a stream of Great Functional consciousness accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and unprompted, led by wisdom and rapture, arose continuously. Unable to contain that momentum of rapture within, it spread and overflowed as if it could not be held inside. Based on that rapture preceded by wisdom, He uttered the inspired verse (Udāna) for the third time:

Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā,
Ātāpino jhāyato brāhmaṇassa.
Vidhūpayaṃ tiṭṭhati mārasenaṃ,
Sūriyova obhāsayamantalikkhaṃ.

Ātāpino = Possessing the ardent effort of Right Exertion which greatly suppresses and burns away the 1,500 defilements. Jhāyato = Because of being intensely and firmly established in meditation, reaching the Jhanic Path during the moment of absorption upon the objects of Samatha such as mindfulness of breathing, and upon the characteristics of
361:
impermanence, suffering, and non-self of all mental and physical phenomena. Brāhmaṇassa = In the continuum of the Arahant who has discarded all evil. Yadā = When. Dhammā = The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Have = Truly. Pātubhavanti = Become manifest and arise. (Tadā = At that time.) Sūriyo = The sun, rising from the edge of Mount Yugandhara and appearing in the east. Antalikkhaṃ = The expanse of the sky. Obhāsayaṃ (Obhāsayanto) = Dispelling the darkness and shining brightly with its thousand rays. Tiṭṭhati iva = Just as it stands. (So brāhmaṇo = That Arahant; Tehi dhammehi = By means of those thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.) Mārasenaṃ = The ten-fold army of Mara, such as sensual desire (kāmarāga). Vidhūpayaṃ (Vidhūpayanto) = Destroying and dispelling them into pieces. Tiṭṭhati = He stands, shining and brilliant with the light of the lamp of wisdom, like the orb of the sun.

(In the Udāna Pali, it is taught that "He contemplated Dependent Origination in the forward order in the first watch of the night, in the reverse order in the middle watch, and in both forward and reverse order in the third watch." This was taught with reference to His contemplation on the seventh night, which completed the Pallanka Sattāha.)

The Blessed One, having contemplated the Law of Dependent Origination in forward and reverse order throughout the three watches of the night of the 1st day of the waning moon of Kason, uttered the three inspired verses mentioned above.
362:
362
Having uttered [the song of victory], the Buddha remained seated on that same Aparājita Throne on the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th days of the waning moon of Kason, entering into and enjoying the bliss of the Fruition of Arahatship (Arahattaphala-samāpatti).

## (2) Animisa-sattāha
(The seven days spent gazing fixedly at the Mahābodhi tree and the Aparājita Throne without blinking the eyes is called "Animisa-sattāha.")

Thus, the Blessed One, after becoming the Buddha, enjoyed the bliss of the Fruition of Arahatship for seven full days at the Aparājita Throne (in a single sitting without changing his cross-legged posture). When the seven days were completed, a doubt arose in the minds of some (worldling) devas and brahmās (except for those noble devas and brahmās who had attained Paths and Fruitions under previous Buddhas and thus partially knew the Buddha's virtues): "The Blessed One has not yet risen from the throne even until now; are there perhaps other virtues yet to be achieved to become a Buddha, besides the virtues he has already attained?"

Then, on the eighth day (the 8th day of the waning moon), the Blessed One rose from the attainment of the Fruition of Arahatship. Knowing the doubt of the devas and brahmās, and in order to dispel their doubt, he ascended into the sky and performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) of emitting pairs of water and fire. (This Twin Miracle performed here at the Mahābodhi-maṇḍa, the Twin Miracle performed at the assembly of relatives in Kapilavatthu, and the Twin Miracle performed at the assembly concerning the ascetic Pāthikaputta in Vesālī—this collection of Twin Miracles of water and fire is identical to the Twin Miracle performed near the Kaṇḍamba mango tree. The detailed account of the Twin Miracle performed near the Kaṇḍamba mango tree will be explained later.)
363:
363
...the Twin Miracle of water and fire performed near the Kaṇḍamba mango tree. The detailed account of the Twin Miracle performed near the Kaṇḍamba mango tree will be explained later.)

After the Blessed One had performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire and dispelled the doubts of the devas and brahmās, he descended from the sky and stood firm like a golden pillar at a spot slightly to the north of the east (= the northeast corner) of the Aparājita Throne. Reflecting, "Indeed, I have attained the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) at this Aparājita Throne," he spent seven days gazing without blinking at the Aparājita Throne and the Mahābodhi tree, where he had attained the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and the Knowledge of Omniscience, which were the fruits of the Perfections (Pāramīs) he had fulfilled for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. That place became known as the Animisa Cetiya.

## (3) Caṅkama-sattāha
Then, when the third week (sattāha) arrived, the Blessed One spent seven days walking back and forth on a jeweled walkway (Ratanacaṅkama) created by devas, which stretched east to west between the Aparājita Throne and the Animisa Cetiya, while contemplating the Dhamma and entering the attainment of Fruition (Phala-samāpatti). That place became known as the Ratanacaṅkama Cetiya.
364:
364
## (4) Ratanaghara-sattāha
Then, when the fourth week arrived, the Blessed One sat in a cross-legged posture in a golden Jeweled House (Ratanaghara) created by devas in the northwest corner of the Mahābodhi tree, reviewing and contemplating the Dhamma of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.

According to the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā:
While sitting cross-legged in the golden Jeweled House and contemplating the Dhamma, as he looked upon the multitude of beings to be tamed (veneyya), he clearly perceived the path of practice consisting of Virtue (Sīla), Concentration (Samādhi), and Wisdom (Paññā)—the way by which beings, including devas, humans, and brahmās worthy of liberation, establish themselves in Virtue, steady their minds with Concentration, and through Wisdom, strive in the practice of Insight (Vipassanā) to reach the Noble Realm of the Paths, Fruitions, and Nibbāna. Thus, he first reviewed the Vinaya Piṭaka, which explains Virtue. Then, he reviewed the Suttanta Piṭaka, which explains Concentration. Thereafter, he reviewed the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, which explains Wisdom.

When he reviewed the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, while he was contemplating the first six books—Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, and Yamaka—his Golden Knowledge of Omniscience was so vast while the methods of the Dhamma were relatively narrow that his Golden Knowledge did not yet find full scope to range freely, and thus the six-colored rays did not yet emit. However, when he reviewed and contemplated the seventh book, the Great Book of Relations (Anantanaya Samanta-paṭṭhāna), (like the great Timiṅgala fish...
365:
365
...like the great Timiṅgala fish, a thousand yojanas in size, which finds room to frolic in the great ocean), his Golden Knowledge of Omniscience found its opportunity to range freely.

When he reviewed and contemplated the extremely subtle, delicate, and profound points of the Dhamma in the Great Book of Relations (Anantanaya Samanta-paṭṭhāna), intense joy and rapture (pīti) arose within the Blessed One. Because of the arising of rapture, his blood became pure and clear. Because his blood was pure, his skin became clear. Because his skin was clear, rays the size of houses or mountains emerged and radiated from the front of his body, and like the king of Chaddanta elephants flying in the sky, they radiated and raced toward the infinite world systems (cakkavaḷas) of the eastern direction.

Similarly, rays emerged and radiated from the back of his body, racing toward the infinite world systems of the western direction. Similarly, rays emerged and radiated from his right side, racing toward the infinite world systems of the southern direction. Similarly, rays emerged and radiated from his left side, racing toward the infinite world systems of the northern direction. From the soles of his feet, rays the color of coral sprouts emerged and radiated, piercing through the mass of earth, water, and air, and descended into the space below. From his head, like a rotating garland of sapphire, masses of dark blue rays emerged one after another and radiated, ascending beyond the six deva realms of the sense sphere and the twenty brahma realms into the upper reaches of space.
366:
366
At that time, all infinite beings in the infinite world systems shone with a bright golden hue.

In particular, the rays that emerged and radiated from the Buddha's body on that day when he contemplated the Paṭṭhāna Dhamma continue to travel through the infinite world systems and universes even today, in the form of successive generations of physical phenomena caused by temperature (utujarūpa).

## Chabbaṇṇaraṃsi-vandanā Gāthās
At this point, I shall present the Pali verses and meanings of the "Chabbaṇṇaraṃsi-vandanā = Homage to the Six-Colored Rays," composed by the Mahāvisuddhārāma Sayadaw, for the benefit of those seeking knowledge.

1. Satta-sattāha-majjhamhi, Nātho yo satta sammasi.
Patvā Samanta-paṭṭhānaṃ, okāsaṃ labhate tadā.

Nātho = The one who is the sole refuge of the three types of beings (humans, devas, and brahmās). Yo Satthā = Which Blessed One. Satta-sattāha-majjhamhi = In the middle of the seven weeks—namely, the Ratanaghara-sattāha, which is the central point among the seven weeks: Pallaṅka, Animisa, Caṅkama, Ratanaghara, Ajapāla, Mucalinda, and Rājāyatana. (Or) In the Ratanaghara week, the central point of the seven-week sequence.
367:
367
...in the [Ratanaghara] week. Satta = The seven books of the Abhidhamma—namely, Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna. Sammasi = He reviewed and contemplated with his Omniscience, which is of great power and depth, incomparable and immeasurable, due to the various Perfections (Pāramīs) he had fulfilled over many aeons. Tadā = At that time of reviewing. Samanta-paṭṭhānaṃ = Upon reaching the Great Book of Samanta-paṭṭhāna, which is diverse in methods and as vast as the ocean waters surrounded by rocky mountains eighty-four thousand yojanas deep. Patvā = Having arrived there according to the range of his knowledge. Ñāṇaṃ = His Golden Knowledge of Omniscience, which is of great power and depth, incomparable and immeasurable, due to the various Perfections he had fulfilled over many aeons. Okāsaṃ = The opportunity to range and frolic freely. Labhate = He did obtain.

2. Yojanānaṃ satāyāmo, pañca Timirapiṅgalo.
Kīḷokāsaṃ samuddeva, gambhīre labhate yathā.

Yathā = To give an illustrative comparison. Yojanānaṃ = Of yojanas (a measure of distance). Pañcasatāyāmo = Five hundred yojanas in length, being very large. Timirapiṅgalo = The great fish named Timirapiṅgala. Gambhīre = In the deep. Samuddeva (Samudde eva) = Only in the ocean, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep.
368:
368
Kīḷokāsaṃ = The opportunity to frolic, play, and swim joyfully with its tail. Labhate yathā = Just as it obtains. Evaṃ tathā = In the same way. Ñāṇaṃ = His Golden Knowledge of Omniscience, which is of great power and depth, incomparable and immeasurable, due to the various Perfections he had fulfilled over many aeons. Okāsaṃ = The opportunity to range and frolic freely. Labhate = He did obtain.

3. Sammasantassa taṃ dhammaṃ, tadā Satthu sarīrato.
Taṃ taṃ dhāvanti chabbaṇṇā, lohitādipasīdanā.

Tadā = At that time when he obtained such opportunity. Taṃ dhammaṃ = That Paṭṭhāna Dhamma, which is as subtle as a fine atom. Sammasantassa = Of the Blessed One who was reviewing and contemplating. Satthu = Of the Buddha, who is capable of teaching the beings of the three realms—brahmās, devas, and humans—with a clear, smiling, and golden heart. Lohitādipasīdanā = Because of the clarity and brightness of his blood and other elements. Sarīrato = From his golden body, which was eighteen cubits in height. Chabbaṇṇā = The rays of six colors—dark blue, golden yellow, white, crimson, tawny, and dazzlingly bright. Taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ = To those various directions, namely left, right, front, back, above, and below. Dhāvanti = They raced and radiated here and there.

4. Nīlāyo nīlaṭṭhānehi, pītodātā ca lohitā.
Tamhā tamhā tu mañjeṭṭhā, nikkhamiṃsu pabhassarā.
369:
369
Nīlaṭṭhānehi = From the dark-blue areas such as the hair and the pupils of the eyes. Nīlā = The dark-blue rays—resembling the scattered petals of blue lotuses, blue water lilies, and blue collyrium, or like the dark-blue emerald fans and dark-blue robes that flutter and wave gently and gracefully—emerged. These rays, which have been shining brilliantly and vividly, as large as houses and mountains, since the day the Buddha contemplated the Great Paṭṭhāna until this very day and night, spread far and wide, enveloping the sky and earth in a deep blue hue.

Pītaṭṭhānehi = From the golden-hued areas of the radiant skin. Pītā = The golden rays—resembling the spreading of golden robes or as if the sky were filled with golden turmeric powder, yellow orpiment, and Mahālekhā flowers—emerged. These rays, which have been shining brilliantly and vividly, as large as houses and mountains, since the day the Buddha contemplated the Great Paṭṭhāna until this very day and night, spread far and wide, making the ten directions bright and golden.

O dātaṭṭhānehi = From the white areas such as the bones, the teeth, and the whites of the eyes. Odātā = The pure white rays—resembling the flow of milk poured from a silver pot,
370:
370
or like a silver canopy filling the sky, or silver fans, silver jasmine, white creepers, white lotuses, and white jasmine flowers fluttering and waving in the high clouds, covering and intertwining with each other—emerged. These rays, which have been shining brilliantly and vividly, as large as houses and mountains, since the day the Buddha contemplated the Great Paṭṭhāna until this very day and night, spread far and wide, shining with pure and beautiful whiteness.

Lohitaṭṭhānehi = From the crimson-red areas such as the flesh, blood, and the red parts of the eyes. Lohitā = The deep red rays—resembling the bright red of vermilion, red blankets, or the blooming of Bandhujīvaka and Kaṇikāra flowers, or like sunset clouds racing across the sky, covering both earth and heaven—emerged. These rays, which have been shining brilliantly and vividly, as large as houses and mountains, since the day the Buddha contemplated the Great Paṭṭhāna until this very day and night, spread far and wide, shining with a bright and intense crimson.

Tu = Furthermore. Mañjeṭṭhā = The rays of madder or brownish-red color, formed by the mixture of dark, red, and blue hues, also emerged. Pabhassarā = The rays of pure brilliance, flashing and scintillating like lightning across the vast sky in the month of Jeṭṭha, or like the sparks of a blazing fire, also emerged. Tammā tammā sarīrapadesā = From various parts of the body,
371:
371
without specific distinction, these rays emerged from every part of the radiant body. Nikkhamiṃsu = Since the day the Buddha contemplated the Great Paṭṭhāna until this very day and night, these rays, as large as houses and mountains, have been shining brilliantly and vividly, spreading far and wide.

5. Evaṃ chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo,
Etā yāvajjavāsarā.
Sabbā disā vidhāvanti,
Pabhā nassanti tatthikā.

Evaṃ = In this manner. Etā chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo = These six-colored rays—namely blue, golden, white, red, crimson, and brilliant—shone forth. Yāvajjavāsarā = Until this very day, as the light of the Sāsana continues to shine. Sabbā disā = To all ten directions, encompassing everything. Vidhāvanti = They have spread far and wide. Tatthikā = In those various places where the six rays reached, such as the celestial trees, gardens, and mansions. Pabhā = The radiance of the bodies and the glory of the Brahmas and Devas, who are capable of illuminating ten thousand universes with their ten fingers, Nassanti = faded and disappeared, being unable to shine in the presence of the Buddha's superior radiance.

6. Iti chabbaṇṇaraṃsittā,
Aṅgīrasoti nāmaso.
Loke patthaṭaguṇaṃ taṃ,
Vande buddhaṃ namassiyaṃ.
372:
372
Iti - evaṃ yathāvuttanayena = In the manner already described. Chabbaṇṇaraṃsittā = Because of possessing these six-colored rays. Nāmaso = By the name that is consistent with His extraordinary qualities. Aṅgīrasoti = He is known as 'Aṅgīrasa'. Loke = In the three worlds and three planes of existence. Patthaṭaguṇaṃ = Being endowed with virtues and attributes that are famous and widespread throughout the universe. Namassiyaṃ = Being worthy of the humble worship and offerings of the entire world. Taṃ buddhaṃ = To that Supreme Buddha, who clearly realized the Four Noble Truths as if holding a precious gem in His hand. Ahaṃ = I, who am but a collection of the thirty-two impure and loathsome parts of the body, Vande - vandāmi = pay homage with deep faith and folded hands, bowing my head repeatedly as if the Living Buddha were present before me.

The Paṭṭhāna Dhamma is filled with infinite methods like the sky; it is as vast as the thickness of the earth and as deep as the volume of the ocean. Nevertheless, because the Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is so great and swift, the contemplation was completed in just seven days. The place where the Buddha sat contemplating this Jewel of Dhamma for seven days is known as the Ratanāghara Cetiya.

## (5) Ajapāla Sattāha
After the Buddha had spent four weeks (28 days) in the vicinity of the Mahābodhi tree in this manner,
373:
373
when the fifth week arrived, the Buddha proceeded from the Mahābodhi tree to the Ajapāla Banyan tree located to the east. There, He stayed for seven days, contemplating the Dhamma and entering the Attainment of Fruition (Phalasamāpatti). (That banyan tree is called the Ajapāla Nigrodha because goatherds frequently came to rest in its shade. Ajapāla = the place where goatherds rest + Nigrodha = banyan tree.)

At that time, a certain Brahmin of an unknown clan, who was of a very proud and arrogant nature (Huhunka), approached the Buddha and exchanged pleasant and friendly greetings. After finishing the conversation, which was memorable and endearing, the (Huhunka) Brahmin stood at a suitable place and asked the Buddha:

"Venerable Gotama, by what qualities does one truly become a Brahmin in this world? What are the qualities that make one a true Brahmin?"

In this regard, even if the Buddha were to preach the Dhamma to this (Huhunka) Brahmin, he would not be able to penetrate the Four Noble Truths. Indeed, for those who heard the verses uttered by the Buddha before the preaching of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta—similar to the giving of the Refuges to the merchant brothers Tapussa and Bhallika—it could only serve as a merit conducive to future realization (vāsanābhāgiya). They could not yet penetrate the Four Noble Truths to reach the Paths and Fruits. This is the natural order of things.
374:
374
(From Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, Vol. 3, p. 148.) Since that (Huhunka) Brahmin was not a suitable vessel for the Dhamma (meaning he would not realize the Four Noble Truths), the Buddha did not take him as a formal listener. However, knowing the meaning of the Brahmin's question, the Buddha uttered this inspired verse (Udāna):

Yo brāhmaṇo bāhitapāpadhammo,
Nihuhuṅko nikkasāvo yatatto.
Vedantagū vusitabrahmacariyo,
Dhammena so brahmavādaṃ vadeyya.
Yassussadā natthi kuhiñci loke.

Yo brāhmaṇo = That Arahant who is called a true Brahmin. Bāhitapāpadhammo = Has expelled all evil. Nihuhuṅko = Is free from the 'huṃ huṃ' sound of arrogance. Nikkasāvo = Is free from the stains of defilements. Yatatto = Has a mind devoted to the practice of meditation. (Or) Yatatto = Has a heart restrained by the discipline of virtue (sīla-saṃvara). Vedantagū = Has reached the end of all conditioned things, which is Nibbāna, by realizing it through the four Path Knowledges. ## Māra Admits Defeat
While the Buddha was staying at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree, Māra the Evil One had been following the Buddha for seven years, looking for any flaw to criticize. However, having failed to find even an atom's worth of fault, he approached the Buddha and said:

"O Monk Gotama, are you sitting here in this forest in dejection because you are overwhelmed by sorrow? Have you lost a thousand pieces of wealth? Or is it because you desire a thousand pieces of wealth?"
376:
“Are you sitting there in dejection, lost in thought? Or have you committed some great unwholesome deed in the town or village, and being unable to face others, have you come to this forest to sit in dejection? Why do you not make friends with people? You seem to have no intimacy or friendship with anyone at all.”

Thus he addressed the Blessed One in verse. Then the Blessed One replied:

“O Māra, having uprooted and destroyed all the causes of sorrow, I sit here without even a speck of unwholesome dust, entirely free from grief, dwelling in the two jhānas. Having completely cut off the craving for existence, I sit here happily, without any attachment or longing. (I am not sitting in dejection because of losing wealth or out of a greedy desire for wealth, as you might think.)”

When he had replied thus, Māra the Evil One spoke again:

“O Monk Gotama, those people and those monks in the world who speak of things such as silver, gold, and other utensils, or the four requisites such as robes, as ‘property’—if your mind is attached to and clings to those people, those monks, that gold and silver, or those robes, you will by no means be able to escape from my domain of the three realms of existence.”

Then the Blessed One said:
377:
“O Māra, I have no attachment or longing for things such as silver, gold, and other utensils, or the four requisites such as robes, as ‘property.’ I am not one who speaks of things as ‘mine’ like others do. O Māra, you should regard me as such an excellent and supreme person. Since I have abandoned the three realms of existence, you will not see the path I travel within your domain of the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth (yoni), the five destinations (gati), the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa).”

When he had said this, Māra the Evil One spoke again:

“O Monk Gotama, if you know the safe and good path that leads to Nibbāna, then go by yourself. Why do you still wish to preach to and liberate others?”

Thus he spoke provocatively. Then the Blessed One said:

“O Māra, (no matter how you try to hinder me), when deities, humans, Brahmās, and other beings who wish to cross to the other shore of Nibbāna ask about the good path that leads to Nibbāna—the state free from death—I shall indeed answer and preach to those humans, deities, and Brahmās the true and good path to Nibbāna.”

When he had said this, Māra the Evil One became helpless, like a crab whose claws (thumbs) have been broken by village children, and then—

## The Coming of Māra’s Daughters to Seduce

After that, Māra the Evil One thought with distress: “Though I have followed this Prince Siddhattha for all this time, seeking an opportunity to find fault, I have not seen even the slightest slip or mistake that could be blamed. Now, this Prince Siddhattha has rebelled against and transcended my domain of the three realms.” Reaching a state of great unhappiness, he sat alone, crouching and brooding on the main road not far from the Blessed One. He repeatedly thought of sixteen reasons and drew sixteen lines on the ground. The sixteen lines were:

(1) “I did not fulfill and accumulate the Perfection of Generosity (Dāna-pāramī) in previous lives as this Prince Siddhattha did. Therefore, I cannot be equal to this Prince Bodhisatta.” Thinking thus, he drew the first line.

(2) “I did not fulfill and accumulate the Perfection of Morality (Sīla-pāramī) in previous lives as this Prince Siddhattha did.

At that time, the three daughters of Māra the Evil One, named Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā, said, “We do not see our father (Māra the Evil One); where could our father be now?” While looking for him, they saw Māra the Evil One sitting alone, crouching and brooding in dejection, drawing lines on the ground. They quickly approached their father and asked, “Father, why are you so unhappy and miserable?” Māra the Evil One told his three daughters, “My dear daughters, this Great Monk Gotama has rebelled against and transcended my domain of the three realms of existence. Although I have followed him closely for seven years, seeking an opportunity to find fault, I have not found even an atom’s worth of fault or mistake in that Great Monk Gotama. That is why your father is unhappy and distressed.” Then the three daughters said, “Father, if that is the case, do not worry or grieve at all. We shall seduce and entice that Great Monk Gotama to follow our will and bring him before you.”

Then Māra the Evil One said, “My dear daughters, no one in the world can bring this Great Monk Gotama to follow their desire—”

When he said this, the three daughters replied, "Father, we are women; we shall bind this Great Ascetic Gotama with the snare of passion (rāga) and other means, and bring him to you quickly. Therefore, father, do not be distressed or worried." After saying this, the three goddesses went to the presence of the Buddha and spoke enticing words: "O Monk, let us stay humbly at your feet and serve you by providing whatever sensual pleasures you desire." The Blessed One paid no attention to the words spoken by the three daughters of Māra; moreover, without even opening His eyes, He remained enjoying the bliss of Nibbāna by entering into the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).

Again, the three daughters of Māra consulted one another, "The desires of men are various. Some men are fond of young maidens. Some men are fond of women in their first prime. Some men are fond of women in their middle age. Therefore, let us entice this Great Ascetic with various ages and appearances." Then, each of them transformed themselves into a hundred forms: (1) the appearance of young maidens, (2) the appearance of women who have not yet given birth, (3) the appearance of women who have given birth once, (4) the appearance of women who have given birth twice...

Then the Blessed One said, "O goddesses, go away. What benefit do you see that you strive to entice Me with such desires? This kind of action is suitable to be performed only in the presence of those who are not yet free from lust (rāga), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha). As for Me, the Buddha, I have completely abandoned lust; I have completely abandoned hatred; and I have completely abandoned delusion." Having said this, He reflected on His own abandonment of the defilements (kilesas) and uttered these verses:

## Living with Respect and Reverence for the Dhamma
## The Arising of the Thought
While the Blessed One was staying during this Ajapāla week, He thought and considered: "To live without showing respect and obedience to another (i.e., having no one to respect and obey) is painful. Whom should I respect, revere, and live in dependence upon, who has calmed all defilements and abandoned evil?" Then, the thought further occurred to the Blessed One: "In order to fulfill the attributes of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), and liberation (vimutti) which are not yet complete or sufficient, I shall live in dependence upon someone superior to Me in virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation." However, when He reflected and looked with His Golden Omniscient Knowledge for someone superior to Himself in virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation, He found no one in the three worlds. Thus, the thought occurred to Him again: "It would be well if I live respecting and revering only the Dhamma which I have realized through My own penetration."

Then, Sahampati Brahmā, knowing the thought in the Blessed One's mind, approached the Buddha in an instant. Placing his robe over his left shoulder, he knelt with his right knee on the ground, raised his joined palms, and said: "Exalted Blessed One... this thought of the Lord Buddha is correct as intended. Blessed One... the Buddhas who appeared in the past also lived respecting and revering only the Dhamma.
388:

In the future, the Buddhas who will arise will also live respecting and revering only the Dhamma. Exalted Blessed One... I desire that the Lord who has now arisen in the present also live respecting and revering only the Dhamma." Having submitted this, he further addressed Him with these three verses:

Yo ca sambuddho = that Buddha. Atthi = exists.

Sabbe = All Buddhas of the three periods without exception. Saddhammagaruno = showing respect and reverence to the True Dhamma.

## (6) Mucalinda Sattāha
The Blessed One, having spent seven days at the foot of that Ajapāla Banyan tree contemplating the Sublime Dhamma, departed from the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree and proceeded to the foot of a Mucalinda tree (Barringtonia acutangula) near the Mucalinda Lake, southeast of the Mahābodhi tree. There, at the foot of that Mucalinda tree, He sat in a single cross-legged posture for seven days, enjoying the bliss of the fruition of Arahatship (arahattaphala).

At that time, an unseasonal heavy rain (rain that falls before the rainy season) fell and drizzled for seven days. (This kind of rain falls only on two occasions: when a Universal Monarch appears and when a Buddha appears.) While that heavy rain was falling, the Mucalinda Naga King, who ruled the Naga realm beneath the Mucalinda Lake and possessed great power and majesty, thought and considered: "This unseasonal heavy rain began to fall as soon as the Blessed One entered my realm. It would be proper if there were a monastery for the Blessed One to reside in." Thus, the Mucalinda Naga King himself [created] a great palace made of the seven kinds of jewels...
391: Even though he was endowed with the power to create things by supernatural means, he thought, "If I were to create a great jeweled palace by such power and offer it, it would not be of great benefit to me. I shall perform a deed of service to the Buddha with my own body." Having so thought, he created a very large physical body and coiled it seven times around the Buddha to prevent cold, heat, gadflies, mosquitoes, and flies from touching or harassing Him, and he spread his hood over the Buddha's head like a canopy. (The interior of the coils was as spacious as the ground floor of the Lohapāsāda palace; the Naga King's intention was for the Buddha to stay in whichever of the four postures—lying, sitting, standing, or walking—He desired. Therefore, he coiled such a wide area. That He might stay in any posture was merely the Naga King's wish; the Buddha, however, spent the seven days in the sitting posture only. In the center of the coils, a jeweled throne was prepared; above that throne, a canopy was hung with fragrant flower garlands adorned with golden stars. In the four corners, fragrant oil lamps were lit brightly. In the four directions, caskets of sandalwood incense were opened. Seated upon the jeweled throne in the center of the coils, the Buddha entered into and enjoyed the bliss of Phalasamāpatti for the entire seven days). (From Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, Vol. 2, p. 90). Thus, the Buddha spent seven days enjoying the bliss of Arahattaphala within the sevenfold coils of the Naga King Mucalinda, as if He were staying in a spacious Gandhakuti chamber. When the seven days had passed, the Naga King Mucalinda, seeing that the sky was clear of high clouds and mists,
392: realized that it was no longer necessary to keep the Buddha enveloped with his coils and hood. He then discarded his Naga form, transformed himself into a beautiful young man, and stood before the Buddha with his hands raised in respectful salutation. At that time, the Buddha, clearly perceiving and rejoicing in the fact that "for one who enjoys the bliss of Nibbāna through Phalasamāpatti, there is happiness in every place where one dwells," could not contain His surge of rapture and uttered this Udāna: Sukho viveko tuṭṭhassa, sutadhammassa passato. Abyāpajjaṃ sukhaṃ loke, pāṇabhūtesu saṃyamo. Sukhā virāgatā loke, kāmānaṃ samatikkamo. Asmimānassa yo vinayo, etaṃ ve paramaṃ sukhaṃ. Viveko = Nibbāna, which is the true state of being secluded from the four types of Upadhi (attachments), is extremely happy. Tuṭṭhassa = For one who is satisfied and fulfilled by the four Path-knowledges. Sutadhammassa = For one who has the Dhamma clearly manifest within the eye of wisdom. (Or) Because of having the Dhamma clearly manifest. Passato = For the person who, with the eye of wisdom, looks upon and reflects with absolute clarity on Nibbāna, the true seclusion from the four Upadhis, and all other things that should be known. Abyāpajjaṃ = Having no ill-will and maintaining loving-kindness toward humans, devas, Brahmas, and all beings.
393:
Loke = In the world. Sukhaṃ = It is indeed pleasant. Pāṇabhūtesu = Towards living beings such as humans, devas, and brahmās. Saṃyamo = Restraint, the cultivation of Karuṇā (compassion) through the Brahma-vihāra without the desire to harm or oppress. Sukho = It is indeed pleasant.

Loke = In the world. Kāmānaṃ = Of the objects of sensual pleasure. Samatikkamo = The transcendence and abandonment through Samuccheda-pahāna (abandonment by eradication). Virāgatā = The noble Anāgāmi-magga (Path of Non-Returning), which is the cause for the arising of wisdom and faith as one who is free from passion. Sukhā = It is indeed pleasant. Asmimānassa = Of the conceit of 'I am', the pride and arrogance. Yo vinayo = That Arahatta-phala (Fruition of Arahatship) which is the absolute removal and eradication. Atthi = There is.
