He uttered these two verses of solemn utterance (Udāna).

## (7) Rājāyatana Sattāha

After seven days had passed and the seventh week (Sattama Sattāha) was reached, while the Buddha was experiencing the bliss of Arahatta-phala at the foot of the Mucalinda tree, he departed from there and went to the Rājāyatana tree (the Lin-lun tree) to the south of the Mahābodhi tree. He sat there, experiencing the bliss of Arahatta-phala, and remained for seven days.

(By this point, the seven times seven days, the Sattasattāha or forty-nine days, were completed. During these forty-nine days, the Buddha did not engage in rinsing the mouth, washing the face, bodily cleansing (excretion), bathing,
395: While they were wondering, a deity who had been their close relative in a previous life appeared visibly on a tree fork and said, "Friends, the Buddha has recently attained Enlightenment. For the duration of the Satta-sattāha (forty-nine days), He has not partaken of any food, enjoying only the bliss of Arahattaphala. He is now staying at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. Friends, go and honor the Buddha with an offering of food. Such an act of honoring and making an offering will lead to your long-lasting welfare and happiness." Hearing these words, the merchant brothers were greatly delighted. Thinking, "It will take a long time if we cook a meal," they took the parched rice cakes and honey balls they had brought with them, approached the Buddha, paid respectful homage, and stood in a suitable place. They respectfully addressed Him, "Exalted Buddha, may the Blessed One accept our parched rice cakes and honey balls. Such acceptance will lead to our long-lasting welfare and happiness." At that time, the Buddha thought (since the earthen bowl offered by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma at the time of His renunciation had disappeared on the day He accepted Sujātā's thick milk-rice), "The Buddhas of the past did not receive food with their hands. In what vessel, then, shall I receive the parched rice cakes and honey balls now offered by these merchant brothers?"
396: Knowing the Buddha's thought, the Four Great Kings of the four directions—Dhataraṭṭha, Virūḷhaka, Virūpakkha, and Kuvera—respectfully offered four sapphire bowls to the Buddha. The Buddha did not accept those sapphire bowls and rejected them. Then, the Four Great Kings again offered four stone bowls of the color of mung beans. The Buddha accepted those four stone bowls, and out of compassion for the Four Great Kings, He placed the four bowls one on top of the other and resolved, "Let them become a single bowl." Upon His resolution, the four bowls became a single bowl with four distinct rims. The Buddha received the parched rice cakes and honey balls offered by the merchant brothers in that bowl, partook of them, and then delivered a suitable discourse of appreciation (Anumodanā) to the brothers. At that time, the two merchant brothers (since the Jewel of the Saṅgha had not yet appeared) approached the Buddha and the Dhamma as their refuge and shelter. By saying, "Ete mayaṃ bhante bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāma dhammañca," referring only to the Buddha and the Dhamma, they became lay disciples established in the Two-Word Refuge (Dvevācika-saraṇagamana). (These two individuals were the very first lay disciples in the world to be established in the Two-Word Refuge.)
397: Then, the merchant brothers requested, "Exalted Buddha, out of compassion, please grant us an object of worship to which we may constantly pay homage and make offerings." The Buddha then stroked His head with His right hand and granted the hair relics (Kesa-dhātu) to the merchant brothers. Receiving the hair relics, the merchant brothers were as overjoyed as if they had been sprinkled with the nectar of immortality. After completing their trading, they returned to their home city of Pokkharavatī in Ukkalā Janapada, placed the hair relics in a golden casket, and built a pagoda to worship them. The Rājāyatana Sattāha ends here. At this point, for the purpose of increasing faith, I shall present the "Sattaṭṭhāna Phaya-shiko" poem composed by the Venerable Ledi Sayadaw. (1) With radiant glory, the Lord Sage, knowing the truth of the faculties of wisdom, at the Bodhi pavilion, the golden Banyan palace, where a marvelous golden throne arose from the earth, having conquered Mara and attained Omniscient Wisdom, He remained for a week, coiled and serene, enjoying the first victory of great glory. (2) For the second time, during that week, having repelled Mara, from the flying throne, He stood facing the Northeast, peaceful and serene...
398:
398
Looking with unblinking eyes at the throne, the Lord of the Three Worlds spent his time in joyful delight, a sight truly inspiring and serene.

(3) In the third week, the Glorious Buddha spent his time walking back and forth along the pleasant jewelled walkway (caṅkama) in the northern direction from the Bodhi tree, reflecting upon the Dhamma.

(4) In the fourth week, in a magnificent and peaceful Golden House (Ratanāghara) to the northwest of the Bodhi tree and the radiant throne, the Buddha repeatedly reflected upon the Abhidhamma with the ocean of his Great Wisdom (Mahā-ñāṇa-sāgara), while the six-colored rays shone brilliantly.

(5) In the fifth week, the Supreme Lord of Glory sat in a respectful and adorable manner under the great and lofty Ajapāla (Goatherd's) Banyan tree in the eastern direction from the Bodhi tree.

(6) In the sixth week, to the southeast of the Golden Banyan throne, at the foot of the Mucalinda tree by the side of the pleasant Mucalinda Lake—which was filled with emerald-like blue water and various lotus flowers—while the Friend of the World sat there, a fierce storm and rain fell. Due to the Buddha's past merits and perfections, the Serpent King protected him by spreading his hood, a wondrous display of power.

(7) In the seventh week, the All-Knowing Buddha spent his time at the foot of the Rājāyatana (Buchanania latifolia) tree on the southern side of the Bodhi tree, opening the great doors of his wisdom.
400:
400
It is sublime. (These two terms refer to the Supramundane Dhamma.) It is not a matter to be reached by mere reasoning (atakkāvacara). (It is a Dhamma to be reached only by wisdom.) It is subtle (nipuṇa), to be experienced only by the wise who practice the right path. However, this generation of beings delights in attachment (ālaya)—namely, the attachment to sensual pleasures (kāmālaya) and the attachment to craving (taṇhālaya) that enjoys those five sensual pleasures. They rejoice in attachment and are captivated by it. For such a generation, this Dhamma of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), which deals with causes and effects, is difficult to see. Furthermore, Nibbāna—the cessation of all conditioned things, the relinquishing of all substrates of existence (upadhi) such as kāmupadhi, khandhupadhi, kilesupadhi, and abhisaṅkhārupadhi, the exhaustion of the 108 types of craving, the fading away of the 1,500 defilements, and the cessation of all suffering—is even more difficult to see. If I were to teach such a profound Dhamma, and if others (devas and humans) whose faculties are weak and who are not ready for liberation do not understand or perceive it, then teaching the Dhamma to such people would only be wearying and troublesome for me." Such was the thought that arose in the Blessed One's mind.

Furthermore, these two most wonderful verses, which he had never heard before, became clear in his mind:
401:
401
(1) Kicchena me adhigataṃ,
Halaṃ dāni pakāsituṃ.
Rāgadosaparetehi,
Nāyaṃ dhammo susambudho.

(2) Paṭisotagāmiṃ nipuṇaṃ,
Gambhīraṃ duddasaṃ aṇuṃ.
Rāgarattā na dakkhanti,
Tamokhandhena āvutā.

(1) Me = By me. Kicchena = Through difficult practice while fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs). Adhigataṃ = This Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths has been attained and realized. Dāni-idāni = At this present moment, when only the internal cause (ajjhattika-nidāna), namely my compassion, is fulfilled, but the external cause (bāhira-nidāna), the request of the Brahma who is respected by the world, is not yet fulfilled. Pakāsituṃ = To clearly preach to devas and humans. Halaṃ = It is not yet suitable or appropriate. Ayaṃ dhammo = This Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. Rāgadosaparetehi = By those overwhelmed and oppressed by the evil states of lust and hatred. Na susambudho = Will not be easily or clearly understood.

(2) Tamokhandhena = By the mass of darkness which is ignorance (avijjā). Āvutā = Being completely covered and blinded so that the eye of wisdom is blocked. Rāgarattā = Those devas and humans who are attached and clinging through sensual lust, lust for existence, and lust for views. Nipuṇaṃ = The subtle. Gambhīraṃ = The very profound (like the mass of water supporting the earth). Duddasaṃ = The very difficult to see (like a mustard seed covered by Mount Meru). Aṇuṃ = The extremely subtle like an atom,
402:
402
Paṭisotagāmiṃ = The excellent Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths that leads to Nibbāna, going against the current of Saṃsāra. Na dakkhanti = They will not be able to see. (This reflection is a natural occurrence for all Buddhas.)

As the Blessed One reflected thus, his mind inclined toward not making an effort to teach the Dhamma for the time being, due to these three reasons: (1) the abundance of defilements in the continuity of beings, (2) the extreme profundity of the Dhamma, and (3) his own great respect for the Dhamma.

This state of mind is like a doctor who arrives at a patient oppressed by various diseases and thinks, "With what method and what medicines can I cure this patient's illness?" Similarly, the Blessed One, seeing the beings oppressed by various diseases of defilements and seeing the extreme profundity and difficulty of the Dhamma, thought, "What Dhamma should I teach to these beings? By what method of teaching should I preach to them?" It was only a mental process reflecting on how beings might understand the Four Noble Truths. (It was not a total abandonment of the thought of teaching. For details, one should look in the Milindapañhā.)

Alternatively, the preaching of the Buddhas has two causal origins: (1) The internal cause (ajjhattika-nidāna), which is the Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā) for beings arising within their own hearts; and (2) The external cause (bāhira-nidāna), which is the request to teach by the Brahma King, who is respected by the whole world (Loka-garu). At the time the Blessed One reflected on the profundity of the Dhamma and the thick defilements of beings,
403:
403
The internal cause, his Great Compassion, was already fulfilled. However, the external cause, the request of the Brahma King (Brahmayācana), was not yet fulfilled at that time. Therefore, his mind inclined toward teaching only when the external cause—the request of the Brahma King—was fulfilled.

Teaching only after being requested by a Brahma is a great tradition (dhammatā) of all Buddhas. The reason for this is that during the times outside of a Buddha's dispensation (bāhira-kāla), laypeople, hermits, wanderers, and those regarded as holy men and brahmins worship and respect only the Brahma. Therefore, if the Great Brahma, who is respected by the whole world, shows respect and bows down to the Buddha, then the whole world will also show respect, bow down, and have faith in the Buddha. For this reason, it is the natural custom of Buddhas to teach only after being requested by a Brahma King. Thus, it was only when the external cause,
404:
404
the request of the Brahma King, was fulfilled that his mind inclined toward teaching.

## The Request of Sahampati Brahma to Teach the Dhamma

(Sahampati Brahma: In the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha, a senior monk named Sahaka attained the first Rūpāvacara Jhāna. When he passed away without losing his Jhāna, he became a Great Brahma in the first Jhāna realm, with a lifespan of sixty-four intermediate eons (antara-kappa), which is one incalculable eon (asaṅkhyeyya-kappa). The Brahmas of that realm recognized and called him "Sahampati Brahma." — From Saṃyutta Aṭṭhakathā 1, 182; Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā 3, 155.)

When the Blessed One's mind thus inclined toward not making an effort to teach the Dhamma, Sahampati Brahma thought: "Nassati vata bho loko, vinassati vata bho loko—Alas, friends, the world is perishing! Alas, friends, the world is being destroyed! For the mind of the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One who has fully penetrated all Dhammas, inclines toward not making an effort to teach the Dhamma." Just as a strong man might stretch his bent arm or bend his stretched arm, Sahampati Brahma disappeared from the Brahma realm along with ten thousand other Brahmas and appeared before the Blessed One. Then, Sahampati Brahma, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder,
405:
Placing his upper robe over his left shoulder and kneeling with his right knee on the ground, Sahampati Brahmā saluted the Blessed One with joined palms and said:

“Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to all beings, including devas and Brahmās. May the Sugata (the Well-Spoken One) teach the Dhamma to all beings. There are beings with little dust in their eyes of wisdom. If they do not hear the Dhamma of the Blessed One, they will decline and lose the noble attainments of the Path and Fruit which they are worthy of achieving. There will be those who can clearly understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One.”

Having spoken thus in prose, Sahampati Brahmā again requested and entreated the Buddha with these verses:

“Venerable Sir, in former times, before the appearance of the Buddha, an impure and false doctrine devised by the six sectarian teachers, such as Pūraṇa Kassapa, who were possessed of defilements, appeared in the land of Magadha. Therefore, O Noble One, please open the great door of the Path to the Deathless (Nibbāna), which has been closed since the disappearance of the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha. May these beings hear the noble Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, which has been realized by the Blessed One, who is free from the
406:
stain of defilements.

O Blessed One, who is virtuous, pure, and wise, possessing the eye of wisdom that can see all around! Just as a man with good sight standing on a rocky mountain peak looks down upon the people all around, even so, O Blessed One, who is free from sorrow, having ascended the palace of wisdom, look down upon the beings—devas, humans, and Brahmās—who are immersed in sorrow, oppressed by birth, aging, sickness, and death.

O Blessed One, who is great and heroic in effort, who is never defeated in any battle but always victorious! Arise, O Hero! You are like a caravan leader who can lead the assembly of beings to be trained out of the difficult journeys of birth and aging to the safe haven of Nibbāna. O Blessed One, who is free from the debt of craving and sensual desire, please wander through the world to establish the assembly of Dhamma. Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One teach the Four Noble Truths to all beings. There will be those who can clearly understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One.”
407:
Thus he requested and entreated. (It is the nature of all Buddhas that when the mind is inclined to hesitate in teaching the Dhamma, considering its depth and the thick defilements of beings, a Brahmā comes to request the teaching. This is from the commentary on the Thirty Natural Laws of the Buddhas in the Buddhavaṃsa Aṭṭhakathā.)

## The Buddha Surveys the World of Beings

When Sahampati Brahmā requested him to teach, the Blessed One, having fulfilled both the external cause (the request of the Brahmā) and the internal cause (the Great Compassion for beings), surveyed the world of beings with his pair of Buddha-eyes: the knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of the degrees of faculties (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa).

While surveying, he saw in a pond of blue, red, and white lotuses: (1) some lotuses that are born in the water, grow in the water, and remain submerged, thriving within the water; (2) some lotuses that are born in the water, grow in the water, and remain level with the surface of the water; (3) some lotuses that are born in the water, grow in the water, and stand high above the water, unsullied and unattached to the water. (Among these three types, those in category 3, standing high above the water, are the lotuses that will bloom today. Those in category 2, level with the water's surface, will bloom tomorrow. Those in category 1, submerged and thriving in the water, will bloom on the third day [the day after tomorrow].)
408:
Apart from these three types, there is (4) a type of lotus that is diseased, which will never rise above the water nor bloom, but will become food for fish and turtles. Similarly, the Buddha perceived beings with little dust in their eyes of wisdom and those with much dust; beings with keen faculties and those with dull faculties (the five faculties: faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom); beings with good qualities and those with bad qualities; beings easy to teach and those hard to teach; and beings who live seeing the dangers of the world (the aggregates, defilements, misconduct, volitional formations, and kamma leading to rebirth) as a terrifying mass of peril, like an enemy with a raised sword ready to strike, and those who do not live so.

(In this context, when the Buddha surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye, he saw four types of persons: (1) The *ugghaṭitaññū* person, who, like the lotuses that rise above the water and bloom today as soon as the sun rises, realizes the Four Noble Truths and attains liberation as soon as a brief summary or heading is taught. (2) The *vipañcitaññū* person, who, like the lotuses level with the water's surface that will bloom tomorrow, does not attain liberation by hearing a brief summary alone, but realizes the Four Noble Truths and attains liberation only when that summary is explained in detail. (3) The *neyya* person, who, like the lotuses submerged and thriving that will bloom on the third day, does not attain liberation in a single sitting even after hearing the Dhamma in brief and in detail, but by relying on good friends, practicing, studying, and reflecting repeatedly, realizes the Four Noble Truths and attains liberation in later days, months, or years. (4) The *padaparama* person, who, like the diseased
409:
lotuses that neither rise nor bloom but become food for fish and turtles, may hear, study, and practice the Dhamma in this life, yet does not attain the Path and Fruit, gaining only the potential habit (vāsanā) for future lives while ending this life as food for the fish and turtles of defilements. He saw these four types of persons in their respective groups.

Having seen this, the Blessed One clearly reflected on the Dhamma that would bring appropriate benefits to these four types of persons and developed a strong desire to teach. Then, he further categorized all beings in the three realms into two groups: the *bhabba* (capable of liberation) and the *abhabba* (incapable of liberation). Among these, he set aside the *abhabba* and took into his golden knowledge only the *bhabba* persons. He then divided them into six groups based on their temperaments: those with a lustful temperament, a hateful temperament, a deluded temperament, a speculative temperament, a faithful temperament, and an intellectual temperament. Having done so, he thought, “I shall teach the Dhamma.”)

Having thus analyzed and understood, the Blessed One addressed Sahampati Brahmā with this verse of acceptance:

*Apārutā tesaṃ amatassa dvārā,*
*Ye sotavanto pamuñcantu saddhaṃ.*
*Vihiṃsasaññī paguṇaṃ na bhāsiṃ,*
*Dhammaṃ paṇītaṃ manujesu brahme.*

The meaning is: O Sahampati Brahmā, for those devas and humans who are capable of liberation, I have not kept the eight great doors of the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the Deathless Nibbāna closed; (I have kept them open at all times). Let those devas and humans who have good ears (the faculty of hearing) release their faith towards me.
410:
(Only those with good hearing will be able to listen to the Dhamma I teach. And only if they have faith in me will they practice the Dhamma with conviction and the doors of Nibbāna will open for them. Even if they have good hearing, if they lack faith in me, they will not believe the Dhamma nor practice it. If they do not believe and practice, the doors of Nibbāna will not open. Therefore, it means: let beings with good hearing listen to the Dhamma by releasing their faith towards me.

Alternatively: From the time the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha disappeared until today, because beings have not encountered a true Buddha or the true Dhamma, the treasure of faith within them has been like a bundle held tightly in the hand; true faith could not arise. The devotion they had towards sectarian teachers during this interval was not true faith, but merely *micchādhimokkha*—an unwholesome mental state of mistaking the false for the true. Now that a true Buddha has appeared, let those devas and humans with good hearing unwrap the bundle of the treasure of faith, which they have held tightly since the disappearance of Kassapa Buddha's dispensation; let them release their clenched hands.)
411:
"O Great Sahampati Brahma, in previous days, because the two conditions for preaching the Dhamma were not yet fulfilled, even if I were to preach, it would not benefit beings and would only result in my exhaustion. Therefore, I did not preach the sublime Dhamma I have realized to humans, devas, and Brahmas."

Then, the Great Sahampati Brahma, thinking, "The Exalted One has given me his word and permission to preach the Dhamma," was delighted and joyful. He paid respectful homage to the Exalted One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and vanished from that very spot (returning to his own Brahma realm).

## For the Preaching of the Dhammacakka Sutta
## Journeying to the Migadāya Forest

After the Great Sahampati Brahma had departed, the Exalted One reflected and considered: "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma? Who will understand the Dhamma I preach quickly?" Then he further reflected: "This Āḷāra Kālāma, of the Kālāma lineage, is endowed with the three types of wisdom: Jāti-paññā (innate wisdom), Bhāvanā-paññā (wisdom through meditation), and Pārihārika-paññā (wisdom of preservation). For a long time, he has been an 'Apparajakkha' person, one with little dust of defilements in his eyes of wisdom. It would be well if I were to preach the Dhamma first to Āḷāra Kālāma of the Kālāma lineage; he will quickly penetrate and understand the Dhamma I preach." Such was the thought that arose in the Exalted One.
412:
Then a deity, without revealing his form, addressed the Exalted One: "Exalted One, Āḷāra Kālāma of the Kālāma lineage has been dead for seven days." The Exalted One, however, did not make a decision or reach a conclusion based solely on the deity's words. He looked with his own Golden Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and clearly saw that, just as the deity had said, Āḷāra Kālāma had passed away seven days ago and had been reborn in the Ākiñcaññāyatana realm (the Sphere of Nothingness), which is the third of the four Formless Brahma realms.

Then the thought occurred to the Exalted One: "Āḷāra Kālāma of the Kālāma lineage has suffered a great loss from the Path and Fruit (Magga-Phala) he was worthy of attaining. If Āḷāra Kālāma had heard this Dhamma preached by me, he would have quickly penetrated the Four Noble Truths." Then he reflected again: "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma? Who will understand the Dhamma I preach quickly?" Then the thought arose: "This Uddaka Rāmaputta, the son of Rāma, like Āḷāra, is endowed with the three types of wisdom. For a long time, he has been an 'Apparajakkha' person, one with little dust of defilements in his eyes of wisdom. It would be well if I were to preach the Dhamma first to Uddaka Rāmaputta, the son of Rāma; he will quickly penetrate and understand the Dhamma I preach."
413:
Then a deity, without revealing his form, addressed the Exalted One: "Exalted One, Uddaka Rāmaputta, the son of Rāma, passed away at midnight last night." The Exalted One did not make a decision or reach a conclusion based solely on the deity's words. He looked with his own Golden Omniscient Knowledge and clearly saw that, just as the deity had said, Uddaka Rāmaputta had passed away at midnight and had been reborn in the Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana realm (the Sphere of Neither-perception-nor-non-perception), also known as Bhavagga, the fourth of the Formless Brahma realms.

Then the thought occurred to the Exalted One: "Uddaka Rāmaputta, the son of Rāma, has suffered a great loss from the Path and Fruit he was worthy of attaining. If Uddaka Rāmaputta had heard this Dhamma preached by me, he would have quickly penetrated the Four Noble Truths." Then he reflected again: "To whom should I first preach the Dhamma? Who will understand the Dhamma I preach quickly?"

Then the thought occurred to the Exalted One: "The five monks (Pañcavaggī) have been very helpful to me. These five monks attended to and served me while I was practicing the great struggle (Dukkaracariyā) for six years in the Uruvelā forest. Therefore, it would be well if I were to preach the Dhamma first to the five monks." Then he continued to reflect:
414:
"Where are the five monks living now?" After this thought, he looked with his Divine Eye (Dibba-cakkhu) and saw the five monks living in the Migadāya forest, at a place called Isipatana, near the city of Bārāṇasī.

(In this matter: The reason the Exalted One considered the helpfulness of the five monks was that the Buddha is one who especially remembers the gratitude of others; it was not that he was unwilling to preach to those who had not helped him.)

Thinking, "I shall go to the Migadāya forest and preach the Dhammacakka Dhamma," the Exalted One stayed near the Bodhi-maṇḍa, going on alms rounds until the 14th day of the waxing moon of Āsāḷha. When the full moon day of Āsāḷha arrived, he prepared his bowl and robes early in the morning, thinking, "I shall go to the city of Bārāṇasī," and set out on foot for the journey of eighteen yojanas.

(The distance between Mahābodhi and Gayā is three gāvutas. The distance between Mahābodhi and Bārāṇasī is eighteen yojanas. Previous Buddhas traveled through the air to the Migadāya forest by means of meditative absorption (jhāna) to preach the Dhammacakka. Our Buddha, however, saw the past merit of Upaka the ascetic, who was to become an Anāgāmī (Non-returner). He knew: "Now Upaka is coming along this road. He will see me, converse with me, and then depart. Later, becoming weary of the world, he will come to me, hear the Dhamma, and become an Anāgāmī in this life. In his second life, he will reach the Aviha realm and become an Arahant." Knowing this, he traveled the eighteen-yojana journey on foot.)
415:
## Meeting Upaka the Ascetic

As the Exalted One was traveling on foot from Mahābodhi to Bārāṇasī, Upaka the ascetic, who was traveling between Mahābodhi and Buddha Gayā, saw the Exalted One. He approached and asked: "Friend, your six faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—are very clear. Your complexion is pure and radiant. Friend, under whom have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you prefer?" Then the Exalted One answered Upaka the ascetic with this verse:

(1) Sabbābhibhū sabbavidūhamasmi,
sabbesu dhammesu anupalitto.
Sabbañjaho taṇhākkhaye vimutto,
sayaṃ abhiññāya kamuddiseyyaṃ.

"Upaka, I am the one who has overcome all things in the three realms. I am the one who knows all things completely and without remainder. I am unstained by the defilements of craving, hatred, and delusion in all things of the three planes. I have abandoned and relinquished all things of the three planes. I am liberated and established in Nibbāna, the destruction of craving. Since I have realized all things by myself without a teacher, whom should I point to and say, 'This is my teacher'? There is no such person."
416:
(2) Na me ācariyo atthi, sadiso me na vijjati.
Sadevakasmiṃ lokasmiṃ, natthi me paṭipuggalo.

"Upaka, I have no teacher. (Not to mention a superior teacher), there is no one even equal to me. In the world of beings including the devas, there is no one who can be my counterpart in virtues such as morality (sīla).

(3) Ahaṃ hi arahā loke, ahaṃ satthā anuttaro.
Ekomhi sammāsambuddho, sītibhūtosmi nibbuto.

"Upaka, I am the Arahant in the world, worthy of special offerings. I am the supreme Teacher of devas and humans in the world. I have penetrated all things correctly through my own self-evolved knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa) and thus I am the peerless One. I am the one whose fires of defilements are extinguished and cooled."

(4) Dhammacakkaṃ pavattetuṃ, gacchāmi kāsinaṃ puraṃ.
Andhībhūtasmiṃ lokasmiṃ, āhañchaṃ amatadundubhiṃ.

"Upaka, I am going to the city of Bārāṇasī in the Kāsī country, to the Isipatana Migadāya forest, to set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion. In this world of devas and humans who are like the blind without the eye of wisdom, I shall beat the great drum of the Deathless (Amata-dundubhi)." (This means: I go to Bārāṇasī in the Kāsī country to beat the great drum of the Deathless, which is the preaching of the Dhamma.)

Then Upaka the ascetic said to the Exalted One: "Friend, if it is as you claim, you must be the Infinite Conqueror (Ananta-jina) who has conquered the five Maras."

The Exalted One replied:
417:
(5) Mādisā ve jinā honti, ye pattā āsavakkhayaṃ.
Jitā me pāpakā dhammā, tasmāhamupaka jino.

"Upaka, those Buddhas like me, who have reached the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints (Āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa or Arahatta-magga) and have conquered and abandoned evil, unwholesome states, are called Conquerors (Jina). I, too, like those Buddhas, have reached the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints and have conquered and abandoned evil, unwholesome states; therefore, Upaka, I am a Conqueror."

Then Upaka the ascetic said, "Friend, it may be as you say," and nodding his head, he left the path and went to the Vankahāra country. (This very conversation and exchange of questions and answers with the Exalted One became a reason for Upaka to rely on for his future ordination. Indeed, Upaka was a person with great merit (adhikāra). That is why the Exalted One traveled on foot to meet him.)

(In this matter: It is the natural law (dhammatā) that those who hear the Dhamma preached by the Exalted One before the preaching of the Dhammacakka Sutta do not attain the Path and Fruit, but only benefit from the impression (vāsanā) of the Dhamma. Therefore, although Upaka heard this profound Dhamma concerning the virtues of the Exalted One, he did not attain the Path and Fruit, but only gained the impression to become a monk later.)

## Brief Story of Upaka

Upaka the ascetic lived in a small hunters' village in the Vankahāra country, depending on the head of that village...
418: He lived in a small monastery, supported and venerated by a hunter. (Because the gadflies and mosquitoes were very prevalent in that district, the ascetic Upaka was made to stay inside a large earthen jar.) The hunter, wishing to go to a distant deer forest, instructed his daughter Cāpā (Sāvā, Suttani-aṭṭhakathā, 1, 248; Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā, 2, 94), saying, 'My daughter, look after and serve our teacher, the noble Arahant, properly and well; do not be negligent,' and then went to the forest with his sons and brothers. The hunter's daughter, Cāpā, was beautiful and attractive to behold, endowed with all the graceful features of a woman. On the day after the hunter's departure, when the ascetic Upaka came to the hunter's house and saw Cāpā approaching to serve him food after making preparations, he was overcome by lust. Unable even to eat the food, he took the food in his bowl, went back to his dwelling, placed the bowl in a suitable spot, and thought, 'I shall live only if I get Cāpā; if not, I shall die.' Thus, he lay down without eating any food. On the seventh day, the hunter returned home and asked his daughter Cāpā about the teacher Upaka. When Cāpā said, 'Father, your teacher Upaka came to the house only one day and has not returned since,' the father, still in his hunting attire from the forest (without even changing clothes), thought, 'I will go to the teacher Upaka and
419: inquire about the matter.' He immediately went to Upaka's dwelling, massaged his feet, and asked, 'What kind of illness is this, Bhante?' The ascetic Upaka did not answer yet, but only groaned and tossed from side to side. When the hunter said, 'Please speak, Bhante; I will do everything within my power,' Upaka replied, 'I shall live only if I get Cāpā; if not, it is better to die right here.' The hunter asked, 'Bhante, do you know any kind of craft or skill?' Upaka replied, 'I do not.' The hunter then said, 'Bhante, one who does not know any craft will not be able to manage a household.' Upaka responded, 'I do not know any craft, but I will carry the meat you obtain and I will sell the meat.' The hunter said, 'We also like such carrying and selling of meat,' and gave him an upper garment to change into lay clothes. He then took him home and gave his daughter Cāpā in marriage to Upaka. From the union of Upaka and his wife Cāpā, a son was born,
420: whom they named Subhadda. Whenever the little son cried, Cāpā would mock and ridicule Upaka by singing a lullaby: 'O son of the meat-carrier, the former ascetic, the follower of a hunter, the foolish one who left the monkhood for me... sleep now, my dear son, while your mother lulls you. Sleep in your jeweled cradle, my golden son. With playful wiles, mother will swing the cradle; stop crying, my golden lump, I want you to sleep. Your father is the lowest among men. Avoid such a path in the future and be free; your mother now leaves this message, my beautiful golden garland.'* Thus, she ridiculed and insulted Upaka by using the lullaby to provoke him. Then Upaka said, 'Woman, do you think I am one without a refuge? I have a great friend named Anantajina. I shall go to that friend Anantajina.' When he said this, Cāpā realized, 'When I speak such provocative words, this Upaka feels deep pain and cannot bear it,' and she sang that lullaby repeatedly. One day, without informing or speaking to Cāpā, Upaka departed for the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). At that time, the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī and had already instructed the monks in advance, saying, 'Monks, if someone comes asking for Anantajina, *Written by Manle Sayadaw.
421: show him to Me.' Upaka came along the way asking those he met, 'Where does Anantajina live?' and eventually reached Sāvatthī. Standing in the middle of the Jetavana Monastery, he asked the monks, 'Venerable sirs, where does Anantajina live?' The monks then led Upaka to the Blessed One. As soon as Upaka saw the Blessed One, he asked, 'Exalted Blessed One, do you still recognize and remember me?' The Blessed One replied, 'Upaka, yes, I recognize you. Where do you live now?' Upaka replied, 'Exalted Blessed One, I live in the Vaṅkahāra district.' Then the Blessed One asked, 'Upaka, you have become old; will you be able to become a monk?' Upaka replied, 'Exalted Blessed One, I will become a monk.' Then the Blessed One had him ordained and gave him a suitable subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). Upaka practiced meditation diligently and, after attaining the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala), passed away from that life and was reborn in the Aviha realm, the lowest of the five Suddhāvāsa Brahma realms. Soon after being born in that Aviha realm, he attained the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala).
422:
## Summary of the Account of Cāpā

When the wanderer Upaka departed, Cāpā became weary of the household life. She entrusted her young son Subhadda to his grandfather and followed the path Upaka had taken. Upon reaching Sāvatthī, she became a bhikkhunī under the guidance of the bhikkhunīs. She practiced Vipassanā meditation with great effort and, through the sequence of the four Paths, attained Arahatta-phala. Having exhausted all defilements (āsavas), she became an Arahant and was known as Cāpā Therī. (From the Commentary on the Therīgāthā, page 231.)

## The Buddha's Arrival at the Migadāya Forest

Then, as the Buddha traveled by stages, he arrived at the presence of the Group of Five (Pañcavaggiya) in the Isipatana Migadāya forest near Bārāṇasī on the evening of the full moon day of Āsāḷha in the year 103 of the Great Era (Mahā-sakkarāj). The five bhikkhus of the Group of Five saw the Buddha coming from afar and made a pact among themselves:

"Friends, this ascetic Gotama is coming. This ascetic Gotama is one who has fallen away from the practice of meditation (a great meditator-turned-layman). He is one who strives for the abundance of the four requisites. He has turned towards the side of luxury. We shall not pay homage to this ascetic Gotama, nor shall we go out to meet him, nor shall we take his bowl and robes. However, we shall prepare a seat for him in case he wishes to sit."

Knowing the thoughts of the five bhikkhus of the Group of Five, the Buddha...
423: the Blessed One directed specific loving-kindness (odhissaka-mettā) towards those five monks. As the Blessed One drew closer and closer to them, they were so affected by the power of His Buddha-majesty and the power of His loving-kindness that they were unable to keep their original pact. All five of them went out to greet the Blessed One. One took the Blessed One's bowl and robe; another prepared the seat; another set out water for washing the feet; another provided the footstool; and another placed the towel for drying the feet. The Blessed One sat on the seat prepared by the Group of Five and washed His feet. (Although these five monks broke their pact and showed physical respect to the Blessed One), when they spoke, they addressed the Blessed One by His name 'Gotama' and as 'Āvuso' (friend), treating Him as an equal. They spoke words of welcome, saying, 'Friend Gotama, when you were practicing meditation in the Uruveḷā forest, we followed you, carrying your bowl and robe. We offered you water for washing and tooth-sticks. We swept the precinct of the hermitage where you lived. After the five of us left, who attended to your needs? Since we departed, have you been free from excessive worldly thoughts?' Thus, they addressed the Blessed One by the name 'Gotama' and as 'Āvuso', treating Him as an equal.
424: Then the Blessed One said, 'O monks of the Group of Five, do not address Me by the name "Gotama" or as "Āvuso", treating Me as an equal. Monks, I have truly become a Buddha, worthy of special offerings, having clearly and fully realized all the truths that should be known. Monks, lend your ears; I have attained the Deathless Nibbāna. I shall instruct you; I shall teach you the Dhamma. If you, dear sons, follow and practice as I instruct, you will, in this very life, soon realize through your own higher knowledge and attain the bliss of the Fruit of Arahantship—the goal for which sons of good family (kulaputta) by birth and sons of good family by conduct leave the household life to become monks.' When He said this, the five monks (unable to believe) said, 'Friend Gotama, even when you practiced the six years of austerities (dukkara-cariyā), such as the Āpānaka-jhāna which is difficult for ordinary men to practice, you did not attain the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship or Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) that can make one a Noble One (Ariya). Now that you have become one who strives for abundance in the four requisites, one who has reverted from the practice, and one who has turned towards a life of luxury, how could you have attained the Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship, which makes one a Noble One and surpasses the ten ordinary wholesome paths of men?'
425:
“Where can omniscience be attained and reached?” they replied (quite honestly).

When they spoke thus, the Blessed One said to the group of five monks: “Monks, I am not one who strives for the abundance of the four requisites, nor am I one who has fallen from the work of striving (an ex-meditator who has returned to the lay life), nor am I one who has turned towards the side of seeking abundance in the four requisites. Monks, I have truly become a Buddha, worthy of special offerings, having clearly and truly penetrated the entire mass of all things that should be known through the Four Noble Truths. Monks, lend your ears; I have attained and reached the Deathless Nibbāna. I shall admonish and teach you; I shall preach the Dhamma to you. If you, dear sons, follow and practice as I admonish, you will, in this very life and before long, personally realize through higher knowledge, fulfill, and dwell in the bliss of the fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala), which is the goal yearned for by noble sons of good family and noble sons of good conduct who have abandoned the household life and entered the monkhood as servants of the Sāsana.” When he spoke thus, the group of five monks (still unable to believe) spoke for a second time in the same manner as before.

Although the Blessed One spoke for the second time in the same manner as before, saying that he was “not one who strives for the abundance of the four requisites,” etc., the group of five monks (still remaining unable to believe) spoke for a third time in the same manner as before.
426:
Then the Blessed One (changing his approach) said: “Monks, do you recall me ever coming to you and speaking to make you think highly of me, saying, ‘Friends, do not have many wandering thoughts of going elsewhere; light and meditation signs (kammaṭṭhāna nimitta) have appeared to me,’ during the time I was striving in the Uruvelā forest, so that you would not be lazy in my presence?” When he spoke thus, the group of five monks reflected: “If this Monk Gotama had said ‘I have become an Arahant’ while he was striving, we would have believed him. However, this Monk Gotama did not speak boastfully or deceitfully at that time; now, however, he speaks only of qualities that truly exist.” Having been reminded by that single statement, they developed a sense of reverence (gārava) towards the Blessed One and believed without hesitation, thinking, “Truly, this Great Monk Gotama has become a Buddha.” They then replied and confessed: “No hetaṃ bhante = Bhante, we do not recall the Lord ever saying such things during the time you were striving in the past (= you never said it).”

The Blessed One was thus able to make the group of five monks well aware that he had become a Buddha. Then, the group of five monks respectfully listened to the words of the Blessed One, lent their ears, and directed their minds forward to reach the fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala). Then, the Blessed One, having made the group of five monks well aware that he was truly a Buddha,
427:
on the evening of the full moon day of Āsāḷha in the year 103 of the Great Era (Mahā-sakarāj), while the sun was still shining with its own light, dispelling the natural darkness and about to set in the west, and while the moon was emerging from the eastern world-element, shining with its own light, dispelling the natural darkness in conjunction with the Uttarāsāḷha nakshatra, he began to preach the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, starting with “Dve me bhikkhave antā.”

(As soon as the phrase “Dve me bhikkhave antā” was recited, the voice that emerged reached from the highest plane of existence (Bhavagga) to the lowest hell (Avīci) and remained spread throughout the entire ten thousand world systems. At that very moment, eighteen crores of Brahmas, whose roots of merit had matured and who had performed special meritorious deeds (adhikāra-kusala) in the past to know the Four Noble Truths, had already assembled in unison.)

When the Blessed One thus preached the Dhammacakka Sutta, Venerable Koṇḍañña followed the discourse and directed his wisdom accordingly; at the conclusion of the Sutta, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) along with the eighteen crores of Brahmas.

In this way, when the Blessed One preached the Dhammacakka Sutta, the thirty-two great extraordinary omens appeared, just as they did at the time of his conception, his birth, and his attainment of Buddhahood.

When Venerable Koṇḍañña was thus established in the fruit of Stream-entry, the Blessed One uttered a joyful exclamation (udāna) loud enough for the devas and humans of the ten thousand world systems to hear: “Aññāsi vata bho Koṇḍañño,
428:
Aññāsi vata bho Koṇḍañño = Oh, Koṇḍañña has indeed understood the Four Noble Truths! Oh, Koṇḍañña has indeed understood the Four Noble Truths!” Because the Blessed One uttered this joyful exclamation starting with “Aññāsi vata,” the name of the Elder Koṇḍañña became famously known as “Elder Aññāsi-Koṇḍañña.”

After becoming a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), Elder Aññāsi-Koṇḍañña requested the Blessed One for novicehood and monkhood, saying: “Glorious Blessed One, may I receive the novicehood in the presence of the Blessed One; may I receive the monkhood.” Then, the Blessed One, extending his golden right hand from within his robes, spoke with a voice like that of the Great Brahma: “(1) Ehi Bhikkhu, (2) Svākkhāto Dhammo, (3) Cara brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāya = (1) Come, monk; receive the monkhood that you, dear son, have requested. (2) The Dhamma has been well-expounded by me. (3) Practice the holy life, which is the three higher paths (magga), with diligence to make an end of suffering.” Among these three sentences spoken by the Blessed One, as soon as the first sentence marked (1) was completed, the matter of Elder Aññāsi-Koṇḍañña’s ordination and becoming a monk was successfully accomplished.
429:
(As soon as the Blessed One called that Elder Koṇḍañña with “Ehi Bhikkhu,” his original lay appearance vanished, and his status as a monk was successfully achieved. His hair was shaved, and he was already clad in robes. With one robe worn around the waist, another single robe (ekaccī) draped over him, another great robe (saṅghāṭī) placed on his shoulder, and an alms-bowl slung over his left shoulder, all eight requisites were ready in their respective places. He stood worshipping the Blessed One, his teacher and preceptor (upajjhāya), endowed with a graceful posture like that of a senior elder of sixty years' standing (eighty years of age).

The requisites obtained by these Ehi Bhikkhu monks are called iddhimaya-parikkhāra (requisites created by psychic power). If a person, after offering the eight requisites such as robes (or even just an alms-bowl and robes if unable to do more) to a Noble One (ariya) such as a Stream-enterer, or to a virtuous worldling monk, makes a prayer (patthanā) saying, “May this current offering of requisites be a support for becoming an Ehi Bhikkhu monk in the future,” and if that offering of requisites is endowed with special merit (adhikāra-kusala), it can lead to obtaining the iddhimaya-parikkhāra (= becoming an Ehi Bhikkhu monk) in the presence of the Buddhas. — From Sārattha-ṭīkā, Vol. 2, p. 51.)

The Blessed One, staying for the Rains Retreat in that very Migadāya forest, remained only at the monastery on the following day (the 1st waning day of Āsāḷha) giving admonition and advice to Elder Vappa (without going for alms). The remaining four monks went for alms. Elder Vappa became a Stream-enterer on that very morning. In the same manner, on the next day (= 2nd waning day of Āsāḷha), he gave advice to Elder Bhaddiya; on the next day (= 3rd waning day of Āsāḷha), to Elder Mahānāma; and on the next day (= 4th waning day of Āsāḷha), to Elder Assaji, remaining only at the monastery without going for alms. Those Elders also,
430:
reached the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) on their respective days and received the Ehi Bhikkhu monkhood in the presence of the Blessed One.

When the 5th waning day of Āsāḷha, a Thursday, arrived, the Blessed One preached the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta to the group of five monks so that they might reach the state of Arahantship with the exhaustion of all taints (āsava). At the conclusion of the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta discourse, the group of five monks became Arahants with the exhaustion of all taints.

(Matters worth knowing regarding the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta and the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta will be presented upon reaching the chapter on the Dhamma-ratana.)

## Chapter 10
## About the Deva Kings Sātāgira and Hemavata
## (Hemavata Sutta)

The Blessed One preached the Dhammacakka Dhamma on the full moon day of Āsāḷha in the year 103 of the Great Era, just as the sun was about to set. At the midnight hour of that same night, he preached the Hemavata Sutta (otherwise known as the Sātāgira Sutta). The detailed background for preaching this Sutta is as follows:

In this Bhadda-kappa (Auspicious Aeon), during the time when the lifespan of humans was 20,000 years, the Kassapa Buddha appeared and remained for a period of 16,000 years (which is four-fifths of the life-aeon) before attaining Parinibbāna. The physical remains (utuja-rūpa-kalāpa) of that Kassapa Buddha were honored with great worship,
431:
They performed the funeral rites with great honor. The bodily relics (sarīradhātu) of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha did not break into fragments but remained as a single solid mass like a block of gold. Such a state is the natural custom of long-lived Buddhas.

Short-lived Buddhas, however, pass into Parinibbāna before all people have had the opportunity to pay their respects. Therefore, out of compassion and consideration, thinking, 'The multitudes of people living in various towns and regions will increase their merit by honoring my relics after I have passed into Parinibbāna,' short-lived Buddhas make a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna): 'May my relics be dispersed into fragments.' Thus, the bodily relics of such short-lived Buddhas are dispersed into fragments like gold dust, just like the relics of our Blessed Buddha.

The people built a relic chamber for the single solid bodily relic of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha and erected a great stupa that was one yojana in height and one yojana in circumference. This great stupa was one gāvuta in length on each of its four sides, and each side had a great entrance gate. Thus, the distance between one gate and another was one gāvuta.

King Kikī, the ruler of Bārāṇasī, sponsored one of the entrance gates. Another gate was sponsored by King Kikī's son,
432:
Prince Pathavindhara. Another gate was sponsored by the ministers led by the General. The remaining gate was sponsored by the citizens led by a wealthy merchant. The bricks used in the construction of the great stupa were only gold and jeweled bricks. Each brick was worth one hundred thousand. They performed the plastering work using vermilion and arsenic, and the masonry work using fragrant oil and ghee to build that great stupa.

After the great stupa was completed, two young men of good family left the household life and were ordained as monks under the Great Disciples (Sāvaka) who had personally served the Buddha. (It should be noted that in the Sāsana of long-lived Buddhas, only the Great Disciples who personally served during the Buddha's lifetime perform the duties of ordaining novices, ordaining monks, and giving tutelage (nissaya). Disciples who arise after the Buddha has passed into Parinibbāna do not have the opportunity to perform such duties.)

At that time, the two young monks of good family asked the Great Disciples, 'Venerable sirs, how many duties of a monk are there to be practiced in the Buddha's Sāsana?' The Great Disciples replied, 'Friends, there are two duties of a monk to be practiced in the Buddha's Sāsana: (1) the duty of practicing Vipassanā meditation, known as Vāsadhura, and (2) the duty of studying and teaching the scriptures, known as Pariyattidhura. Between these two—'
433:
(1) A monk of good family, after residing with his teachers and preceptors for five years and fulfilling his major and minor duties, should master the Pātimokkha and the Suttas consisting of about two or three bhāṇavāras. Having properly learned the method of practicing Vipassanā meditation, he should sever attachments to his group of disciples and lay supporters, enter the deep forest away from people, and strive in meditation to realize the fruit of Arahatship. Such striving is called the duty of practicing Vipassanā meditation, or Vāsadhura. (2) According to one's ability, one should master one Nikāya of the Piṭaka, two Nikāyas, three Nikāyas, four Nikāyas, or all five Nikāyas of the Piṭaka. One should then strive in the Pariyatti Sāsana to ensure the words and meanings are pure and unerring. Such striving is called the duty of studying and teaching the scriptures, or Pariyattidhura.'

Then, the two young monks of good family said, 'Among the two duties of a monk, Vāsadhura is indeed more noble and praiseworthy.' However, they consulted each other, saying, 'We are still young. We shall fulfill this duty of Vāsadhura meditation when we are older. Before we grow old, we will first complete the duty of studying and teaching the scriptures, known as Pariyattidhura.' They then applied themselves to the study of the scriptures. Being naturally wise, before long,
434:
they became proficient and reached the further shore of all three Piṭakas, and they also became extremely skilled in matters of Vinaya judgments. Because of their mastery of the scriptures, these two monks of good family became famous in the Sāsana and gained a large following of disciples. Due to this large following, they also received an abundance of offerings. Each of them had a retinue of five hundred monks.

These two elders lived while instructing and preaching the true teachings and advice of the Buddha to the fourfold assembly who came to visit them. Thus, the three aspects of the Sāsana flourished and shone brightly, as if a Buddha had appeared once again.

## The Vinaya Case of the Dhammavādī Monk and the Adhammavādī Monk

At that time, a Dhammavādī (righteous) monk and an Adhammavādī (unrighteous) monk were living in a village monastery. Of these two, the Adhammavādī monk was cruel, rude, and harsh in speech. One day, the Dhammavādī monk clearly heard and knew of an offense committed by the Adhammavādī monk against the Vinaya rules. The Dhammavādī monk rebuked him, saying, 'Friend, this act you have committed is not suitable for the Sāsana.' Then the Adhammavādī monk replied, 'Friend, what did you see? What did you hear? Do not accuse me randomly.' He spoke in such a way as to obscure the original matter.
435:
The Dhammavādī monk said, 'Friend, the great elders who are experts in the Vinaya (Vinayadhara) will know about this.'

Then the Adhammavādī monk thought, 'If these great Vinayadhara elders decide this case according to the path of the Dhamma, I will certainly have no standing or support in the Sāsana.' Wishing to win those great Vinayadhara elders over to his side, he immediately took monastic requisites (parikkhāra) as gifts and approached the two great Vinayadhara elders. He respectfully offered the requisites he had brought and sought to live under their tutelage (nissaya). He pretended to be one who wished to respectfully serve them and fulfill all major and minor duties perfectly.

Then one day, the Adhammavādī monk approached the place where the two great Vinayadhara elders were meeting. After paying respects, even though the elders gave him leave to depart, he remained standing there persistently. The elders then asked the Adhammavādī monk, 'Friend, do you have any special matter to speak about?' The Adhammavādī monk replied, 'Yes, venerable sirs. I have had a dispute with another monk regarding a violation of a training rule. If that accusing monk comes to your presence and reports this matter, please do not decide the case according to the law or as it should be decided.' The elders said, 'It is not proper not to decide a matter that has come before the Saṅgha as it should be decided.'
436:
When the elders said it was improper, the Adhammavādī monk pleaded, 'Venerable sirs, if you decide the case in such a manner, I will have no standing or support in the Sāsana. Let that evil deed be my own evil deed (I will bear the karmic consequences myself). Please, just do not decide that case.'

Since the Adhammavādī monk pleaded so insistently (leaving them no choice), the great Vinayadhara elders finally gave their word, saying, 'Very well, friend.' Having obtained this promise from the great Vinayadhara elders, the Adhammavādī monk returned to the village monastery. Thinking, 'All matters to be done with the great Vinayadhara elders have been completed,' he dominated, oppressed, and looked down upon the Dhammavādī monk even more than before, speaking to him with great cruelty and harshness.

The Dhammavādī monk thought, 'This Adhammavādī monk is truly devoid of any sense of shame.' He immediately left the village monastery and approached the one thousand monks who were the followers of the great Vinayadhara elders. He said, 'Friends, should not a matter that has come before the Saṅgha be decided according to the law? Or, without bringing the matter before the Saṅgha, should not the accusing monk and the accused monk be made to confess their faults to each other and be reconciled? Now, however, these great Vinayadhara elders neither decide the matter nor bring about reconciliation. Why is it that they neither decide nor reconcile?'
437:
He reported and complained. The one thousand disciple monks also heard the words spoken by the Dhammavādī monk, but thinking, "The two great Vinaya-expert elders must have known some special reason," they remained silent without saying anything in return.

Then, the Adhammavādī monk took the opportunity and oppressed the Dhammavādī monk, saying, "Friend, you previously said, 'The Vinaya-expert elders will know.' Well, now go ahead and report that matter to the Vinaya-expert elders!" He then spoke harshly, saying, "From today onwards, you have suffered a great defeat. Do not ever return to our forest village monastery," and then he departed.

After that, the Dhammavādī monk approached the great Vinaya-expert elders and lamented with a loud voice, "Venerable sirs, you have no regard for the Sāsana of the Buddha; you only have regard for the person, thinking, 'This Adhammavādī monk serves us and pleases us.' (You look at the face of the person instead of the face of the Sāsana). You do not protect the Sāsana, but only protect the shameless (alajji) and immoral (dussīla) person. From today onwards, you should no longer deliver Vinaya judgments. It is only today that the Blessed One Kassapa has truly attained Parinibbāna!" He wept, saying, "The Sāsana of the Blessed One Kassapa has met with a miserable destruction!" and then he departed from the presence of those Vinaya-experts.

At that time, the two great Vinaya-expert elders felt a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and alarm, thinking, "While protecting only the shameless and immoral
438:
person, we have cast the great treasure of the Sāsana into a deep abyss." They were filled with remorse (kukkucca) and anxiety. Because their hearts were oppressed by the blow of that remorse, when they passed away, they were unable to be reborn in the higher celestial realms. Instead, one of the two elders became a Yakkha king named Hemavata on the mountain named Hemavata in the Himalayan forest. The other became a Yakkha king named Sātāgiri on the mountain named Sāta in the Majjhimadesa. The one thousand monks who were the followers of those two great elders, having followed only the example of those two elders, were also unable to be reborn in the higher celestial realms and became attendant Yakkhas, five hundred each, in the presence of those two great Yakkha kings. However, the lay donors of the four requisites for those Vinaya-expert elders were reborn in the higher celestial realms.

These two, Hemavata Yakkha king and Sātāgiri Yakkha king, were among the twenty-eight Yakkha generals and were great Yakkha kings of immense power and majesty. Eight times every month, it was the custom for an assembly of devas to be held at the pavilion named Nāgavatī (according to the Sri Lankan version, on the mountain named Bhagalavatī) on the Manosila plateau in the Himalayan forest to settle matters of justice. In that assembly, it was the custom for Hemavata Yakkha king and Sātāgiri Yakkha king to participate.

At that time, Sātāgiri Yakkha king and Hemavata Yakkha king met each other at that great assembly of devas and,
439:
remembering the events from the human world, they asked and answered each other about their respective places of rebirth, saying, "Friend, where were you reborn? And friend, where were you reborn?" They then said, "Friend, we have suffered a great ruin. Although we formerly strove in the practice of a monk for twenty thousand years during the Sāsana of the Blessed One Kassapa, because we relied on a single shameless and immoral evil friend (pāpamitta), we have been reborn in the race of Yakkhas. Our lay donors of the four requisites, however, have been reborn in the higher celestial realms of the sensuous sphere (kāmāvacara)." Saying this, they became intensely distressed.

## Making a Pact

Thereafter, Sātāgiri Yakkha king said, "Friend Hemavata, your abode, the Himalayan forest, is known as a forest of wonderful and extraordinary things. Therefore, if you see or hear any wonderful or extraordinary event, please come and tell me." Hemavata Yakkha king also said, "Friend Sātāgiri, your abode, the Majjhimadesa, is the place where noble persons arise and reside, and is thus known as an extraordinary region. Therefore, if you see or hear any wonderful or extraordinary event, please come and tell me." In this way, the two friends, Sātāgiri Yakkha king and Hemavata Yakkha king, made a pact and a promise to each other. Unable to abandon that state of being Yakkhas, they lived in association with each other while a single incalculable aeon (asaṅkheyya-kappa) of the interval between Buddhas (buddhantara) passed away.
440:
During this period, the great earth rose upwards by one yojana and three gāvutas.

At that time, our Bodhisatta, from the time he made the aspiration for Buddhahood and received the definite prophecy (niyata-byādisa) at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara until his life as King Vessantara, fulfilled and perfected the ten perfections (pāramīs) for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand world-cycles. After being reborn in the Tusita heaven and remaining there for the full lifespan of a deva, as previously mentioned, the devas from the ten thousand world-systems came and requested him to become a Buddha. He then made the five great investigations, gave his word to the assembly of devas and Brahmas that he would become a Buddha, and while the thirty-two great omens appeared clearly, causing the ten thousand world-systems to tremble, he took conception in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā in this human world.

When these two friends, Sātāgiri Yakkha king and Hemavata Yakkha king, saw the thirty-two great omens that appeared when the Bodhisatta took conception, they did not consider, reflect, or know that "these great omens have appeared because the Bodhisatta has taken conception." When the Bodhisatta was born, when he renounced the world, and when he attained Buddhahood, the thirty-two great omens appeared clearly. Even though they saw those great omens, the two Yakkha kings, as before, did not consider, reflect, or know that "these great omens have appeared because of these reasons."
441:
When the Blessed One called the five monks of the group of five (pañcavaggiya) and preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which has three phases and twelve modes, only Sātāgiri Yakkha king among the two was the first to see the great earthquake and the thirty-two wonderful and extraordinary omens that appeared. Knowing that the cause of those thirty-two great omens was the Blessed One currently preaching the Dhammacakka sermon, he approached the presence of the Blessed One together with his retinue of five hundred Yakkhas. However, although he listened to the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, he was unable to attain any special Dhamma of the Path or Fruit (magga-phala).

The reason was that while Sātāgiri Yakkha king was listening to the Dhammacakka sermon, he remembered his friend Hemavata Yakkha king and thought, "Has my friend Hemavata come to this great assembly of Dhamma or not?" While looking at the audience, he did not see his friend Hemavata and thought, "How slow my friend Hemavata is! He is missing the Blessed One's Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which is so profound in meaning and beautiful in phrasing." Because of this distraction of mind, he was unable to attain the special Dhamma of the Path or Fruit.

Even though the sun had set, the Blessed One had not yet finished preaching the Dhammacakka sermon. At that time, Sātāgiri Yakkha king thought, "I will go and fetch my friend Hemavata, and then I will come back with him to listen to the Dhamma sermon." He then created vehicles such as elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and garuḍa-vehicles, and with his five hundred Yakkhas,
442:
he traveled through the sky towards the Himalayas.

## The Two Deva Kings Meeting in the Sky

When the thirty-two great omens appeared at the time of the Bodhisatta's conception, birth, renunciation, enlightenment, and Parinibbāna, they did not last long but disappeared and ceased within a moment. However, when the Blessed One preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, those thirty-two great omens were wonderful and extraordinary, and they did not disappear in an instant but remained for a considerable time before ceasing. Thus, Hemavata Yakkha king also saw those thirty-two great omens appearing wonderfully and extraordinarily in the Himalayan forest. He thought, "Since the time I was born in this forest, this great mountain has never been so full of wonderful, extraordinary, and delightful things as it is now. Well then, right now (according to our pact), I will go and fetch my friend Sātāgiri, and together with him, I will come and enjoy the glory and bliss of these marvelous Himalayan forest flowers." Having so planned, just like Sātāgiri Yakkha king, he created vehicles such as elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and garuḍa-vehicles, and with his five hundred Yakkhas, he traveled through the sky towards the Majjhimadesa.

At that time, the two great Yakkha kings met face to face in the sky above the city of Rājagaha and...
443:
443
When they inquired about the reason for their meeting, the deity Hemavata said, "Friend Sātāgira, since the time I became a deity in the Himavanta forest, this great Himavanta mountain has never been so delightful with trees blooming out of season like this. Therefore, I thought that I would enjoy the glory and splendor of these wonderful Himavanta forest flowers together with you, and thus I have come to call for you."

When Sātāgira asked Hemavata, "Friend Hemavata, do you know the reason for this extraordinary blooming of flowers out of season?", Hemavata replied, "I do not know, friend Sātāgira."

Then Sātāgira said to Hemavata, "Friend Hemavata, this wonderful and extraordinary phenomenon has not occurred in the Himavanta forest alone; indeed, it has occurred equally throughout the ten thousand world systems. Friend Hemavata, the Exalted Buddha has appeared in the three worlds. That Buddha is currently preaching the Dhammacakka sermon in the great Migadāya forest called Isipatana near the city of Vārāṇasī. Because the Buddha is preaching the Dhammacakka sermon, thirty-two great and extraordinary omens, never seen before, have appeared throughout the entire world."

In this way, Sātāgira informed his friend Hemavata that the Buddha had appeared.
444:
444
Having spoken thus, wishing to take his friend Hemavata to the presence of the Buddha, he said:

Ajja pannaraso uposatho,
dibbā ratti upaṭṭhitā,
anomanāmaṃ satthāraṃ,
handa passāma gotamaṃ.

(Friend Hemavata,) Today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth day, the full moon. Tonight is a most delightful night, as if the entire island of Jambudīpa were beautifully adorned, lit by the radiance of the bodies, garments, ornaments, and mansions of the devas and brahmās (who have come from the ten thousand world systems to hear the Dhamma on the day the Buddha preaches the Dhammacakka), as well as by the light of the moon, stars, and constellations, and the bodily radiance of the Buddha, the deity of purity. (Friend Hemavata,) Do not remain in doubt, wondering whether he is truly the Buddha or not. Come! Let us go now to pay homage to the Buddha of the Gotama lineage, who has attained extraordinary titles such as Buddha and Bhagavā through undiminished virtues and has become the supreme Teacher of humans, devas, and brahmās.

Thus he spoke to the deity Hemavata.

At that time, Hemavata, hearing the words of Sātāgira, thought: "This Sātāgira speaks boldly, saying 'Anomanāmaṃ satthāraṃ' and so on, that the person he saw is indeed the Omniscient Buddha. In this world,
445:
445
Omniscient Buddhas are rare and difficult to find. Persons like Pūraṇa Kassapa and others merely claim to be Omniscient Buddhas, and being associated with wrong knowledge, they greatly oppress and destroy many people. If the ascetic Gotama whom Sātāgira saw is indeed the Omniscient Buddha, he must certainly be endowed with the Tādi quality (the quality of being unshakable by the eight worldly conditions). Therefore, I will first investigate whether he is endowed with the Tādi quality, which can only be possessed by Buddhas."

Thinking thus and wishing to ask about the characteristics of Tādi, he recited this verse of inquiry:

Kacci mano supaṇihito,
sabbabhūtesu tādino.
Kacci iṭṭhe aniṭṭhe ca,
saṅkappassa vasīkatā.

(Friend Sātāgira,) How is it? Is the mind of the Buddha you saw well-directed, as befits one endowed with the Tādi quality, remaining naturally steadfast without any love or hatred toward all beings? How is it? Has the Buddha Gotama you saw practiced so as to overcome and be free from sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka), thoughts of ill will (byāpāda-vitakka), and thoughts of cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka) that tend to arise through love and hatred toward pleasant and unpleasant objects?

At that time, Sātāgira, having already firmly decided that the Buddha was indeed the Omniscient Buddha, wished to confirm and answer regarding all the virtues of the Omniscient Buddha that Hemavata had inquired about:
446:
446
Mano cassa supaṇihito,
sabbabhūtesu tādino.
Atho iṭṭhe aniṭṭhe ca,
saṅkappassa vasīkatā.

(Friend Hemavata,) The mind of the Buddha I saw is well-directed, as befits one endowed with the Tādi quality, remaining naturally steadfast without any love or hatred toward all beings. (Not to mention his being endowed with the Tādi quality now that he is a Buddha, even while fulfilling the Perfections to become a Buddha, in his birth as the Chaddanta elephant king, he bore no grudge against the hunter Sonuttara who attempted to kill him, but instead cut off and offered his own tusks. In his birth as the monkey king, he bore no anger toward the enemy brahmin who struck his head with a stone to kill him, but instead showed him the way. In his birth as the wise Vidhura, he bore no anger toward the Yakkha Puṇṇaka who cruelly threw him head-first into the abyss below the sixty-league-high Kāḷa mountain while holding his feet, but instead preached the Dhamma to him. Therefore, Sātāgira answered boldly with "Mano cassa supaṇihito" and so on.) Friend Hemavata, the Buddha I saw has practiced so as to overcome and be free from sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty that tend to arise through love and hatred toward pleasant and unpleasant objects.

Thus he recited this verse in reply.
447:
447
In this way, Hemavata first inquired whether the Buddha was endowed with the Tādi quality in relation to the mind-door, and having heard Sātāgira's confirmation, he now wished to inquire about purity in relation to the three doors (body, speech, and mind) to be more certain. (Alternatively) Having first inquired briefly about the Tādi quality in relation to the three doors and heard the confirmation, he now wished to inquire in detail to be more certain:

Kacci adinnaṃ nādiyati,
kacci pāṇesu saññato.
Kacci ārā pamādamhā,
kacci jhānaṃ na riñcati.

(Friend Sātāgira,) How is it? Is the Buddha you saw free from taking the property of others that is not given by body or speech? How is it? Is he well-restrained and abstinent from the misconduct of killing and harming living beings? How is it? Is he far and free from heedlessness (pamāda), which is the delight and attachment to the five strands of sensual pleasure (referring to misconduct in sensual pleasures and unchaste conduct)? How is it? Is he one who does not neglect the meditative attainments (jhāna), having abandoned the five hindrances?

Thus he recited this verse of inquiry again.
448:
448
At that time, Sātāgira (knowing that the Buddha did not only abstain from taking what is not given and so on now that he is a Buddha, but had also abstained from them for a long time in the past, and by the power of the merit of such abstinence (virati), he attained the various marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa Lakkhaṇa), and the whole world speaks of the Buddha's virtues saying, "The ascetic Gotama abstains from the misconduct of taking what is not given," and so on) wished to answer with pure and bold words:

Na so adinnaṃ ādiyati,
atho pāṇesu saññato.
Atho ārā pamādamhā,
buddho jhānaṃ na riñcati.

(Friend Hemavata,) The Buddha I saw is indeed free from taking the property of others that is not given by body or speech. He is well-restrained and abstinent from the misconduct of killing and harming living beings. He is far and free from heedlessness, which is the delight and attachment to the five strands of sensual pleasure. He is also one who does not neglect the meditative attainments, having abandoned the five hindrances.

Thus he recited this verse in reply.

After hearing the answer regarding purity in the door of the body, Hemavata now wished to inquire about purity in the door of speech:
449:
449
Kacci musā na bhaṇati,
kacci na khīṇabyappatho.
Kacci vebhūtiyaṃ nāha,
kacci samphaṃ na bhāsati.

Friend Sātāgira, how is it? Is the Buddha you saw one who does not speak lies? How is it? Is he one who does not speak harsh and wicked words (pharusavācā) that oppress and defile the minds of beings? How is it? Is he one who does not speak slanderous words (pisuṇavācā) that destroy the love between two people? Does he not speak frivolous talk (samphappalāpa) which is useless and without essence, like empty or hollow grain?

Thus he recited this verse of inquiry.

At that time, Sātāgira (knowing that the Buddha did not only abstain from verbal misconduct now that he is a Buddha, but had also abstained from lies and so on for a long time in the past, and by the power of the merit of such abstinence, he attained the marks of a Great Man such as having only one hair growing from each pore and the appearance of the Unṇā hair-tuft, and the whole world speaks of the Buddha's virtues saying, "The ascetic Gotama abstains from the misconduct of lying," and so on) wished to answer with pure and bold words:
450:
450
Musā ca so na bhaṇati,
atho na khīṇabyappatho.
Atho vebhūtiyaṃ nāha,
mantā atthaṃ subhāsati.

Friend Hemavata, the Buddha I saw is indeed one who does not speak lies. He is indeed one who does not speak harsh and wicked words. He is indeed one who does not speak slanderous words. He speaks only words that are beneficial and distinguished by wisdom.

Thus he recited this verse in reply.

After hearing the answer regarding purity in the door of speech, Hemavata now wished to inquire about purity in the door of the mind, and whether he has transcended delusion and is endowed with the five kinds of vision (cakkhu):

Kacci narajjati kāmesu,
kacci cittaṃ anāvilaṃ.
Kacci mohaṃ atikkanto,
kacci dhammesu cakkhumā.

Friend Sātāgira, how is it? Is the Buddha you saw indeed free from covetousness (abhijjhā), which is the attachment to sensual objects? How is it? Is the Buddha you saw free from the disturbance of ill will and anger (byāpāda-dosa)? How is it? Is the Buddha you saw [free from] the root cause of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi)...
451:
“Has he overcome and transcended the four delusions? Is he truly one who possesses the eye of wisdom, perceiving all things without any obstruction or hindrance?”

He recited this verse to inquire. (In this verse, he inquired with the thought, “One is not yet a Buddha merely by the purity of the three doors; only one endowed with Omniscience (or the five eyes) can truly be a Buddha,” thus asking, “Kacci dhammesu cakkhumā = Is he truly one who possesses the eye of wisdom that perceives all things?”)

Then, the Yakkha King Sātāgira (reflecting that: since the Blessed One had already abandoned the defilements of sensual lust and ill-will at the moment of the Path of Non-Returning (Anāgāmi-magga) before reaching the Fruit of Arahatship, he was free from attachment to sensual objects; he also possessed a mind free from the disturbance and turbidity of ill-will (byāpāda); since he had already abandoned the delusion that veils the Four Noble Truths (saccapaṭicchādaka-moha), which is the cause of wrong view, at the moment of the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga), he was one who had transcended delusion; and since he had realized the Four Noble Truths through his own self-enlightened knowledge (svayambhū-ñāṇa) without a teacher, he had already attained the title of Buddha and the eyes of wisdom; therefore), wishing to proclaim boldly that the Blessed One possessed purity in the door of the mind and had truly become a Buddha by attaining the golden knowledge of Omniscience, he replied:

Na so rajjati kāmesu,
atho cittaṃ anāvilaṃ.
Sabbamohaṃ atikkanto,
buddho dhammesu cakkhumā.
452:
“Friend Hemavata, the Blessed One whom I have seen is indeed one who has abandoned and is free from covetousness, which is the longing and attachment for sensual objects. The mind of the Blessed One whom I have seen is also free from the disturbance and turbidity of ill-will (byāpāda). The Blessed One whom I have seen is indeed one who has abandoned and transcended all four delusions, which are the fundamental causes of wrong view. Because he has realized all things through self-enlightened knowledge, he has attained the name ‘Buddha’ and is also endowed with the five eyes.”

He recited this verse in reply.

In this way, the Yakkha King Hemavata, having heard and being greatly delighted and joyful to learn of the Blessed One’s purity in the three doors and his true state as an Omniscient Buddha, and being one whose speech was unhindered and hit the mark due to the very pure wisdom gained from great learning (bāhusacca-maṅgala) during the dispensation of the past Kassapa Buddha, wished to continue listening to the extraordinary and marvelous qualities of the Blessed One:

Kacci vijjāya sampanno,
kacci saṃsuddhacaraṇo.
Kaccissa āsavā khīṇā,
kacci natthi punabbhavo.

“Friend Sātāgira, is the Blessed One whom you have seen truly endowed with the eye of knowledge (vijjā) that all Buddhas should possess?”
453:
“Is he truly one who possesses the fifteen kinds of pure conduct (caraṇa), which are like good feet for going to Nibbāna?
