Have the four taints (āsavas) in the continuum of the Blessed One whom you have seen been completely exhausted and ended? Is the Blessed One whom you have seen free from being born again in a new existence (rebirth)?”

He recited this verse to inquire.

Then, the Yakkha King Sātāgira, having a heart that was deeply convinced and settled in the fact that the Blessed One was truly an Omniscient Buddha, wished to confirm and answer that all the qualities Hemavata asked about were clearly and fully present in the Blessed One:

Vijjāya ceva sampanno,
atho saṃsuddhacaraṇo.
Sabbassa āsavā khīṇā,
natthi tassa punabbhavo.

“Friend Hemavata, the Blessed One whom I have seen is indeed endowed with the eye of knowledge (vijjā) that all Buddhas should possess. Furthermore, he is indeed one who possesses the fifteen kinds of pure conduct (caraṇa), which are like good feet for going to Nibbāna. All the taints (āsavas) in the continuum of the Blessed One whom I have seen have been completely exhausted and ended. For that Blessed One whom I have seen, being born again in a new existence (rebirth) is also no more.”

He recited this verse in reply.
454:
Then, the Yakkha King Hemavata, having become free from doubt regarding the Blessed One, thinking, “The Blessed One whom Sātāgira has now seen is indeed the Sammāsambuddha, the Supreme One of the three worlds,” and wishing to praise the Blessed One while standing in the sky, as well as to make Sātāgira rejoice:

Sampannaṃ munino cittaṃ,
kammunā vyappathena ca.
Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ,
dhammato naṃ pasaṃsasi.

“Friend Sātāgira, the mind of the Blessed One whom you have seen is indeed endowed with the quality of steadfastness (tādi-guṇa); he is also endowed with purity of bodily action, purity of verbal action, and purity of mental action. Friend Sātāgira, you indeed speak words of praise according to the truth for that Blessed One who is endowed with the three knowledges, the eight knowledges, and the fifteen kinds of conduct.”

He recited this verse, praising and causing great delight.

Then, the Yakkha King Sātāgira, with the intention of saying, “Friend Hemavata, what you have said is exactly as it is; you have understood the qualities of the Blessed One very well and have rejoiced well,” and wishing to make Hemavata rejoice in turn:
455:
Sampannaṃ munino cittaṃ,
kammunā vyappathena ca.
Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ,
dhammato anumodasi.

“Friend Hemavata, the mind of the Blessed One whom I have seen is indeed endowed with the quality of steadfastness (tādi-guṇa). He is also endowed with purity of bodily action, purity of verbal action, and purity of mental action. Friend Hemavata, you indeed appreciate and rejoice according to the truth in the Blessed One who is endowed with the three knowledges, the eight knowledges, and the fifteen kinds of conduct.”

Having said this, wishing to urge, inspire, and invite Hemavata to go to the Blessed One:

Sampannaṃ munino cittaṃ,
kammunā vyappathena ca.
Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ,
handa passāma gotamaṃ.

“Friend Hemavata, the mind of the Blessed One whom I have seen is indeed endowed with the quality of steadfastness (tādi-guṇa). He is also endowed with purity of bodily action, purity of verbal action, and purity of mental action. Let us go now to pay homage to the Blessed One of the Gotama lineage, who is endowed with the three knowledges, the eight knowledges, and the fifteen kinds of conduct.”

He recited this verse to invite him.

Then, the Yakkha King Hemavata, being one who possessed the power of wisdom and great learning brought from previous lives, wishing to accept the invitation to go and see the Buddha while praising the Blessed One with the qualities he cherished:
456:
Eṇījaṅghaṃ kisaṃ vīraṃ,
appāhāraṃ alolupaṃ.
Muniṃ vanasmiṃ jhāyantaṃ,
ehi passāma gotamaṃ.
Sīhaṃ vekacaraṃ nāgaṃ,
kāmesu anapekkhiṇaṃ.
Upasaṅkamma pucchāma,
maccupāsappamocanaṃ.

“Friend Sātāgira, come, let us go. Let us go and pay homage to the Lord Buddha of the Gotama lineage, who has legs as shapely and beautiful as those of an antelope (eṇī), who is endowed with the major and minor physical characteristics—five parts long, four parts short, three parts thin, six parts high, and well-rounded in the appropriate places—who possesses the heroic energy capable of repelling and destroying both internal and external enemies, who is accustomed to taking only enough food to sustain the body, who has abandoned the greed for food, who is endowed with the fourfold Path-knowledge, and who dwells practicing jhāna in the secluded forest.

Friend Sātāgira, like a maned lion, he is difficult for ordinary people to approach, able to endure the worldly conditions (lokadhamma), and free from fear. In a single world-system, he is like a Chaddanta elephant king,
457:
who is the only one to appear and is endowed with great physical and intellectual power, and who is free from desire and lust for all sensual objects. Let us approach the Blessed One and inquire about Nibbāna, the true escape from the suffering of the three realms of existence (tebhūmaka-vaṭṭa), which is the snare of death.”

Reciting these verses, he urged and invited Sātāgira along with their retinue of a thousand Yakkhas to go to the Buddha to pay homage and listen to the Dhamma.

## Kāḷī the Woman Attaining Stream-entry

That day was the day of the great full-moon festival of the month of Āsāḷha in the city of Rājagaha. At that time, like a celestial maiden enjoying grand divine luxury in the city of Tāvatiṃsa adorned with noble ornaments all around, a woman named Kāḷī, a resident of the town of Kuraraghara, had ascended to the upper story of her parents' mansion in Rājagaha. She was standing there to catch the gentle breeze, wishing to relieve the weariness of her pregnancy as she was about to give birth.

(Kāḷī was a woman of Rājagaha. When she reached maturity, she married into Kuraraghara. When she became pregnant with the future Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa, she thought, “I will give birth at my parents' home,” and returned to her parents' house in Rājagaha. While she was on the mansion balcony catching the breeze to relieve the exhaustion of her impending labor, she overheard the conversation about the Buddha’s qualities spoken by the two Yakkha kings.)
458:
The woman Kāḷī heard the Dhamma discourse concerning the qualities of the Buddha spoken by the two Yakkha generals in its entirety—the beginning, the middle, and the end. Thinking, “Indeed, the Buddhas are endowed with such marvelous and extraordinary qualities,” she developed a sense of joy (pīti) by focusing on the Buddha’s attributes. Through that joy, she removed the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and practiced Vipassanā meditation. While standing right there, she attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Among the women of the noble families, Kāḷī was the first to become a Stream-enterer and a noble female disciple (ariya-sāvikā), becoming like an eldest sister among the women. That very night, Kāḷī gave birth to the young boy (the future Venerable Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa). After staying at her parents' house as long as she wished, she returned to her own place in Kuraraghara.

Because she attained the Fruit of Stream-entry by merely hearing the news and gaining faith in the Buddha’s qualities without ever having seen the Blessed One before—like one who easily eats a meal prepared for another—the Blessed One, while later seated among the assembly of monks at the Jetavana Monastery and conferring titles of pre-eminence (Etadagga) upon the laywomen, declared:

“Monks, among my female lay disciples who have gained settled faith in the Three Jewels through hearing reports (anussava), the woman named Kāḷī, a resident of Kuraraghara, is the foremost, the most excellent.” Thus, he placed her in the position of Etadagga for being ‘one whose faith is based on hearing’ (anussava-pasāda).
459:
## The Arrival of the Two Celestial Generals Before the Buddha

The two celestial kings, Sātāgira and Hemavata, accompanied by their retinue of one thousand Yakkhas, went to the Isipatana Migadāya forest in the city of Vārāṇasī during the middle watch of that very night. They approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, who was still sitting in the same cross-legged posture he had assumed while teaching the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, and said:

*Akkhatāraṃ pavattāraṃ,*
*Sabbadhammāna pāraguṃ.*
*Buddhaṃ verabhayātītaṃ,*
*Mayaṃ pucchāma gotamaṃ.*

"We wish to ask the Lord Buddha of the Gotama lineage about matters we do not know or see—the Buddha who has taught the Noble Truths in both brief and detailed ways; who has reached the far shore of all phenomena through the six modes of higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), full understanding (*pariññā*), abandonment (*pahāna*), development (*bhāvanā*), realization (*sacchikiriya*), and attainment (*samāpatti*); who has awakened from the sleep of delusion; and who has transcended the five dangers and enmities such as killing."

With this verse, they praised the Blessed One and requested permission to ask questions. Having received permission, the celestial king Hemavata, who was superior in power and wisdom between the two, wished to ask the matter he had in mind:
460:
*Kismiṃ loko samuppanno,*
*Kismiṃ kubbati santhavaṃ.*
*Kissa loko upādāya,*
*Kismiṃ loko vihaññati.*

"Exalted Buddha, in what does the world of beings (*satta-loka*) and the world of formations (*saṅkhāra-loka*) arise? In what do all beings—humans, devas, and Brahmas—form intimacy through craving and views (*taṇhā-diṭṭhi*) as 'I' and 'mine'? Depending on what does the designation of 'world of beings' and 'world of formations' occur? In what (or because of what) are all beings—humans, devas, and Brahmas—distressed?"

Thus he questioned the Blessed One with this verse.

Then, the Blessed One, wishing to answer Hemavata's question by way of the six internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*)—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and the six external sense bases (*bāhirāyatana*)—form, sound, odor, flavor, touch, and mental objects—said:

*Chasu loko samuppanno,*
*Chasu kubbati santhavaṃ.*
*Channameva upādāya,*
*Chasu loko vihaññati.*

"Hemavata, when the six internal sense bases and the six external sense bases exist and arise, the world of beings and the world of formations
461:
manifest and arise. (The world of beings, consisting of humans, devas, and Brahmas, is in ultimate reality nothing but the six internal sense bases—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and the six external sense bases—the collection of form, sound, odor, flavor, touch, and mental objects. Apart from these twelve sense bases, there are no 'humans, devas, or Brahmas.' The world of formations, such as fields, lands, gold, silver, and crops, is also in ultimate reality only the six external sense bases. Apart from these six external sense bases, there is no 'world of formations' consisting of inanimate things. Therefore, the Blessed One answered: '*Chasu loko samuppanno*' = 'When the six internal sense bases and the six external sense bases exist and arise, the world of beings and the world of formations manifest and arise.')

Hemavata, all beings—humans, devas, and Brahmas—form intimacy in this collection of the six internal sense bases and six external sense bases as 'I' and 'mine' through craving and views. (All the things that beings perceive as 'I', 'another', 'man', 'woman', 'field', or 'land', and which they cling to and form intimacy with through craving and views as 'I' and 'mine', are in ultimate reality only the aforementioned collection of the six internal and six external sense bases. Indeed, beings perceive the eye as 'I' and 'mine' and form intimacy with it through craving and views; they also perceive the ear
462:
as 'I' and 'mine' and form intimacy with it through craving and views. They do the same with the nose, tongue, body, mind, form, sound, odor, flavor, touch (such as coarse, fine, hot, or cold), and mental objects known by the mind, perceiving them as 'I' and 'mine' and forming intimacy through craving and views. Therefore, the Blessed One answered: '*Chasu kubbati santhavaṃ*' = 'All beings—humans, devas, and Brahmas—form intimacy in this collection of the six internal and six external sense bases as "I" and "mine" through craving and views.')

Hemavata, it is depending on these very six internal sense bases and six external sense bases that the designations 'world of beings' and 'world of formations' arise. (It is clear that based on the twelve sense bases mentioned, the conventional terms for the world of beings—humans, devas, Brahmas—and the world of formations—fields, lands, rice, water, crops—manifest.)

Hemavata, when these six internal sense bases and six external sense bases exist (or because of these things), all beings—humans, devas, and Brahmas—are distressed. (According to the *Ādittapariyāya* teaching, the twelve sense bases are constantly burning with the eleven fires, such as the fire of passion, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion. The world of beings, consisting of humans, devas, and Brahmas, is
463:
in ultimate reality only the twelve sense bases (six internal and six external). These sense bases are always burning with the eleven fires respectively. Because sense bases exist, one is burned by the fires; because one is burned by the fires, one suffers distress. If there were no sense bases, there would be no fuel, and thus no fire could burn; if no fire burns, there can be no distress. Therefore, the Blessed One answered: '*Chasu loko vihaññati*' = 'When these six internal sense bases and six external sense bases exist (or because of these things), all beings—humans, devas, and Brahmas—are distressed.')

The section on the questions and answers regarding the Round (*Vaṭṭa*) ends here.

At that time, Hemavata was unable to clearly distinguish the Blessed One's brief explanation (starting with '*Chasu loko samuppanno*') regarding the twelve sense bases in relation to suffering. Wishing to know the specific nature of those sense bases and their opposite, and desiring to ask briefly about both the Round of Suffering (*Vaṭṭa*) and the Cessation of the Round (*Vivaṭṭa*), he asked:

*Katamaṃ taṃ upādānaṃ,*
*Yattha loko vihaññati.*
*Niyyānaṃ pucchito brūhi,*
*Kathaṃ dukkhā pamuccati.*
464:
"Exalted Buddha, (according to your answer '*Chasu loko vihaññati*') what are those six things that, when they exist, cause all beings—humans, devas, and Brahmas—to be distressed? What are those six things that are clung to, which cause beings to be distressed? (With this statement, he asks about the Truth of Suffering (*Dukkha-sacca*); by asking directly about the Truth of Suffering, the Truth of the Origin (*Samudaya-sacca*) is also asked, as it is the cause of that suffering.)

What is the way out (*niyyāna*) from the Round of Rebirth? By what means (what extraordinary Dhamma) is one released from the suffering of the Round? O Lord Buddha, having been asked about the way out from the Round of Rebirth, please answer us. (With the latter half of this verse, he directly asks about the Truth of the Path (*Magga-sacca*); by asking directly about the Truth of the Path, the Truth of Cessation (*Nirodha-sacca* or Nibbāna) is also asked, as it is the object of that Path, like 'pulling a vine brings the whole cluster.')"

When Hemavata thus asked the question concerning the Four Noble Truths—explicitly mentioning the Truth of Suffering and the Truth of the Path, and implicitly mentioning the Truth of the Origin and the Truth of Cessation—the Blessed One, wishing to answer in the same manner as Hemavata had asked, taught this verse:
465:
*Pañca kāmaguṇā loke,*
*Manochatṭhā paveditā.*
*Ettha chandaṃ virājetvā,*
*Evaṃ dukkhā pamuccati.*

The meaning is:

"Friend Hemavata, I have clearly taught the five strands of sensual pleasure in the world—form, sound, odor, flavor, and touch—with the mind as the sixth. (In the first half of this verse, by the word 'mind', the mind-base (*manāyatana*) is directly taught. By directly teaching the mind-base, the base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*) is also taught, as it is the object of that mind. By the five strands of sensual pleasure—form, sound, odor, flavor, and touch—the five bases of form (*rūpāyatana*), sound (*saddāyatana*), odor (*gandhāyatana*), flavor (*rasāyatana*), and touch (*phoṭṭhabbāyatana*) are directly taught. By teaching these five, the five sense bases that perceive these objects—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—are also taught and included. Thus, with the first half of this verse, the Blessed One answered regarding the twelve sense bases (six internal and six external), which are the things to be clung to (*upādāna*) or the phenomena of the Round (*vaṭṭa-dhamma*) that cause the world's distress.)

Friend Hemavata, in this collection of the twelve sense bases, which are the Truth of Suffering and the phenomena of the Round,
466:
one must entirely abandon and destroy sensual desire (*chanda-rāga*) (by defining them as aggregates, sense bases, elements, or simply mind-and-matter, and then practicing insight (*vipassanā*) by applying the three characteristics, culminating in the Path of Arahatship). By abandoning and destroying it in this way, one is released from the suffering of the Round. (With the latter half of this verse, the Blessed One answered the question about the Cessation of the Round (*Vivaṭṭa*) and also showed the Truth of the Path (*Magga-sacca*). The Truth of the Origin (*Samudaya-sacca*) and the Truth of Cessation (*Nirodha-sacca*) are already included as they were in the previous question. Alternatively, the first half of this answer-verse shows the Truth of Suffering. In the latter half, the word 'desire' (*chanda*) shows the Truth of the Origin. In the word '*virājetvā*' (having abandoned/destroyed), the term '*virāga*' shows the Truth of Cessation, which is Nibbāna, the fading away and cessation of craving. By the phrase 'in this way', the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path, which is the way out of the Round of Rebirth, is expressed, thus showing the Truth of the Path. In this way, the Blessed One taught the Four Noble Truths in this answer-verse.)

Having thus shown the excellent way out (*niyyāna*)—the Eightfold Noble Path—through this answer-verse which fully contains the Four Noble Truths within its meaning, the Blessed One wished to firmly state that very way out in the natural sequence of language (*sabhāva-nirutti*) and bring the discourse to a conclusion:
467:
He then preached this verse:

“This is the way out of the world,
Declared to you exactly as it is.
This I declare to you,
Thus one is released from suffering.”

The meaning is: “O Hemavata, I have preached to you this Niyyāna-dhamma, the Noble Eightfold Path, which is the means of escape from the triple realm of conditioned existence—the sensual realm, the fine-material realm, and the immaterial realm—exactly as it is. Only through this Noble Eightfold Path can one be liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirths (Saṃsāra); there is no other way to liberation. (Therefore, even if you were to ask a thousand times,) I will only preach this Noble Eightfold Path to you as the excellent Niyyāna-dhamma for escaping the round of rebirths. (This means I will not preach any other way.)”

(Alternatively) “Since one can only be liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirths through this Noble Eightfold Path and there is no other way, I will preach only this Noble Eightfold Path as the excellent Niyyāna-dhamma for you, who have already attained the lower Paths and Fruits, so that you may reach the higher Paths and Fruits. (This means I will not preach any other way.)”
468:
## The Deities and Spirits Attain Stream-entry

In this way, the Blessed One concluded the Dhamma teaching, crowning it with the Fruit of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, the deity Sātāgira and the deity Hemavata, along with their retinue of one thousand spirits (yakkhas), were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). (They became Sotāpanna Ariyas.)

The section on the questions and answers regarding the Round and the Ending of the Round is finished.

At that time, the deity Hemavata, who was naturally respectful of the Dhamma and was now established as a Sotāpanna Ariya, could not be satisfied enough with hearing the Blessed One’s Dhamma teaching, which was rich in profound meaning and phrasing. Desiring to ask the Blessed One about the stage of the Learner (Sekkhabhūmi) and the stage of the Non-learner (Asekkhabhūmi), he recited this verse:

“Who here crosses the flood?
Who here crosses the ocean?
In the deep without footing or support,
Who does not sink?”

The meaning is: “O Blessed One, what kind of person endowed with what practice and virtue can cross the fourfold flood in this world? What kind of person endowed with what practice and virtue can cross the vast and deep ocean of Saṃsāra in this world?”
469:
“Who is the one who does not sink and remains safely in the very deep ocean of Saṃsāra, where there is no footing below and no support to cling to above?” (In this verse, the first half asks about the stage of the Learner, and the second half asks about the stage of the Non-learner.)

Then, the Blessed One, wishing to answer regarding the stage of the Learner (Sekkhabhūmi) asked in the first half of the verse, spoke this verse:

“Always possessed of virtue,
Wise and well-concentrated,
Reflecting within and mindful,
One crosses the flood so difficult to cross.”

The meaning is: “O Hemavata, that monk who is always possessed of virtue (Sīla) (protecting and guarding the precepts without transgression even at the cost of life); who is possessed of mundane and supramundane wisdom (Paññā); who is well-concentrated, being possessed of access concentration and absorption concentration (Samādhi); and who repeatedly contemplates his own mind and body (Niyakajjhatta) with insight-knowledge (Vipassanā-ñāṇa) by applying the three characteristics—such a monk, possessed of the mindfulness (Sati) to constantly practice these three trainings (Sīla, Samādhi, Paññā), is able to cross the fourfold flood which is difficult for ordinary people to cross.”
470:
Having thus answered regarding the stage of the Learner, the Blessed One, now wishing to answer regarding the stage of the Non-learner (Asekkhabhūmi), spoke this verse:

“Detached from the perception of sensual pleasure,
Having transcended all fetters,
With delight in existence exhausted,
He does not sink in the deep.”

The meaning is: “O Hemavata, that person who has completely abstained from all perceptions associated with craving and attachment to sensual objects; who has broken and transcended the ten fetters (Saṃyojana) with the four Paths; and who has entirely exhausted the three types of craving (Nandī) and the three types of existence (Bhava)—such an Arahant, endowed with these qualities, does not sink in the vast and deep ocean of Saṃsāra, where there is no footing below and no support to cling to above. (Because craving is exhausted, he reaches the safety of Nibbāna with residue; and because existence is exhausted, he reaches the safety of Nibbāna without residue, arriving at the state of greatest peace and bliss.)”

The section on the questions and answers regarding the stage of the Learner and the Non-learner is finished.
471:
## The Spirits Depart Reciting Verses of Praise

Then, the deity Hemavata looked at his friend Sātāgira and the retinue of one thousand spirits. Feeling delighted, satisfied, and joyful, he praised the Blessed One with the following five verses. Then, together with his friend Sātāgira and the retinue of one thousand spirits, he paid respectful homage and returned to his own abode. The five verses of praise are as follows:

(1) “Behold the Great Seer, of profound wisdom,
Who sees the subtle meaning, who possesses nothing,
Who is unattached to the realm of sensual existence,
Liberated in every way, walking the divine path.”

(O friends, O deities!) He is of profound wisdom (Gambhīrapañña), possessing the wisdom that can analyze and understand deep phenomena such as the aggregates. He sees the subtle meaning (Nipuṇatthadassi), seeing clearly and truly the meaning of questions posed by subtle wise men. He possesses nothing (Akiñcana), having not even a trace of the seven kinds of defilements such as lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, misconduct, and impurities. He is unattached (Asatta) to the two types of sensuality and the three types of existence. He is completely liberated (Vippamutta) from the bonds of desire and lust in all objects such as the aggregates and sense bases. He is one who repeatedly enters and walks (Kamamāna) the divine path (Dibba-patha) of the eight attainments. He is the Great Seer (Mahesi) who has sought and practiced the special qualities of virtue, etc. Behold (Passatha) that Blessed One of the Gotama lineage clearly with your own eyes.
472:
(2) “Behold the one of noble name, who sees the subtle meaning,
Who bestows wisdom, who is unattached to the lair of sensuality,
Behold the All-knower, the wise one,
Walking the Noble path, the Great Seer.”

(O friends, O deities!) He has a noble name (Anomanāma), possessing great names such as ‘Sammāsambuddha’ praised for undiminished qualities. He sees the subtle meaning (Nipuṇatthadassi), seeing clearly and truly the meaning of questions posed by subtle wise men. He bestows wisdom (Paññādada), distributing special wisdom by teaching the good practice that leads to wisdom in a gentle and pleasant manner. He is unattached (Asatta) to the various sensual objects which are the lair of attachment for craving and wrong view. He is the All-knower (Sabbavidū), having understood all phenomena distinctly. He is the wise one (Sumedha), possessing the wisdom of the perfections which is the foundation of Omniscience. He is one who enters and walks (Kamamāna) the Noble path (Ariya-patha) known as the attainment of the Fruit (Phala-samāpatti) whenever he has time. He is the Great Seer (Mahesi) who has sought and practiced the special qualities of virtue, etc. Behold (Passatha) that Blessed One of the Gotama lineage clearly with your own eyes.
473:
(3) “Truly, it is a sight well seen by us today,
A beautiful dawn, a beautiful rising,
For we have seen the Fully Enlightened One,
Who has crossed the flood and is free from taints.”

(O friends, O deities! We) have seen the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) who has crossed the fourfold flood and whose four taints (Āsava) are exhausted. Because (Yaṃ) we have seen him clearly so as to attain the Paths and Fruits by good fortune, therefore (Tasmā), our seeing (Diṭṭha) with our eyes today is a truly good seeing, having gained the opportunity of the ‘unsurpassed seeing’ (Dassanānuttariya). Our reaching the time of dawn (Pabhāta) is a truly beautiful dawn, being free from all faults. Our rising (Uṭṭhita) from the sleep of the life-continuum is a truly good rising, being free from greed, hatred, and delusion.

(4) “These ten hundred spirits,
Powerful and famous,
All go to you for refuge;
You are our unsurpassed Teacher.”

O Blessed One, whose glory shines like the sun! All these spirits (Yakkhas), numbering ten hundreds (one thousand), who are endowed with the power of karma-born psychic success (Kammajiddhi) and have great gains and retinues, go to You for refuge, being imbued with the Great Supramundane Refuge. You are our unsurpassed Teacher (Satthā), the supreme master who can guide and help us to build the great palace of the first Ariya stage.
474:
(5) “We shall wander from village to village,
From mountain to mountain,
Paying homage to the Fully Enlightened One,
And the excellence of the Dhamma.”

O Blessed One, whose glory shines like the sun! We (from this day forward) shall wander, paying homage to the true state of the Buddha, who is endowed with the vast and abundant qualities of the Lord of the Three Worlds, and to the excellence of the Dhamma, the ten-fold teaching of the Paths, Fruits, Nibbāna, and the Scriptures, which is the excellent teaching for escaping the round of rebirths.

(Our Lord, the Head of the Three Worlds, is truly the glorious Buddha who possesses the peak of Omniscient Knowledge. The Noble Conqueror, the Incomparable One, has the quality of goodness in the beginning, middle, and end of the ten-fold Dhamma...)
475:
...fully and clearly taught. The eight noble Saṅgha also, who are praised for the three trainings, practiced the complete and detailed methods with a joyful heart.)—
Thus, praising the various and wonderful qualities of the Three Jewels repeatedly, with hands joined in reverence above the head, and being filled with joy and devotion as those seeking Nibbāna: 'From one village of devas to another, from one mountain of devas to another, we shall wander and proclaim, O Blessed One.' (This Hemavata Sutta is found in the Sutta Nipāta, 1-Uragavagga.)
Here ends the account of the Deva King Sātāgira and the Deva King Hemavata (Hemavata Sutta).
**********
## Chapter 11
## Teaching the Practice of Sagehood
## (From the Nalaka Sutta)
(Whenever a Buddha arises, it is a natural law that a monk who practices the Moneyya-paṭipadā [Practice of Sagehood] also appears. When our incomparable Lord of the Three Worlds, the Buddha, appeared, the monk who inquired about and practiced that Moneyya-paṭipadā was the monk Nalaka [the nephew of the great hermit Kāladevila], mentioned previously on pages 63 and 64. It was already stated on those pages that the youth Nalaka had gone forth as a monk even before the Buddha's enlightenment.)
476:
The Blessed One (as previously mentioned) taught the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, leading eighteen crores of Brahmas and the Venerable Koṇḍañña to the realization of the Dhamma. On the 5th day after that full moon, He taught the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta to the five monks of the group of five (Pañcavaggiya), leading them to the fruit of Arahatship. When the 7th day after the full moon arrived, the deities who were among the audience of the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta and who wished for the welfare of the Venerable Nalaka, informed him: 'Venerable Nalaka, the Blessed One has already taught the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, in the Isipatana Deer Park near Bārāṇasī. The Buddha, the Noble One among the three types of beings, has clearly appeared.' Thus, they informed the Venerable Nalaka that the Buddha had appeared and that the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta had been taught.
The Venerable Nalaka had become a hermit-monk thirty-five years ago. Thinking, 'If I dive into water frequently, my ears will be impaired; if my ears are impaired, I will not hear the Dhamma and will suffer loss from the teaching,' he abandoned the traditional practice of his relatives, which was frequent diving, and waited for the time the Buddha would appear. Upon hearing the news from the deities, he rejoiced, thinking, 'The time that my uncle, the hermit Kāladevila, told me about has truly arrived.' Joyfully, on the 7th day after the full moon of Āsāḷha, he left the Himālaya and went to the Isipatana Deer Park. The Blessed One, anticipating his arrival and intending to teach him the Moneyya-paṭipadā, was waiting for him.
477:
Seeing the Blessed One sitting in the cross-legged posture on the noble Buddha-seat, he was filled with overflowing faith and devotion. After paying respectful homage to the Blessed One, he asked by reciting these two verses:
Aññātametaṃ vacanaṃ,
asitassa yathātathaṃ.
Taṃ taṃ gotama pucchāmi,
sabbadhammāna pāraguṃ.
Anagāriyupetassa,
bhikkhācariyaṃ jigīsato.
Muni pabrūhi me puṭṭho,
moneyyaṃ uttamaṃ padaṃ.
The meaning is:
O Blessed One of the Gotama lineage, I have now personally realized that the words spoken to me by my uncle, the hermit Kāladevila (Asita), thirty-five years ago are perfectly true and unerring (now that I see the Blessed One face to face). Therefore, I ask the Blessed One, who has reached the further shore of all phenomena (sabbadhamma) in six ways, out of a desire to know and practice.
O Great Sage (Mahāmuni), who excels the five types of sages (Āgā-muni, Anāgā-muni, Sekkha-muni, Asekkha-muni, and Pacceka-muni) due to Your many virtues, please teach me out of compassion. I ask about the noble practice of sagehood (Moneyya), the excellent state that leads to the four Path Knowledges for a monk who has entered the homeless life and
478:
lives by seeking alms.
Then, the Blessed One taught the practice of sagehood (Moneyya-paṭipadā) in detail through twenty-three verses, beginning with 'Moneyyaṃ te upaññissaṃ'.
(In this context, 'Moneyya' refers to the four Path Knowledges, specifically the Arahatta-magga-ñāṇa. Therefore, the noble and correct practice that leads to the four Path Knowledges is called Moneyya-paṭipadā or the Practice of Sagehood.)
The Pali and Burmese prose of the twenty-three verses of the Moneyya-paṭipadā are as follows:
(1) Moneyyaṃ te upaññissaṃ,
dukkaraṃ durabhisambhavaṃ.
Handa te naṃ pavakkhāmi,
santhambhassu daḷho bhava.
'Dear Nalaka, I shall declare to you the practice of sagehood (Moneyya), which is extremely difficult to perform and hard to attain.
(Dear Nalaka, the practice of sagehood you ask about is a practice to be undertaken with great persistence from the time of being a worldling, without allowing the mind to be overwhelmed by defilements; thus, it is a practice that is difficult to perform and difficult to accomplish.)
479:
Dear Nalaka, I shall now teach you the practice of sagehood in detail. (You are one who has accumulated merit.) Therefore, make yourself firm with the energy to do what is difficult, and practice steadfastly with unremitting effort.'
(2) Samānabhāgaṃ kubbetha,
gāme akkuṭṭhavanditaṃ.
Manopadosaṃ rakkheyya,
santo anuṇṇato care.
'Dear Nalaka, in villages and towns, one should practice maintaining equanimity, whether people abuse and insult one out of anger, or pay homage and respect with devotion. A virtuous person should guard against resentment and ill-will (due to being insulted) and should practice with unremitting effort to ensure there is no conceit or pride arising from being honored and respected. (If those living in villages and towns abuse you, you must guard against ill-will and anger. Even if a king pays homage, you must not let pride arise. In this way, one should practice to be equal towards both abuse and homage.)'
480:
(By this verse, the Buddha taught the removal of defilements related to the village.)
(3) Uccāvacā niccharanti,
dāye aggisikhūpamā.
Nāriyo muniṃ palobhenti,
tာ su taṃ mā palobhayuṃ.
'Dear Nalaka, in the forest also, various objects arise that are like flames of fire. (Alternatively: Just as when a forest fire burns, flames of various colors—with or without smoke, blue, yellow, red, large or small—appear; similarly, in the forest, various objects that are fearful, pleasant, hateful, or delusive—such as humans, ogres, lions, leopards, tigers, various birds, their various sounds, fruits, flowers, and young leaves—appear. Among these various objects:) Women who come to the forest for recreation, or to collect firewood, flowers, vegetables, or fruits, may try to entice and seduce a monk living alone in seclusion by smiling, speaking flirtatiously, weeping, or dressing loosely. Let not those women seduce you. (Practice with effort so that those women cannot seduce you.)'
(By this verse, the Buddha taught the removal of defilements related to the forest.)
481:
(4) Virato methunā dhammā,
hitွာ kāme paropare.
Aviruddho asāratto,
pāṇesu tasathāvare.
(5) Yathā ahaṃ tathā ete,
yathā ete tathā ahaṃ.
Attānaṃ upamaṃ katvā,
na haneyya na ghātaye.
'Dear Nalaka, you should be one who keeps far away from sexual intercourse, having abandoned various sensual pleasures, whether superior or inferior. Without showing opposition or hatred towards beings (belonging to others' groups) and without showing attachment or affection towards beings (belonging to your own group), one should use oneself as an example (having empathy): "Just as I wish to live and not die, and desire happiness and not suffering, so do these beings wish to live and not die, and desire happiness and not suffering." Thus, one should not personally kill or harm, nor cause others to kill or harm, trembling beings (tasa—worldlings, Sotāpannas, Sakadāgāmīs, and Anāgāmīs who are not yet free from craving) and firm beings (thāvara—Arahants who are free from craving).
(In these verses, by the phrase "hitvā kāme paropare = having abandoned various superior and inferior sensual pleasures," the Buddha taught Indriya-saṃvara-sīla [restraint of the senses]. By the remaining
482:
With these words, the Buddha taught the Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla, beginning with abstinence from sexual misconduct and abstinence from taking life.)

(6) Hitvā icchañca lobhañca,
yattha satto puthujjano.
Cakkhumā paṭipajjeyya,
tareyya narakaṃ imaṃ.

Dear Nālaka, the multitude of worldlings (puthujjanas) remain attached and clinging to the four requisites—robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicine—and to the sensual pleasures of a monk. You, dear son, should avoid and abandon the desire for what has not yet been obtained (icchā) and the greed or stinginess for what has already been obtained (lobha). Being one with the eye of wisdom, you must practice the noble Moneyya practice which has been, is being, and will be taught. By practicing in this way, you will be able to cross over the craving for the four requisites which leads to wrong livelihood, called the 'abyss' (naraka) because it is difficult to fulfill.

(With this verse, the Buddha taught the Ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla, beginning with the abandonment of craving that clings to the four requisites.)

(7) Ūnūdaro mitāhāro,
appicchassa alolupo.
Sadā icchāya nicchāto,
aniccho hoti nibbuto.
483:
Dear Nālaka, a monk who wishes to practice the Moneyya-paṭipadā (the practice of a sage) must be one with a lean stomach (by eating four or five mouthfuls less than a full meal). (It is not enough to simply eat less; he must also) be one who is moderate in food, having reflected upon it through Paccavekkhaṇā (considering its benefits and faults). (Furthermore, he must) be endowed with these four types of Appicchatā (fewness of wishes): (1) Paccaya-appiccha: having few desires regarding the four requisites; (2) Dhutaṅga-appiccha: not wishing others to know that he is practicing the noble Dhutaṅga; (3) Pariyatti-appiccha: not wishing others to know of his learning and expertise in the scriptures; and (4) Adhigama-appiccha: not wishing others to know of his attainment of the Paths and Fruits. (Even this is not enough;) he must strive to completely abandon the fickleness of craving (taṇhā) through the Path of Arahantship. (When he has thus become free from the craving of greed,) he will be like a person who is not driven by the intense greed for the four requisites, like one who is perpetually tormented by hunger, and he will become free from the hunger of defilements. In doing so, he will become one whose fires of defilements are entirely extinguished.

(With this verse, the Buddha taught the practice starting with Bhojane mattaññutā (moderation in eating),
484:
Paccayasannissita-sīla (or Paccaya-paribhoga-sīla) and the sequential practice leading up to the Fruit of Arahantship.)

(8) Sa piṇḍacāraṃ caritvā,
vanantamabhihāraye.
upaṭṭhito rukkhamūlasmiṃ,
āsanūpagato muni.

(9) Sa jhānapasuto dhīro,
vanante ramito siyā.
jhāyetha rukkhamūlasmiṃ,
attānamabhitosayaṃ.

Dear Nālaka, that monk practicing Moneyya, after wandering for alms (= after finishing the meal), should go only to the forest, his dwelling place (without lingering to talk with people for a long time). The monk practicing Moneyya (upon reaching the forest) should sit either at the foot of a tree or in his designated seat.

(In this context, the phrase "after wandering for alms" indicates the Piṇḍapātika-dhutaṅga. Since a monk who undertakes the strict Piṇḍapātika-dhutaṅga also practices Sapadānacārika-dhutaṅga, Ekāsanika-dhutaṅga, Pattapiṇḍika-dhutaṅga, Khalupacchābhattika-dhutaṅga, Ticīvarika-dhutaṅga, and Paṃsukūlika-dhutaṅga, these six dhutaṅgas are also considered taught here.

The phrase "should go only to the forest" indicates the Āraññika-dhutaṅga. The phrase "should sit either at the foot of a tree or in his designated seat" indicates the Rukkhamūlika-dhutaṅga
485:
and Nesajjika-dhutaṅga. By teaching these ten dhutaṅgas in sequence, the other three—Abbhokāsika-dhutaṅga, Yathāsaṃthatika-dhutaṅga, and Sosānika-dhutaṅga—are also implied as they are consistent with them. Thus, with this verse, the Buddha taught the thirteen dhutaṅgas to the Elder Nālaka.)

Dear Nālaka, the monk who practices the noble Moneyya-paṭipadā while observing these thirteen dhutaṅgas should be one who strives in the mundane jhānas—attaining those not yet attained and mastering those already attained through the five masteries (vasī). Being endowed with Appanā-samādhi (fixed concentration), he should delight in the forest, secluded from the noise of people. (Striving only for mundane jhāna is not enough;) at the foot of a tree in that forest, he should dwell absorbed in jhāna (including supramundane jhāna associated with the Path of Stream-entry, etc.), greatly gladdening and satisfying himself.

(With this verse, the Buddha taught delighting in the forest through striving in mundane and supramundane jhānas, as well as the Fruit of Arahantship.)

Upon hearing this Dhamma teaching, Ven. Nālaka was extremely eager to fulfill the Moneyya practice even without eating food; however, he was not able to strive in the monk's practice without food. Indeed, for one who strives in the monk's practice without eating, long life is not possible.
486:
In fact, one must seek food without allowing defilements to arise. Seeking food in this way, without giving rise to defilements, is the proper method in the Dispensation. Therefore, the Buddha, wishing to show Ven. Nālaka that "in the following days, he should wander for alms in the village, but should not let defilements arise," and desiring to teach the alms-gathering duty that culminates in the Fruit of Arahantship, spoke these six verses.

(10) Tato ratyāvivasāne,
gāmantamabhihāraye.
avhānaṃ nābhinandeyya,
abhihārañca gāmato.

Dear Nālaka, the monk practicing Moneyya, after the aforementioned (wandering for alms and going to the forest), should go to the alms-village on subsequent days when the night has passed and dawn has broken (having performed duties such as the Cetiyangaṇa-vatta within the monastery before alms-time, and having developed physical and mental seclusion while contemplating the meditation subject on the way to and from the village).

Upon reaching the village, he should not delight in or accept invitations such as "Venerable Sir, please take your meal at our house" (nor should he accept alms while harboring various wandering thoughts such as "Will they give me alms at this house?
487:
Will they not give? Will they give good food? Will they give poor food?"). (If, however, the lay devotees take his bowl by force, fill it with food, and offer it, he should eat that food and strive in the monk's practice. The dhutaṅga practice is not broken. But he should not enter the village with the expectation of receiving such food.)

(When a Moneyya monk enters a village and lay devotees, without inviting him to their homes, come to where the monk is before he walks for alms from house to house and offer food with many side dishes, this is called 'Abhihāra' alms.) He should not accept even a single portion of such Abhihāra alms (even if offered with hundreds of side dishes). (The meaning is that he must only collect alms by walking from house to house.)

(11) Na munī gāmamāgamma,
kulesu sahasā care.
ghāsesanaṃ chinnakatho,
na vācaṃ payutaṃ bhaṇe.

Dear Nālaka, when the monk practicing Moneyya reaches the village, he should not socialize with lay families (in a manner unsuitable for the Dispensation, sharing their joys and sorrows). He should be like one who is mute and should not speak words of hints, signs, or indirect talk to obtain alms-food.
488:
(12) Alatthaṃ yadidaṃ sādhu,
nālatthaṃ kusalaṃ iti.
ubhayeneva so tādī,
rukkhaṃvupanivattati.

Dear Nālaka, when the monk practicing Moneyya enters the village for alms, if he receives even a little food, he should reflect, "It is good to receive this." If he receives nothing, he should reflect, "It is blameless not to receive." Being thus unshaken by both receiving and not receiving alms, and being endowed with the quality of Tādi (equanimity), he should depart from the lay devotees' houses (just as a man seeking fruit approaches a tree and, whether he gets fruit or not, leaves that tree without hate or affection, remaining indifferent).

(13) Sa pattapāṇi vicaranto,
amūgo mūgasammato.
appaṃ dānaṃ na hīḷeyya,
dātāraṃ nāvajāniyā.

Dear Nālaka, that Moneyya monk wandering for alms with bowl in hand, though not mute, should act so that people regard him as mute (meaning he should not engage in idle talk). He should not despise or disparage even a small gift. He should not look down upon a donor for giving only a small amount.
489:
(14) Uccāvacā hi paṭipadā,
samaṇena pakāsitā.
na pāraṃ diguṇaṃ yanti,
nayidaṃ ekaguṇaṃ mutaṃ.

(Dear Nālaka, when the Moneyya monk becomes endowed with the alms-gathering duty as described, he should not be satisfied with just that, but must practice and complete the superior and noble Paṭipadā. Indeed, the Dispensation has the Paṭipadā (practice) as its essence. It means, "The practice is the essence of the Dispensation; only by practicing will one reach the essence of the Dispensation.") The Buddha has taught that good practice leading to the Path in two ways: the superior and the inferior.

(To clarify: from the start of striving in the monk's practice until the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are abandoned, this interval is called the field or domain of Paṭipadā. If one can abandon the five hindrances easily and without hardship during this time, it is called Sukhā-paṭipadā. If one abandons them only through painful and difficult practice, it is called Dukkhā-paṭipadā. From the time the five hindrances are abandoned until the Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) is reached, this interval is called the field of Abhiññā (insight wisdom). If insight-knowledge reaches Path-knowledge quickly after abandoning the hindrances, it is called Khippābhiññā. If it reaches Path-knowledge slowly, it is called Dandhābhiññā.
490:
(1) For some individuals, while striving in the monk's practice, they abandon the five hindrances easily and without hardship, and then quickly reach Path-knowledge. This type of practice is called Sukhā-paṭipadā Khippābhiññā (the Buddha taught this as the superior practice). (2) Some abandon the five hindrances easily but reach Path-knowledge slowly. This is called Sukhā-paṭipadā Dandhābhiññā. (3) Some can only abandon the five hindrances through painful and difficult practice but reach Path-knowledge quickly. This is called Dukkhā-paṭipadā Khippābhiññā. (4) Some abandon the five hindrances through painful and difficult practice and also reach Path-knowledge slowly. This is called Dukkhā-paṭipadā Dandhābhiññā (the Buddha taught these three types, 2, 3, and 4, as the inferior practice).

Dear Nālaka, in reaching the other shore called Nibbāna through these superior and inferior practices, one cannot reach Nibbāna twice with a single Path-knowledge. (Once Path-knowledge arises, it completely eradicates the defilements it is meant to abandon; since it does not arise again in that same mental continuum, it is taught that "one cannot reach Nibbāna twice with a single Path-knowledge.") This Nibbāna is
491:
It is not a type of Dhamma that can be reached all at once (with a single path-knowledge). (It means that all defilements cannot be abandoned by a single path-knowledge; only through the four path-knowledges can the respective defilements be abandoned without remainder. Therefore, one cannot reach Nibbāna or the Fruition of Arahatship with a single stroke of path-knowledge; one can only fully reach Nibbāna and the Fruition of Arahatship through the four stages of path-knowledge.)

(15) Yassa ca visatā natthi,
Chinnasotassa bhikkhuno.
Kiccākiccaprahīnassa,
Pariḷāho na vijjati.

Dear Nālaka, for that monk of sagehood (who has practiced until reaching the Fruition of Arahatship through the two modes of practice taught), there are no cravings that spread in 108 ways (as they have been completely abandoned and destroyed by the Path of Arahatship). In such a monk of sagehood, who has completely cut the stream of defilements (through the Path of Arahatship) and has abandoned both wholesome and unwholesome actions, there is not even a slight fever of passion (rāga) or fever of hatred (dosa).

(With this verse, the Buddha shows the benefits and advantages of the practice.)

Upon hearing these verses, the thought occurred in the mind of the Venerable Nālaka: "If the practice of sagehood is only this much,
492:
it is quite easy and not difficult; I will be able to fulfill it easily without any hardship or exhaustion." Therefore, the Buddha, wishing to show the Venerable Nālaka again that "Dear Nālaka, the practice of sagehood is not an easy task to practice as you think; it is indeed a difficult practice," spoke these verses:

(16) Moneyyaṃ te upaññissaṃ,
Khuradhārūpamo bhave.
Jivhāya tālumāhacca,
Udare saññato siyā.

Dear Nālaka, I shall further explain the practice of sagehood to you. A monk who practices sagehood must be like the edge of a razor. (The meaning is: just as one who licks a blade smeared with honey must be careful and mindful of the danger of cutting the tongue, so too a monk of sagehood, when using the four requisites obtained rightfully, must guard his mind against the danger of defilements arising. Indeed, it is very difficult to obtain the four requisites through pure means, and once obtained, it is also difficult to use them blamelessly. Therefore, the Buddha repeatedly taught the virtue of restraint regarding requisites (paccayasannissita-sīla).) Dear Nālaka, a monk practicing sagehood should press his tongue against the palate (and by abandoning the craving for tastes,
493:
without resorting to the four requisites obtained through wrong livelihood), he should be restrained in his stomach. (The meaning is: if he does not obtain the requisites rightfully for his stomach, he must abandon the craving for tastes, grit his teeth, and be able to endure; he should never, under any circumstances, use things sought through wrong livelihood.)

(17) Alīnacitto ca siyā,
Na cāpi bahu cintaye.
Nirāmagandho asito,
Brahmacariyaparāyaṇo.

Dear Nālaka, a monk practicing sagehood must have an unsluggish mind (by constantly practicing the cultivation of wholesome states). He should not think many diverse thoughts such as about relatives, lineages, towns, or villages. He should be free from the 'raw smell' of defilements, unattached to any existence great or small through craving and wrong view, and should rely on the holy life (brahmacariya) which consists of the three trainings (sikkhā) of the Dispensation.

(18) Ekāsanassa sikkhetha,
Samaṇūpāsanassa ca.
Ekattaṃ monamakkhātaṃ,
Eko ce abhiramissasi.
Atha bhāhisi dasa disā.

Dear Nālaka, a monk practicing sagehood must train himself to live in solitude without a companion, and
494:
to repeatedly strive and exert himself in the thirty-eight subjects of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) which are the resort of monks. (Here, by living alone, the Buddha teaches physical seclusion (kāya-viveka); by exerting and developing the subjects of meditation, He teaches mental seclusion (citta-viveka)). Such living alone without a companion through both physical and mental seclusion is what I, the Buddha, call the practice of sagehood. Dear Nālaka, if you can delight in being alone without a companion through both physical and mental seclusion, you will become famous and illustrious in the ten directions.

(19) Sutvā dhīrānaṃ nighosaṃ,
Jhāyīnaṃ kāmacāginaṃ.
Tato hiriñca saddhañca,
Bhiyyo kubbetha māmako.

Dear Nālaka, when you hear the shouts of praise from the wise who have abandoned both the objects of sensual desire and the defilements of sensuality, and who repeatedly enter into both the jhāna of fixed meditation and the jhāna of insight, you should (without letting your mind wander because of that praise) increase your sense of moral shame (hiri) and your faith (saddhā) (believing that this practice of sagehood is the good practice for liberation from saṃsāra) even more than before. By repeatedly developing this liberating practice, you will truly be a son of mine (the Buddha).
495:
(20) Taṃ nadīhi vijānātha,
Sobbhesu padaresu ca.
Saṇantā yanti kusobbhā,
Tuṇhī yanti mahodadhī.

Dear Nālaka, that instruction (which says "when hearing the praise of the wise, do not let the mind wander or be agitated, but increase moral shame and faith even more") should be understood through the following analogies of great rivers and small streams. Small streams and rivulets flow with a gurgling sound and agitation. Great rivers like the Ganges, however, flow silently without agitation or noise. (Similarly, one who is not a true son of mine is agitated like small streams, thinking "I am one who fulfills the practice of sagehood." But one who is a true son of mine, by developing the aforementioned moral shame and faith, remains silent with a humble mind like the great rivers.)

(21) Yadūnakaṃ taṃ saṇati,
Yaṃ pūraṃ santameva taṃ.
Aḍḍhakumbhūpamo bālo,
Rahado pūrova paṇḍito.

Dear Nālaka, (I wish to further point out another way): Whatever vessel is not full of water is deficient. That vessel makes a sound as it splashes. Whatever vessel is full of water,
496:
that water-filled vessel is silent and calm. A fool is like a vessel that makes noise with half-filled water. A wise man is like a full lake.

In this context, a question might arise: "If a fool is like an unfilled pot because of being restless and noisy, and a wise man is like a full lake because of being silent and calm, why does the Buddha make an effort to teach the Dhamma and speak so many words?" To address this, He spoke these last two verses:

(22) Yaṃ samaṇo bahuṃ bhāsati,
Upetaṃ atthasañhitaṃ.
Jānaṃ so dhammaṃ deseti,
Jānaṃ so bahu bhāsati.

(23) Yo ca jānaṃ saṃyatatto,
Jānaṃ na bahu bhāsati.
Sa munī monamarahati,
Sa munī monamajjhagā.

Dear Nālaka, I, the Great Recluse, speak much of that which is endowed with meaning and text and is connected with benefit. (That speech is not spoken with agitation or restlessness; rather,) I, the Great Recluse, teach the Dhamma only after knowing and discerning with the wisdom of what is beneficial and what is not. (Even if I teach all day, I am not dragging it out to waste time.) In thus teaching only the Dhamma,
497:
I speak much only by discerning specifically, "This Dhamma is for the benefit and welfare of this person; this Dhamma is for the benefit and welfare of that person." (It means I am not speaking many words without essence just because I am naturally talkative.)

Dear Nālaka, that monk who practices sagehood, having understood the Dhamma taught by me through discernment (with penetrative wisdom capable of destroying defilements), and having a mind well-guarded, does not speak much because he knows (what speech would not lead to the welfare of beings). Only such a monk practicing sagehood is worthy of the practice of sagehood. (Not only is he worthy, but indeed) that monk of sagehood will certainly attain the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship.

In this way, the Buddha concluded the great Dhamma teaching related to the practice of sagehood, culminating in the Fruition of Arahatship.

## The Three Types of Fewness of Desires of Venerable Nālaka

Upon hearing the Buddha's detailed teaching on the practice of sagehood culminating in the Fruition of Arahatship, the Venerable Nālaka became one with fewness of desires (appicchatā) in these three areas: (1) seeing the Buddha, (2) hearing the Dhamma, and (3) asking about the practice of sagehood. To elaborate:
498:
(1) At the end of hearing the Dhamma teaching related to the practice of sagehood, the Venerable Nālaka, with a very clear, joyful, and satisfied mind, paid respects to the Buddha with great devotion and entered the forest. From the time he entered the forest, the desire "It would be good if I could see the Buddha again" never arose even once in the mind of the Venerable Nālaka. This is his fewness of desires regarding seeing the Buddha.

(2) Similarly, the desire "It would be good if I could hear the Dhamma again" never arose even once in the mind of the Venerable Nālaka. This is his fewness of desires regarding hearing the Dhamma.

(3) Likewise, the desire "It would be good if I could ask the Buddha about the practice of sagehood again" never arose even once in the mind of the Venerable Nālaka. This is his fewness of desires regarding asking about the practice of sagehood. (As he was a special individual and a special disciple who appears only once per Buddha, he was fully satisfied and his desires were fulfilled by seeing the Buddha just once, hearing the Dhamma just once, and asking about the practice of sagehood just once. Therefore, the desires to see the Buddha again, hear the Dhamma again, or ask questions again did not arise; it was not because of a lack of faith that he did not want to see the Buddha, hear the Dhamma, or ask questions.)
500:
He adjusted and wore his undergarment neatly, fastened his waistband, and then, after donning the double-layered outer robe and the upper robe, he faced towards the city of Rājagaha where the Blessed One was residing. He paid homage with the five-point prostration (placing the two hands, two knees, and the forehead on the ground), and with palms joined in reverence, he stood leaning against the mountain named Hiṅgulaka, where he entered Parinibbāna, the final cessation, ending the cycle of existence.

## Building a Stupa for the Relics
At that time, the Blessed One, perceiving that the Elder Nālaka had entered Parinibbāna, went to that place together with the community of monks. The Buddha himself supervised and managed the cremation ceremony. After having the relics collected and a stupa built to enshrine them, he returned to the city of Rājagaha.

The account of the teaching of the Moneyya practice is finished.
**********
## Chapter 12
## The Ordination of the Merchant's Son Yasa
While the Blessed One was residing for the rainy season retreat at the Isipatana Deer Park in Bārāṇasī, after having taught and liberated the group of five monks and the Elder Nālaka through the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta, and the Nālaka Sutta, there was a noble youth named Yasa. He was the son of Sujātā, the daughter-in-law of the merchant of Bārāṇasī (the one who offered the ghana-milk rice) from the market town of Sena. He was refined in body, speech, and mind, and was also endowed with great wealth and a large retinue.
501:
The merchant's son Yasa had three palaces: one for the winter season, one for the summer season, and one for the rainy season. At that time (while the Blessed One was residing in the Deer Park), it was the rainy season. Thus, for the four months of the rains, Yasa remained in the palace suitable for the rainy season, surrounded by a troupe of female dancers and musicians skilled in playing, dancing, and singing. In that entire palace, there was not a single man; from the doorkeeper to the entertainers, all were women. He enjoyed and indulged in great sensual pleasures without descending from the palace. (Yasa's father, the great merchant, had arranged only women for all duties within the palace with the intention: "Let my son, who is enjoying such magnificent and great wealth, not feel any disgust or fear upon seeing any man.")

While he was thus enjoying the great sensual pleasures with the five kinds of musical instruments and the company of women without any men, one day, the merchant's son Yasa fell asleep early. The troupe of entertainers, seeing that the merchant's son was asleep and they were no longer needed, also fell asleep, each clutching, embracing, or pillowing their respective instruments. In that great hall of the performance chamber, lamps were kept burning brightly throughout the night.
502:
Then, the merchant's son Yasa woke up before the others. He saw his retinue of female entertainers asleep: some clutching lutes, some with drums on their necks, some embracing large drums, some with disheveled hair, some with saliva trickling from their mouths, and some muttering in their sleep. Seeing them in such a state of deep sleep, which appeared as repulsive as a cemetery, the nature of the disadvantages (ādīnava) of sensual pleasures became clear to Yasa. A sense of detachment and weariness towards sensual pleasures arose and persisted in him.

At that time, Yasa, being deeply moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), uttered this exclamation born of the power of his wisdom: "Upaddutaṃ vata bho, upassatthaṃ vata bho = Oh, how distressed it is! Oh, how oppressed it is! This wretched body, this great vessel of suffering of all beings, including myself, is indeed afflicted and oppressed by various defilements."

Then, the merchant's son Yasa (weary of his experiences and sensory objects) rose from his bed, put on his golden slippers, and left (without informing anyone). When he reached the door of the house, the deities, intending that "no one shall hinder or obstruct the merchant's son Yasa in his quest to become a monk," had already opened the door in advance. Thus, he left the house easily. When he reached the city gate, the guardian deities of the city had likewise opened the gate in advance.
503:
He left the city easily without any hindrance or obstruction and continued his journey, arriving early in the morning at the great Isipatana Deer Park near the city of Bārāṇasī.

At that time, the Blessed One had risen early in the last watch of the night and was walking to and fro (caṅkama) in the open air. Seeing the merchant's son Yasa coming from afar, the Buddha descended from the walking path and sat down on the seat prepared for him. When Yasa approached the presence of the Blessed One, he again uttered the same exclamation of spiritual urgency he had uttered before.

Then the Blessed One addressed Yasa: "Come, Yasa! This Nibbāna, which I, the Buddha, have realized, is a state that is not oppressed or afflicted by various defilements. Come, Yasa, sit here. I, the Buddha, will preach to you the excellent Dhamma that leads to Nibbāna." Hearing this invitation and encouragement, Yasa thought, "It is said that this Nibbāna realized by the Blessed One is a state not oppressed or afflicted by various defilements," and with a joyful, glad, and uplifted mind, he took off his golden slippers, approached the Blessed One respectfully, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place.

Then the Blessed One preached to the merchant's son Yasa, who was seated in a suitable place, the gradual discourse (anupubbīkathā), which is the excellent path to the attainment of the Path and Fruit: (1) Dānakathā = discourse on giving, (2) Sīlakathā = discourse on virtue,
504:
(3) Saggakathā = discourse on the celestial realms, and (4) Maggakathā = discourse on the excellent practice that leads to the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna. He preached these in order.

## Dānakathā
Dānakathā, the discourse on giving, means: "This meritorious deed of giving is the cause of happiness in the present life, happiness in the future life, and the happiness of Nibbāna. It is the root cause of various types of wealth, such as human wealth and celestial wealth. It is the basis for material objects of use and the happiness derived from using those objects. It is a good protection for beings who encounter disasters (vyasana). It is a refuge, a destination, and a support. In this present life and in future lives, there is no good support, basis, attachment, protection, refuge, destination, or reliance equal to giving.

Indeed, because this meritorious deed of giving is a support, it is like a lion-throne adorned with jewels; because it is a foundation, it is like the great earth; because it is something to hold onto, it is like a rope for the blind to grasp and rely upon. Furthermore, because this meritorious deed of giving is the means to cross over the suffering of the woeful states (apāya), it is like a ship. Because it can free one from and alleviate the danger of enemies such as greed and stinginess, it is like a brave commander in a battlefield. Because it protects one from the danger of poverty, it is like a well-fortified, well-managed, and well-adorned great city. Because it is not smeared or attached to the stains of unwholesome states such as envy (issā) and stinginess (macchariya),
505:
it is like a Paduma lotus. Because it can burn away the rubbish of unwholesome states like stinginess, it is like fire. Because it is difficult for those unwholesome enemies to approach, it is like a venomous snake. Because it can remove dread and fear, it is like a lion king. (The donor does not have to fear any enemy in this life, let alone in the next.) Because it is of great strength, it is like a noble elephant. (The donor is strong in this life and will be very strong in physical and intellectual power in future lives.) Because it is recognized by the wise and virtuous as a noble blessing that leads to extraordinary prosperity in both the present and future lives, it is like a pure white bull. Because it carries one away from the poor soil of the four failures (vipatti) to the safe and good soil of the four accomplishments (sampatti), it is like the Valāhaka Sindh horse king.

This meritorious deed of giving is the excellent path, the track, and the right way traveled by the Buddhas; it is the lineage of the Buddhas. While I, the Buddha, was fulfilling the perfections (pāramī), I performed many great offerings such as the great offering of Velāma, the great offering of Mahāgovinda, the great offering of Mahāsudassana, and the great offering of Vessantara. When I was the wise hare, a Bodhisatta, I sacrificed my own body in a blazing fire and completely won over the hearts of the recipients. (In this instance, the heart of the Brahmin recipient, who was Sakka, the King of Devas...)
506:
Without wandering to any other object, he remained repeatedly focused only on the courageous generosity of the Bodhisatta Hare. This state is elegantly expressed through the rhetorical device of circumlocution (vaṅkavutti-alaṅkāra) as: "I have completely captured the hearts of the recipients."

(In this context, with the phrase "sacrificing one's own self," the Great Bodhisattas, because they clearly see the fruits of generosity, sacrifice even their own lives. Therefore, what wise person should cling to external objects? Indeed, one should not.)

Furthermore, the merit of generosity (dāna) can provide worldly attainments such as the glory of Sakka, Māra, Brahmā, and Universal Monarchs. In the supramundane aspect, it can also provide the wisdom of a Disciple's Enlightenment (sāvaka-bodhi), Private Enlightenment (pacceka-bodhi), and Supreme Enlightenment (sammā-sambodhi).

In this manner and others, the Buddha preached the discourse related to generosity to Yasa, the son of the wealthy merchant.

## Sīlakathā (Talk on Morality)

(Since only those who perform the merit of generosity can observe morality, the Buddha preached the talk on morality immediately after the talk on generosity. To clarify further: generosity is the relinquishing of one's own property to others, either out of a desire for their welfare or out of a desire to honor them. Thus, a person who performs the merit of generosity is a noble person who truly desires the welfare of beings, and has no reason to kill others or steal the property of others.)
507:
Therefore, since only those who perform the merit of generosity can observe morality, the Buddha preached the talk on morality immediately after the talk on generosity.)

Sīlakathā = The discourse related to morality is as follows: "This merit of morality is the support, the foundation, the refuge, the great protection, the shelter, the destination, and the resting place of beings. This merit of morality is the lineage of the Buddhas. When I was the Naga King Saṅkhapāla, the Naga King Bhūridatta, the Naga King Campeyya, King Sīlava, the Elephant King Mātuposaka, the Elephant King Chaddanta, and in countless and boundless lives, I have protected and fulfilled morality so that it was neither broken, nor breached, nor spotted, nor mottled."

Indeed, for the wealth of this present life and the wealth of the life hereafter, there is no support, foundation, refuge, great protection, shelter, destination, or resting place equal to morality. There is no ornament like the ornament of virtue, no flower like the flower of virtue, and no perfume like the perfume of virtue. Furthermore, the multitude of humans and devas can never tire of looking at one who wears the flower of virtue, applies the perfume of virtue, and is adorned with the ornament of virtue.

In this manner and others, the Buddha preached the discourse related to morality to Yasa, the son of the wealthy merchant.

## Saggakathā (Talk on Heaven)

(In order to show that by means of this merit of morality, such heavenly wealth is obtained, immediately after the talk on morality, the Buddha preached Saggakathā = the discourse related to heaven.)
508:
Saggakathā = The discourse related to heaven is as follows: "This heavenly realm, the happy destination, is desired and cherished by everyone; it causes the hearts of everyone to flourish and be refreshed. In this heaven, one obtains constant joy and luxurious pleasures. The devas of the Realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika) enjoy heavenly pleasures for nine million years by human reckoning. The devas of the Realm of the Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa) enjoy heavenly pleasures for thirty-six million years by human reckoning."

In this manner and others, the Buddha also preached the discourse related to the bliss of heaven to Yasa, the son of the wealthy merchant. (Indeed, because heavenly wealth is so vast and grand, even the mouths of the Buddhas who preach about that heavenly wealth are as if insufficient to contain it.)

## Maggakathā (Talk on the Path)

After preaching about the bliss of heaven, the Buddha intended to show that "That heavenly bliss is constantly oppressed and afflicted by defilements such as lust (rāga), whereas the Noble Path (ariya-magga) is completely liberated from defilements and thus not oppressed or afflicted by them." Therefore, immediately after the talk on heaven, he was to preach the discourse related to the Noble Path. Wishing to preach that Maggakathā, and because they are the means to attain that Path, the Buddha also preached Kāmānaṃ Ādīnavakathā (Talk on the Danger of Sensual Pleasures) and Nekkhamma Ānisaṃsakathā (Talk on the Benefits of Renunciation).
509:
## Kāmānaṃ Ādīnavakathā and Nekkhamma Ānisaṃsakathā

After the Buddha had attracted and drawn Yasa's mind with the discourse related to heavenly bliss, he then spoke (like one who, after decorating an elephant to be most beautiful, cuts off its trunk): "This heavenly bliss is also merely impermanent (anicca); it is unstable (addhuva). One should not develop desire and lust (chanda-rāga) for that heavenly bliss. Sensual pleasures (kāmaguṇa) provide little gratification but much suffering and exhaustion. In this mass of sensual pleasures, the gratification is as small as a red bean, while the faults are as large as Mount Meru."

In this manner and others (just as he had reflected and known during his own Great Renunciation), the Buddha preached extensively on the dangers of sensual pleasures, their low nature which is resorted to by the vulgar and not by the noble, and how these sensual things oppress and burn beings.

Then, just as there are many faults in those sensual things, he preached extensively on the benefits of the group of Dhamma known as renunciation (nekkhamma), from the state of monkhood up to Nibbāna, showing how it is free from faults and has little suffering.
510:
## Yasa Attaining the Stage of a Stream-Enterer

Having thus preached to Yasa the progressive discourse starting with the talk on generosity, and when he knew that Yasa's mind was ready, soft, free from hindrances, uplifted, and clear, the Buddha revealed to Yasa the Sāmukkaṃsika Dhamma Desanā, the teaching of the Four Noble Truths: the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca), the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca), the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca), and the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca).

(To explain clearly: when the Buddha preached the progressive series of discourses starting with the talk on generosity to Yasa, the faults of the mind such as lack of faith, laziness, heedlessness, distraction, and delusion were cleared away from Yasa's mental continuum. Thus, he was in a state capable of receiving the profound teaching of the Four Truths. Being free from defilements such as wrong view and conceit, he was in a soft state like pure Jāmbūnada gold, ready to be shaped or drawn. He was free from the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa). He remained endowed with great joy and rapture (pīti-pāmojja) in the good practice leading to Nibbāna. Being endowed with faith, he was extremely clear. Only then did the Buddha, using the method of teaching that only Buddhas can employ to lead beings to the Path and Fruition according to their inclinations and temperaments, preach the profound Four Noble Truths to Yasa.)

When he preached thus, just as a clean cloth from which all stains have been washed and removed
511:
would perfectly take the dye of yellow, red, or other colors applied by a dyer (kavā) and would have a brilliant glow, even so, the Eye of Dhamma (dhamma-cakkhu), the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa), arose in Yasa's continuum. It took the cessation of the Truth of Nibbāna as its direct object, while abandoning the dust of defilements such as lust that lead to the lower realms, and completely eradicating the stains of defilements like wrong view (diṭṭhi) and doubt (vicikicchā). He clearly perceived with certainty (which no one could destroy) that "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease." Being one of quick insight, sharp wisdom, and one who attains direct knowledge easily and quickly (sukha-paṭipadā-khippābhiññā), that vision of the Path of Stream-entry became manifest right there in that single sitting. This means he became a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna).

(In this regard, just as a dyer cannot successfully dye a cloth that is stained and dirty with whatever color he desires, such as yellow or red, so too, the dye of the Four Noble Truths cannot be successfully applied to the mind of a being that is stained with the dirt of hindrances like sensual desire and ill-will. But if a dyer takes a dirty cloth, places it on a stone, sprinkles it with water, and scrubs it with soap, cow dung, and ash—these three—until it is clean, and then dyes it, the dye will take well and produce the desired brilliant color. Similarly, the Buddha, the Great Dyer who dyes with the four truths, placed the cloth-like mind of Yasa, which was stained with defilements, on the stone-like progressive discourse (anupubbīkathā).)
512:
He repeatedly sprinkled it with the pure water of Yasa's faith, and scrubbed it with his mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā)—these three. When the mind was clean and free from the stains of the hindrances, he applied the dye of the Four Noble Truths. At that moment, the vision of the Path (sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa) appeared in Yasa's mind, and the dye of the Four Noble Truths took hold so firmly that no one could destroy it.

## The Wealthy Father's Attainment of Stream-entry and
## Yasa's Attainment of Arahantship

When morning dawned, Yasa's mother, the wealthy lady Sujātā, rose early and went up to Yasa's mansion to look for him. Not seeing her son Yasa, she was overcome with grief and went to Yasa's father, the wealthy merchant, saying, "O Merchant, I do not see your son Yasa." Then the father quickly sent out swift messengers on horseback to the four directions, while he himself went toward the Isipatana Deer Park to search. He saw the golden footprints of Yasa and, following those very footprints, he tracked him.

The Buddha saw Yasa's father coming from afar and thought, "It would be best if I hide Yasa by psychic power so that his father cannot see him." He then used his psychic power to conceal Yasa from his father's sight.
513: Then the wealthy merchant father came to the Blessed One and asked, "Venerable Sir, have you seen the noble son Yasa?" The Blessed One replied, "Merchant, if you wish to see your son, sit down here. While sitting in this very place, you shall see your son, the noble son Yasa, who is sitting nearby." Hearing this, the merchant father was delighted and joyful, thinking, "While sitting here, I shall see my son Yasa sitting nearby." He paid homage to the Blessed One with great respect and sat in a suitable place. When he was seated, the Blessed One preached to him the gradual discourse (anupubbīkathā), which is the noble path to the realization of the Path and Fruit, in the following order: (1) Dānakathā = talk on giving, (2) Sīlakathā = talk on virtue, (3) Saggakathā = talk on heaven, and (4) Maggakathā = talk on the path (renunciation), which leads to the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna. When the Blessed One perceived that the merchant father's mind was ready, softened, free from hindrances, uplifted, and clear, He then preached the Sāmukkaṃsika Dhamma-desanā (the teaching special to the Buddhas), the Four Noble Truths. Thereupon, the merchant father was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). (This merchant father of Yasa became the very first noble disciple among male lay followers in this Buddha's Dispensation to attain Stream-entry.)
514:
Then the merchant father of Yasa said, "Excellent, Venerable Sir! Excellent, Venerable Sir! It is as if, Venerable Sir, one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what had been hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. In the same way, the Blessed One has revealed the Dhamma in many ways. Venerable Sir, I go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka) who has taken refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts." Thus he took the supramundane refuge. (This merchant father of Yasa was the first noble lay disciple in the world to be established in the three-word refuge (tevācika) as a Stream-enterer.)

## Yasa Attaining Arahantship
Even while the Blessed One was preaching to his father, the noble son Yasa, reflecting on the Four Noble Truths according to the path he had realized when reaching the Path of Stream-entry, attained the higher three paths in succession and became an Arahant. Thus, the mind of the noble son Yasa, through craving and wrong view, was no longer attached to anything
515:
He had completely severed the attachment of "I" and "mine" even towards the Dhamma, and was fully liberated from the taints (āsavas) which had ceased through non-arising.

## The Wealthy Father Seeing His Son
## Inviting the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a Meal

At that time, the Blessed One thought: "Yasa, the noble son, has become an Arahant with the destruction of the taints. He will never again return to the lay life to enjoy sensual pleasures as he did before.
