Therefore, it is now appropriate to cease the psychic arrangement that prevented the father and son from seeing each other." Having thought thus, He ceased that psychic arrangement and made a resolution that the father and son should see each other.

The wealthy merchant, while sitting in his place, suddenly saw his son, the noble son Yasa, sitting near him. With a heart full of great joy, he said to Yasa: "Dear son Yasa, your mother is in great sorrow, lamenting and weeping because she cannot see you. Please give life to your mother."

Then the young Yasa (without replying to his father) looked up at the Blessed One. The Blessed One then addressed the wealthy merchant: "Great Merchant, what do you think of what I am about to ask? Just as you have realized the Four Noble Truths through the vision of a trainee (sekha-ñāṇa), so too, another person has realized the Four Noble Truths through the vision of a trainee..."
516:
That person, reflecting on the Four Noble Truths according to the path he realized when reaching the Path of Stream-entry, has attained the higher three paths in succession and become an Arahant, with taints exhausted. Would such a person, who has become an Arahant, return to the lay life to enjoy sensual pleasures as he did before?" The merchant father replied, "No, Venerable Sir."

Then the Blessed One said (to bring the point home), "Merchant, just as you have seen the Four Noble Truths with the vision of a trainee, your son Yasa had already seen the Four Noble Truths with the vision of a trainee (even before you arrived). Reflecting on the Four Noble Truths according to the path he realized when reaching the Path of Stream-entry, he attained the higher three paths in succession and has now become an Arahant with taints exhausted. Merchant, the noble son Yasa will never again return to the lay life to enjoy sensual pleasures as he did before." When the Blessed One said this, the merchant father exclaimed, "Venerable Sir, since the noble son Yasa's mind is completely liberated from the taints, without any attachment to anything as 'I' or 'mine' (meaning he has become an Arahant), it is a great gain for the noble son Yasa,
517:
and he has made good use of his human life. Venerable Sir, for the sake of today's morning merit and joy, may the Blessed One, together with the noble son Yasa as his attendant monk, accept my meal invitation." The Blessed One accepted the merchant's invitation by remaining silent.

Then the merchant, knowing that the Blessed One had accepted, rose from his seat, paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, performed the circumambulation, and returned to his home.

## Yasa's Ordination
Shortly after his father had left, the noble son Yasa paid respectful homage to the Blessed One and requested ordination, saying, "Venerable Sir, may I receive the initial ordination (pabbajjā) and the full ordination (upasampadā) in the presence of the Blessed One?" The Blessed One stretched out his golden hand and said, "Ehi Bhikkhu, svākkhāto dhammo, cara brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāya = Come, monk! Receive the ordination you requested. The Dhamma is well-preached. Practice the noble life (brahmacariya) for the complete ending of suffering until your final moment of passing away (parinibbāna)." As soon as the Blessed One called him with the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' invitation, the noble son Yasa was instantly transformed into the appearance of a monk of sixty years' standing, complete with the eight miraculous requisites (iddhimaya-parikkhāra), and he paid respectful homage to the Blessed One.
518:
(The Blessed One’s utterance of "Ehi Bhikkhu" (Come, monk) was itself the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination for the Venerable Yasa; there was no need for a formal assembly in a Sīmā). (When the Venerable Yasa became a monk, there were seven Arahants in the world of men: the Blessed One, the five monks of the group of five, and the Venerable Yasa.)

## The Wealthy Mother Sujātā and
## Yasa’s Former Wife Attaining Sotāpanna

After the young Yasa had received the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination, the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taking His bowl and robes, went to the house of the wealthy merchant with the Venerable Yasa as His attendant monk. He sat down on the prepared noble seat. Then, the wealthy lady Sujātā, the mother of Venerable Yasa, and his former wife approached the Blessed One, paid respectful homage, and sat in a suitable place.

When they were seated, the Blessed One preached to the mother and the former wife the gradual discourse, the noble path leading to the attainment of Path and Fruit, in the manner previously described: (1) Dānakathā = discourse on giving, (2) Sīlakathā = discourse on virtue, (3) Saggakathā = discourse on heaven, (4) Maggakathā = discourse on the practice leading to Nibbāna, including the discourse on the danger of sensual pleasures and the benefits of renunciation. When He knew that their minds were ready, soft, free from hindrances...
519:
uplifted, joyful, and clear, He then preached the Sāmukkaṃsika Dhamma-desanā, the Four Noble Truths, to Yasa's mother, the merchant's wife Sujātā, and his former wife. Thereupon, both Yasa's mother Sujātā and his former wife were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

Then Yasa's mother Sujātā and his former wife said, "Excellent, Venerable Sir! Excellent, Venerable Sir! It is as if, Venerable Sir, one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what had been hidden, or to take one by the hand and show the way to one who was lost, or to hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. In the same way, the Blessed One has revealed the Dhamma in many ways. Venerable Sir, we both go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May the Blessed One accept us as female lay followers (upāsikā) who have taken refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts." Thus they took the supramundane refuge. (Yasa's mother Sujātā and his former wife were the very first in the world to become female lay followers...)
520:
...they became female lay followers (upāsikā) who were established in the Three Refuges and had attained the stage of Sotāpanna.)

Then the mother, father, and former wife of the Venerable Yasa personally served the Blessed One and the Venerable Yasa with choice food with their own hands. Knowing that the Blessed One had finished His meal, they sat in a suitable place free from the six faults. The Blessed One then instructed and encouraged the mother, father, and former wife of the Venerable Yasa with a Dhamma discourse, after which He rose from His seat and departed for the Isipatana Migadāya forest.

(In this regard, the reason the Blessed One preached to Yasa’s mother and former wife before the meal was that they were pierced with grief due to Yasa’s ordination. If they were not joyful, they would not be able to give alms properly, might feel resentment toward the Blessed One, and would not be able to attain the Path and Fruit. Therefore, the Blessed One preached first to remove their grief before accepting the meal—so it should be noted from the Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā.)

## The Ordination of Fifty-four Former Friends
## of the Venerable Yasa

In the city of Bārāṇasī, four young men of merchant families—Vimala, Subāhu, Puṇṇaji, and Gavampati—who were former friends of the Venerable Yasa during his lay life, heard the news that their friend Yasa had renounced his great wealth and become a monk...
521:
they reflected: "Our friend Yasa, a son of a good family, has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the yellow robes, and gone forth from the home life into homelessness. The Dhamma-Vinaya (the teaching and discipline) in which he has become a monk cannot be a low thing; it must surely be supreme. That monkhood itself cannot be a low thing; it must surely be supreme." Having thus reflected, the four merchant sons approached the Venerable Yasa, paid homage to him with respect, and stood in a suitable place.

Then the Venerable Yasa took those four merchant sons, who were his former friends from lay life, and approached the Buddha. After paying homage to the Buddha, he sat in a suitable place and addressed the Buddha: "Venerable Sir, these four—Vimala, Subāhu, Puṇṇaji, and Gavampati—are sons of good families descended from merchant lineages in Vārāṇasī. They were my former friends during my lay life. May the Blessed One instruct and admonish these four merchant sons who are my friends."

To these four merchant sons, the Buddha preached the gradual discourse, which is the noble path to the attainment of the Paths and Fruits, in the following order: (1) Dānakathā (Talk on Giving), (2) Sīlakathā (Talk on Virtue), (3) Saggakathā (Talk on Heaven), (4) Maggakathā (Talk on the Path), which includes Kāmānaṃ Ādīnava (The Danger of Sensual Pleasures) and
522:
Nekkhamme Ānisaṃsakathā (Talk on the Benefits of Renunciation). When the Buddha knew that the minds of those four were ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and clear, he preached to them the Sāmukkaṃsika Dhamma-desanā (the teaching unique to the Buddhas), which is the Four Noble Truths. Then those four merchant sons, the former friends of the Venerable Yasa, were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).

Having been established in the Fruit of Stream-entry, they requested the Buddha for the going forth (pabbajjā) and the full ordination (upasampadā), saying: "Venerable Sir, may we receive the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, may we receive the full ordination."

Then the Buddha, stretching out his golden hand, granted them the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination, saying: "Etha bhikkhavo—Come, monks! Receive the monkhood you have requested. The Dhamma is well-preached. Lead the holy life (brahmacariya) to make an end of suffering through the three higher paths."

As soon as the Buddha spoke these words, the four merchant sons were instantly adorned with the eight miraculously created requisites (iddhimaya-parikkhāra), each in its proper place. They appeared like elders of sixty years' standing and respectfully paid homage to the Buddha, having already become monks. Their lay appearance miraculously disappeared and was replaced by the appearance of monks. (The very act of the Buddha calling them with the words "Etha bhikkhavo" constituted the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination for those four merchant sons; there was no need for a formal ordination in a Sīmā.)
523:
After the four merchant sons had received the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination, the Buddha instructed and admonished those four monks with Dhamma talks. While being thus instructed and admonished, those four merchant-son monks soon became free from taints (āsavas) and attained Arahantship. When those four merchant sons became Arahants, the number of Arahants in the world of humans was eleven: the Buddha, the five monks of the group of five (pañcavaggiya), the Venerable Yasa, the Venerable Vimala, the Venerable Subāhu, the Venerable Puṇṇaji, and the Venerable Gavampati.

## The Renunciation of the Fifty Friends of the Venerable Yasa

At that time, fifty friends of the Venerable Yasa from the countryside (janapada), who were also sons of good families from long-standing lineages, heard the news that their friend, the merchant's son Yasa, had renounced his great wealth and entered the monkhood. They reflected: "Our friend Yasa, a son of a good family, has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the yellow robes, and gone forth from the home life into homelessness. The Dhamma-Vinaya of the Buddha in which he has become a monk cannot be a low thing; it must surely be supreme. That monkhood itself cannot be a low thing; it must surely be supreme."

Having thus reflected, those fifty former friends approached the Venerable Yasa, paid homage to him with respect, and stood in a suitable place.
524:
Then the Venerable Yasa took those fifty sons of good families from the countryside, who were his former friends from lay life, and approached the Buddha. After paying homage to the Buddha, he sat in a suitable place and addressed the Buddha: "Venerable Sir, these fifty sons of good families living in the countryside are from long-standing noble lineages. They were my former friends during my lay life. May the Blessed One instruct and admonish these fifty sons of good families who are my former friends."

To these fifty sons of good families, the Buddha preached the gradual discourse, which is the noble path to the attainment of the Paths and Fruits, in the following order: (1) Dānakathā, (2) Sīlakathā, (3) Saggakathā, (4) Maggakathā, which includes Kāmānaṃ Ādīnava and Nekkhamme Ānisaṃsakathā. When the Buddha knew that the minds of those fifty were ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and clear, he preached to them the Sāmukkaṃsika Dhamma-desanā, the Four Noble Truths. Then those fifty sons of good families, the former friends of the Venerable Yasa, were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala).

Having been established in the Fruit of Stream-entry, they requested the Buddha: "Venerable Sir,
525:
may we receive the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One, may we receive the full ordination."

When they requested the monkhood, the Buddha (in the same manner as before), stretching out his golden hand, granted them the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination, saying: "Etha bhikkhavo—Come, monks! Receive the monkhood you have requested. The Dhamma is well-preached. Lead the holy life to make an end of the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha) through the three higher paths."

As soon as the Buddha spoke these words, those fifty sons of good families were instantly adorned with the eight miraculously created requisites, each in its proper place. They appeared like elders of sixty years' standing and respectfully paid homage to the Buddha, having already become monks. Their lay appearance miraculously disappeared and was replaced by the appearance of monks. (The very act of the Buddha calling them with the words "Etha bhikkhavo" constituted the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination for those fifty sons of good families; there was no longer any need for a formal ordination in a Sīmā.)

After the fifty sons of good families had received the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination, the Buddha instructed and admonished those fifty monks with Dhamma talks. While being thus instructed and admonished, those fifty monks soon became free from taints and attained Arahantship. When those fifty sons of good families became Arahants, the number of Arahants in the world of humans, including the previous eleven, became sixty-one.
526:
## The Past Merit of Venerable Yasa and His Friends

In the distant past, fifty-five friends formed an association to perform voluntary charitable deeds. They lived by providing free funeral services for the destitute who had passed away. One day, they found the body of a destitute pregnant woman who had died and carried it to the cemetery for cremation.

Among those fifty-five charitable friends, fifty of them said to the other five, "You five please finish the cremation," and after assigning the task, they entered the village ahead of them.

Then, among the remaining five, the youth who was the leader (the future Yasa) used a stick to poke and turn the corpse while performing the cremation, and he attained the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā). That youth, the future Yasa, also spoke to the other four friends to alert them, saying, "Friends, look at this impure and loathsome corpse." Following the leader's words and demonstration, those four friends also attained the perception of foulness in that corpse.

After completing the cremation, when those five friends reached the village, they recounted the matter of the foulness as they had seen it to the fifty members who had gone ahead. Consequently, those fifty friends also attained the perception of foulness.
527:
The youth who was the leader, the future Yasa, did not stop at telling his friends; when he returned home, he also recounted the matter of the foulness to his mother, father, and his wife. Thus, his beneficent mother and father, as well as his wife, also attained the perception of foulness.

Those fifty-eight people, led by the future Yasa, took the perception of foulness they had attained as a foundation and continued to develop the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā). This was the past merit of those fifty-eight people.

Because of that past merit, in his present life as the son of a wealthy merchant in Vārāṇasī, the perception of a cemetery arose in Venerable Yasa regarding the female dancers. It was because they were endowed with the supporting condition (upanissaya) of the merit from the meditation on foulness practiced in that past life that those fifty-eight people attained the extraordinary Dhamma of the Path and Fruit (Magga-Phala).

The account of the son of the merchant Yasa entering the monkhood ends.
**********
## Chapter 13
## Sending the Sixty Arahants on Mission

After becoming the Buddha, the Blessed One spent the first rainy season (vassa) in the Isipatana Deer Park. He stayed in that Deer Park until the full moon day of Thadingyut (Pavāraṇā). One day, the Blessed One called the sixty Arahants and said:
528:
“Monks, I am released from all snares, both those of the devas and those of humans, which are the snares of craving and greed dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure. Monks, you too are released from all snares, both those of the devas and those of humans, which are the snares of craving and greed dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure.

Monks, go forth for the welfare and benefit of many beings—humans, devas, and Brahmas—and for their mundane and supramundane happiness, wandering through the eight directions (setting a maximum of one yojana per day). Do not two of you go by a single way (for if two monks go together on one path, while one preaches, the other would have to sit idly in silence).

Monks, preach the Dhamma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, complete in meaning and phrasing. Proclaim to devas and humans the holy life (brahmacariya), which is the training of the three—virtue, concentration, and wisdom—which is entirely complete, without excess or deficiency, and pure from the stains of misconduct.”
529:
“Monks, there are beings—humans, devas, and Brahmas—with little dust of defilements in their eyes. If they do not hear the Dhamma, they will perish from attaining the extraordinary Dhamma of the Path and Fruit. There will certainly appear devas and humans who will clearly understand the profound nature of the Dhamma.

Monks, I too (will not remain in this Deer Park merely to have monasteries built and to receive the four requisites from lay supporters; rather...) will go to Senānigama in the Uruvelā forest to liberate and preach to the thousand matted-hair ascetics.”

Thus he spoke the words of the mission.

(Special Note: Among the five paragraphs of the speech mentioned, regarding the phrase in the third paragraph, “excellent in the beginning, middle, and end,” there are two types of excellence (kalyāṇa): the excellence of the Dispensation (Sāsana) and the excellence of the Teaching (Desanā).

Of these two, virtue (sīla) is called the excellence in the beginning of the Sāsana; calm (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and the four Path-knowledges are called the excellence in the middle of the Sāsana; the four Fruits and Nibbāna are called the excellence in the end of the Sāsana. (Alternatively) Virtue and concentration are the beginning; insight-knowledge and Path-knowledge are the middle; Fruit and Nibbāna are the end. (Alternatively) Virtue, concentration, and insight-knowledge are the beginning; the four Paths are the middle; the four Fruits and Nibbāna are the end.
530:
Regarding the excellence of the Teaching (Desanā): if it is a verse of four lines (pāda), the first line is the beginning, the second and third lines are the middle, and the fourth line is the end. If it is a verse of five or six lines, the first line is the beginning, the last (fifth or sixth) line is the end, and the remaining (third and fourth) lines are the middle. If it is a Sutta with only one sequence of connection, the introduction (nidāna) is the beginning, the concluding phrase starting with 'Idamavoca' is the end, and the remaining body of text is the middle. If it is a Sutta with many sequences of connection, the introduction is the beginning, the concluding phrase starting with 'Idamavoca' is the end, and the many intermediate sequences are the middle. It refers to the Dhamma teachings, verses, or Suttas that express one, two, or all three types of the Sāsana's excellence.)

## Māra Coming to Interfere

When the Blessed One spoke these words of the mission to the sixty Arahants, Māra the Evil One thought, "This Great Ascetic Gotama is sending out sixty Arahant heroes, the commanders of the Sāsana, saying, 'Do not two of you go by a single way; preach the Dhamma,' as if he were organizing a great battle. If even one of these sixty preaches the Dhamma, my mind will not be at ease. How could it be possible if sixty Arahants preach as the Great Ascetic Gotama has arranged? I shall go and hinder that Great Ascetic Gotama right now." Having thus planned, he approached the Blessed One and said:
531:
Baddhosi sabba-pāsehi,
ye dibbā ye ca mānusā.
Mahābandhana-baddhosi,
na me samaṇa mokkhasi.

"O Ascetic Gotama, you are caught and bound by all the snares of craving and greed, both those of the devas and those of humans, which are the snares of defilements. You are also one who is tied by the bonds of defilements in the prison of the three realms of existence. O Ascetic Gotama, (for the reasons mentioned) you will by no means escape from my domain, the three realms of existence."

Thinking, "If I speak thus, this Great Ascetic will not make an effort for other beings to escape from Saṃsāra," he spoke these words of hindrance.

Then the Blessed One (wishing to show that Māra's words and his own reality were as far apart as the sky and the earth, and as directly opposed as fire and water) replied to Māra:

Muttāhaṃ sabba-pāsehi,
ye dibbā ye ca mānusā.
Mahābandhana-mutto'mhi,
nihato tvamasi antaka.

"You vile and wicked Mara, the False Killer! I, the Buddha, am completely released from all the snares of craving and greed, both those of the devas and those of humans.
532:
I am also completely released from the great bonds of defilements in the prison of the three realms of existence. In this battle of defilements, I have conquered you once and for all. (You are the great loser)."

When he spoke these bold words, Māra spoke again:

Antalikkha-caro pāso,
yvāyaṃ carati mānaso.
Tena taṃ bādhayissāmi,
na me samaṇa mokkhasi.

"O Ascetic Gotama, that snare of lust (rāga) which arises in the inner minds of beings can bind even those who possess direct knowledge (abhiññā) and attainments (jhāna) and can fly through the air. I will bind and oppress you with that snare of lust. O Ascetic Gotama, you will by no means escape from my domain, the three realms of existence."

Then the Blessed One replied:

Rūpā saddā rasā gandhā,
phoṭṭhabbā ca manoramā.
Ettha me vigato chando,
nihato tvamasi antaka.

(Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and touches that are pleasing; my desire for these is gone. I have defeated you, Ender.)
533:
“O vile and wicked Māra, the murderer! In this world, there exist the five cords of sensual pleasure—various sights, sounds, tastes, smells, and touches—which can cause the hearts of devas and humans to rejoice and be delighted. (Only those who are not free from craving and greed, who pursue and are attached to those five cords of sensual pleasure, can you bind with your snare of passion.) As for me, the Buddha, the craving, greed, and lustful desire that pursue and delight in these five cords of sensual pleasure have been entirely eradicated. (Therefore, in this battle of defilements,) I have conquered you once and for all. (You have suffered a great defeat.)”

When these bold and fiery words were spoken, the Māra-deva—who had initially spoken thinking, “Will he withdraw and give up, thinking a powerful deva has come to forbid him?”—realized upon the Buddha’s declaration, “O Māra, I have conquered you once and for all,” that: “The Blessed One knows me; the Well-Spoken One knows me.” Feeling unhappy and dejected, both physically and mentally, he vanished from that very spot.

## Permission for Ordination by the Three Refuges
## The Reason for Granting Permission

(At that time of the first rainy season, when the Blessed One sent forth the monks to propagate the Dhamma, it was a time when
534:
residence during the rainy season (vassa) had not yet been prescribed for the monks. Therefore,) when the Blessed One sent the monks on their missionary journeys, the monks, thinking, “The Blessed One himself will grant the 'Going Forth' (pabbajjā) and the 'Admission' (upasampadā) to these candidates,” would bring candidates who wished to go forth and be ordained from various regions and various districts to the presence of the Blessed One. In doing so, both the monks who brought them and the candidates themselves became extremely weary, exhausted, and fatigued.

(When the missionary monks preached the Dhamma, not only those endowed with the past merit to become 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks, but also those not so endowed would develop the desire to go forth and be ordained. It was not the custom of the Buddhas to personally ordain those who lacked the past merit for 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination. Therefore, as the number of candidates—both those worthy and unworthy of being called 'Ehi Bhikkhu'—increased and became mixed, the Blessed One wished to prescribe the procedure for ordination for those not eligible for 'Ehi Bhikkhu' status.) The Blessed One then had this thought: “At present, the monks are bringing candidates from various regions and districts to me, thinking, 'The Blessed One himself will grant them the Going Forth and the Admission.' Consequently, those
535:
monks and the candidates are becoming extremely weary, exhausted, and fatigued. It would be well if I were to grant permission to the monks, saying: 'Monks, from now on, you yourselves may grant the Going Forth and the Admission to those candidates who wish for it in those various regions and districts.'”

Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from his solitary seclusion and delivered a suitable and appropriate Dhamma discourse concerning that matter. After relating the thought that had occurred to him during his solitary seclusion during the day, he said: “Monks, from now on, you yourselves may grant the Going Forth and the Admission to those candidates who wish for it in those various regions and districts. I allow you (my dear sons) to grant the Going Forth and the Admission yourselves.

Monks, the Going Forth and the Admission should be granted in this way: First, the hair and beard must be shaved off. Then, the candidate must be made to don the saffron-dyed robes. Then, having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder (= making them pay respects), having made them prostrate at the feet of the monks, having made them sit in a squatting position, and having made them raise their joined hands (añjali), you should instruct them to say:

Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.
Dutiyampi Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Dutiyampi Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Dutiyampi Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi.
536:
Tatiyampi buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Tatiyampi dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Tatiyampi saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi—
(The Three Refuges must be administered in this way.)

"Monks, I allow you to give the going-forth (pabbajjā) and the full ordination (upasampadā) by these three refuges," the Blessed One declared.

(In this context, giving the going-forth and full ordination consists of: (1) Shaving the hair and beard = kesacchedana, (2) Donning the saffron-dyed robes = kāsāyacchādana, (3) Giving the refuges = saraṇadāna. These three constitute the process.)

## Māra’s Second Visit and
## His Words of Obstruction

Then the Blessed One, having resided in the Isipatana Migadāya forest for the four months of the rainy season until the full moon day of Kattikā, called the monks together and said:

"Monks, I am delivered from all snares, both celestial and human. By right attention and right effort, I have attained and reached the unsurpassed Fruit of Arahatship. I have realized the unsurpassed Fruit of Arahatship (and frequently enter the attainment of the Fruit of Arahatship). Monks, you too, through right attention and right effort, attain and reach the unsurpassed Fruit of Arahatship..."
537:
(constantly enter the attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship).”

(This exhortation was given so that the monks would not fall into the habit of discouragement carried over from their lives as worldlings, thinking, “We are Arahants whose taints are exhausted; what benefit is there for us in further practice? There will be no further special benefit.” It was to prevent them from retreating and to encourage them to spend their time in the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) in forest dwellings on the outskirts of towns and villages, and also so that other monks, seeing these Arahants in such attainment, might follow their example (diṭṭhānugati).)

Then, the Māra-deva approached the Buddha and said:

Baddhosi mārapāsehi,
ye dibbā ye ca mānusā.
Mahābandhanabaddhosi,
na me samaṇa mokkhasi.

“O Ascetic Gotama, you are bound by the snare of craving and greed connected to divine sensual pleasures, and by the snare of craving and greed connected to human sensual pleasures. You are bound by these snares of defilements. You are also tied by the bonds of defilements in the prison of the three realms of existence. O Ascetic Gotama, (for the reasons stated) you shall by no means escape from my domain, the three realms of existence.”

Thus did he speak words of obstruction.
538:
Then the Blessed One (wishing to show Māra that his claims and the Buddha's reality were as far apart as the sky and the earth, and as diametrically opposed as fire and water) addressed him:

Muttāhaṃ mārapāsehi,
ye dibbā ye ca mānusā.
Mahābandhanamuttomhi,
nihato tvamasi antaka.

“O Māra, I am completely liberated from the snare of craving and greed connected to divine sensual pleasures, and from the snare of craving and greed connected to human sensual pleasures. It is true that I am also entirely liberated from the great bonds of defilements in the prison of the three realms of existence. In this battle of defilements, I have conquered you once and for all; I have slain you so that you are utterly defeated. (You are the great loser.)”

Thus did he speak these bold and fiery words. Then Māra, realizing, “The Blessed One knows me; the Well-Spoken One knows me,” vanished from that very spot, feeling unhappy and dejected, both physically and mentally.

The account of Māra’s second attempt to obstruct is finished.
539:
## The Ordination of the Thirty Princes
## of the Bhaddavaggiya Group

(For the Blessed Ones residing in any place, there is no lack of delight or dissatisfaction based on the deficiency of shade, shelter, water, or the hardship of living, nor based on the lack of faith among the local people. Likewise, they do not stay long in a place thinking, "We live happily here," based on the abundance of shade, shelter, water, or the faith of the people. Indeed, the Blessed One resides in a place only with the intention (āsaya) of establishing beings in the Three Refuges, the five, eight, or ten precepts, or in the monkhood, provided there is the sufficing condition (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruit and special merit. After liberating those who are to be liberated, and when there are no more such beings, it is the natural custom of the Buddhas to depart for another place.)

Then the Blessed One, having stayed in the Isipatana Migadāya forest of Bārāṇasī until His wish to liberate the five monks of the group of five and others was fulfilled, took His bowl and robes and departed alone...
540: While traveling on the journey to the Uruvelā forest, the Buddha entered a forest named Kappāsika and stayed at the foot of a certain tree. At that time, thirty brothers and friends of the princes known as the Bhaddavaggiya (so named because they were handsome, virtuous, and traveled and lived together as a group) were enjoying themselves in that Kappāsika forest, each accompanied by his wife. One of the princes, who had no wife, had brought along a prostitute by paying her a fee. While those princes were indulging in drink and were heedless, the hired prostitute stole their belongings and fled. Then, those friends, out of concern for their companion's matter, wandered through the Kappāsika forest searching for the missing woman. Seeing the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a tree, they approached him and (without yet paying homage) asked, "Venerable Blessed One, have you seen a woman?" The Blessed One asked, "Princes, what business do you have with a woman?" They replied, "Venerable Blessed One, we thirty friends of the Bhaddavaggiya group were enjoying ourselves in this Kappāsika forest with our respective wives. One friend, having no wife, brought a prostitute by paying her a fee..."
541: "...While we were indulging in drink and were heedless, that prostitute stole our belongings and fled. We, being friends, are wandering through this Kappāsika forest searching for that missing woman out of concern for our companion's matter." Then the Blessed One asked, "Princes, which do you think is better for you: seeking the missing woman or seeking yourselves?" They replied, "Venerable Blessed One, for us, seeking ourselves is indeed superior." "Princes, if that is so, then sit down; I shall preach the Dhamma to you," the Blessed One said. They replied, "Very well, Venerable Sir," and the thirty Bhaddavaggiya friends respectfully paid homage to the Blessed One and sat in a suitable place free from the six faults. To those thirty Bhaddavaggiya friends, the Blessed One preached the progressive discourse (anupubbīkathā) which is the noble path to the attainment of the Paths and Fruits, in the same manner as previously mentioned: (1) Discourse on Giving (dāna-kathā), (2) Discourse on Virtue (sīla-kathā), (3) Discourse on Heaven (sagga-kathā), (4) Discourse on the Path (magga-kathā) consisting of the discourse on the danger of sensual pleasures (kāmānaṃ ādīnava) and the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma-ānisaṃsa). When the Blessed One knew that the thirty princes had minds that were ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and clear...
542: ...knowing their state of mind, the Blessed One preached to those thirty princes the Sāmukkaṃsika Dhamma-desanā (the teaching peculiar to the Buddhas), namely the Four Noble Truths. Thereupon, among those thirty Bhaddavaggiya friends, some were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), some in the Fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-phala), and some in the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala). (Not a single one remained a worldling.) Having been established in their respective fruits of Sotāpatti, Sakadāgāmi, and Anāgāmi, the thirty Bhaddavaggiya friends requested the Blessed One, "Venerable Blessed One, may we receive the novice ordination and the higher ordination in the presence of the Blessed One." The Blessed One, in the same manner as before, extended his golden hand and called them with the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' formula: "Etha bhikkhavo—Come, monks! Receive the ordination you have requested. The Dhamma has been well-preached by me; practice the noble life (brahmacariya) to make an end of suffering through the higher paths." As soon as he called them, the thirty Bhaddavaggiya friends were instantly adorned with miraculously created requisites (iddhimaya-parikkhāra) in their proper places, looking like elders of sixty years' standing. They respectfully paid homage to the Blessed One, having already become monks. Their wondrous human appearance vanished, and they were transformed into the appearance of monks. (The very act of the Blessed One calling them with 'Ehi bhikkhavo' constituted the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination for those thirty princes. There was no further need for a formal assembly in a Sīmā.)
543:
(In this regard, those thirty princes were the thirty drunkards in the Tuṇḍila Jātaka of the Chakkanipāta. At that time, they listened to the exhortation of the Bodhisatta, the Great Tuṇḍila Pig King, and observed the five precepts well. This observance of the five precepts was the prior merit for these thirty princes to realize the Four Noble Truths together in this life. Apart from observing the five precepts together, they also had significant merits tending toward liberation (vivaṭṭanissita-kusala) from listening to the Dhamma, taking refuge, giving alms, keeping precepts, and practicing Samatha and Vipassanā meditation under previous Buddhas. Therefore, on the very day they met the Blessed One, they were endowed with special qualities such as attaining the lower Paths and Fruits and receiving the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination.

These thirty Bhaddavaggiya monks were half-brothers of King Pasenadi of Kosala. Because they mostly resided in the city of Pāveyya in the western part of the Kosala kingdom, they are known in the Pāḷi texts as the "Pāveyyaka" monks. It was on their account that the Blessed One later allowed the Kathina robe. These thirty Pāveyyaka Bhaddavaggiya monks later attained Arahatship while the Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha, after hearing the Anamatagga Dhamma discourse found in the Tiṃsamatta Sutta, second chapter of the Anamatagga Saṃyutta (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1, 394).)

## Chapter 14
## The Liberation of the One Thousand Hermit Brothers

After the Blessed One had established the thirty Bhaddavaggiya princes in the three lower Paths and Fruits and they had become monks...
544: ...and having converted them, he traveled by stages and arrived at the Uruvelā forest. At that time, three matted-hair ascetic brothers were living in the Uruvelā forest: (1) Uruvela Kassapa (the eldest), (2) Nadī Kassapa (the middle brother), and (3) Gayā Kassapa (the youngest). Among them, the ascetic Uruvela Kassapa was the leader and teacher of five hundred ascetic disciples. The ascetic Nadī Kassapa was the leader and teacher of three hundred ascetic disciples. The ascetic Gayā Kassapa was the leader and teacher of two hundred ascetic disciples. Then the Blessed One went to the hermitage of the ascetic Uruvela Kassapa and said, "O Kassapa, if it is not a burden to you, I would like to stay for one night in your fire-chamber." The ascetic Uruvela Kassapa replied, "O Great Samana, it is no burden to me. (However, I wish to inform you that) in this fire-chamber, there is a serpent king of great power, fierce, venomous, and swift. I do not want that serpent king to harm or oppress you, Great Samana." When the Blessed One requested a second time and a third time in the same manner, Uruvela Kassapa replied as before, saying it was no burden to himself, but he was concerned that the serpent king in the fire-chamber, who was of great power, swift, and venomous, would harm or oppress the Blessed One.
545: When the Blessed One requested for the fourth time, saying, "O Kassapa, that serpent king certainly cannot harm or oppress me; I only urge you to give me permission to stay in the fire-chamber," Uruvela Kassapa replied, "O Great Samana, stay as comfortably as you wish." Having received permission from the ascetic Uruvela Kassapa, the Blessed One entered the fire-chamber, spread a small grass mat, and sat down cross-legged, keeping his body erect and establishing mindfulness directed toward the object of meditation. When the serpent king saw the Blessed One entering the fire-chamber, he became extremely angry and (intending to destroy the Blessed One into fine powder like chaff and ash) emitted clouds of smoke toward the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One thought, "It would be well if I, without harming or hurting this serpent's outer skin, inner skin, flesh, sinews, bones, or marrow, were to overwhelm and extinguish its power with my own power." Having resolved not to harm or hurt any part of the serpent king's body, the Blessed One exercised his psychic power and emitted smoke even more intense than that of the serpent king. The serpent king, unable to restrain his anger, then emitted flames of fire. The Blessed One also entered the Tejokasiṇa-jhāna (meditative absorption on the fire-device) and emitted even larger and more intense flames of fire.
546:
The whole fire-chamber seemed to be ablaze with the great flames of both the Buddha and the Naga. Then, the matted-hair ascetics led by the teacher Uruvela Kassapa surrounded the fire-chamber and spoke with concern: "O friends, the Great Ascetic, who is so beautiful, is indeed being tormented by the Naga King."

Then, when the night had passed and dawn broke, the Blessed One, without harming or hurting any part of the Naga King's body, subdued the Naga King's power with His own psychic power. Placing the Naga King in His alms-bowl, He said to the teacher Uruvela Kassapa, "O Kassapa, here is your Naga. Its power has been subdued by my power." He then showed the Naga to the teacher Uruvela Kassapa. At that, the teacher Uruvela Kassapa thought:

"The Great Ascetic is indeed of great power and majesty, for he can subdue the power of the Naga King, who is of fierce and swift poison, with his own power. Yet, although he is of such great power and majesty, he is not an Arahant like me."

Then, the teacher Uruvela Kassapa, being greatly impressed by this first miracle of subduing the Naga King, invited the Blessed One, saying: "O Great Ascetic, please stay and reside in this very place. I..."
547:
"...will always provide you, Great Ascetic, with regular offerings of food."

The first chapter on the display of miracles is finished.

Thereafter, the Blessed One stayed in a certain forest grove near the hermitage of the teacher Uruvela Kassapa. Then, when the first watch of the night had passed and it was midnight, the Four Great Kings, possessing a most pleasing appearance, illuminating the entire forest grove with their radiance, approached the Blessed One. Having paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, they stood in the four directions, surrounding Him like four great masses of fire.

Then, when the night had passed and dawn broke, the teacher Uruvela Kassapa came to the Blessed One and said: "O Great Ascetic, it is time for the meal; the food is ready. Please come for the meal. O Great Ascetic, who were those who, when the first watch of the night had passed and it was midnight, possessing a most pleasing appearance and illuminating the entire forest grove with their radiance, approached you, paid respectful homage to you, and stood in the four directions surrounding you like four great masses of fire?"

The Blessed One replied: "O Kassapa, those four whom you ask about are the Four Great Kings. They approached me to hear the Dhamma."
548:
When this was said to the teacher Uruvela Kassapa, he thought:

"Even the Four Great Kings come to this Great Ascetic to hear the Dhamma. Thus, this Great Ascetic is indeed of great power and majesty. Yet, although he is of such great power and majesty, he is not an Arahant like me."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in the mind of the teacher Uruvela Kassapa, yet remaining patient (as his faculties were not yet mature), partook of the food offered by the teacher Uruvela Kassapa and continued to stay in that forest grove.

The second chapter on the display of miracles is finished.

Then, when the first watch of the night had passed and it was midnight, Sakka, the King of Devas, possessing a most pleasing appearance, illuminating the entire forest grove with his radiance, approached the Blessed One. Having paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, he stood in a suitable place, his radiance surpassing that of the previous Four Great Kings, being delightful and exceptionally noble, like a great and brilliant mass of fire.

Then, when the night had passed and dawn broke, the teacher Uruvela Kassapa came to the Blessed One...
549:
...and said: "O Great Ascetic, it is time for the meal; the food is ready. Please come for the meal. O Great Ascetic, who was he who, when the first watch of the night had passed and it was midnight, possessing a most pleasing appearance and illuminating the entire forest grove with his radiance, approached you, paid respectful homage to you, and stood in a suitable place, his radiance surpassing that of the previous Four Great Kings, being delightful and exceptionally noble, like a great and brilliant mass of fire?"

The Blessed One replied: "O Kassapa, he whom you ask about is Sakka, the King of Devas. He approached me to hear the Dhamma."

When this was said to the teacher Uruvela Kassapa, he thought:

"Even Sakka, the King of Devas, comes to this Great Ascetic to hear the Dhamma. Thus, this Great Ascetic is indeed of great power and majesty. Yet, although he is of such great power and majesty, he is not an Arahant like me."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in the mind of the teacher Uruvela Kassapa, yet waiting for the time when his faculties would mature and remaining patient, partook of the food offered by the teacher Uruvela Kassapa...
550:
...and continued to stay in that forest grove.

The third chapter on the display of miracles is finished.

Then, when the first watch of the night had passed and it was midnight, Sahampati Brahmā, possessing a most pleasing appearance, illuminating the entire forest grove with his radiance, approached the Blessed One. Having paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, he stood in a suitable place, his radiance surpassing that of the previous Four Great Kings and Sakka, being delightful and exceptionally noble, like a great and brilliant mass of fire.

Then, when the night had passed and dawn broke, the teacher Uruvela Kassapa came to the Blessed One and said: "O Great Ascetic, it is time for the meal; the food is ready. Please come for the meal. O Great Ascetic, who was he who, when the first watch of the night had passed and it was midnight, possessing a most pleasing appearance and illuminating the entire forest grove with his radiance, approached you, paid respectful homage to you, and stood in a suitable place, his radiance surpassing that of the previous Four Great Kings and Sakka, being delightful and exceptionally noble, like a great and brilliant mass of fire?"

The Blessed One...
551:
...replied: "O Kassapa, he whom you ask about is Sahampati Brahmā. He approached me to hear the Dhamma."

When this was said to the teacher Uruvela Kassapa, he thought:

"Even Sahampati Brahmā comes to this Great Ascetic to hear the Dhamma. Thus, this Great Ascetic is indeed of great power and majesty. Yet, although he is of such great power and majesty, he is not an Arahant like me."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in the mind of the teacher Uruvela Kassapa, yet waiting for the time when his faculties would mature and remaining patient, partook of the food offered by the teacher Uruvela Kassapa and continued to stay in that forest grove.

The fourth chapter on the display of miracles is finished.

In this manner, while the Blessed One was staying in the Uruvela forest, the people of the Anga and Magadha regions used to organize a great monthly sacrifice to honor and make offerings to the teacher Uruvela Kassapa. When the day of that great sacrifice arrived, on the day before, they were preparing various kinds of food and provisions (to go to the teacher Uruvela Kassapa at dawn)...
552:
...and were making arrangements to go and pay homage. Then, the teacher Uruvela Kassapa thought:

"Now a great sacrifice for me is about to take place and is being prepared. (When dawn breaks), all the people of Anga and Magadha will come to my hermitage bringing many kinds of food and provisions. If, when those people have assembled, the Great Ascetic (being one of great power and majesty) performs a great miracle in their midst, the people will be greatly impressed by him. Then, the gains and honor for the Great Ascetic will increase day by day. For me, however, (as their faith and devotion will decrease), my gains and honor will diminish and decline day by day. Therefore, it would be good if the Great Ascetic, being considerate, does not come to my hermitage for the meal tomorrow."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the thought in Uruvela Kassapa's mind with His own mind through the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariya-abhiññā), went to the northern continent of Uttarakuru. Having received alms-food from that northern continent, He partook of the meal near Lake Anotatta in the Himalayas and spent the day in the sandalwood forest near that lake.
553: (According to the Mahāvaṃsa: In the evening, knowing that it would be the place where the Sāsana would shine in the future, the Buddha traveled alone to the island of Sīhaḷa, known as Lankādīpa. After subduing and teaching the yakkhas, he granted a handful of hair relics to the Great Deva Sumana for perpetual worship.) Then, before dawn the next day, he returned to the Uruvela forest and resided there as before. When it was time for the morning meal the following day, the matted-hair ascetic Uruvela Kassapa approached the Blessed One and said: "O Great Ascetic, it is time for the meal; the food is prepared. At that time, the great earth shook, the sky thundered...

## Analysis of Antaraṭṭhaka

‘Antaraṭṭhaka’ means “the eight days in between” (the period of eight days occurring in the interval). If this term ‘Antaraṭṭhaka’ is compared and analyzed with the term ‘Aṣṭakā’ found in Sanskrit texts, the following meaning is obtained.
565:
“Aṣṭakā refers to (1) the offering and worship dedicated to deceased parents, grandparents, etc., and (2) the day of such offering and worship,” as defined in Vācaspati (1, 516) and Kappaduma (1, 148).

Among the many traditions regarding the ritual of this offering and the designation of the day for worship, some traditions for designating the day are as follows:

(1) “Tadapī phussamāghaphagguṇānaṃ kaṇhapakkhasattamyādīsu kattabbaṃ = That (special offering and worship dedicated to deceased parents, grandparents, etc., completed over a period of three days) should be performed on the seventh day, etc., of the waning fortnight of the months of Phussa, Māgha, and Phagguṇa,” as cited from the Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra in Vācaspati (1, 516).

(2) “Aṣṭakā (feminine) phussamāghaphagguṇānaṃ kaṇhapakkhaaṣṭamī = Aṣṭakā refers to the eighth day of the waning fortnight of the months of Phussa, Māgha, and Phagguṇa,” as stated in the Sanskrit Śabdakostubha Dictionary (100).

## Interjection

“In the months of Phussa and Māgha, when silver mist soaks the air with gentle breezes, between these two months (1); and likewise between Māgha and Phagguṇa, four days each before and after (2); designated as Antaraṭṭh, during these eight nights, at the break of dawn with radiant light, the shivering cold is extreme and constant.” This composition in the Maghadeva Laṅkā Thit, stanza (280), is to be considered as to whether it is based on the two aforementioned traditions.
566: (3) "Atrāyaṃ bhedo.. hemantasisirānaṃ catunnamaparapakkhānamaṭṭhamīsvatṭhakā ekassāṃ vā = Here, this is the distinction.. the Aṣṭakā (offering to deceased parents, grandparents, etc.) should be performed on the eighth days of the four waning fortnights of the Hemanta and Sisira seasons (the four months of winter), or on the eighth day of one waning fortnight," as stated in the Āśvalāyana Sūtra cited in Vācaspatya (1, 517). (4) "Aṣṭakā is the eighth day after the full moon (specifically, the eighth day after the full moon during the four winter months of Hemanta and Sisira, on which ancestors or the deceased are worshipped)," as found in Williams' Sanskrit-English Dictionary (117). According to the two traditions shown in (3) and (4), it is clear that there are four types of Aṣṭakā days in the two seasons (the four months of winter): two Aṣṭakā days in the Hemanta season (the 8th waning day of Kattika and the 8th waning day of Māgasira) and two Aṣṭakā days in the Sisira season (the 8th waning day of Phussa and the 8th waning day of Māgha). In the same way, the Antaraṭṭhaka days mentioned in the religious texts should also be of four types within the four months of winter. However, in the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries...
567:
567
“Antaraṭṭhaka refers to the eight days between two months, specifically the last four days of the month of Tabodwe and the first four days of the month of Tabaung”—
This is the unanimous interpretation given by the commentators.

Among these interpretations, one must consider whether some are literal (mukha) and others are figurative or metaphorical (upacāra pariyāya).

In particular, regarding the Antaraṭṭhaka mentioned in the context of the conversion of the thousand ascetics (Sārattha, 3, 207), one should reflect on whether it is a figurative interpretation. Within such an interpretation, it remains to be considered whether it was intended to be understood through the methods of synecdoche (upalakkhaṇa), illustration (nidassana), or inclusive indication (antadīpaka).

Indeed, the author of the Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā was well aware of the passages in the Jātaka Commentary (Jā-aṭṭha, 1, 100) and the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary (Buddhavaṃsa-aṭṭha, 5), which explain that the Buddha arrived at the city of Rājagaha on the full moon day of Pyatho. He was also aware of the passage in the Majjhima Commentary (Ma-aṭṭha, 3, 145-6), which explains that the Venerable Sāriputta attained Arahantship on the full moon day of Tabodwe. Despite this knowledge, his definition of the Antaraṭṭhaka days as “the eight days between Tabodwe and Tabaung” in relation to the conversion of the thousand ascetics suggests even more strongly that it is an interpretation intended to be understood through the three aforementioned methods.

If interpreted in this way, the specific phrase “the eight days between the two months, being the last four days of Tabodwe and the first four days of Tabaung, occurring within the winter season (Hemanta),” which describes a part, a specific instance, or the end, is used to represent the whole, including the other three types of Antaraṭṭhaka days (nights) that occur or could occur during the four months of winter. Thus, by that phrase alone—
568:
568
(1) The eight nights between the end of Tazaungmon and the beginning of Nadaw (four days each), (2) The eight nights between the end of Nadaw and the beginning of Pyatho (four days each), (3) The eight nights between the end of Pyatho and the beginning of Tabodwe (four days each), and (4) The eight nights between the end of Tabodwe and the beginning of Tabaung (four days each)—
All these four types of Antaraṭṭhaka days (nights) are thus encompassed.

Among these four types of Antaraṭṭhaka, if one analyzes “which Antaraṭṭhaka should be the one related to the conversion of the thousand ascetics while the Buddha was dwelling in the Uruvelā forest”—

According to the Majjhima Commentary (Ma-aṭṭha, 3, 146), it is explained that “the Venerable Sāriputta became an Arahant on the full moon day of Tabodwe.” Therefore, the Antaraṭṭhaka marked as (4), between the end of Tabodwe and the beginning of Tabaung, is not possible.

Furthermore, since the Jātaka Commentary (Jā-aṭṭha, 1, 100) and the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary (Buddhavaṃsa-aṭṭha, 5) state that “the Buddha arrived at the city of Rājagaha on the full moon day of Pyatho,” the Antaraṭṭhaka marked as (3), between the end of Pyatho and the beginning of Tabodwe, is also not possible.
569:
569
If that is the case, which Antaraṭṭhaka could it be? Upon deep reflection—

In both the Jātaka Commentary (Jā-aṭṭha, 1, 100) and the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary (Buddhavaṃsa-aṭṭha, 5), it is stated that after attaining Enlightenment, the Buddha spent the first Vassa at the Migadāvana forest in Bārāṇasī. After the Vassa, He journeyed to the Uruvelā forest and dwelt there for three months, during which He disciplined and converted the thousand ascetics led by the three brothers. Therefore, within that three-month period of residence, only one of the two types of Antaraṭṭhaka could be possible: either (1) the Antaraṭṭhaka between the end of Tazaungmon and the beginning of Nadaw, or (2) the Antaraṭṭhaka between the end of Nadaw and the beginning of Pyatho.

Between these two, the second Antaraṭṭhaka—the eight nights comprising the four days before and after the transition from Nadaw to Pyatho—is the most likely to be the one in this context.

Only by deciding, accepting, and believing that the Antaraṭṭhaka mentioned in the conversion of the thousand ascetics refers to “the eight nights between the end of Nadaw and the beginning of Pyatho” will the following accounts be consistent and without contradiction: the Buddha’s itinerary from the end of Vassa until the month of Tabaung as found in Jā-aṭṭha (1, 100) and Buddhavaṃsa-aṭṭha (5); the “day the Venerable Sāriputta became an Arahant” as found in the Dīghanakha Sutta (Ma, 3, 168) and its commentary (Ma-aṭṭha, 3, 146); and the
570:
570
“Antaraṭṭhaka days” mentioned in the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pāḷi (Vi, 3, 41) and its sub-commentary, the Sāratthadīpanī (Sārattha, 3, 207).

This concludes the analysis of the Antaraṭṭhaka.

571
When asked, the Buddha replied, “Yes, Kassapa, it is I,” and while the ascetics were watching, He rose into the air and descended to stand upon their boat. Then the elder ascetic Uruvelā Kassapa thought:

“Even the swift-flowing torrent of the river cannot carry away this Great Ascetic. Thus, this Great Ascetic possesses great power and majesty. However, even though he is so powerful and majestic, he is not yet an Arahant whose taints are exhausted like me.”

## The Ordination of the Elder Uruvelā Kassapa and His Five Hundred Disciples

In the preceding days, the Buddha had been waiting for the spiritual faculties (indriya) of those ascetics to mature. He had patiently endured their condescension for nearly three months. Now, as their faculties had matured, He would speak to them openly and clearly to discipline and convert them.

Even though He had displayed the miracle of not being submerged by the flood, the elder ascetic Uruvelā Kassapa, as before, wrongly thought that only he was an Arahant whose taints were exhausted, while the Buddha was not. At that moment, the Buddha thought:
572:
572
“(If I remain indifferent,) this vain man (Uruvelā Kassapa), who is far from the Path and Fruit, will continue for a long time to have the wrong thought: ‘This Great Ascetic has great power and majesty, yet he is not an Arahant whose taints are exhausted like me.’ It would be well if I were now to cause this ascetic Uruvelā Kassapa to feel spiritual urgency (saṃvega).”

Having had this thought, He spoke to the elder ascetic Uruvelā Kassapa with these three clear and direct statements:

“O Kassapa, (1) You are not an Arahant whose taints are exhausted; (2) You are not one who has reached the Path of Arahantship; (3) (Let alone reaching it,) you do not even have the right practice to reach the Path and Fruit of Arahantship.”

Upon hearing these words, the elder ascetic Uruvelā Kassapa was struck with great spiritual urgency. He bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet and pleaded for ordination, saying: “Exalted Buddha, may I receive the initial ordination (pabbajjā) and the full ordination (upasampadā) in the presence of the Blessed One.”

Then the Buddha, knowing that the spiritual faculties of the five hundred ascetics had also matured, said to the elder ascetic Uruvelā Kassapa:

“O Kassapa, you are the leader, the chief, and the teacher of these five hundred ascetics.
573:
573
(It would not be proper if you do not inform your disciples.) Go and speak to those five hundred disciples first, so that they may also do as they see fit.”

When the Buddha said this, the elder ascetic Uruvelā Kassapa went to the place where his five hundred disciples were and said: “O teachers, I wish to live the holy life as a disciple of the Great Ascetic. You may do as you see fit.” Then the five hundred ascetics replied: “O Great Teacher, we have long held great faith in the Great Ascetic (since the time he subdued the Naga king). If you, Great Teacher, are to live the holy life as a disciple of the Great Ascetic, then all five hundred of us will also live the holy life as his disciples.”

Then the elder ascetic Uruvelā Kassapa and the five hundred ascetics cast their hair, matted locks, fire-drills, water pots, needles, and other ascetic requisites, as well as their carrying poles and utensils for fire sacrifice, into the current of the Nerañjarā River. They then approached the Buddha, bowed their heads at His feet, and requested ordination, saying: “Exalted Buddha, may we receive the initial ordination and the full ordination in the presence of the Blessed One.”
574:
Then the Blessed One, saying "Etha bhikkhavo" and so forth, stretched out his golden hand and called them with the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination: "Come, monks! Accept the monkhood you have requested. The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by me. Lead the noble life of the three trainings to make an end of the suffering of the round of rebirths." Immediately, the great teacher Uruvela Kassapa and those five hundred ascetics became fully ordained monks, appearing like senior elders of sixty years' standing (eighty years of age), complete with supernaturally created requisites in their proper places, and respectfully paid homage to the Blessed One. Their ascetic appearance miraculously vanished and was replaced by the appearance of monks. (The Blessed One's calling them with the words "Etha bhikkhavo" from his golden mouth was the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination for those ascetics; there was no longer any need for the formal procedure in a consecrated boundary.)

## The Ordination of the Great Teacher Nadī Kassapa (the Middle Brother) and His Disciples

When the teacher Nadī Kassapa, who lived at the downstream landing, saw the ascetic requisites of the great teacher Uruvela Kassapa and his five hundred disciples floating down the Nerañjarā River, he thought, "May no harm befall my elder brother!" He then said, "Go and find out what has happened to my elder brother," and first sent two or three disciples. He himself, together with three hundred disciples, then approached the place where the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa was staying. Upon reaching the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa,
575:
he asked, "O elder brother Kassapa, is this monkhood commendable (noble)?"

Then the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa replied to (his middle brother) Nadī Kassapa, "Yes, friend, this monkhood is indeed most commendable and noble." Upon hearing this, the teacher Nadī Kassapa and his three hundred ascetics, following the previous example, cast their ascetic requisites and fire-worshipping utensils into the Nerañjarā River. They then approached the Blessed One, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and requested to be ordained, saying, "Exalted Buddha, may we receive the novice ordination and the full monkhood in the presence of the Blessed One."

Then the Blessed One, saying "Etha bhikkhavo" and so forth, stretched out his golden hand and called them with the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination: "Come, monks! Accept the monkhood you have requested. The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by me. Lead the noble life of the three trainings to make an end of suffering." Immediately, the teacher Nadī Kassapa and those three hundred ascetics became fully ordained monks, appearing like senior elders of sixty years' standing (eighty years of age), complete with supernaturally created requisites in their proper places, and respectfully paid homage to the Blessed One. Their ascetic appearance miraculously vanished and was replaced by the appearance of monks. (The Blessed One's calling them with the words "Etha bhikkhavo" from his golden mouth was
576:
the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination for those ascetics; there was no longer any need for the formal procedure in a consecrated boundary.)

## The Ordination of the Great Teacher Gayā Kassapa (the Youngest Brother) and His Disciples

When the teacher Gayā Kassapa (the youngest brother), who lived at the downstream landing, saw the ascetic requisites of the great teacher Uruvela Kassapa and his five hundred disciples, and the middle brother Nadī Kassapa and his three hundred disciples, floating down the Nerañjarā River, he thought, "May no harm befall my elder brothers Uruvela Kassapa and Nadī Kassapa!" He then said, "Go and find out what has happened to my elder brothers," and first sent two or three disciples. He himself, together with two hundred disciples, then approached the place where the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa was staying and asked him, "O elder brother Kassapa, is this monkhood indeed most commendable and noble?"

Then the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa replied to (his youngest brother) Gayā Kassapa, "Yes, friend, this monkhood is indeed most commendable and noble." Upon hearing this, the teacher Gayā Kassapa and his two hundred ascetics, following the previous example, cast their ascetic requisites and fire-worshipping utensils into the Nerañjarā River. They then approached the Blessed One, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and requested to be ordained, saying, "Exalted Buddha, may we receive the novice ordination and the full monkhood in the presence of the Blessed One."
577:
Then the Blessed One, saying "Etha bhikkhavo" and so forth, stretched out his golden hand and called them with the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination: "Come, monks! Accept the monkhood you have requested. The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by me. Lead the noble life of the three trainings to make an end of suffering." Immediately, the teacher Gayā Kassapa and those two hundred ascetics became fully ordained monks, appearing like senior elders of sixty years' standing (eighty years of age), complete with supernaturally created requisites in their proper places, and respectfully paid homage to the Blessed One. Their ascetic appearance miraculously vanished and was replaced by the appearance of monks. (The Blessed One's calling them with the words "Etha bhikkhavo" from his golden mouth was the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination for those ascetics; there was no longer any need for the formal procedure in a consecrated boundary.)

(In this section of the display of miracles, the five hundred logs that the ascetics could not split, their miraculous splitting all at once, the ascetics being unable to light fires, the miraculous lighting of fires all at once, the ascetics being unable to extinguish the fires, the miraculous extinguishing of the fires all at once, and the creation of five hundred fire-vessels—all these various extraordinary events occurred due to the Blessed One's resolution. In this way, the miracles performed by the Blessed One in the Uruvela forest to
578:
convert the one thousand Kassapa brothers and their disciples are sixteen that are directly mentioned in the Pāḷi texts, and three thousand five hundred that are not directly mentioned—making a total of three thousand five hundred and sixteen (3,516) miracles.)

## Preaching the Ādittapariyāya Sutta

Then the Blessed One, having stayed in the Uruvela forest until his wish to convert the one thousand former ascetics was fulfilled, traveled together with the one thousand monks who were formerly ascetics to the place where there was a large rock called Gayāsīsa (resembling an elephant's head) near the village of Gayā. He sat upon the Gayāsīsa rock together with the one thousand monks.

While sitting there, he considered, "What kind of discourse would be suitable for these one thousand monks?" He then reflected, "These people used to serve and worship fire every night and morning. Therefore, if I preach the Ādittapariyāya Dhamma discourse to these one thousand monks, explaining how the twelve sense bases are repeatedly burned by the eleven kinds of fire, they will be able to attain the fruit of Arahatship." Having made this decision, he taught:

The six internal bases, the six external objects, the six consciousnesses, the six contacts, and the eighteen feelings born of contact—all these things are burning with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion, the fire of birth, the fire of aging, the fire of death, the fire of sorrow,
579:
the fire of lamentation, the fire of pain, the fire of grief, and the fire of despair. Showing in detail how they are burning with these eleven kinds of fire,

when he preached the Ādittapariyāya Sutta, those one thousand monks attained the four stages of the Path in succession and became Arahants with the exhaustion of the taints (āsavas). Thus, the minds of those one thousand monks were completely liberated from the taints, being entirely free from the grasping of "I" and "mine" through craving and wrong view, and the taints were extinguished by the cessation of non-arising.

(Matters to be noted regarding the Ādittapariyāya Sutta will be explained upon reaching the chapter on the Dhamma Ratana.)
