## Chapter 15
## The Buddha's Journey to the City of Rājagaha

Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Gayāsīsa until his wish to convert the one thousand former ascetics to the fruit of Arahatship was fulfilled, kept in mind the words of King Bimbisāra, who had requested (on page 218 above) when they met while the Buddha was first seeking renunciation: "Venerable Sir, I make this request: when you have attained Buddhahood, please come first to my kingdom."
580:
Accompanied by the one thousand Arahants who were formerly ascetics, he journeyed toward the city of Rājagaha. Upon reaching the Laṭṭhivana garden, a grove of young palm trees near Rājagaha, he stayed at the foot of the Suppatiṭṭha Banyan tree, which provided wide shade and was a place of worship and reverence for the people.

(In this regard, after becoming the Buddha, the Blessed One spent the first Vassa at the Isipatana Migadāya wood. When the Vassa ended and the Pavāraṇā ceremony was completed, he went to the Uruvela forest. He stayed in the Uruvela forest for three months, converting and disciplining the one thousand Kassapa brothers and their disciples until they attained Arahatship. Then, accompanied by the one thousand Arahants, he arrived at Rājagaha on the full moon day of Phussa (Pyatho) and stayed in Rājagaha for two months. From Jātaka Commentary Vol. 1, page 100, and Buddhavamsa Commentary, page 24.)

At that time, according to the report of the gardener, King Bimbisāra heard the good news that the Blessed One had arrived at Rājagaha. The details of the news he heard were:

"O friends, the Blessed One of the Gotama clan, a Sakyan prince born of the pure Sakyan lineage who renounced the Sakyan clan to become a monk, has now arrived at our city of Rājagaha and is staying at the foot of the Suppatiṭṭha Banyan tree in the Laṭṭhivana garden near Rājagaha."

"The reputation of this Blessed One of the Gotama clan has spread as far as the highest heaven in the following manner: 'For these reasons, the Blessed One is...'"
581:
581
He is endowed with the nine supreme qualities beginning with 'Arahant' and ending with 'Bhagavā'. Having realized this world of beings, including the devas and brahmas, through His own higher knowledge, He makes it known and proclaims it to others.

That Blessed One of the Gotama lineage teaches the Dhamma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it is complete in meaning and phrasing. He reveals the holy life (brahmacariya) which is perfectly complete and pure, free from the stains of misconduct, consisting of the three trainings of virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā) to devas and humans.

"It is truly excellent and sublime to have the opportunity to pay respects to and associate with such noble masters, the Worthy Ones, who are endowed with such special qualities and graces"—thus the good news was heard.

Then, King Bimbisāra, accompanied by 120,000 brahmin householders of the Magadha country, approached the Blessed One. After paying respectful homage to the Blessed One, he sat down in a place free from the six faults (not too far, not too near, not in front, not behind, not too high, and not upwind).

Among the 120,000 brahmin householders who came with King Bimbisāra: (1) Some brahmin householders paid respectful homage to the Blessed One and sat down in a place free from the six faults. (2) Some brahmin householders...
582:
582
...exchanged pleasant and memorable greetings with the Blessed One and sat down in a place free from the six faults. (These two groups of brahmins were those who stood on the side of Right View.)

(3) Some brahmin householders extended their joined palms in anjali towards the Blessed One and sat down in a place free from the six faults. (These brahmins were those who stepped on both sides of the boat, between Wrong View and Right View. Their thought was: (a) "If those with Wrong View criticize us, saying 'Why do you pay homage to the ascetic Gotama?', we shall tell them, 'How can merely raising joined palms be called paying homage?'; (b) If those with Right View criticize us, saying 'Why do you not pay homage to the Blessed One?', we shall tell them, 'What, must one strike the ground with one's head for it to be called paying homage? Indeed, raising joined palms is also paying homage.'" Thus they sat there so they could speak to both sides.)

(4) Some brahmin householders announced their names, saying, "O Venerable Gotama, I am Datta, I am Mitta, the son of such-and-such person, and I have come into the presence of the Venerable One," and sat down in a place free from the six faults. Some brahmin householders announced their clans, saying, "O Venerable Gotama, I am of the Vāseṭṭha clan, I am of the Kaccāyana clan, and I have come into the presence of the Venerable One," and sat down in a place free from the six faults.
583:
583
(These brahmins were those who were poor and undistinguished. They announced their names and clans thinking that by doing so in the midst of the assembly, they would become well-known.)

(5) Some brahmin householders remained silent and sat down. (These brahmins were either those with crooked intentions or those who were ignorant and foolish. Among these two types, those with crooked intentions (the calculating ones) thought, "If I speak a word or two, it will lead to intimacy. If intimacy develops, it would not be proper if I do not offer a meal or two." Fearing the need to offer meals due to intimacy, they remained silent. The ignorant and foolish ones, because of their lack of knowledge, sat down in whatever place they found, remaining silent like large clods of earth placed on the ground.)

## The Brahmins' Doubt

After they had sat down, a thought arose in the minds of those 120,000 brahmin householders of Magadha: "How is it? Does the Great Ascetic practice the holy life under the teacher Uruvela Kassapa, or does the teacher Uruvela Kassapa practice the holy life under the Great Ascetic?" Then the Blessed One, knowing the thoughts of those 120,000 brahmin householders with His own mind (cetopariya-abhiññā), addressed the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa:
584:
584
"Kiṃ meva disvā Uruvelavāsi,
Pahāsi aggiṃ kisakovadānā.
Pucchāmi taṃ Kassapa etamatthaṃ,
Kathaṃ pahīnaṃ tava aggihuttaṃ."

"O Kassapa, dweller of the Uruvelā forest, you who were a teacher who instructed ascetics with emaciated bodies (through austere practices), what fault did you see that you abandoned the fire-sacrifice? O Kassapa, I ask you this matter: For what reason have you abandoned the practice of fire-worship?"

Thus the Blessed One questioned him with a verse. Then the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa replied:

"Rūpe ca sadde ca atho rase ca,
Kāmitthiyo cābhivadanti yaññā.
Etaṃ malantī upadhīsu ñatvā,
Tasmā na yiṭṭhe na hute arañjiṃ."

"Exalted Buddha, (sacrificial priests) proclaim that through sacrifices, one can attain the five cords of sensual pleasure—visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and touches—and women who are like tigers that devour with their five sensual claws. Having clearly seen that these five objects and women are merely stains among the acquisitions (upadhi) of the five aggregates, I no longer delight in great sacrifices,
585:
585
nor do I delight or find pleasure in the daily fire-sacrifice, O Blessed One."

Thus he replied to the Blessed One with a verse. Then the Blessed One asked:

"Ettheva te mano na ramittha (Kassapāti Bhagavā),
Rūpesu saddesu atho rasesu.
Atha ko carahi devamanussaloke,
Rato mano Kassapa brūhi metaṃ."

"O Kassapa, if your heart does not delight or find pleasure in the five cords of sensual pleasure—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and touches—and in women, then, O Kassapa, in this world of devas and humans, in what does your heart find delight? Tell me this matter."

When questioned by the Blessed One with this verse, the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa replied:

"Disvā padaṃ santamanūpadhikaṃ,
Akiñcanaṃ kāmabhave asattaṃ.
Anaññathābhāvimanaññaneyyaṃ,
Tasmā na yiṭṭhe na hute arañjiṃ."

"Exalted Buddha, I have clearly seen Nibbāna, which has the characteristic of peace, which is the state of being free from the four types of acquisitions (upadhi), being entirely without the anxieties of passion and so forth, and being completely unattached and liberated from the world of desire and the world of existence. (Because it is free from rebirth, aging, and death,
586:
586
it is entirely without change. It is a state that is not led by another, as it must be reached and attained only through the Path one has developed oneself.) Because I have clearly and distinctly realized this Nibbāna, I no longer delight in great sacrifices, nor do I delight or find pleasure in the daily fire-sacrifice, O Blessed One."

After replying with this verse, the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa, in order to make it clearly known that he was a disciple of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and placed his head upon the feet of the Blessed One, saying, "Exalted Buddha, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am the disciple of the Blessed One." Then, he rose into the air to the height of one palm tree and descended to pay homage to the Blessed One again. He did this a second time to the height of two palm trees, a third time to the height of three palm trees, and so on, up to the height of seven palm trees. After rising into the air and descending seven times to pay homage to the Blessed One, he sat down in a place free from the six faults.

Seeing that miracle, the great multitude of brahmin householders praised the qualities of the Blessed One, saying, "Oh, the Blessed One is of great power and majesty! He has tamed even the great ascetic teacher Uruvela Kassapa, who possessed such strong and firm Wrong View and who considered himself an Arahant, by breaking the net of his views."
587:
587
Hearing their words of praise, the Blessed One said, "O brahmin householders, it is not surprising that I, having now attained Omniscient Wisdom, have tamed Uruvela Kassapa. In the past, when I was still a Bodhisatta not yet free from passion, as the King of Brahmas named Nārada, I also broke the net of Wrong View of this Uruvela Kassapa's predecessor (King Aṅgati)." At the request of the assembly of brahmin householders, He then preached the Mahā-Nārada-Kassapa Jātaka. (The details of the Mahā-Nārada-Kassapa Jātaka should be read in the Stories of the Ten Great Jātakas.)

Through the admission of the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa, the Blessed One perceived with His mind (cetopariya-abhiññā) that the 120,000 brahmin householders had become free from doubt, thinking, "Indeed, the great teacher Uruvela Kassapa is practicing the holy life as a disciple under the Great Ascetic Gotama." Then, to King Bimbisāra and those 120,000 brahmin householders, He preached the progressive discourse (anupubbīkathā), the noble path leading to the attainment of the Path and Fruition, in the order of: (1) Discourse on Giving (dānakathā), (2) Discourse on Virtue (sīlakathā), (3) Discourse on Heaven (saggakathā), (4) Discourse on the Path (maggakathā), which includes the discourse on the danger of sensual pleasures (kāmānaṃ ādīnava) and the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma-ānisaṃsa). When the Blessed One knew that King Bimbisāra and the 120,000 brahmin householders had ready minds, soft minds, minds free from hindrances (nīvaraṇa), uplifted and joyful minds, and clear minds...
588:
When the Blessed One preached the Sāmukkaṃsika Dhamma, the Four Noble Truths, to King Bimbisāra and the wealthy brahmins, one hundred and ten thousand brahmins and householders, headed by King Bimbisāra, were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) right there. The remaining ten thousand brahmins and householders became lay followers (upāsakas) established in the Three Refuges.

## The Five Wishes of King Bimbisāra

Then King Bimbisāra, the ruler of Magadha, who had become a Stream-enterer, said: "Magnificent, Blessed One! Lord, when I was formerly a prince, five wishes arose in me. Those five wishes have now been fulfilled for me.

(1) Lord, when I was formerly a prince, the wish arose: 'If only the people of Magadha would anoint me as king.' Lord, this was my first wish. That first wish of mine has been fulfilled.

(2) Lord, when I was formerly a prince, the wish arose: 'When I am king, if only the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, would visit my kingdom.' Lord, this was my second wish. That second wish of mine has now been fulfilled.

(3) Lord, when I was formerly a prince, the wish arose: 'If only I might pay respects to that Blessed One who has visited my kingdom.'
589:
Lord, this was my third wish. That third wish of mine has now been fulfilled.

(4) Lord, when I was formerly a prince, the wish arose: 'If only that Blessed One who has visited my kingdom would preach to me the noble Dhamma that leads to Nibbāna.' Lord, this was my fourth wish. That fourth wish of mine has now been fulfilled.

(5) Lord, when I was formerly a prince, the wish arose: 'If only I might clearly understand the Dhamma preached by that Blessed One.' Lord, this was my fifth wish. That fifth wish of mine has now been fulfilled.

Lord, these five wishes arose in me when I was formerly a prince, and all five of those wishes have now been fulfilled for me.

Magnificent, Blessed One! Magnificent, Blessed One! Lord,
590:
Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way, the Blessed One has made the Dhamma clear in many ways. Lord, I go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts. Lord, may the Blessed One together with the Saṅgha of monks accept tomorrow's meal from me for the sake of merit." The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent.

Then King Bimbisāra, the ruler of Magadha, knowing that the Blessed One had accepted, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed for his golden palace.

(In this context, King Bimbisāra took refuge after attaining Stream-entry. Although the matter of refuge is already completed at the moment of the Path of Stream-entry, where one realizes, "The Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha are indeed the true refuge and reliance,"
592:
Because the entire garden and the whole road were packed with people who had come to see the Buddha, there was almost no space even for a single monk to pass. If it continued like this, the Blessed One might miss his meal for that day. As if saying, "Let not the Blessed One miss his meal," the Paṇḍukambala emerald stone throne of Sakka, the king of devas, showed signs of heat. Sakka, reflecting on the cause and seeing it clearly, transformed himself into a young man (māṇava). Singing praises related to the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—he suddenly appeared before the Blessed One. By his divine power, he cleared a path for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha to proceed, and like a herald of Nibbāna, he sang:

"The Tamed, with the tamed,
With the former matted-hair ascetics,
Liberated, with the liberated,
Golden like a Singī gold plate,
The Blessed One has entered Rājagaha."

(O people of the country!) Golden like a Singī gold plate: Having a complexion as bright as a Singī gold plate, which is the eighth and most excellent of the eight kinds of gold, such as Jātarūpa. The Blessed One: The Lord of Glory.

Liberated: Because the Leader himself is already liberated from the three realms of existence and the three rounds of suffering. With the liberated: With those who have been liberated from the three realms of existence and the three rounds of suffering by the essence of the Dhamma (dhamm-oja) shown by the Lord. With the former matted-hair ascetics: Together with the thousand Arahants who were formerly matted-hair ascetics (jaṭilas). Has entered Rājagaha: At the invitation of the ruler of Magadha, he has entered the city called Rājagaha, moving like the sun or the moon.

"The Freed, with the freed,
With the former matted-hair ascetics,
Liberated, with the liberated,
Golden like a Singī gold plate,

(O people of the country!) Golden like a Singī gold plate: Having a complexion as bright as a Singī gold plate, which is the eighth and most excellent of the eight kinds of gold. The Blessed One: The Lord of Glory. The Freed: Because he himself is freed from the round of fifteen hundred defilements and the snare of Māra. With the freed: With those who have been freed from the round of defilements and the snare of Māra by the Dhamma instructions (dhamm-upadesa) given by the Lord. Liberated: Because the Leader himself is already liberated from the three realms of existence and the three rounds of suffering. With the liberated: With those who have been liberated from the three realms of existence and the three rounds of suffering by the essence of the Dhamma shown by the Lord.

With the former matted-hair ascetics: Together with the thousand Arahants who were formerly matted-hair ascetics. Has entered Rājagaha: At the invitation of the ruler of Magadha, he has entered the city called Rājagaha, moving like the sun or the moon.

"The One who has crossed, with those who have crossed,
With the former matted-hair ascetics,
Liberated, with the liberated,

With those who have crossed: With those who have crossed the rough waters of the four floods and reached the other shore by the beautiful vehicle of the Eightfold Path (Aṭṭhaṅgika-magga) provided by the Lord. Liberated: Because the Leader himself is already liberated from the three realms of existence and the three rounds of suffering. With the liberated: With those who have been liberated from the three realms of existence and the three rounds of suffering by the essence of the Dhamma shown by the Lord. Has entered Rājagaha: At the invitation of the ruler of Magadha, he has entered the city called Rājagaha, moving like the sun or the moon.
595:
Santo santehi saha purāṇajaṭilehi,
Vippamutto vippamuttehi.
Siṅgīnikkhasavaṇṇo,
Rājagahaṃ pāvisi bhagavā.

(O citizens and people!) The Blessed One, whose complexion is as radiant as the finest Siṅgī gold—the most excellent among the eight kinds of gold, weighing as much as a nikkha—has entered the city of Rājagaha. He is the Peaceful One, having personally extinguished all the fires of defilements, and He is accompanied by a thousand former matted-hair ascetics who have also become peaceful, their fires of defilements extinguished by the nectar of Dhamma shared by the Lord. He is the Liberated One, having personally escaped from the three realms of existence and the cycle of rebirth, and He is accompanied by those who are also liberated, having escaped the three realms through the essence of the Dhamma He pointed out. Together with these thousand Arahants who were formerly matted-hair ascetics, He has entered the city of Rājagaha, at the invitation of the supreme King of the Magadha country, moving like the sun and the moon.

Dasavāso dasabalo,
Dasadhammavidū dasabhi cupeto.
So dasasataparivāro,
Rājagahaṃ pāvisi bhagavā.

(O citizens and people!) He who is endowed with the ten Ariyan abodes (dasavāsa),
596:
who is endowed with the ten physical powers and the ten powers of knowledge (dasabala); who clearly understands the ten paths of wholesome action (dasadhamma); who is fully accomplished in the ten qualities of an adept (asekha-dhamma); that Blessed One, surrounded by a retinue of a thousand former matted-hair ascetics, has entered the city of Rājagaha, at the invitation of the supreme King of the Magadha country, moving like the sun and the moon.

Sakka, the king of devas, singing these verses of praise in a melodious and pleasant voice, went before the company of monks led by the Buddha, alerting the people.

At that time, when the citizens of Rājagaha saw Sakka, the king of devas, who had transformed himself into the likeness of a young man, they said to one another:

“Friends, this young man is indeed very beautiful!
Friends, this young man is indeed wonderful to behold!
Friends, this young man is indeed inspiring!
Whose servant might this young man be?”

When they spoke thus to one another, Sakka, the king of devas, replied:
597:
Yo dhīro sabbadhi danto,
Suddho appaṭipuggalo.
Arahaṃ sugato loke,
Tassāhaṃ paricārako.

(O citizens and people!) In this world, that Buddha who is the Wise One, the master of all-knowing wisdom; who is restrained and disciplined at all six sense-doors, free from the taints of unwholesomeness; who is pure, untainted by the dust of the fifteen hundred defilements; who is the Peerless Person, without equal in the three realms of existence; who is the Worthy One, deserving of the special offerings of men, devas, and brahmas; who is the Well-Gone One, speaking only words that are true and beneficial, leading to the paths and fruits—I, in this form of a young man, am the servant and attendant of that Blessed One who is endowed with such marvelous attributes.

Thus he replied to the people with these verses.

## King Bimbisāra’s Donation of the Veḷuvana Monastery

The Blessed One, traveling along the path prepared for Him by Sakka, the king of devas, entered the city of Rājagaha surrounded by a thousand monks.
598:
King Bimbisāra invited the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, to the golden palace. He personally served them with excellent food and delicacies with his own hands, with great respect and devotion. After the meal, he sat in a place free from the six faults. While sitting there, King Bimbisāra reflected:

“In what kind of place should the Blessed One reside? It should be a place that is:
(1) Not too far from the town,
(2) Not too close to the town,
(3) Provided with good access roads,
(4) Easy for everyone to visit whenever they wish,
(5) Quiet and secluded from the five kinds of sensory noise, such as the sounds of the city, villages, and people.”

As he considered this, he realized that his own Veḷuvana (Bamboo Grove) garden was endowed with these five qualities. He thought it would be excellent to donate this Veḷuvana garden to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. He then addressed the Blessed One:

“Most Reverend Blessed One, I cannot live apart from the Triple Gem. I wish to come to the presence of the Buddha at all times, whether suitable or not. The Laṭṭhivana (Palm Grove) garden where the Buddha is currently staying is very far from the city. Our Veḷuvana garden, however, is neither too far nor too close to the city.”
599:
“It is provided with good access and is a place worthy of the Buddhas. Therefore, I wish the Blessed One to accept this Veḷuvana garden of mine.”

Having said this, he took a golden pitcher filled with scented water and, desiring to donate the Veḷuvana garden, he made the formal dedication:

“Etāhaṃ bhante veḷuvanaṃ udyānaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dammi = Venerable Blessed One, I donate this Veḷuvana garden to the community of monks headed by the Buddha.”

After speaking these words of donation, he poured the water of libation onto the hand of the Blessed One. When this Veḷuvana monastery was accepted, the Great Earth shook and trembled, like a woman dancing with joy, as if to say, “The roots of the Buddha’s Dispensation are now firmly established.”

(Note: It is mentioned in the Buddhavamsa Commentary and other texts that, apart from the Veḷuvana monastery in Jambudīpa, there is no other monastery whose donation caused the earth to shake.)

## Ten Verses of Appreciation for a Monastery from the Buddhavamsa Commentary

Then, after accepting the Veḷuvana garden, the Blessed One preached the Dhamma of appreciation for the donation of a monastery to King Bimbisāra, the ruler of Magadha:

(1) Āvāsadānassa panānisaṃsaṃ,
Ko nāma vattuṃ puriso samattho.
Aññatra buddhā pana lokanāthā,
Yutto mukhānaṃ nahutena cāpi.
600:
(O Great King!) Apart from the Buddhas, who are the refuge and mainstay of the three worlds, what man would be able to fully explain the great benefits of the gift of a dwelling (āvāsa-dāna)? Even if one were uniquely endowed with ten thousand mouths, no ordinary person in this world could possibly describe it completely.

(2) Āyuñca vaṇṇañca sukhaṃ balañca,
Varaṃ pasatthaṃ paṭibhānameva.
Dadāti nāmāti pavuccate so,
Yo deti saṅghassa naro vihāraṃ.

(O Great King!) Whatever person, with a joyful heart of faith, builds and offers a monastery (vihāra) to the Saṅgha for their residence, that person is said to be a giver of life, a giver of beauty, a giver of happiness, a giver of strength, and a giver of superior and praiseworthy wisdom (paṭibhāna).
601:
This is said because the attainment of these benefits is based on the cause of the gift.

(3) Dātā nivāsassa nivāraṇassa,
Sītādino jīvitupaddavassa.
Pāleti āyuṃ pana tassa yasmā,
Āyuppado hoti tamāhu santo.

(O Great King!) Because a person who joyfully builds and offers a dwelling that can ward off various dangers to life, such as cold and heat, thereby well protects the lives of the community of monks residing in that monastery, the virtuous ones, headed by the Buddha, praise that donor as a “giver of life.”

(4) Accuṇhasīte vasato nivāse,
Balañca vaṇṇo paṭibhā na hoti.
Tasmā hi so deti vihāradātā,
Balañca vaṇṇaṃ paṭibhānameva.

(O Great King!) For a monk who must reside in an open space or a field, suffering from the severity of the climate—being too hot or too cold—his strength, his beauty, and his wisdom cannot become firm and stable due to the lack of supportive conditions. (The meaning is that these can only flourish when residing in a secure monastery.) Therefore,
602:
the donor who offers a monastery for residence is truly one who gives strength, beauty, and wisdom.

(5) Dukkhassa sītūṇhasarīsapa ca,
Vātātapādippabhavassa loke.
Nivāraṇānekavidhassa niccaṃ,
Sukhappado hoti vihāradātā.

(O Great King!) In this world full of dangers, the donor of a monastery is one who gives the gift of happiness. This is because by providing a monastery, he constantly wards off and prevents the various kinds of suffering caused by cold, heat, and reptiles (such as snakes, scorpions, and lice), as well as the many forms of suffering arising from harsh winds and the fierce sun.
603:
(6) Because the donor of a monastery wards off the suffering caused by cold, heat, wind, sun, gadflies, mosquitoes, unseasonal rain, snakes, scorpions, and wild animals, therefore he finds happiness in the next world.

(O Great King), because the donor of a monastery wards off the suffering caused by cold, heat, wind, sun, gadflies, mosquitoes, unseasonal rain, snakes, scorpions, and wild animals by providing a dwelling, therefore that donor of a monastery certainly and without fail attains both physical and mental happiness in the afterlife.

(7) One who, with a clear mind, joyfully gives a delightful monastery—the cause of existence and wealth—to those endowed with virtues like morality, is called a 'giver of everything'.

(O Great King), that person who, with a heart overflowing with faith and joy, gives a monastery—which is the cause of both the success of existence (bhava-sampatti) and the success of wealth (bhoga-sampatti), and which is delightful and pleasing to the hearts of all who see it—to the venerable monks who are flourishing in the five groups of virtue such as morality (sīla-kkhandha)...
604:
...to the venerable monks who are flourishing in the five groups of virtue such as morality. Such a donor is praised and proclaimed by the Buddhas as a 'giver of everything' (Sabbadada)—one who gives all four: strength, beauty, happiness, and vision. (This refers to the Saṃyutta Nikāya verse: 'He who gives a dwelling gives everything.')

(8) Having abandoned the stain of stinginess along with greed, one gives a dwelling to those who are abodes of virtue. Just as a burden is dropped by carriers at its destination, so too is he born in heaven by the carriers of his volitional formations, free from sorrow.

(O Great King), that person who, having abandoned the stain of stinginess (macchariya) along with greed (lobha), gives a dwelling to the venerable Saṅgha who are the abode of virtues such as morality. Just as a burden carried by porters is dropped at the desired destination, so too is that donor (or) so too is that donor by the porters known as volitional formations (kamma-saṅkhāra)...
605:
...being brought to a happy destination, he is born in that heaven, a collection of five beautiful and suitable sense objects, completely free from the sorrow of seeking food, clothing, and shelter.

(9) A wise man should have grand and beautiful monasteries built. There, he should invite learned monks to reside. He should always respectfully and with a clear mind provide them with various kinds of food, drink, and robes.

(O Great King), therefore, a wise man who considers his own welfare should have grand, magnificent, and beautiful monasteries built by paying the necessary costs and wages. In those completed monasteries, he should invite and request learned monks to reside. To those resident monks, he should always respectfully and with a heart full of faith provide and support them with various kinds of food, drink, and robes.
606:
(10) Therefore, O Great King, after repeatedly enjoying delightful pleasures in various happy existences through the fruit of donating a monastery, you will eventually attain the peaceful, sorrowless bliss of Nibbāna.

O Great King, therefore, through the merit of this monastery donation given with a clear heart, you will repeatedly enjoy abundant and delightful wealth and possessions in various happy existences (sugati). Afterwards, you will certainly reach and realize the peaceful bliss of Nibbāna, which is free from all sorrow, through the four Path Knowledges and four Fruit Knowledges.

In this way, the Buddha, having preached the Vihāra-anumodanā (discourse on the appreciation of monastery donation) to King Bimbisāra, rose from his seat and, surrounded by a thousand monks, proceeded to reside at the Veluvana monastery.

(Note: Regarding the statement that King Bimbisāra donated the Veluvana garden to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha, this is described primarily as the donation of the garden. However, according to the Buddhavamsa Commentary, the Veluvana garden was adorned with delightful gabled mansions (pāsāda),
607:
flat-roofed mansions (hammiya), celestial-like dwellings (vimāna), four-roofed dwellings, two-roofed dwellings, and pavilions. Thus, it should be understood that buildings suitable for monks to reside in were already included.)

## Permission to Accept the Monastery Garden
Then, the Buddha, having preached on the occasion of King Bimbisāra's donation of the Veluvana garden, addressed the monks:

“Anujānāmi bhikkhave ārāmaṃ = Monks, I allow the acceptance of a monastery garden (ārāma)”—

Thus, he gave permission to the monks to accept monastery gardens.

## Preaching the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta
## (From the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha)
The day after accepting the Veluvana monastery, the Buddha preached the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta. The detailed background is as follows:

Counting back from this aeon, ninety-two aeons ago, King Jayasena ruled in the city of Kāsī. (The Dhammapada Commentary on the Yamaka Vagga, in the story of Venerable Sāriputta, and the Aṅguttara Commentary on the Ekaka Nipāta, in the story of Uruvela Kassapa, name him King Mahinda.) His Chief Queen, Sirimā, gave birth to the Bodhisatta named Phussa. In due course, the Bodhisatta Phussa...
608:
...attained Enlightenment. King Jayasena thought, "My eldest son has renounced the world and become a Buddha." Therefore, feeling great affection and thinking "My Buddha, My Dhamma, My Sangha," he served the Buddha and the Sangha himself at all times. He did not give others the opportunity to serve or worship. He had bamboo fences built on both sides from the monastery gate to his golden palace. Above, he had a canopy decorated with golden stars and hanging fragrant flower garlands. Below, he had pure white sand spread and various flowers scattered. He arranged for the Buddha to travel only by that path.

Phussa Buddha, wrapped in his robes and surrounded by monks, would go to the palace within the screens, eat his meal, and return to the monastery within the screens. Not a single citizen had the chance to offer even a spoonful of alms. Then the people criticized:

"Although a Buddha has appeared in the world, we have no chance to perform merit. Just as the sun and moon appear to give light to all people, so do Buddhas appear for the welfare and happiness of all beings. But this king has monopolized the great field of merit for himself alone."
609:
Then, the three half-brothers of Phussa Buddha also thought:

"Buddhas appear for the benefit of the entire world of beings. They do not appear for the benefit of a single person. Our father, the King, does not give others the chance to serve the Buddha. How can we get the opportunity to serve him?"

They conspired with the citizens, saying, "Let's use a stratagem," and arranged for a mock rebellion at the border. 

When the King heard the news that the border regions were in unrest, he sent his three sons to suppress the rebellion. When the princes returned after quelling the rebellion, King Jayasena was very pleased and said, "Sons, take whatever boon you desire."

The three princes replied, "Father, we desire no other boon. We only wish for the boon of respectfully serving and attending to the Buddha."

The King said, "Sons, leave this boon aside and take another."
610:
When the princes said, “Great King, our father, we desire no other boon,” the King replied, “My sons, if that is so, take it for a limited period.” The princes then requested a period of seven years. When the King refused, saying seven years was too long, they reduced it year by year to six, five, four, three, two, and one year. Then they reduced it to seven months, six, five, and four months. Still, the King did not grant it. Finally, they requested the boon to serve and support the Buddha for only three months, and the King granted it, saying, “Very well, take it.”

The three brother princes, having received the boon from their father the King to support the Buddha for the three months of the Vassa (Rains Retreat), were exceedingly joyful. They went to the presence of the Phussa Buddha, paid their respects, and said, “Exalted Buddha, we wish to support the Buddha for the three months of the Vassa. May the Exalted Buddha accept our invitation to reside in our province for these three months.” The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Then, the three brother princes, knowing that the Buddha had accepted, sent a royal message to the Minister in their province:

“Minister, for these three months of the Vassa, we wish to attend to, serve, and honor the ninety thousand (90,000) monks headed by our elder brother, the Phussa Buddha, with the four requisites. You must quickly arrange and build the necessary structures, such as monasteries, for the Buddha and the assembly of monks to reside in.”
611:
The Minister completed everything as commanded in the royal message with great speed. He then sent word back, reporting, “Everything, including the monasteries and other buildings, has been completed according to the royal command.”

Then, the three princes, together with one thousand (1,000) soldiers, wore garments dyed with astringent juice (ochre robes). They had two thousand five hundred (2,500) attendants serve the Sangha headed by the Buddha to ensure their comfort with the four requisites. They invited the Sangha headed by the Buddha to their province, handed over the newly built monasteries and surroundings to them, and had them reside in those monastic grounds.

## The Faithful Treasurer and His Wife
The son of a treasurer (seṭṭhi), who served as the treasurer for those three princes, together with his young wife, was endowed with faith and devotion to the Triple Gem. This treasurer (acting on behalf of the princes) faithfully handed over the materials to be offered to the monks headed by the Buddha from the princes' treasuries, turn by turn, to the Minister.
612:
The Minister took those offerings provided by the treasurer and, together with eleven thousand (11,000) residents of the province, prepared and cooked them to the highest quality, offering them daily without fail to the assembly of monks headed by the Buddha. (As for the three princes, together with their one thousand (1,000) soldiers, they wore garments dyed with astringent juice, observed the precepts, and stayed at the monastery itself, performing various major and minor duties for the Sangha headed by the Buddha while listening to the Dhamma.)

## The Evil-Minded Relatives of the Minister
Among the eleven thousand (11,000) people performing the service as directed by the Minister, some of the Minister’s relatives possessed crooked and wicked minds. They created various obstacles and dangers to the alms-giving. They themselves snatched and stole the food prepared for the Buddha and the Sangha to eat, and also fed their children. They even set fire to the alms halls (maṇḍapas).

## Sending the Buddha back to the Father
When the Vassa ended and the Sangha had performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, the three princes held a great festival of worship for the Buddha. Then, according to their original promise to their father the King, they escorted the Buddha back to the King’s country. They arrived at the royal city of Kāsi, where King Jayasena resided.
613:
Not long after arriving, the Buddha attained Parinibbāna. (According to the Saṃyutta Commentary, the Phussa Buddha attained Parinibbāna while still with the princes.)

King Jayasena, the three brother princes, the Minister, and the Treasurer all passed away in due course and, along with their retinues, were reborn in the heavenly realms. However, the relatives of the Minister who were crooked and wicked were reborn in the hell realms.

In this manner, as these two groups wandered from one heaven to another and from one hell to another, ninety-two aeons (kappas) passed. Later, in this Bhadda-kappa, when the Kassapa Buddha appeared in the world, those crooked and wicked relatives (of the Minister) were reborn in the realm of Petas (hungry ghosts). At that time, people gave alms for their own deceased relatives and shared the merit, saying, “Idaṃ amhākaṃ ñātīnaṃ hotu = May this merit be for our relatives.” When they dedicated the merit in this way, their Peta relatives received celestial wealth and happiness.

Seeing other Petas endowed with such wealth and happiness, the Minister’s Peta relatives approached the Kassapa Buddha and asked, “Exalted Buddha, will we also ever receive such wealth?” The Kassapa Buddha replied, “O Petas, you will not receive such wealth at this time.”
614:
“Indeed, in the future, after one intermediary aeon (antara-kappa) has passed, the Gotama Buddha will appear in the world. During the time of the Gotama Buddha, a king named Bimbisāra will arise. This King Bimbisāra was formerly your close relative (the Minister) ninety-two aeons ago. That King Bimbisāra will give alms to the Gotama Buddha and share the merit with you. At that time, you shall receive this kind of wealth and happiness.” Thus did the Buddha give the prophecy.

When the Kassapa Buddha spoke these words, it was so joyful for those Petas that it felt as if he had said they would receive it “tomorrow.”

Then, after a long period between the Buddhas (the interval between Kassapa Buddha and Gotama Buddha) had passed, our Buddha appeared in the world. The three brother princes, along with their one thousand followers, passed away from the heavenly realm and were reborn into brahmin families in the Magadha country. In due course, they became ascetics and were the one thousand matted-hair ascetics (Jaṭilas) at Gayāsīsa. At that time, the Minister of the three princes became the present King Bimbisāra, ruler of Magadha. The Treasurer became the present Visākha Seṭṭhi, and the Treasurer’s wife became the present Dhammadinnā, the treasurer’s daughter.
615:
The rest of the retinue from that time became the present retinue of King Bimbisāra. 

As previously mentioned, on the day our Incomparable Buddha, the Supreme One of the Three Worlds, arrived at Rājagaha, He established King Bimbisāra along with one hundred and ten thousand (110,000) brahmins and householders in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). On the following day, led by Sakka, the King of Devas, who acted as a herald, the Buddha accepted a great alms-offering at King Bimbisāra’s golden palace.

At that time, all those former relatives of King Bimbisāra who were Petas surrounded the place, waiting and hoping, thinking, “Our former relative King Bimbisāra will surely share the merit of this alms-giving with us now; he will share it now.” However, after giving the great alms, King Bimbisāra was only considering where the Buddha should reside, thinking, “Where will the Exalted Buddha stay?” Because he was preoccupied with the monastery location, he did not share or dedicate the merit of that alms-giving to anyone. The King’s former relatives, the Petas, having their hopes cut off, made a terrifying, agonizing wailing and crying sound in the King’s palace during the night.

King Bimbisāra, hearing that sound, was greatly afraid, terrified, and shaken. When morning dawned, he went to the presence of the Exalted Buddha, paid his respects with great devotion, and said, “Exalted Buddha, last night I heard such a terrifying sound. For me—”
616:
"What kind of benefit or harm will come from that sound?" he asked the Buddha. Then the Buddha replied, "Great King, do not fear. No harm whatsoever will come to you because of that sound. In truth, your former relatives have been reborn in the realm of the Petas (hungry ghosts). Throughout an entire incalculable aeon during the interval between Buddhas, those former relatives of yours, now a host of Petas, have been wandering about, looking forward to and longing only for you, thinking, 'After giving a donation to the Buddha, he will dedicate the merit to us.' Great King, yesterday you did not dedicate the merit of your good deeds to that host of former relatives. Therefore, having lost their hope, your former relatives made such a terrifying sound."

When the Buddha answered thus, King Bimbisāra asked again, "Exalted Buddha, if I were to give a donation and dedicate the merit now, would they still receive it?" The Buddha replied, "Yes, Great King, they can receive it."

Then King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, "Exalted Buddha, if that is so, may the Buddha accept my donation today for the sake of merit; I shall dedicate the merit of the good deed to that host of former relatives." The Buddha accepted King Bimbisāra's invitation by remaining silent.

The King returned to the golden palace, prepared a great donation, and sent word that it was time for the Buddha to come and receive the offering. The Buddha...
617:
...proceeded to the golden palace and sat together with the assembly of monks on the noble seats prepared. The host of former relatives also came to the golden palace, thinking, "Today we will surely receive the share of merit," and stood waiting behind the walls and in other such places.

Through His psychic power, the Buddha made it possible for the King to see that host of former relatives who were in distress. While pouring the water of libation into the Buddha's hand, the King dedicated the merit, saying: "Idaṃ me ñātīnaṃ hotu = May this donation of clear water be for my relatives."

At that very moment (as the Peta relatives received their share of the merit), ponds filled and covered with five kinds of lotuses suddenly appeared for the use of those former relatives. Those Peta relatives drank from and bathed in those ponds; their distress, exhaustion, and thirst vanished, and their bodies became bright and golden in hue.

Then the King offered gruel, hard food, and soft food in due order to the Sangha headed by the Buddha, and dedicated the merit as before. At that very moment, divine gruel, hard food, and soft food appeared for the use of those former relatives. Those Peta relatives partook of that divine gruel and food heartily (making up for their past hunger), and they became endowed with full and refreshed sense faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.

Thereafter, the King offered robes and bedding to the Sangha headed by the Buddha and dedicated the merit as before. At that very moment...
618:
...divine clothes, divine vehicles, divine mansions and palaces, and various kinds of divine rugs, blankets, bedding, and ornaments appeared for the use of those Peta relatives. The Buddha made an asseveration (adhiṭṭhāna) so that King Bimbisāra could see all those riches. According to that asseveration, King Bimbisāra saw all those riches clearly with his own eyes and became exceedingly joyful.

(According to the Story of Venerable Sāriputta Thera in the Dhammapada Commentary, Volume 1, page 66, those Peta relatives abandoned their state as Petas and were established in divine bodies.)

Then, when the Buddha had finished His meal, He preached this Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, adorned with twelve verses, to King Bimbisāra, the ruler of Magadha, in order to give a talk of appreciation (anumodanā):

Tirokuṭṭesu tiṭṭhanti,
sandhisiṅghāṭakesu ca.
dvārabāhāsu tiṭṭhanti,
āgantvāna sakaṃ gharaṃ.

(This Tirokuṭṭa Sutta appears in the Khuddakapāṭha Pāḷi and the Petavatthu Pāḷi. The detailed meaning of the Pāḷi should be noted in the Myanmar translations of the Khuddakapāṭha and Petavatthu Pāḷi.)
619:
At the conclusion of this Tirokuṭṭa Sutta discourse, eighty-four thousand beings, having become terrified and moved (saṃvega) by the Buddha's explanation and opening up of the faults and suffering of being reborn in the Peta realm, and having practiced accordingly, realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation.

On the second day as well, the Buddha preached this same Tirokuṭṭa Sutta to devas and humans. He continued to preach in this manner until the seventh day, and in the same way, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) each day.

## This concludes the Second Volume of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas.

## Regarding the Five Tumults (Kolāhala)
A tumult (kolāhala) refers to a widespread, noisy, and sudden announcement or rumor made by one or two people initially and then by many in unison, saying, "Such and such is going to happen," before the event actually occurs.

In this context, "tumult" refers only to the noisy collective talk of many people as a precursor or omen, occurring a long time before something that will definitely happen in the future. It does not refer to the noisy and sudden talk that happens randomly in various towns and villages about things that cannot truly happen, such as "A Universal Monarch is about to appear."

In the world, there are five kinds of such tumults that occur in advance as omens:
(1) Kappa-kolāhala (Aeon Tumult),
(2) Cakkavatti-kolāhala (Universal Monarch Tumult),
(3) Buddha-kolāhala (Buddha Tumult),
(4) Maṅgala-kolāhala (Blessing Tumult),
(5) Moneyya-kolāhala (Sagehood Tumult).
Among these five:
621:
(ā)
## (1) Kappa-kolāhala
The noisy uproar that the world is about to perish is called Kappa-kolāhala. When the end of the aeon approaches, one hundred thousand years before the destruction, the Kāmāvacara devas known as Lokabyūha dress in red garments, let their hair hang disheveled, wipe tears from their weeping faces, and with an appearance of great distress, wander through the paths frequented by humans, proclaiming:

"Friends, one hundred thousand years from this year, this world-system will perish. The great oceans will dry up. The great earth and Mount Sineru—all these will be destroyed by fire (if it is an aeon destroyed by fire), or by water (if it is an aeon destroyed by water), or by violent and harsh winds (if it is an aeon destroyed by wind). This world-system, from this great earth where Mount Sineru and the oceans stand up to the Brahma realm, will be destroyed. O friends, develop loving-kindness (mettā); develop compassion (karuṇā); develop sympathetic joy (muditā); develop equanimity (upekkhā) as the sublime abodes. Respectfully care for and serve your parents; respect the elders and those worthy of respect. Be constantly vigilant in performing meritorious deeds; do not be negligent!"

They proclaim this widely enough for all people to hear. Based on this proclamation, the noisy collective talk of many people gathered in various places, saying, "The world is about to perish! The world is about to perish!" is called "Kappa-kolāhala."

## (2) Cakkavatti-kolāhala
The noisy uproar among people saying, "A Universal Monarch is about to appear," who will rule over the entire human world, including the four great islands and two thousand small surrounding islands, is called...
622:
(i)
...Cakkavatti-kolāhala. The Kāmāvacara devas who are world-protectors (Lokapāla) and who know in advance that a Universal Monarch is about to appear in the human world, wander through the main roads frequented by humans one hundred years before the Universal Monarch appears, proclaiming:

"Friends, one hundred years from today, a Universal Monarch will arise in this human world!"

They proclaim this widely enough for all people to hear. Based on this proclamation, the noisy collective talk of many people gathered in various places, saying, "A Universal Monarch is about to appear! A Universal Monarch is about to appear!" is called "Cakkavatti-kolāhala."

## (3) Buddha-kolāhala
The noisy uproar among people saying, "A Buddha is about to be enlightened," in the human world is called Buddha-kolāhala. The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, who know in advance that an Omniscient Buddha is about to be enlightened in the human world, dress themselves in the garments and ornaments of Brahmas, wear the Brahma crowns on their heads, and with clear, joyful, and delighted minds, wander through the main roads frequented by humans one thousand years before the Buddha's enlightenment, proclaiming:

"Friends, one thousand years from today, an Omniscient Buddha will manifest and be enlightened in this human world!"

They proclaim this widely enough for all people to hear. Based on this proclamation, the noisy collective talk of many people gathered in various places, saying, "The Buddha is about to be enlightened! The Buddha is about to be enlightened!" is called "Buddha-kolāhala."

(Regarding this Buddha-kolāhala, the statement that "Buddha-kolāhala arises one thousand years before the Buddha's enlightenment"...)
623:
(It should be noted that this statement is made only in accordance with the lifespan of the Buddhas who are to appear; it should not be taken as a general statement made without regard for the lifespan of all Buddhas who will appear. The reason is that in eras of long lifespans, the Bodhisattas such as Prince Dīpaṅkara, Prince Koṇḍañña, and Prince Maṅgala, having descended to the human world to become Buddhas, enjoyed royal splendor as humans for about ten thousand or nine thousand years before renouncing the world, practicing austerities, and attaining Enlightenment. As for the Buddha-kolāhala [the uproar concerning a Buddha], it first arises in the celestial realms, and following that uproar, the devas and brahmas of the ten thousand world-systems approach and entreat the Bodhisatta. Only after receiving the Bodhisatta's consent do the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas travel through the human world and make the proclamation. Therefore, since long-lived Buddhas appear only after about ten thousand or nine thousand years—more than one thousand or five thousand years—after the Buddha-kolāhala has arisen in the human world, the statement "one thousand years for the Buddha-kolāhala" should not be taken as a statement for every Buddha, but should be understood as a statement only for Buddhas with short lifespans like Gotama Buddha.)

## (4) Maṅgala-kolāhala
Maṅgala-kolāhala (the uproar concerning blessings) refers to the great commotion where many people gather and, unable to decide the exact nature and meaning of the Maṅgala Dhamma (the doctrine of blessings), speak of their own opinions, saying, "This is Maṅgala," or "That is Maṅgala," and "This is what is called Maṅgala." The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, who know in advance that the Buddha will preach the Maṅgala Dhamma in this human world, and who know the thoughts of the people who desire the Maṅgala Dhamma, travel along the main roads frequented by people twelve years before the Buddha preaches it, and proclaim—
624:
"Friends, twelve years from today, the Buddha will preach the Maṅgala Dhamma."

They proclaim this widely so that all people may hear. Taking this proclamation as the cause, the great commotion and discussion among many people gathered in various places regarding the Maṅgala Dhamma is called "Maṅgala-kolāhala."

## (5) Moneyya-kolāhala
Moneyya-kolāhala (the uproar concerning sagehood) refers to the great commotion regarding the Moneyya practice. (The detailed account of this Moneyya practice is written extensively in the section on the Elder Nāḷaka in the Saṅgha-ratana Thera-vaṃsa.) The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, who know in advance that a monk in the human world will approach the Buddha and ask about the Moneyya practice, travel along the main roads frequented by people seven years before it is preached, in the same manner as before, and proclaim—

"Friends, seven years from today, a monk will approach the Buddha and ask about the Moneyya practice."

They proclaim this widely so that all people may hear. Taking this proclamation as the cause, the great commotion and discussion among many people gathered in various places regarding the word "Moneyya practice" is called "Moneyya-kolāhala."

These are the five kinds of uproars (kolāhala). The accounts of these uproars are explained in the Buddhavaṃsa-aṭṭhakathā, Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā, Kosala-saṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā, Khuddakapāṭha-aṭṭhakathā, Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā, and Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā.

End of the account of the five uproars.
626:
(4) Regarding the fading of physical appearance, throughout their entire celestial lifespan, these devas never experience any physical decay or loss of complexion, such as broken teeth, gray hair, or wrinkled skin. Devis (goddesses) always remain at the age of sixteen, and devas (gods) at the age of twenty. Thus, while the devas and devis remain youthful, fresh, and radiantly beautiful due to their great meritorious deeds, when the time to pass away approaches, their physical bodies become dry, soiled, weary, and withered, resulting in the fading of their physical appearance.

(5) Regarding the lack of delight in one's own celestial mansion, throughout their entire celestial lifespan, these devas never experience any lack of enjoyment or dissatisfaction with their celestial mansions. It is only when they are about to pass away that they find themselves unable to delight in or enjoy their own dwellings.

## The Five Omens Do Not Occur for Every Deva
Although it is said that these five omens appear when one is about to pass away, it should not be understood that they occur for every single deva. Just as in the human world, omens such as falling meteors, earthquakes, and eclipses of the sun and moon occur only for powerful kings and ministers, so too in the celestial realm, these five omens appear only for devas and devis of great power and merit. For devas of little power and merit, these five omens do not appear.

Furthermore, just as the benefits and harms of omens in the human world are known only to wise omen-readers, the significance of these five omens is known only to wise devas; unwise devas do not know them.

When these omens of passing away appear, devas with little merit become intensely afraid and tremble, thinking, "Who knows where I will be reborn now?" Devas with great merit—
627:
—however, have no fear at all, reflecting, "Based on the merit of the gifts we have given, the Uposatha precepts we have observed, and the meditation we have practiced, we shall enjoy splendor in the higher celestial realms." (From the Commentary to the Mahāpadāna Sutta, Mahāvagga, Dīgha Nikāya, DA. 2.21).

## On Conception in the Second Stage of Life
One might ask: Why did Queen Māyā conceive the Bodhisatta during the third part of the second stage of life (majjhima-vaya)? The answer is: In the physical bodies of beings still in the first stage of life, sensual desire (chanda-rāga-taṇhā) is usually intense and powerful. Therefore, women who conceive during this first stage are often unable to protect or maintain their pregnancy safely. Consequently, the pregnancies of such women are prone to many diseases and ailments.

When the second stage of life, called majjhima-vaya—which is the middle third of the lifespan—is further divided into three parts, and after passing two of those parts and reaching the third part, the womb (gabbhāsaya) of such women is pure and clean. Children born from a pure and clean womb are free from diseases.

It is the natural law (dhammatā) that the mother of a Bodhisatta in his final existence enjoys royal splendor in the first stage of life, gives birth to the Bodhisatta in the third part of the second stage, and then passes away. (The passing away of the mother seven days after the birth of the Bodhisatta is also a natural law; it is not because she gave birth to the son. In fact, when the Bodhisatta Deva performed the Five Great Observations and looked at the lifespan of the mother, he would only pass away from the celestial realm after seeing that the mother had only ten months and seven days of life remaining from the time of the Bodhisatta's conception. By reflecting on this fact, one should note that even before the Bodhisatta's conception, the mother's remaining lifespan was only ten months and seven days.)

## About the Hermit Kāḷadevila
(The name of this hermit is explained as Devala in the Sinhalese version and as Devila in the Burmese version.) I shall present the account of this Hermit Devila, taking it from the Sutta Nipāta Commentary, Volume II, page 203.

This Hermit Devila was the chaplain (purohita) of King Sīhahanu, the ruler of Kapilavatthu and father of King Suddhodana. Because his complexion was dark, he was also called Asita. He was a wise minister and royal teacher who had to devise and advise on all matters of state, royal affairs, and administrative issues that came before King Sīhahanu, resolving them completely.

During the reign of King Sīhahanu, even when Prince Suddhodana was still a young prince and had not yet been consecrated, he was the royal tutor who had to teach Prince Suddhodana various royal customs, arts, sciences, and skills.
632:
After King Sīhahanu, when his son Prince Suddhodana succeeded to his father’s throne and was consecrated as the ruler of Kapilavatthu, that same former chaplain (the Brahmin Asita) became the chaplain to King Suddhodana once again.

Thus, after Prince Suddhodana was consecrated and ruled the kingdom, King Suddhodana no longer showed the same special reverence and humble respect to that chaplain (the Brahmin Asita), who had been his childhood teacher, as he did when he was a young prince. Instead, when entering the royal assembly by night or day, he merely showed respect by joining his palms (añjali) according to the custom of consecrated Sakyan kings.

Because he no longer received the profound and humble respect as in the past, the chaplain Asita, with the pride of his Brahmin birth and his status as a teacher, became dissatisfied and displeased. Feeling weary of attending the King, he requested permission from King Suddhodana to become a hermit.

King Suddhodana, knowing the firm decision of his chaplain, said to him, “If you wish to become a hermit, please do so. However, after becoming a hermit, do not go to live in a distant place; stay in my royal garden so that I may easily see and pay respects to my teacher regularly.” The chaplain agreed, saying, “Very well, let it be so.” After becoming a hermit, he received the support of King Suddhodana and lived in the royal garden, practicing meditation on the kasina devices. He attained the five mundane superknowledges (abhiññā) and the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti). From the time he became a hermit and attained these jhānas and attainments, after having his daily meal in King Suddhodana’s palace, he would regularly go to places such as the Himalayas, the Cātumahārājika heaven, and the Tāvatiṃsa heaven to spend the heat of the day.

This is the account of the Hermit Kāḷadevila, also known as the Hermit Asita.

## A Brief History of the Bodhisatta's Royal Lineage
In connection with the *Kula-olokana* (investigation of the family) by the Bodhisatta Setaketu Deva, the *Rājakkama* (royal succession) of the Sākiyan kings shall be presented in brief as follows. By noting this, one understands the *Jātimahatta-guṇa* (the quality of greatness of birth) of the Buddha-to-be.

In the first *Antara-kappa* of the *Vivattaṭṭhāyī Asaṅkhyeyya-kappa* (the incalculable aeon of world-evolution and stability) of this *Bhadda-kappa*, the very first king of the humans at the beginning of the world was our Noble Bodhisatta. His original name was Manu.

That Noble Bodhisatta, King Manu, was exceedingly handsome, extremely pleasant to behold, and very inspiring of faith among all the people of the early world. He possessed great majesty and power and was endowed with all excellent virtues.

In that early era of the world, during the first part, the conduct of those early humans was extremely pure. However, after a long time had passed, those who committed evil deeds such as stealing the property of others (*adinnādāna*) began to appear. In order to be free from such evils and to live in peace as before, all the people of the early world gathered and consulted together. They unanimously decided and decreed to select and appoint someone who would suitably judge and rule over them.

According to that decision, they reached a consensus that only Manu, the Bodhisatta, was endowed with the most suitable qualities and virtues. Having reached this agreement, all the people of the early world approached the Noble Being named Manu and requested him to rule over them with good and appropriate governance.

As he performed the duty of governing and ruling, all the people who were under his rule, each and every one...

## Acquisition of Three Names
Because all the people, without objection and with one accord, well-designated the Noble Bodhisatta as the one who would rule and govern righteously in exchange for the taxes offered, the Noble Being Manu received the name *Mahāsammata* (The Great Elect).

Because he had the authority to decide, manage, and rule so that there would be no disputes or quarrels over land ownership (or to settle them if they arose), the Noble Being Manu also received the name *Khattiya* (Lord of the Fields).

Because he was able to please and endear the people by governing and protecting them with good and upright royal virtues, the Noble Being Manu also received the name *Rāja* (The One who Pleases).

Among all the kings of men in this *Bhadda-kappa*, only this Noble Bodhisatta Manu was the first to receive these three names: *Mahāsammata*, *Khattiya*, and *Rāja*.

Just as the sun gives sight, form, and light to beings and carries a thousand rays, so too, because he was like the eyes of the early world and carried the radiance of many virtues as if a second sun had arisen, he was also known and recorded by his lineage as *Ādiccavaṃsa* (The Solar Dynasty/Lineage of the Sun).
