(Tha). The last of the 57 kings mentioned above was named Nāgadeva. The son of King Nāgadeva re-founded the city of Mithilā for the second time and ruled there. Including him, there were twenty-five (25) successive generations of his sons and grandsons in that city of Mithilā.

(Da). The last of those twenty-five kings was named Samuddadatta. The son of King Samuddadatta ruled in the city of Rājagaha. Including him, there were twenty-five (25) successive generations of his sons and grandsons in that city of Rājagaha.

(Dha). The last of those twenty-five kings was named Tidhaṅkara. The son of King Tidhaṅkara founded and ruled the city of Takkasilā. Including him, there were twelve (12) successive generations of his sons and grandsons in that city of Takkasilā.

(Na). The last of those twelve kings was named Tālissara. The son of King Tālissara founded and ruled the city of Kusinārā. Including him, there were twelve (12) successive generations of his sons and grandsons in that city of Kusinārā.

(Pa). The last of those twelve kings was named Purinda. The son of King Purinda founded and ruled the city named Tāmalittiya. Including him, there were nine (9) successive generations of his sons and grandsons in that city of Tāmalittiya.
643:
(Khā)
The account of these 83 kings in five groups mentioned in notes (Tha), (Da), (Dha), (Na), and (Pa) is composed in the Maghadeva Alaṅkāra, Part 2, Chapter 1 (Chronicle Section), Verse 30:

"In the era of the palace grounds in the new city of Campā, the last to take the shade of the white parasol was King Nāga, the ruler of Jambudīpa. His lineage, numbering twenty-five (pañcavī), were kings who practiced the Dhamma. In the Videha country, according to ancient history, they established the second city of Mithilā on the earth and resided in the palace. From the noble King Samuddadatta, twenty-five descendants followed, ending with King Tidhaṅkara, residing joyfully in the beautiful city of Rājagaha while the drums sounded. From the lineage of the famous King Tidhaṅkara, twelve (dvādasa) great kings, ending with King Tālissa, established their permanent residence in the noble, dark-hued city of Takkasilā. From King Tālissa, twelve (dvādasa) kings descended, who, possessing the ten kingly virtues without fail, took possession of the golden palace in the city of Kusinārā. From the lineage of the noble King Purinda, nine kings resided in the great golden city of Tāmalittiya, ending with King Sāgaradeva, ruling according to the ten kingly virtues in a prosperous and wide kingdom."
So it is composed.

(Pha). The last of the 83 kings mentioned above was named Sāgaradeva. The son of King Sāgaradeva was named Maghadeva. Starting from King Maghadeva, his sons, grandsons, and successive descendants ruled in the city of Mithilā for eighty-four thousand (84,000) generations.

(Ba). The last of those eighty-four thousand kings of the Maghadeva lineage was King Nimi, the Bodhisatta. The son of the Bodhisatta King Nimi was named Kaḷārajanaka. His son was named Samaṅkara. His son was named Asoca (also found as Asoka). These kings, Kaḷārajanaka,
644:
(Ga)
Samaṅkara, and Asoca, along with their successive sons and grandsons, totaling eighty-four thousand and three (84,003) kings, re-founded and ruled in the city of Bārāṇasī.

(Bha). The last of those eighty-four thousand and three kings was named Sihappati.
(1) King Vijitasena, son of King Sihappati,
(2) King Dhammasena, his son,
(3) King Nāgasena, his son,
(4) King Samiddha, his son,
(5) King Disampati, his son,
(6) King Reṇu, his son,
(7) King Kusa, his son,
(8) King Mahākusa, his son,
(9) King Navaraṭṭha, his son,
(10) King Dasaraṭṭha, his son,
(11) King Rāma, the Bodhisatta, his son,
(12) King Viḷāraṭṭha, his son,
(13) King Cittaraṃsī, his son,
(14) King Ambaraṃsī, his son,
(15) King Sujāta, his son,
(16) King Okkāka, his son.
These sixteen (16) kings also continued to rule in the city of Bārāṇasī.

From King Mahāsammata, the Bodhisatta at the beginning of the aeon, to King Okkāka, there were two hundred fifty-two thousand five hundred fifty-six (252,556) kings in the lineage of sons and grandsons.
645:
(c)
Including the 84,000 kings mentioned in note (pha), the 84,003 kings mentioned in note (ba), and the 16 kings mentioned in note (bha), counting from King Mahāsammata to King Okkāka, there were a total of 252,556 kings. This is recorded in the *Mahāsutakārī Maghadeva Laṅkā* treatise, Volume II, (1) Section on Royal Chronicles, Verse 31:

From Sāgaradeva, of majestic power, the lineage continued. With rising glory, starting from the Bodhisatta Maghadeva, all became monks. Following the ancient traditions and established customs, they held noble intentions. Through the line of Royal Sages (Rājisi), up to the Bodhisatta King Nemi, there were 84,000 illustrious and noble kings who reigned in the golden palace of Mithilā.

Then came the beloved son of the sovereign King Nemi, Kālājanaka, whose glory was like the sun. From Samaṅkara and Asoka onwards, in a direct line, there were 84,003 kings who established the second dynasty and ruled in the golden city of Bārāṇasī.

Of the last of those famous kings named Vijita, his glorious son, like a deity, was Vijitasena. Then came Dhammasena and Nāgasena, of fierce power. From Samiddha, the great Disampati, Reṇu, Kusa Rājā, and Mahākusa, followed by Navaraṭṭha, Dasaratha, and the Bodhisatta Rāma. Their sons continued the line: Viḷāraṭṭha, Cittaraṃsī, Ambarāṃsī, the famous Sujāta, up to Okkāka. These sixteen supreme kings ruled in the city of Bārāṇasī, where the golden drums resounded with sweet music. Counting from King Mahāsammata to King Okkāka, the total number is 252,550 plus six, making 252,556 kings. This is the first division of the Royal Chronicles recorded in golden ink.

Thus it was composed.

(In this regard, the commentaries on the *Ambaṭṭha Sutta* of the *Sīlakkhandha Vagga* and the *Muni Sutta* of the *Suttanipāta* explain that after the 84,000 kings of the Maghadeva lineage, there were three lineages of Okkāka kings. The third King Okkāka had five chief queens, each with five hundred attendants, and so forth.)
646:
(gi)
It should be understood that the Sakyan (Sakya) princes are the descendants of the lineage of the third King Okkāka. The Okkāka king mentioned as the 252,556th king should also be identified as the third King Okkāka.

## About King Okkāka
Among those 252,556 kings, the last one, King Okkāka, had five queens: Hatthā, Cittā, Jantu, Jālini, and Visākhā. Each queen had five hundred female attendants.

(The reason he was called King Okkāka is explained in the *Ambaṭṭha Sutta* commentary of the *Sīlakkhandha Vagga*: when the king spoke, a brilliant light like a torch (ukkā) issued from his mouth. In the Burmese Royal Chronicles, it is also noteworthy that special men like King Kyansittha and King Manuha of Thaton were believed to have a brilliant radiance, or a torch-like light, or a unique glow issue from their mouths, similar to King Okkāka.

Furthermore, the residence of King Okkāka should not be definitively identified as the city of Bārāṇasī. This is because the *Ambaṭṭha Sutta* commentary itself states that the eldest daughter of this King Okkāka, Princess Piyā, and King Rāma of Bārāṇasī were wed. Therefore, it should be understood that the capital of the present King Okkāka (the third Okkāka), who is the primary ancestor of the Sakyan lineage, was a city other than Bārāṇasī.)

From the eldest of these five queens, Queen Hatthā, four sons were born: Okkāmukha, Karakaṇḍu, Hatthinika, and Sinisūra; and five daughters: Piyā, Suppiyā, Ānandā, Vijitā, and Vijitaseṇā.

After the birth of these four sons and five daughters, when Queen Hatthā passed away, King Okkāka appointed a young, youthful, and exceedingly beautiful princess as his chief queen.
647:
(gī)
From this queen, a young son named Jantu was born. On the fifth day after his birth, the young prince Jantu was adorned beautifully and presented to the king. King Okkāka was so delighted that he granted the queen a boon, saying, "Take whatever boon you desire."

After consulting with her relatives, the queen asked for the boon of granting the kingship (the throne) to her young son Jantu. King Okkāka refused, rebuking and threatening her, saying, "Wretched woman, be gone! You desire harm for my sons." However, whenever the opportunity arose, the queen would soothe the king and repeatedly plead, "Great King, a king should not let his word (promise) become a lie. I request you to grant it as you promised," asking him to hand over the throne to Prince Jantu. Consequently, King Okkāka summoned his elder sons, including Okkāmukha, and with a heavy and sorrowful heart, spoke to them thus:

"My sons, because your father was so delighted upon seeing your younger brother, Prince Jantu, I granted his mother whatever boon she desired. Now, Jantu's mother intensely desires to hand over the throne and royal wealth to her son. Except for your father's auspicious state elephant, auspicious state horse, and auspicious state chariot, take as many elephants, horses, and chariots as you wish and depart from this city to a place of safety before I pass away. After my death, return and take possession of the throne of this kingdom."

Having said this, he sent the elder princes away along with eight great ministers.

Prince Okkāmukha and the other elder princes, with heavy hearts and much weeping, said, "Father, if we have committed any faults, please forgive us." They paid their respects and apologized to their father the king and the royal concubines. Then, saying, "Father, let our sisters also accompany us," they requested permission and took their five elder and younger sisters with them. Surrounded by the fourfold army and accompanied by the eight great ministers, they departed from the capital. Thinking, "The elder princes will surely rule the kingdom when their father passes away; let us serve and attend to them from now on," a great multitude of people followed the princes.
648:
(gu)
Asking their father for permission, the five sisters also joined them and left the city. They departed from the capital accompanied by the eight ministers and the fourfold army. A great number of people followed the princes, thinking, "The elder princes will certainly rule the kingdom when their father passes away. Let us serve and attend to them early on."

The size of the following crowd was one yojana on the first day, two yojanas on the second day, and three yojanas on the third day, increasing day by day. The princes then consulted each other: "Our military strength and following are very great. If we were to use this force to attack and seize the kingdom of a neighboring minor king, no king or country would dare to resist us. However, what benefit is there in seizing another's country through oppression and force? There is no benefit. This Great Island of Jambudīpa is very vast. Let us establish a new city and palace in an unoccupied forest area." Having agreed upon this, they headed towards the Himavantā forest and searched for a site to build their city.

## The Founding of Kapilavatthu
At that time, our Great Bodhisatta was born into a wealthy Brahmin family of high status (Brāhmaṇa Mahāsāra). His name was Kapila. He renounced his wealth, went into the forest, and became an ascetic. He was living in a leaf-roofed hermitage near a clear, clean pond within a large teak forest on the slopes of the Himavantā mountains.

That ascetic Kapila, the Bodhisatta, was learned in the science called *Bhūmijāla* (the science of ground signs), through which he could perceive the merits and defects of the ground eighty cubits below and eighty cubits above. In the area around where the ascetic Kapila had built his leaf-roofed hermitage, the grass, trees, and shrubs grew
649:
(gū)
circumambulating to the right, and the shoots and tendrils of those grasses, trees, and shrubs grew facing only towards the eastern direction. Not only that, but when predatory animals such as lions and tigers chased their prey like deer and pigs, or when snakes and cats chased frogs and mice, upon reaching that spot, they could no longer chase or catch them. Instead, the deer, pigs, frogs, and mice would turn back and threaten those predatory animals, lions, snakes, and cats, causing them to retreat and flee. Because the Bodhisatta, the ascetic Kapila, saw these signs, he knew, "This area is the supreme and most excellent ground where enemies can be overcome," and thus he had created and built his leaf-roofed hermitage in that place.

The princes, led by Prince Okkāmukha, who wished to establish a city and kingdom, were wandering in search of a site when they arrived at the place of the Bodhisatta ascetic Kapila's leaf-roofed hermitage. When questioned by the ascetic, they informed him that they were searching for a site to establish a city. The Bodhisatta ascetic Kapila, knowing this and feeling great compassion for the princes, said:

"Princes, a city established on the site of this hermitage of mine will be the most excellent city in the whole of Jambudīpa. Among the men born in this city, even a single man will be able to overcome and master a hundred or a thousand men born elsewhere. Therefore, establish and create a new city on the site of this hermitage of mine. Build your royal palace on the site of this hermitage. To describe the goodness and excellence of this ground: if supported by this place, even the son of an outcaste (caṇḍāla) would become one greatly praised through the power of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti)."

Thus he spoke. The princes then asked, "Venerable Ascetic, is this not the place currently occupied and used by you?"
650:
Kapila the hermit said, "Princes, do not be overly concerned thinking that this place is my current dwelling. Build a hermitage for me at one side, and build your city and palace right here where I point. Name the city Kapilavatthu."

Prince Okkāmukha and the other three princes, along with their ministers and the army, built the city and palace as instructed by the Bodhisatta Kapila the hermit. They named the city and the country Kapilavatthu and resided there.

## The Origin of the Sakyans

As they lived there, the princes reached the age for marriage. The ministers thought, "Ministers, these princes have come of age. If their father, King Okkāka, were near, he would arrange their marriages. Now it is our responsibility." They then consulted with the princes.

The princes said, "O friends, there are no princesses of our lineage here, nor are there princes of our lineage for our sisters. If we marry those of different lineages, our descendants will be impure from both the father's and mother's sides, leading to the confusion of lineage (jātisambheda). Therefore, let us elevate our eldest sister, Princess Piyā, to the position of mother, and let the remaining four brothers and four sisters marry among ourselves to prevent the mixing and destruction of our lineage." Having agreed, and fearing the corruption of their lineage, they elevated the eldest sister, Princess Piyā, to the position of mother...
651:
...and lived as married couples, paired with their four sisters.

As they lived thus, the households of Prince Okkāmukha and the other princes and princesses flourished with children. When King Okkāka heard that Prince Okkāmukha and the other children had founded Kapilavatthu and, instead of marrying into other lineages, had married their own siblings of the same father and mother and were living prosperously, he was greatly delighted. In the midst of his ministers and relatives, he exclaimed:

"Sakyā vata bho kumārā = O friends, my sons and daughters are indeed capable!"

"Paramasakyā vata bho kumārā = O friends, my sons and daughters are exceedingly noble and capable!"

Based on this exclamation "Sakyā vata" (they are capable) by King Okkāka, the word "Sakya"—meaning "capable"—became the name for Prince Okkāmukha and the other princes and princesses, as well as their descendants. They became known as the Sakya, Sākiya, or Sākiyans.

(This is the account of the origin of the Sakyan lineage.)

## The Founding of the Koliya Kingdom

Later, Princess Piyā, the eldest sister of the married siblings like Okkāmukha, was afflicted with leprosy (kuṭṭha). On her body, pustules and patches appeared, resembling the flowers of the kalao (or the sea-coral tree).
652:
Because of this, her younger brothers, the princes, thought, "If we live and eat closely with our elder sister Piyā, who has such a loathsome disease, this leprosy will spread to us." After consulting, they pretended to go for a pleasure trip in the garden one day. They took their elder sister Piyā in a carriage to a suitable place in the forest. There, they had a large square pit dug, sufficient for the four postures of reclining, sitting, standing, and walking. They stocked this underground chamber with ample food and supplies, placed Princess Piyā inside, and to protect her from dangers, covered the pit with a wooden roof. They then covered the edges and top of the roof with earth and returned to their capital, Kapilavatthu.

At that time, King Rāma of Bārāṇasī was also afflicted with leprosy. Being loathed by his harem and courtiers, he felt a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega). He handed over the kingship to his eldest son and entered the forest. He built a leaf-hut and lived on roots and fruits. Before long, his leprosy was cured, and his skin became golden. While wandering here and there, he found a large tree with a hollow trunk. He cleared a space sixteen cubits wide inside the tree, fitted it with a main door, a window, and a ladder, making it like a small palace chamber. He was living in that tree-house.

King Rāma would keep a fire in a large brazier. At night, he would listen to the sounds of deer, wild boars, and other animals to mark their locations. At dawn, he would go to those places, collect the remains of deer or boars left by lions, leopards, or tigers, and cook them for food.
653:
One day, a tiger, catching the scent of Princess Piyā from her underground chamber not far from King Rāma's dwelling, began scratching and opening the wooden roof with its claws. The princess, terrified, screamed loudly. King Rāma, who was sitting by his brazier near dawn, heard the sound and thought, "This is a woman's voice." Early in the morning, he went to the underground chamber and asked, "Who is inside this pit?" When she replied, "I am a woman," he asked, "Of what lineage?" She answered, "Lord, I am the daughter of King Okkāka." He said, "Come out." She replied, "Lord, I cannot come out." When asked why, she said, "Lord, I have a skin disease." King Rāma then inquired about all the circumstances. To the princess, who refused to come out due to her Khattiya pride, he revealed his own royalty, saying, "I too am of the Khattiya lineage." He lowered a ladder, brought her out of the chamber, and took her to his dwelling. He gave her the same medicine he had used, and after her leprosy was cured and her skin became golden, they lived together as husband and wife by mutual consent.

While living thus, Queen Piyā gave birth to twins sixteen times, resulting in thirty-two sons. As these sons grew up, King Rāma taught them all the arts and sciences that princes should master.

One day, a hunter from Bārāṇasī, King Rāma's original capital, came to that forest near the Himālayas in search of treasures. He saw King Rāma and, recognizing him, said, "Great King, I know you well." While the king was asking the hunter about his country and kingdom...
654:
...the thirty-two sons arrived at that spot. Seeing the princes, the hunter asked, "Great King, who are these youths?" When the king replied, "They are my sons," the hunter inquired about their maternal lineage. Realizing the situation, the hunter thought, "I have found a great piece of news to report to the King of Bārāṇasī." He returned to Bārāṇasī and informed the king of everything.

The King of Bārāṇasī, who was King Rāma's son, was overjoyed at the prospect of bringing his father back. He traveled with the fourfold army to where King Rāma was, paid respectful homage, and pleaded, "Great Father, please accept the kingship of Bārāṇasī once again." King Rāma replied, "My son, I no longer desire the kingship of Bārāṇasī, nor will I return there. Right here, clear this tree where I live, and build a palace for me at the site of this kalao tree. Found a new city and palace for my sake." As instructed by his father, the King of Bārāṇasī founded the new city.

This new city was named Koliyanagara because it was built after clearing the kalao tree at his father's dwelling, and also Vyagghapajja because it was built on a path frequented by tigers. After paying homage to his father, the King of Bārāṇasī returned to his own city.

While King Rāma and Queen Piyā were residing in the new city of Koliya, one day Queen Piyā said to her grown sons:

"My sons, your uncles, the Sakyan kings, rule in the city of Kapilavatthu. The daughters of your uncles dress and adorn themselves in such a way; they have such appearances and manners. When these princesses come to the bathing ghat to bathe..."
655:
(Gā)
"O young men, take hold of and bring back the princesses whom you love and cherish."

Thus, she instructed and guided them.

Following their mother's instructions and guidance, the princes went to the bathing ghat of the daughters of their maternal uncles, the Sakyan kings of Kapilavatthu. After observing and choosing the princesses they each preferred, at the moment when the princesses were drying their hair after bathing, the princes took hold of them, announced their names and lineage, and brought them back.

When the Sakyan kings heard of this, they said, "Friends, let it be. These Koliyan princes are the sons of our elder sister; they are but our own nephews and close relatives." Thus, they accepted the matter with pleasure and remained silent, without taking any offense.

In this manner, the Sakyan and Koliyan royalties intermarried, and this lineage continued unbroken until the time of the Buddha.

Thus, the Sakyan royal clan flourished and expanded their lineage in a pure, beautiful, and noble manner through intermarriage among close relatives. From King Okkāka, the original ancestor of the Sakyans, down to Prince Siddhattha, the Bodhisatta, there was no break or deviation in the lineage. Therefore, these Sakyans reached the pinnacle of royal history as the "Asambhina Khattiya" (the pure and unbroken line of Khattiyas).

## The Founding of the Kingdom of Devadaha
The Sakyan kings residing in Kapilavatthu used to go to a large, pleasant, and beautiful lake for water sports. Because that lake was the place where the Sakyan kings played in the water, it came to be known as Devadaha. (Deva = the Sakyan kings who are conventional deities + Daha = the lake where they played).
656:
(Gha)
Later, the Sakyans who came to this lake for water sports did not return to Kapilavatthu but built royal pavilions (rest houses) and resided near the lake. As the settlement gradually became prosperous and grand, it turned into a kingdom. Taking the name from the Devadaha lake, the kingdom was also called Devadaha.

The Sakyan kings residing in that kingdom also came to be known as the Devadaha Sakyans, based on the name of the kingdom.
(Based on the commentary to the Devadaha Sutta, Uparipaṇṇāsa Aṭṭhakathā, page 1.)

## The Lineage of King Okkāmukha Sakya
Among the three Sakyan kingdoms—Kapilavatthu, Koliya, and Devadaha—the following kings established Kapilavatthu:

(1) King Okkāmukha (When this king spoke, brilliant rays of light issued from his mouth, just like his father, King Okkāka),
(2) His son, King Nipuṇa,
(3) His son, King Candima,
(4) His son, King Candamukha,
(5) His son, King Sivi,
(6) His son, King Sañjaya,
(7) His son, the Bodhisatta King Vessantara,
(8) His son, King Jālī,
(9) His son, King Sīhavāhana,
(10) His son, King Sīhassara.

These ten Sakyan kings, and subsequently the 82,000 Sakyan kings ending with King Jayasena, who were the descendants of King Sīhassara, were successive rulers in the great city of Kapilavatthu in the Sakka country.
657:
(Ghā)
Among those 82,010 Sakyan kings, the last one, King Jayasena, had two children: a son named Sīhahanu and a daughter named Yasodharā.

At that time, King Okkāsakka and Queen Yasavatī, who were reigning in the kingdom of Devadaha, also had two children: a son named Añjana and a daughter named Kañcanā.

Having two children each, Prince Sīhahanu, the son of King Jayasena of Kapilavatthu, and Princess Kañcanā, the daughter of King Okkāsakka of Devadaha, were wedded. They had seven children: five sons and two daughters. The five sons were (1) Suddhodana, (2) Amitodana, (3) Dhotodana, (4) Sakkodana, and (5) Sukkodana. (This is presented according to the commentary on the Sammaparibbājaniya Sutta in the second volume of the Sutta Nipāta Aṭṭhakathā.) The two daughters were (1) Princess Amittā and (2) Princess Pālitā.

Furthermore, Prince Añjana, the son of King Okkāsakka of Devadaha, and Princess Yasodharā, the daughter of King Jayasena of Kapilavatthu, were wedded. They had four children: two sons and two daughters. (In this context, King Añjana is also referred to as Mahāsuppabuddha.) The two sons were (1) Prince Suppabuddha and (2) Prince Daṇḍapāṇi. The two daughters were (1) Princess Sirīmahāmāyā and (2) Princess Pajāpatī Gotamī.

When Prince Suddhodana, the son of King Sīhahanu, wedded both sisters, Princess Sirīmahāmāyā and Princess Pajāpatī Gotamī, the daughters of King Añjana, the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha was born to the elder sister, Queen Sirīmahāmāyā. To the younger sister, Princess Pajāpatī Gotamī, were born a daughter, Princess Rūpanandā, and a son, Prince Nanda.
658:
(Ghi)
According to the sequence of words briefly explained above, from King Okkāmukha, who first established Kapilavatthu, down to his descendant King Sīhassara, there were 10 kings.

From the descendants of King Sīhassara down to King Jayasena, there were 82,000 kings.

(1) King Sīhahanu, the son of King Jayasena,
(2) King Suddhodana, his son,
(3) The Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha, his son.

Thus, the total of these three groups is 82,013 Sakyan kings, all of whom were the sovereign kings of the unbroken Sakyan lineage (Asambhina Sakya) who reigned in the royal capital of Kapilavatthu. (This is a brief presentation of the Sakyan lineage of Kapilavatthu.)

Combining the 252,556 kings from the beginning of the world cycle, starting from King Mahāsammata down to King Okkāka, with the 82,013 Sakyan kings from King Okkāmukha down to the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha, the total number of kings in the entire lineage is 334,569.

Therefore, in the second part of the Mahāsutakārī Maghadeva Laṅkā, in the section on Royal History, verses 32 and 33 state:

(32) From that King Okkāka, the lord of men, his four sons and five daughters of celestial beauty came forth to the great Himavantā forest. In the Sakavane, the site of the hermitage of the great sage Kapila, at the auspicious and victorious spot, they established a new palace and throne. They designated the country as Sakka and the city as Kapilavatthu, marking it as the pinnacle of Jambudīpa with a golden record. The four brothers wedded their younger sisters to keep the lineage pure and established the kingdom. From the mouth of the first of these later kings, King Okkāmukha, brilliant rays of light issued. From him descended King Nipuṇa, Candima, and Candamukha; then Sivi, then Sañjaya, and the famously powerful Vessantara of great glory.
659:
(Ghī)
From King Jālī came his own son Sīhavāhana, and from the glorious King Sīhassara onwards, the noble Sakyan clan, the Sakya race, continued in an unbroken line (Asambhina). Then came the lordly King Jayasena, his son Sīhahanu, and the peerless and famous King Suddhodana, ending with the Bodhisatta Siddhattha as the pinnacle. In the central capital of Kapilavatthu, the total number of Sakyan kings was eighty-two thousand and thirteen. Renowned throughout the island and as majestic as the celestial devas, they were the supreme buds of the Solar Dynasty. This is the second golden chronicle of royal history.

Thus it is written.

(33) In this manner, in the continuous line of the Great Chronicle (Mahāvaṃsa) and Royal History, the righteous kings were divided into two main groups: the Sammata group and the Okkāka group. When viewed by the divisions of countries and kingdoms, there are twenty-four groups. All those sovereign lords, when summarized into two main categories and then totaled, number three hundred and thirty-four thousand, five hundred and sixty, with nine more at the end. This is the brief record of the royal lineage to be remembered.

Thus it was composed.

In brief, the term 'Sakkara' (Era) is defined as the designation of yearly intervals established by kings capable of protecting and governing people. Alternatively, it is called 'Sakara' because it is the designation of yearly intervals established by the king named Saka. The measurement of time based on the movements of the sun and moon is designated as 'Koza' or 'Goza'. (The term 'Sakkara' is derived from the compound 'Sakka-rāja'. 'Sakka' means capable of protecting people + 'rāja' means king; thus, 'Sakkara' refers to the yearly intervals established by kings capable of protecting people. The term 'Sakara' is derived from 'Saka-rāja'. 'Saka' means the king named Saka + 'rāja' means king; thus, 'Sakara' refers to the yearly intervals established by the king named Saka. Regarding 'Koza' and 'Goza', the word 'Ko' refers to the sun, and 'Go' refers to both the sun and the moon. The word 'za' refers to movement or circulation. Thus, the duration of time it takes for the sun and moon to complete one quadrant (pāda) in their movement through the twelve signs of the zodiac is called a Koza year or a Goza year. It is also commonly written as 'Gocāra' year.)

## The Use of Kali Yuga and Era (Sakkara)

When the qualifying term 'Kali Yuga' is placed before the word 'Sakkara', as in 'so many years of the Kali Yuga Era', it does not mean that Kali Yuga and Sakkara have the same meaning. It means 'this many years of the Era within the period of the Kali Yuga'. To make this a bit clearer:
662:
(dhe)
According to secular treatises, within each pair of ascending and descending cycles known as an intermediate aeon (antarakappa), there are four ages (yugas) or time periods: Kata Yuga, Tretā Yuga, Dvāpara Yuga, and Kali Yuga, which appear and disappear in rotation. An ascending cycle ends after these four yugas have appeared and disappeared sixty times. The same applies to the descending cycle. Among these four yugas, the Kata Yuga comes first and lasts for 1,728,000 years. Then the Tretā Yuga begins, lasting for 1,296,000 years. Following that is the Dvāpara Yuga, which lasts for 864,000 years. Finally, the Kali Yuga begins, lasting for 432,000 years. (It should be noted that the duration of the Dvāpara Yuga is twice that of the Kali Yuga, the Tretā Yuga is three times, and the Kata Yuga is four times.) The total duration of the four yugas combined is 4,320,000 years.

During the Kata Yuga, just as a creature stands on four legs, if beings were divided into four parts, all four parts would observe the Dhamma. In the Tretā Yuga, like standing on three legs, only three parts observe the Dhamma, while one part does not. In the Dvāpara Yuga, two parts (half) observe the Dhamma, while the other two parts (half) do not. In the Kali Yuga, only one part observes the Dhamma, while the remaining three parts do not.

Our teacher, the Blessed One of the Gotama lineage, appeared in the 2,570th year of the Kali Yuga. This is stated in the first section of the Gotama Purāṇa:

"Kale rārab bhato suñña-satta pañca duke gate.
Saṃvacchare babhūva ve, dhammavidū gotamābhidho."

In the year when 2,570 years had passed since the beginning of the Kali Yuga, the Blessed Buddha named Gotama, the knower of the Dhamma, appeared in this world.
663:
(dhai)
If one wishes to know the current Sāsana year and the current Kali Yuga year, according to the ancient mnemonic: "Take the current Era (Sakkara), add two-eight (82) and one-one (11), and that is the past Sāsana year." For example, to find the past Sāsana years for the current year 1323, add 1323 and 1182. The resulting 2505 is the past Sāsana year.

Once the Sāsana year is known, according to the mnemonic: "Zero-seven (70), five-two (25), add to the Kali Yuga," add 2570 to the current Sāsana year 2505. The resulting 5075 is the current Kali Yuga year.

In summary, when people write or use the phrase "this many years of the Kali Yuga Era," it should be noted that it means "this many years of the Era within the Kali Yuga period." As mentioned, the Kali Yuga lasts for 432,000 years, while the Era (Sakkara) is the count of years to be followed as decreed by kings.

Regarding the four yugas and the Buddha's appearance in the 2570th year of the Kali Yuga, it is composed in verse 553 of the Dhammacariyānisaṃsa section of the Mahāsutakārī Magghadeva Laṅkā:

"Among the four yugas, in the Kata age, all people without exception lived entirely in truth (sammā). In the Tretā age, if divided into four parts, three parts remained in the Dhamma while one part fell away. In the Dvāpara cycle, good and evil were equal, half and half. In the Kali age, beings with right understanding and good conduct are very few; only one part remains while three parts are devoid of Dhamma. In that very Kali Yuga, in the human realm, when over two thousand five hundred and seventy years had passed and begun to exceed, during the period of a hundred-year lifespan (hāyana), the Supreme One of the world, the Great Buddha named Sakyasīha Gotama, appeared and was born in the human world..."

## The Melodious Voice of the Karavīka Bird King and
## The Story of Queen Asandhimittā

Queen Asandhimittā, the consort of King Dhammāsoka, (regarding the melodious nature of the Buddha's voice) asked the Saṅgha, "Is there anyone in this world whose voice is like that of the Blessed One?" The Saṅgha replied, "There is; the voice of the Karavīka bird king is like the voice of the Blessed One." When Queen Asandhimittā further asked, "Where do those Karavīka birds live?", the Saṅgha replied, "They live in the Himavantā region."

Queen Asandhimittā said to King Asoka, "Great King, I wish very much to see a Karavīka bird." King Asoka then issued a command, "This Karavīka bird must come and stay in this cage," and sent forth a golden cage. The cage traveled and stopped in front of a Karavīka bird. The bird reflected, "This cage has come by the king's authority. I cannot stay without following it in defiance of that authority," and it perched in the cage. The cage then traveled back and stopped before the King.

Although the Karavīka bird had arrived, it did not sing. King Asoka asked, "Friends, by what means do these Karavīka birds sing?" The ministers replied, "Great King, these Karavīka birds sing when they see their relatives." King Asoka then ordered the Karavīka bird to be surrounded by mirrors.

When the Karavīka bird saw its own reflection, it thought, "My relatives have come." It flapped its wings and began to sing melodiously and gently, like the sound of a ruby flute. Upon hearing the singing of the Karavīka bird king, Queen Asandhimittā and the citizens of Pāṭaliputta...

(gho)
...became as if intoxicated by the voice of the Karavīka bird king, feeling extremely joyful and delighted as if they were about to dance.

Queen Asandhimittā reflected: "If even the voice of this Karavīka bird, which is but an animal, is this sweet and melodious, what must the voice of the Blessed One be like—He who has reached the pinnacle of glory and power through His Omniscient Wisdom (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)? It would be impossible to even define or limit how sweet and melodious it must be." Focusing her mind on the Buddha, she developed great joy (pīti). Without letting go of that joy, she practiced successive stages of insight meditation (vipassanā) and, together with seven hundred female attendants, established herself in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). (From the Commentary on the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, page 263).

## Thirty-Two Marks of a Great Man

According to the Jinālaṅkāra-ṭīkā, the thirty-two Marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa Lakkhaṇa) are only properly explained when four points are clearly presented for each mark: (1) Kamma (Action), (2) Kammasarikkaka (Similarity to the Action), (3) Lakkhaṇa (The Mark), and (4) Lakkhaṇānisaṃsa (The Benefit of the Mark). Therefore, I will first briefly explain the meaning of these four points.

Among these four: (1) Kamma refers to the foundation of past wholesome deeds performed and accumulated with the aspiration to become a Buddha, which cause the great marks to arise. (2) Kammasarikkaka refers to the various powers and qualities of the marks that arise in accordance with that kamma. (3) Lakkhaṇa refers to the thirty-two types of marks obtained in the present life due to the foundation of past wholesome deeds, such as the level soles of the feet and the 108 signs of the wheel. (4) Lakkhaṇānisaṃsa refers to the subsequent results and ultimate benefits of the past wholesome kamma that produced the marks.

Because of this mark, the Great Bodhisatta was able to stand and walk firmly, strongly, and uprightly, such that no human, deva, brahma, or being could move or shake him. Due to that very same meritorious kamma, external enemies—both those who clearly opposed him and those who did not—could not cause the Great Lord to tremble or be frightened by the internal enemies such as greed, hatred, and delusion.

In this context, the collection of past meritorious deeds practiced firmly and unshakably in many previous lives, which no one could hinder, is called (1) Kamma. Having level soles (or) the level soles themselves, because they are the means of recognizing the cause of past meritorious kamma, are called (3) Lakkhaṇa (Mark). The power and quality of that mark, which is the ability to stand and walk firmly, strongly, and uprightly, is called (2) Kammasarikkaka (Resembling the Kamma). Just as the causal kamma possessed the power of firm and unshakable effort, the resultant mark also possesses the power of being able to stand and walk firmly, strongly, and uprightly. This quality in the resultant mark that is similar to the special quality in the causal past kamma is called Kammasarikkaka (the nature resembling the kamma). Just as when one takes a gourd containing water, the act of taking also includes the water inside...)

## Four Things That Cannot Be Harmed

Even when others spoke many things that might provoke anger, he had no resentment, anger, perversion, or stubbornness in his mind through the power of anger. Not only that, he also gave gifts of very soft and delicate rugs, robes, and fabrics. Due to those wholesome kammas, and in accordance with those kammas, after enjoying celestial bliss as before, when he was reborn as a human, he obtained the (11) great mark of having a skin complexion as golden as pure Singī gold. Because the Great Being-to-be was endowed with this great mark, whether he lived in the household life as a Cakkavatti or went forth as a Sabbaññu Buddha, he obtained the benefit of easily receiving delicate and soft robes, garments, and rugs.

In this context, not having been angry and having given soft robes and rugs in many lives is called (1) Kamma. The skin complexion of an angry person is dull, and their face is ugly and difficult to look at. In the world, there is no...
679:
(Ngā)
...decoration like wearing clothes. Therefore, those who were angry and did not give gifts of robes and rugs have an unattractive appearance, as if to show others their past bad deeds such as anger. The face of one who is not angry is beautiful, and their skin complexion is clear. Indeed, beings obtain the benefit of having a pleasant and inspiring appearance due to these four causes:
1. Having given food in previous lives,
2. Having given clothes in previous lives,
3. Having swept and cleaned in previous lives,
4. Not having been angry.

The Great Being-to-be had performed all four of these causes in many previous lives. Therefore, as if to clearly show all devas and humans that he had performed these four wholesome deeds, the (11) great mark of a Great Man—having a skin complexion as golden as pure Singī gold—appeared clearly. Thus, the golden and beautiful skin complexion that makes those four wholesome deeds well known is called (2) Kamma-sarikkhaka. The physical substance of the skin and flesh that is as golden as pure Singī gold is called (3) Lakkhaṇa. Obtaining delicate and soft robes, garments, and rugs is called (4) Lakkhaṇānisamsa.

(For recitation): Even when insulted and oppressed, he bore no anger and remained calm; because of giving soft, smooth, and delicate robes and rugs, with the mark of a complexion shining like Jambu gold, receiving constant offerings of silk, velvet, wool, and fine soft silk from humans, Brahmas, and devas, to the Buddha, I pay homage.

## Having the Male Organ Enclosed in a Sheath

(11) In many previous lives, the Great Being-to-be worked to reconcile and unite relatives and friends who had been long separated. If a mother and son were at odds, or...
680:
(Ca)
...if a father and son were at odds, or if brothers, sisters, or siblings were at odds, he worked to bring them into harmony. He also greatly rejoiced when friends, mother and son, father and son, brothers, and sisters lived in harmony because of his efforts. Due to that wholesome kamma, and in accordance with that kamma, after enjoying celestial bliss as before, when he was reborn as a human, he obtained the (10) great mark of a Great Man—having the male organ enclosed in a sheath, like the King of Elephants, Chaddanta. Because the Great Being-to-be was endowed with this great mark, if he lived in the household life, he would become a Cakkavatti and have more than a thousand excellent sons who are full of courage and able to crush the enemy's army. If he went forth, he would become a Sabbaññu Buddha and have more than a thousand (many thousands) of Ariya-sāvaka (Noble Disciples) as sons who are full of courage and able to crush the army of the enemy, the defilements.

In this context, the wholesome deed of having united relatives in many lives is called (1) Kamma. "When relatives are united with one another, they cover each other's faults. Even when those relatives have quarrels, if someone's fault appears, they do not want others to know. If someone says, 'This is his fault,' they all rise up and say, 'Who saw it? Who heard it? There is no one in our family who would commit such a fault.' Thus they cover the fault." The Great Being-to-be, by reconciling divided relatives in many previous lives, is said to have performed this 'covering of faults'. Therefore, as if to show all devas and humans that he had reconciled divided relatives so they could cover each other's faults, his male organ, which is like a fault, appeared enclosed in a sheath. Thus, the male organ being enclosed in a sheath, which makes known the past kamma of reconciling relatives so they could live happily and cover each other's faults, is called (2) Kamma-sarikkhaka.
683:
He desired their prosperity and meditated on how to increase their welfare. Due to that wholesome kamma, after enjoying celestial bliss as before, when he returned to the human world, he obtained these three Great Marks: (17) "Having a torso as full as that of a king of lions," (18) "Having a back as smooth and full as a golden slab, with no furrow visible from the waist up to the neck," and (20) "Having a neck that is both symmetrical and well-rounded." Because the Great Being was endowed with these three Great Marks, if he lived the household life, he would become a Wheel-turning Monarch, never diminishing in any royal enjoyments or wealth. If he became a monk, he would become a Fully Enlightened Buddha, never diminishing in mundane and supramundane qualities such as Faith, Virtue, Learning, Generosity, and Wisdom.

In this context, desiring the welfare of all people is called (1) Kamma. The quality of the torso, back, and neck being full and rounded, as if clearly demonstrating his desire for the growth and progress of others' welfare, is called (2) Kammasarikkhaka. The full and rounded torso, back, and neck themselves are called (3) Lakkhaṇa. Not diminishing in wealth, prosperity, faith, etc., is called (4) Lakkhaṇānisaṃsa.

(For Memorization): Because of the wholesome kamma of desiring others to be well, and worrying about how they might increase in merit, wisdom, wealth, and companions... His upper body is like the front half of a golden lion dwelling in the forest; His torso is full, His golden back has no furrow, and His neck is as beautiful and rounded as a drum; by these three... He is the Buddha who does not diminish in any mundane or supramundane qualities.
684:
## Having 7,000 taste nerves that are upturned and centered in the throat.

(13) In many past lives, the Great Being did not oppress or harm sentient beings with his hands, stones, sticks, or weapons like swords. Due to that wholesome kamma, after enjoying celestial bliss as before, when he returned to the human world, he obtained the (21st) Great Mark: "Having 7,000 taste nerves with their ends meeting and centered in the throat, capable of distributing even a tiny amount of flavor, the size of a sesame seed, throughout the entire body." Because the Great Being was endowed with this Great Mark, whether he lived as a Wheel-turning Monarch or became a Fully Enlightened Buddha, he obtained the benefit of having little illness or disease.

In this context, the wholesome merit of not harming sentient beings is called (1) Kamma. For a person who is struck by hands or other objects, blood clots or serous fluid form at the site of the blow, which can lead to internal suppuration and many diseases. As if to clearly demonstrate to devas and humans that the Great Being performed the merit of not harming beings—the cause of being free from disease—he obtained the mark of taste nerves with upturned ends centered in the throat. Thus, the quality of the taste nerves being positioned and developed in such a way, unlike others, is called (2) Kammasarikkhaka. The taste nerves with upturned ends centered in the throat are called (3) Lakkhaṇa. Being free from disease is called (4) Lakkhaṇānisaṃsa.

In this regard, the Great Being's taste nerves carry even a sesame-seed-sized essence of flavor to permeate the whole body; his gastric fire is neither too weak nor too intense but moderate, digesting all food consumed perfectly. Therefore, he is freer from disease than others.

(For Memorization): By avoiding the harming of all beings and performing merit... he has seven thousand taste nerves with ends meeting in the throat; his gastric fire and digestive power are perfectly balanced, digesting food well...
686:
(Ce)
Being loved and revered by beings is called (4) Lakkhaṇānisaṃsa (the benefit of the mark).

(Verse for memorization): Because he did not look askance, nor with a frown, but looked directly with love and clarity, he possesses eyes of clear blue and eyelashes as beautiful as a cow's, beyond compare. By this mark, like a divine medicine of Piyasiddhi, he is loved and revered by the monks and laypeople of the three realms, by Sakka, Brahmā, and the Asuras. To such a Sublime Buddha, I pay homage.

## On Having a Fleshy Protuberance on the Forehead

(15) In many previous lives, the Great Being took the lead and was the foremost in performing various wholesome deeds, such as good conduct of body, speech, and mind, giving and generosity, observing the precepts, keeping the Uposatha, and caring for parents. Due to that wholesome kamma, after enjoying divine bliss in accordance with that kamma as before, when he was reborn as a human, he obtained the 32nd Great Mark: "having a fleshy protuberance on the forehead as if a golden turban were naturally placed there" (Uṇhīsa-sīsa).

Because the Great Being was endowed with this Great Mark, if he lived the household life, he would become a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch); if he went forth, he would become a Sabbaññū (Omniscient) Buddha. He obtained the consequence of being the leader and forerunner of all beings, with many people following him.

In this context, the wholesome deed of taking the lead and managing meritorious acts is called (1) Kamma. A person who takes the lead and manages wholesome acts like dāna (giving) can move about in the midst of an assembly with a joyful and delighted head, held high without any gloom, and has many followers. The Great Being also took the lead and managed wholesome acts in many previous lives. To make this known to gods and humans, the fleshy protuberance naturally appeared on his forehead (alternatively, a well-rounded and full head was formed). Thus, the fleshy protuberance...
688:
(So)
...only one hair grows, and the Uṇṇā-loma grows miraculously. The quality of having one hair per pore and the Uṇṇā-loma, which makes it known that he spoke only one truthful word, is called (2) Kammasarikkaka. The substance of those hairs and the Uṇṇā-loma is called (3) Lakkhaṇa. The fact that various beings and many people follow his will and desire is called (4) Lakkhaṇānisaṃsa.

(Verse for memorization): Because of the original Dhamma of being honest and upright, keeping the truth without deceit, only one hair grows clearly and appropriately in each pore without being crowded. And in the center between the eyebrows, there is the Uṇṇā-loma, which, when pulled, extends about half a fathom, and when released, curls to the right, shining with a white glow like the morning star on the golden forehead, soft as a tuft of cotton. By this mark, the people of the three realms follow his will. To such a Sublime Buddha, I pay homage.

## On Having Forty Teeth, Even and Without Gaps

(17) In many previous lives, the Great Being avoided divisive speech (slander) that causes people to lose affection for one another. He reconciled those who were divided and encouraged those who were united. He delighted and rejoiced in harmony (sāmaggī) and in those who were united. He was very pleased to see or hear of people being in harmony. He spoke only words that promoted unity. Due to that wholesome kamma, after enjoying divine bliss as before, when he was reborn as a human, he obtained two Great Marks: the 23rd mark, "having forty teeth" (Cattālīsadanta), and the 25th mark, "having teeth that are close together without gaps" (Avivaradanta).

Because the Great Being was endowed with these two Great Marks, if he lived the household life, he would become a Cakkavatti; if he went forth, he would become a Sabbaññū Buddha. He obtained the consequence of having a retinue of followers who cannot be divided or destroyed by others...
690:
(Saṃ)
...the 28th Great Mark. Because the Great Being was endowed with these two Great Marks, if he lived the household life, he would become a Cakkavatti; if he went forth, he would become a Sabbaññū Buddha. He obtained the consequence of having his words followed by humans, gods, and Brahmās, and his speech being influential, widespread, and possessing great authority.

In this context, not speaking harsh, mean, or abusive words (pharusavācā) that are unpleasant to others' ears throughout many lives in Saṃsāra, and speaking only subtle, polite, sweet, and peaceful words is called (1) Kamma. Those who speak harsh and abusive words, to let others know they spoke such words by twisting their tongues, receive defects such as a thick tongue, a sagging tongue, or a cracked tongue. For the Great Being, to make it known to gods and humans that he did not speak such harsh and abusive words but spoke only subtle, polite, sweet, and peaceful words, he obtained the mark of a long, broad, soft, and thin tongue. Those who speak harsh words, to let others know they spoke with cracked and harsh voices, receive defects such as a cracked or hoarse voice. For the Great Being, as if to clearly demonstrate to gods and humans that he did not speak with a cracked or harsh voice over many lives, he obtained the benefit of having a voice endowed with eight qualities. Thus, the long, broad, and soft tongue, and the voice endowed with eight qualities, are called (2) Kammasarikkaka. The substance of the subtle, long, and soft tongue, and the substance of the eightfold voice, is called (3) Lakkhaṇa. The fact that humans and gods follow his words, and his speech is influential, widespread, and possesses great authority, is called (4) Lakkhaṇānisaṃsa.

(Verse for memorization): Because he did not speak mean or harsh words that are unpleasant to others, but spoke sweet and peaceful words, he possesses a long, broad, and soft tongue. With a clear, sweet, and pleasant voice that does not falter in an assembly, a deep and resonant voice like the eightfold Brahma-voice or the Karavīka bird, he speaks with great influence. By this mark, his words are followed especially, his influence spreads wide, and he possesses great authority. To such a Sublime Buddha, I pay homage.
691:
(Sa)
## Like the Moon on the 12th Waxing Day and the Jaw of the Lion King
## Having a Full Jaw
(19) In many previous existences, the Bodhisatta refrained from frivolous speech (samphappalāpa), which is useless like empty grain or chaff. He spoke only words that were timely, truthful, beneficial, consistent with the Dhamma, and consistent with the Vinaya (discipline). He spoke words that were worth treasuring in the hearts of the listeners, accompanied by reasons, examples, and guidelines, being well-defined and meaningful. Due to that wholesome kamma, after enjoying celestial bliss according to that kamma as before, when he returned to the human state, he obtained the 22nd major mark: "having a full jaw like that of a lion king (with the appearance of an impending smile)." Because the Bodhisatta was endowed with this great mark, if he lived the household life, he would become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti); if he went forth, he would become a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, obtaining the benefit of being unconquerable and unbreakable by any internal or external enemy.

In this context, the refraining from frivolous speech (samphappalāpa) is called (1) Kamma. Those who spoke frivolous speech in past lives, in order to make their useless chatter known to others, receive defects related to the jaw, such as a sunken jaw or a crooked jaw. The Bodhisatta, however, to make known to devas and humans his refraining from such frivolous speech and his speaking of only meaningful words, obtained the benefit of a full jaw. Thus, the quality of the fullness of the jaw, which makes known the speaking of meaningful words in past lives, is called (2) Kamma-sarikkaka (resemblance to the deed). The physical substance of the full jaw possessing this quality is called (3) Lakkhaṇa (the mark). Being unconquerable and unbreakable by any internal or external enemy is called (4) Lakkhaṇānisaṃsa (the benefit of the mark).

(For Recitation): Because of the merit of not speaking empty, useless, and frivolous words that lack substance, [He obtained] a jaw as full and radiant as that of a lion king.
692:
(Sa)
...with a full and rounded jaw, appearing as if about to smile, like the radiant orb of the moon on the twelfth waxing day; with such a noble jaw, no person can overcome or break Him, O Exalted Buddha, Exalted Buddha.

## Having Even Teeth and
## Having Four Very White Canines
(20) In many previous existences, the Bodhisatta avoided wrong livelihood and lived by pure right livelihood. He refrained far from various forms of deception such as cheating with scales, cheating with measures, and cheating with coins; from crookedness through bribery, from deception by various stratagems, and from fraudulent imitation; and from mutilating, killing, binding, robbing, plundering, and coercing. Due to that wholesome kamma, after enjoying celestial bliss according to that kamma as before, when he returned to the human state, he obtained two major marks: the 24th mark, "having even teeth," and the 26th mark, "having four canines that are exceedingly pure and white, shining like the morning star." Because the Bodhisatta was endowed with these two great marks, if he lived the household life, he would become a Universal Monarch; if he went forth, as in his final existence as Siddhattha, he would become a Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, obtaining the benefit of having a pure retinue of followers.

In this context, the purity of livelihood over many lifetimes is called (1) Kamma. For those whose livelihood was not pure, as if to make that fact known to all, their teeth grow unevenly—upper and lower, inside and outside—and their canines are dull. The Bodhisatta, however, as if to make known to devas and humans that his livelihood was pure throughout many existences in Saṃsāra, has teeth that grow evenly and four canines that are extremely white and pure. Thus, the qualities of the evenness of the teeth and the whiteness and purity of the four canines, which clearly indicate the purity of livelihood in previous existences, are...
693:
(Sā)
...called (2) Kamma-sarikkaka. The physical objects of the white canines and even teeth are called (3) Lakkhaṇa. Having a pure retinue of followers is called (4) Lakkhaṇānisaṃsa.

(For Recitation): Because of avoiding livelihood through cheating with large or small measures, short or long scales, fraud, robbery, theft, and oppression, His teeth are as even as set diamonds, and His four canines are pure white. By these two characteristics of His teeth, He is surrounded by a pure and noble retinue, like the moon among the stars, free from wicked, crooked, or evil people, O Exalted Buddha, Exalted Buddha.

## Concluding Salutation to the Marks of the Buddha
(For Recitation): Having performed such merits, the Lord is now endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. It was prophesied that He would become a Universal Monarch, possessing the seven treasures—the Wheel, Elephant, Horse, Jewel, Woman, Householder, and Minister—and a thousand sons, ruling over the four islands. However, treating such worldly glory like spit, He renounced it and became the Great King of Dhamma, renowned throughout the ten thousand worlds. I pay humble and respectful homage with joined palms to the Lord Buddha, who is always adorned with the six glories (Bhaga), infinite attributes, various wisdoms, and the benefits of the marks, O Exalted Buddha, Exalted Buddha.

## Poem on the Manual of the Thirty-Two Marks of a Great Man
Here, I shall also include the "Dvattiṃsa Mahāpurisa Lakkhaṇa Dīpanī Poem," which shows the four aspects—Kamma, Kamma-sarikkaka, Lakkhaṇa, and Lakkhaṇānisaṃsa—composed by the Most Venerable Mahāvisuddhārāma Sayadaw, for the sake of general knowledge. It begins:

I shall compose the account of how the Universal Monarchs and the Buddhas obtain the thirty-two marks according to their kamma, as expounded and detailed in the Lakkhaṇa Sutta of the Pāthika Vagga.
694:
(Chi)
In the ancient past, because of being firmly established in wholesome deeds, He enjoyed long life, beauty, happiness, and power, surrounded by attendants. After being a deva endowed with the ten attributes of celestial form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, when He reached the human world, He obtained the mark of level feet (supatiṭṭhita-pāda), which touch the ground evenly without being high or low, and thus He is free from enemies. (1)

Because of protecting the masses for their welfare and giving gifts, when He became a deva, it was as before. In this human realm, He is endowed with the mark of the wheel (cakka-lakkhaṇa) on His soles, with a thousand spokes and a perfect rim, and thus His retinue increases. (2)

Because of the noble merit of not killing living beings, He obtained three marks: long heels (āyata-paṇhi), long fingers (dīghanguḷi), and a straight body like that of Brahma, and thus He enjoys a long life. (3)

Because of the merits of offering excellent tastes, He obtained the mark of the seven convexities (sattussada)—on the hands, feet, shoulders, and trunk—and thus He receives excellent tastes and gains. (4)

Because of practicing the four bases of sympathy (sangaha-vatthu), His hands and feet are soft and delicate (mudu-taluna) and net-like (jāla-hatthapāda), and thus His retinue never separates from Him. (5)

Because of explaining the Dhamma and showing the way to welfare for all people, He obtained high ankles and upward-growing body hairs, and thus He is superior to others. (6)

Because of teaching blameless arts and sciences quickly, He has calves like an antelope (eṇijaṅgha), and thus He quickly attains wealth. (7)

Because of the habit of asking questions seeking wisdom, He has delicate skin, and His wisdom is like falling rain. (8)

Because of abandoning anger and having strong faith, and offering soft and fine coverings, He has a golden complexion and very smooth skin, and thus He has an abundance of robes and coverings. (9)
695:
(Chī)
Because of the merit of seeking out and reuniting long-lost relatives and friends, He has a sheath-enclosed organ (kosohita-vatthaguyha), and thus He has many sons, more than a thousand. (10)

Because of the kamma of supporting and elevating people according to their strength, He is proportionate like a banyan tree (nyagrodha-parimaṇḍala) and His hands reach His knees without bending, and thus He is filled with wealth and good results. (11)

Because of the habit of desiring the welfare of all beings, He has the front of a lion, a well-filled back, and a well-rounded neck; having these three, His wealth and attendants never decrease. (12)

Because of loving all beings and wishing them happiness without harm, the seven thousand taste nerves in His throat are perfectly aligned, and thus He is free from illness and His food digests well. (13)

Because of looking with straightforward and loving eyes, He has deep blue eyes and long eyelashes; with these two marks, He is loved by many. (14)

Because of leading the people in performing various merits, He has a turban-like forehead (uṇhīsa-sīsa), and thus many beings follow His practice. (15)

Because of avoiding falsehood, He has one hair per pore and a white urna (uṇṇā) hair between His brows; with these two marks, His servants and followers do as He desires. (16)

Because of abandoning divisive speech (pisuṇavācā), He has forty teeth which are not gaps; with these two marks, His retinue is harmonious and peaceful. (17)

Because of avoiding harsh speech, He has a long and broad tongue and a voice like Brahma; with these two marks, many people accept His words. (18)
696:
(Chu)
Because of avoiding frivolous speech (samphappalāpa), He has a jaw like a lion's, full and rounded; thus enemies stay far away and cannot harm Him. (19)

Because of avoiding wrong livelihood (micchājīva), He has even teeth and bright white canines; with these two qualities, He is endowed with a pure retinue. (20)

If one is fully endowed with all these thirty-two great marks, those learned in the Vedas have declared that one will certainly become either a famous Universal Monarch in the human world or a Buddha. This is a worthy example for all to follow.

This concludes the explanation of the causal kammas and other details of the thirty-two major marks.
